agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Two realistic routes: (1) extend the $n=3$ toolkit (envy-cycle elimination with champion graphs, or the rainbow-cycle-number LP/combinatorial argument) to $n=4$, likely requiring a genuinely new invariant since direct extensions have stalled at 'one good unallocated'; (2) computational search — exhaustive or SAT/ILP-based enumeration of small additive instances (small $n$, small $m$, small integer valuations) to either find a counterexample or build confidence toward a positive conjecture, following the methodology of the 2026 SAT-solving paper but restricted to the additive valuation class specifically (their existing counterexamples require non-additive, e.g. submodular, valuations).
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed existence proof for $n=4$ must produce (or algorithmically construct) an explicit EFX allocation for an ARBITRARY 4-agent additive instance and verify the EFX condition (a finite, polynomial-time-checkable set of $O(n \cdot m)$ inequalities) directly; watch for proofs that secretly assume extra structure (e.g., generic/non-degenerate valuations) not present in the general statement. A claimed counterexample must be a fully specified finite instance (agents, goods, valuation matrix) together with a proof or brute-force check (feasible for small instances) that NO allocation satisfies all EFX inequalities; this is machine-checkable by enumerating the (finite but combinatorially large) space of allocations. Common failure mode: confusing EFX with EF1 or with EFX-with-charity (partial allocations), which are much easier and already solved — a valid contribution must address the COMPLETE allocation, unrestricted additive case.

title: Existence of EFX allocations for chores (three agents)
short_statement: For indivisible chores (which impose costs), an EFX allocation is one where any envy agent $i$ feels toward $j$ vanishes after dropping any single chore from $i$'s own bundle. Does an EFX allocation always exist for additive chores with three agents?
full_statement: Let $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ be a set of agents and $M$ a set of indivisible chores, with each agent $i$ having an additive cost function $c_i$ (chores impose costs / disutilities, $c_i(S)=\sum_{e\in S}c_i(\{e\})$). An allocation $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ partitioning $M$ is EFX (for chores) if for all agents $i,j$ and every chore $e\in X_i$ with $c_i(\{e\})>0$: $c_i(X_i\setminus\{e\})\le c_i(X_j)$. In words, any envy agent $i$ feels toward agent $j$ vanishes upon dropping any single (positively costly) chore from $i$'s own bundle. Unlike the goods setting, the chores setting is harsher: with additive costs restricted to only three distinct values (tri-valued) and four or more agents, EFX allocations can provably fail to exist (He, Tao 2026), which — since tri-valued costs are a special case of unrestricted additive costs — resolves the general $n\ge4$ additive-chores existence question in the negative. The precise remaining gap: does an EFX allocation always exist for chores with (unrestricted) additive costs and exactly $n=3$ agents?
known_results: The general chores analogue of the EFX-for-goods conjecture is now FALSE: He and Tao (arXiv, June 2026) prove that even for tri-valued additive cost functions (only three distinct positive cost levels), for every $n\ge4$ there is an instance with no EFX allocation; since tri-valued costs are additive costs, this resolves the $n\ge4$ general-additive-chores existence question negatively. Their construction is tight: EFX is known to always exist for chores with at most two distinct cost values (bi-valued), so three values is the minimum needed for a counterexample. They further show that even for bi-valued instances, EFX can be incompatible with Pareto-optimality once $n\ge4$ (the first such example with strictly positive costs), while an EFX allocation itself is guaranteed to exist for every bi-valued 4-agent instance. Earlier, Christoforidis and Santorinaios (IJCAI 2024) had shown EFX can fail to exist for only $n=3$ agents under SUPERADDITIVE cost functions (six chores suffice), establishing the first goods/chores separation and NP-completeness of EFX-existence-checking for general monotone costs, but that result does not apply to additive costs. For (unrestricted) additive costs specifically, positive existence results hold when the number of chores is at most $n+2$, when all but one agent share an identical ordering over chores, and (via Kobayashi et al. 2025 and Garg et al. 2023) for three-agent personalized bi-valued costs. In general, a 2-EFX allocation (envy vanishes after removing the two costliest chores) always exists for additive chores (Zhou, Wu 2022/2024), and this approximation factor has since been sharpened further by several 2024-2026 papers (e.g., 'Existence of 2-EFX Allocations of Chores', 2025; 'Constant-Factor EFX Exists for Chores', 2024). As of July 2026, the single remaining open case that gives this problem its name — complete EFX existence for additive costs with exactly $n=3$ agents — has NOT been resolved by the He-Tao nonexistence result (which requires $n\ge4$) and remains open.

where_posed.text: Nonexistence for chores under superadditive costs (n=3) established in Christoforidis, Santorinaios, 'On the Pursuit of EFX for Chores: Non-Existence and Approximations', IJCAI 2024; the sharper additive-costs, general-n nonexistence result (n>=4) is due to He, Tao, 'EFX for Additive Chores: Nonexistence, Pareto Incompatibility, and Bi-Valued Existence', arXiv, June 2026, which explicitly frames itself as resolving 'the long-standing open problem for the existence of EFX allocations with additive cost functions'; the n=3 additive case is left open by both.
where_posed.quote: We consider the fair division problem of indivisible chores and resolve the long-standing open problem for the existence of EFX allocations with additive cost functions. We show that, even for tri-valued additive cost functions, for every n≥4, there exists an instance with n agents where no EFX allocation exists. Our counterexample only uses three types of chores, which is also tight on the number of types, as an EFX allocation is known to exist for two types of chores.

background: Once envy-freeness up to any good (EFX) was proposed for indivisible goods, it was natural to ask about its mirror image for chores — indivisible tasks or costs that agents dislike rather than desire, such as household duties, unwanted job assignments, or waste-disposal responsibilities. The chores setting is not a trivial relabeling of the goods setting: negating valuations flips incentives in ways that break many of the arguments that work for goods, and indeed the two settings have turned out to have surprisingly different answers. For goods, no EFX nonexistence example is known for additive valuations at any number of agents; for chores, by contrast, nonexistence had long been suspected and was confirmed for small cases, revealing a genuine asymmetry between the two models that is itself an interesting structural finding in fair division theory. This makes the chores side of EFX a natural stress-test for which techniques from the goods literature (envy-cycle elimination, rainbow cycle numbers, champion graphs) transfer and which break down, and why. Beyond its theoretical interest, chore division is arguably the more common real-world scenario — splitting caregiving duties, unpleasant shifts, or cost-sharing obligations among roommates, partners, or coworkers — so pinning down exactly where EFX allocations do and do not exist for chores has direct implications for designing fair task-assignment mechanisms. The problem also serves as a proving ground for the interaction between fairness and efficiency (Pareto-optimality), since a recurring theme in the chores literature is that EFX and Pareto-optimality can conflict even when EFX by itself is achievable, unlike in most known goods settings.

progress.summary: Major 2026 development: He and Tao (arXiv 2606.08872, submitted 7 June 2026) proved that EFX allocations can fail to exist for additive chores whenever $n\ge4$, using a tri-valued (hence additive) counterexample, and additionally proved every EFX allocation can fail to be Pareto-optimal for bi-valued chores when $n\ge4$. This settles the general-$n$ question negatively but their construction explicitly requires $n\ge4$; the specific $n=3$, fully general additive-costs case (the version this problem entry is about) is NOT addressed by their counterexample and remains open as of July 2026. Positive existence for the $n=4$ bi-valued special case was also newly shown by the same paper. No paper found claims to resolve $n=3$ additive chores either way.

counterexample_rationale: The problem is specifically about a small, finite case ($n=3$ agents, additive costs); the 2026 nonexistence breakthrough for $n\ge4$ was itself found via an explicit small hand/computer-aided construction (three cost values, few chores), and the same search methodology (careful case analysis or automated SAT/ILP search over small instances) is a natural and directly applicable route to settling $n=3$ either way.
alphaevolve_rationale: Because the remaining question is about one exact, small finite case ($n=3$), an evolutionary/LLM-guided search over cost matrices combined with a fast EFX-feasibility oracle (brute-force or SAT-based, since $n=3$ keeps the allocation space and the number of EFX inequalities small) is very well matched to this problem: it could either surface an $n=3$ counterexample (mirroring how He-Tao's $n\ge4$ counterexample was found) or, by exhaustively failing to find one across systematically varied instances, build strong empirical evidence for an existence conjecture that a human could then try to prove.

literature.synthesis: The chores side of EFX has followed a 'divide and conquer by number of distinct cost values' pattern: bi-valued instances are well understood (existence holds quite broadly, including for $n=3$ personalized bi-valued costs per Garg et al. 2023 and Kobayashi et al. 2025, and for $n=4$ per He-Tao 2026), while tri-valued and general additive instances are where the picture darkens. Christoforidis and Santorinaios (IJCAI 2024) first showed a goods/chores asymmetry by exhibiting nonexistence for $n=3$ under superadditive costs and proving NP-completeness of EFX-checking for monotone costs, but left the additive case open. The 2026 breakthrough by He and Tao closes the general-$n$ additive question by constructing a tri-valued (hence additive), $n\ge4$ nonexistence example — tight in the sense that only two distinct cost values would not suffice — and separately shows EFX and Pareto-optimality can conflict for bi-valued costs once $n\ge4$, extending known EFX/PO incompatibility results (which previously needed zero-cost items) to strictly positive costs. Crucially, their counterexample construction inherently needs at least four agents; nothing in the current literature settles whether $n=3$, unrestricted-additive-cost EFX allocations always exist. This leaves $n=3$ as a sharply delineated remaining gap: below it (bi-valued or $n\le2$) existence is known, and just above it (tri-valued, $n\ge4$) nonexistence is now known, so $n=3$ general additive costs is the precise unresolved boundary case. In parallel, the approximation literature has matured quickly, with 2-EFX (Zhou-Wu) and various constant-factor / conditional bounds (2024-2026) narrowing the practical gap even while exact existence remains unsettled for the hardest cases.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Because the target case is fixed and small ($n=3$, unrestricted additive costs), the most promising approaches are: (1) adapt the He-Tao tri-valued construction technique — try to push their nonexistence gadget down to $n=3$, or prove structurally why it cannot go below $n=4$ (which would itself be informative); (2) exhaustive or SAT/ILP-based search over small 3-agent additive-cost instances (bounded number of chores, small integer costs) to find a counterexample directly, mirroring the SAT-solving methodology used for the analogous goods problem; (3) attempt to extend the existing $n=3$ positive results (bi-valued, personalized bi-valued, identical-ordering) toward general additive costs by relaxing their structural assumptions one at a time to see where the proof breaks.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A nonexistence proof for $n=3$ must exhibit a fully specified instance (3 additive cost vectors over a finite chore set) and verify NO partition satisfies all EFX inequalities — for $n=3$ and a modest number of chores this is a finite check that a solver (SAT/ILP or brute force) can perform exactly, so numerics/computer verification suffice as long as the search is exhaustive over allocations (not just heuristic). A positive existence proof must give an algorithm (or nonconstructive argument) guaranteeing an EFX allocation for EVERY 3-agent additive instance; check especially that the construction does not implicitly assume bi-valued, superadditive-free, or other restricted cost structure, since nearly all current $n=3$ positive results rely on some such restriction. Any claimed resolution should be checked against the He-Tao paper's framing carefully, since their abstract's claim to 'resolve the long-standing open problem' refers to the general-$n$ (not $n=3$-specific) question.

title: Optimal approximation factor for Nash Social Welfare
short_statement: Nash Social Welfare is the geometric mean of agents' utilities; maximizing it over indivisible goods is NP-hard. What is the best constant approximation factor achievable in polynomial time, for additive, submodular, and subadditive valuations?
full_statement: There is a set of agents $N$ ($|N|=n$) and a set of indivisible goods $M$, with each agent $i$ having a monotone valuation $v_i:2^M\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. For an allocation $A=(A_1,\dots,A_n)$ partitioning $M$, the Nash Social Welfare is the geometric mean of the agents' utilities, $$\mathrm{NSW}(A)=\left(\prod_{i\in N} v_i(A_i)\right)^{1/n}.$$ A deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is an $\alpha$-approximation (for $\alpha\ge 1$) if it always outputs an allocation $A$ with $\mathrm{NSW}(A)\ge \mathrm{OPT}/\alpha$, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the maximum NSW over all allocations. Maximizing NSW exactly is NP-hard already for two agents with additive valuations. Determine $\alpha^*=\inf\{\alpha:$ a poly-time $\alpha$-approximation exists$\}$ for each valuation class in the hierarchy additive $\subset$ submodular $\subset$ XOS $\subset$ subadditive (assuming appropriate value/demand oracle access for the richer classes). For unweighted additive valuations, the new randomized upper bound is strictly below $e^{1/e}$; see the What Is Known section. For randomized algorithms, distinguish an expected-welfare guarantee $\mathbb E[\mathrm{NSW}(A)]\ge\mathrm{OPT}/\alpha$ from a per-execution guarantee; the new result is randomized.
known_results: Additive valuations: the earlier polynomial-time algorithm achieves $e^{1/e}+\varepsilon\approx 1.445$ (Barman, Krishnamurthy, Vaish, EC 2018), and the same factor was extended to the weighted (asymmetric) NSW objective by Feng and Li (ICALP 2024). The best hardness is $\sqrt{8/7}\approx 1.069$ (Garg, Hoefer, Mehlhorn, SODA 2018 / Math. Oper. Res. 2024, via Max-E3-Lin-2). Bei, Feng, Hu, Li, Zhang (arXiv 2504.09669, 2025) show the configuration LP for weighted additive NSW has integrality gap $e^{1/e}-\varepsilon$ (so configuration-LP-based algorithms cannot beat 1.445), and for unweighted additive NSW they show an integrality gap of $2^{1/4}\approx 1.189$, strictly above the known $1.069$ NP-hardness. Submodular valuations: Garg, Husic, Li, Vegh, Vondrak (STOC 2023) gave a $(4+\varepsilon)$-approximation (unweighted); Feng, Hu, Li, Zhang (STOC 2025) gave the first constant, $(233+\varepsilon)$, for the weighted case; and Bei, Feng, Hu, Li, Zhang (2025) improved both to $(3.56+\varepsilon)$ for weighted (hence also unweighted) submodular NSW. Hardness for submodular is $e/(e-1)\approx 1.582$ (Garg, Kulkarni, Kulkarni, SODA 2020), and the submodular configuration LP has integrality gap at least $2^{\ln 2}\approx 1.617$. Subadditive valuations: Dobzinski, Li, Rubinstein, Vondrak (STOC 2024) gave the first constant-factor approximation with demand oracles (a large, unoptimized constant). Viswanathan, 'A Better-than-e^{1/e} Approximation Algorithm for Nash Social Welfare under Additive Valuations' (arXiv:2607.13340v1), Theorem 1.1, reports an efficient randomized $(e^{1/e}-c)$ approximation for an absolute $c>0$ by rounding the configuration LP. This concerns unweighted additive NSW, not the weighted objective. The exact optimum approximation factor is not established. No explicit numerical value for c is asserted here.

where_posed.text: The constant-factor approximability question was opened by Cole, Gkatzelis, 'Approximating the Nash Social Welfare with Indivisible Items', STOC 2015 (SICOMP 2018), which gave the first constant factor for additive valuations; the quest for the optimal constant in each valuation class is restated throughout the subsequent literature.

background: The Nash Social Welfare (NSW) objective — the geometric mean of agents' utilities — occupies a sweet spot between the utilitarian objective (sum of utilities, efficient but potentially very unfair) and the egalitarian objective (minimum utility, fair but potentially very inefficient). It is scale-free (multiplying one agent's valuation by a constant does not change the optimizer), and for divisible goods its maximizer coincides with the celebrated competitive equilibrium from equal incomes. Caragiannis, Kurokawa, Moulin, Procaccia, Shah, and Wang further showed that for indivisible goods the NSW maximizer is envy-free up to one good and Pareto-optimal, cementing NSW maximization as a canonical 'fairness plus efficiency' benchmark used in deployed systems such as Spliddit. For indivisible goods, however, maximizing NSW is NP-hard even with two agents (via Subset-Sum-type reductions), so the algorithmic question becomes one of approximation. The breakthrough of Cole and Gkatzelis (STOC 2015) gave the first constant-factor approximation for additive valuations via a spending-restricted Fisher-market relaxation, launching a decade-long program that has produced a rich toolkit: market equilibria and price-based rounding, stable polynomials and real stability, configuration LPs with nontrivial separation oracles, and mixed local-search/matching algorithms. The problem has become a proving ground for approximation-algorithm techniques in the same way max-cut or scheduling problems once were, and progress has marched up the valuation hierarchy from additive to budget-additive, Rado, submodular, and finally subadditive valuations. Yet in every class the optimal approximation constant remains unknown: the gaps between the best algorithms and the best hardness results are still substantial, and closing them — even just for additive valuations — is a central open problem in fair division and approximation algorithms.

title: Best approximation factor for Maximin Share (MMS) fair division
short_statement: An agent's maximin share is the value of the worst bundle when she optimally partitions all goods into $n$ bundles. Exact MMS allocations need not exist, so what is the largest constant $\alpha$ such that $\alpha$-MMS allocations always exist for additive valuations?
full_statement: There is a set of agents $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a set of indivisible goods $M$, with each agent $i$ having a nonnegative additive valuation $v_i$. Let $\Pi_n(M)$ be the set of all partitions of $M$ into $n$ bundles. Agent $i$'s maximin share is $$\mathrm{MMS}_i=\max_{(B_1,\dots,B_n)\in\Pi_n(M)}\ \min_{j} v_i(B_j),$$ i.e., the best value she can guarantee herself if she partitions all goods into $n$ bundles and receives the worst one. An allocation $A=(A_1,\dots,A_n)$ is $\alpha$-MMS if $v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\cdot\mathrm{MMS}_i$ for all agents $i$. Exact ($\alpha=1$) MMS allocations do not always exist, even with additive valuations. Determine $$\alpha^*=\sup\{\alpha:\ \text{every additive instance admits an }\alpha\text{-MMS allocation}\}.$$ Here the quantifier includes all agent counts; for fixed n write $\alpha_n^*$, so $\alpha^*=\inf_n\alpha_n^*$. The reviewed universal bounds are $7/9\le\alpha^*\le20/21$. The polynomial-time computability of the guarantee is a closely related companion question.
known_results: Huang and Zhou, 'A Strongly Polynomial-Time 7/9-Approximation Algorithm for Maximin Share Allocations' (arXiv:2511.13056v3, November 5, 2026), Theorem 8.1, give a complete $7/9$-MMS allocation in strongly polynomial time, improving $10/13$. Ezra and Garbuz, 'Improved Impossibility Bounds for Maximin Share Allocations' (arXiv:2609.15085v2), Theorem 2, give a four-agent eleven-good instance bounding the universal guarantee by $20/21$. Their Theorem 1 separately gives $\alpha_n^*\le1-\Omega((\log n)^{-2})$ for sufficiently large n. These are nonnegative additive goods with equal entitlements. The sharp universal constant remains between the stated bounds.

where_posed.text: The MMS notion is due to Budish, 'The Combinatorial Assignment Problem: Approximate Competitive Equilibrium from Equal Incomes', JPE 2011. The approximation question was posed by Procaccia and Wang, 'Fair Enough: Guaranteeing Approximate Maximin Shares', EC 2014, extended in Kurokawa, Procaccia, Wang, JACM 2018, after showing exact MMS allocations need not exist.

title: Competition complexity of multi-item auctions (general regime)
short_statement: How many extra i.i.d. bidders does a simple mechanism (selling items separately, or VCG) need to out-earn the optimal mechanism on the original bidders, in multi-item settings? The additive independent case is now settled at $\Theta(\sqrt{nm})$ for $m<n$; constants, the $m\ge n$ regime, non-additive valuations, and correlated items remain open.
full_statement: Fix $m$ items with values drawn from a product distribution $D=D_1\times\cdots\times D_m$, and $n$ bidders each with additive values drawn i.i.d. from $D$. Let $\mathrm{Rev}_n(D)$ be the optimal revenue of any Bayesian incentive-compatible mechanism for the $n$ original bidders, and $\mathrm{SRev}_{n+c}(D)$ the revenue of selling each item separately by second-price auction to $n+c$ bidders. The competition complexity is $$C(n,m)=\min\{c\in\mathbb{N}:\ \mathrm{SRev}_{n+c}(D)\ge \mathrm{Rev}_n(D)\ \text{for all product}\ D\},$$ with the VCG analogue defined similarly for richer valuation classes. Bulow-Klemperer (1996) is the statement $C(n,1)=1$ for regular distributions. Known: for additive bidders over independent items, $C(n,m)=\Theta(\sqrt{nm})$ when $m<n$ and $C(n,m)=O(n\ln(m/n))$ when $m\ge n$ (with $\Omega(n)$-type lower bounds). Open: (i) the exact constants and the tight bound in the regime $m\ge n$; (ii) competition complexity for non-additive valuations (unit-demand, XOS, subadditive) where no finite bounds or only much weaker bounds are known; (iii) correlated item distributions; (iv) the competition complexity of other simple formats such as grand-bundle auctions beyond the single-bidder case.
known_results: Additive values, independent items: Eden, Feldman, Friedler, Talgam-Cohen, Weinberg (EC 2017) initiated the framework and proved $C(n,m)\le n+2m-2$-type bounds via Cai-Devanur-Weinberg duality; Feldman, Friedler, Rubinstein (EC 2018) showed $O(n\ln(m/n))$ bidders suffice for $99\%$ of optimal revenue and $\Omega(n\ln(m/n))$ are needed under standard regularity; Beyhaghi, Weinberg (STOC 2019) proved $C(n,m)=O(\sqrt{nm})$ for $m<n$ and $O(n\ln(m/n))$ for $m\ge n$; Derakhshan, Ryu, Weinberg, Xue (EC 2024) settled the $m<n$ regime at $\Theta(\sqrt{nm})$ by improving the lower bound from $\Omega(\ln n)$ to $\Omega(\sqrt{nm})$, showing truncated equal-revenue distributions witness the worst case. Beyond regularity/VCG: Beyhaghi, Cai, Feng, Li, Weinberg (arXiv 2506.09291, 2025) show that under $\alpha$-strong regularity the competition complexity of selling separately drops to $\Theta(n/\alpha)$ — independent of $m$ — and give constant bounds for grand bundling with a single bidder when $m$ is small or the distribution is MHR. For multi-unit auctions, 2026 work strengthens Bulow-Klemperer-style results in the duplicates model (arXiv 2602.11959, building on Feng-Fu-Li 2024, showing e.g. that one duplicate suffices for Vickrey to $10$-approximate optimal revenue). For a single unit-demand bidder ($n=1$), Eden et al. also gave bounds, but general non-additive (XOS/subadditive) competition complexity remains wide open, as do exact constants and correlated items.

where_posed.text: Posed in Eden, Feldman, Friedler, Talgam-Cohen, Weinberg, 'The Competition Complexity of Auctions: A Bulow-Klemperer Result for Multi-Dimensional Bidders', EC 2017, generalizing Bulow, Klemperer, 'Auctions versus Negotiations', AER 1996.

background: Bulow and Klemperer's 1996 theorem is one of the most quoted results in auction theory: for a single item and $n$ i.i.d. regular bidders, a simple second-price auction with $n+1$ bidders earns at least as much revenue as Myerson's optimal auction with $n$ bidders. The managerial message — investing in competition beats investing in mechanism-design sophistication — is compelling, but the single-item assumption is restrictive: real sellers (ad exchanges, spectrum auctions, e-commerce platforms) sell many items, and multi-item optimal mechanisms are notoriously complex, randomized, and prior-dependent (they can even require infinite menus). Eden, Feldman, Friedler, Talgam-Cohen, and Weinberg (EC 2017) introduced the competition complexity of an auction environment: the number of extra bidders that simple mechanisms — selling every item separately via second-price auctions (SRev), or running VCG — need in order to beat the optimal Bayesian incentive-compatible mechanism's revenue on the original bidders. This framework converts the vague 'simple vs. optimal' tradeoff into a sharp quantitative question and connects to the duality-based revenue-benchmark machinery of Cai, Devanur, and Weinberg. A decade of work has pinned down the additive/independent case up to constants: Beyhaghi and Weinberg (STOC 2019) proved $O(\sqrt{nm})$ (for $m<n$) and $O(n\ln(m/n))$ (for $m\ge n$) upper bounds, and Derakhshan, Ryu, Weinberg, and Xue (EC 2024) proved the matching $\Omega(\sqrt{nm})$ lower bound via truncated equal-revenue distributions. What remains open is everything beyond this base case: exact constants, the fine structure of the $m\ge n$ regime, non-additive valuations (unit-demand, XOS, subadditive), correlated items, and the power of other simple formats such as grand bundling.

progress.summary: The core additive regime $m<n$ was settled at $\Theta(\sqrt{nm})$ by Derakhshan, Ryu, Weinberg, Xue (EC 2024). Since then: Beyhaghi, Cai, Feng, Li, Weinberg (June 2025, arXiv 2506.09291) moved beyond standard regularity, proving $\Theta(n/\alpha)$ competition complexity under $\alpha$-strong regularity (removing the dependence on $m$ entirely) and giving the first grand-bundling competition-complexity bounds; a February 2026 paper (arXiv 2602.11959) strengthens Bulow-Klemperer-style results for multi-unit auctions in the duplicates model. Exact constants, the fine $m\ge n$ regime, non-additive valuations, and correlated items remain open.

counterexample_rationale: Lower bounds in this area are exactly explicit constructions — the EC 2024 settlement came from identifying truncated equal-revenue distributions as worst cases — so new hard distributions (for the $m\ge n$ regime, for VCG with unit-demand bidders, or for correlated items) are a concrete constructive target; however, verifying a candidate requires reasoning about the optimal multi-item mechanism's revenue, which is analytically demanding rather than a finite check.
alphaevolve_rationale: A search loop could evolve parameterized families of value distributions (e.g. truncation points and mixtures of equal-revenue curves) and numerically estimate SRev/VCG revenue with extra bidders versus duality-based upper bounds on optimal revenue, hunting for instances that certify larger competition complexity; the bottleneck is that certifying $\mathrm{Rev}_n(D)$ from below requires constructing explicit Bayesian IC mechanisms, which is harder to automate but was the key innovation of the 2024 lower bound.

literature.synthesis: The field is organized around the Cai-Devanur-Weinberg duality framework, which upper-bounds optimal multi-item revenue by tractable benchmarks, and progress has consisted of matching those benchmarks with the revenue of simple auctions with extra bidders. Eden, Feldman, Friedler, Talgam-Cohen, Weinberg (EC 2017) proved the first multi-item Bulow-Klemperer results this way ($n+2m-2$ extra bidders for additive bidders over independent regular items; also a single unit-demand bidder). Feldman, Friedler, Rubinstein (EC 2018) showed $O(n\ln(m/n))$ extra bidders suffice even for $99\%$ of the benchmark, with a matching $\Omega(n\ln(m/n))$ necessity under regularity. Beyhaghi and Weinberg (STOC 2019) sharpened the upper bounds to $O(\sqrt{nm})$ for $m<n$, and Derakhshan, Ryu, Weinberg, Xue (EC 2024) closed that regime with an $\Omega(\sqrt{nm})$ lower bound built from an explicit Bayesian IC auction for truncated equal-revenue distributions, also proving these truncations always witness worst-case competition complexity. The 2025 'Beyond VCG and Regularity' paper (Beyhaghi, Cai, Feng, Li, Weinberg) shows the entire $m$-dependence is an artifact of bare regularity: under $\alpha$-strong regularity the answer is $\Theta(n/\alpha)$, and grand bundling admits constant competition complexity in natural single-bidder cases. The main remaining gaps: no tight answer (even asymptotically, with constants) in the $m\ge n$ regime; essentially nothing tight beyond additive valuations — for unit-demand, XOS, or subadditive bidders the duality benchmarks lose constant factors, so new benchmark technology or direct coupling arguments are needed; and correlated items break the per-item second-price analysis entirely.

reviewed.result: Single item, $n$ i.i.d. regular bidders: a second-price auction with $n+1$ bidders revenue-dominates the optimal auction with $n$ bidders, i.e. $C(n,1)=1$.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: For lower bounds: construct explicit Bayesian IC mechanisms whose revenue exceeds SRev with $c$ extra bidders on candidate worst-case distributions — the EC 2024 result shows truncated equal-revenue families are the right search space for additive values, and analogous families for unit-demand/XOS are unexplored; numerical optimization over truncation parameters plus duality certificates is a plausible pipeline. For upper bounds: sharpen Cai-Devanur-Weinberg flow/benchmark choices, or exploit distributional structure ($\alpha$-strong regularity, MHR) as in the 2025 work. The $m\ge n$ regime likely needs a new benchmark, since the current one is provably loose there.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: An upper-bound claim must show $\mathrm{SRev}_{n+c}\ge\mathrm{Rev}_n$ for ALL distributions in the stated class — referees should check the revenue benchmark used to upper-bound $\mathrm{Rev}_n$ is valid for randomized Bayesian IC mechanisms (not just deterministic/DSIC ones) and that the coupling between original and augmented auctions handles the highest-order statistics correctly. A lower-bound claim needs an explicit distribution plus an explicit (possibly randomized) BIC mechanism whose revenue is certified to exceed $\mathrm{SRev}_{n+c}$; the BIC constraints and revenue computation for specific parametric families can be verified numerically, but the final claim must hold exactly, so closed-form or interval-arithmetic verification is expected.

title: Menu complexity of approximately revenue-optimal multi-item auctions
short_statement: When selling $n$ items to one additive buyer with independent values, how many menu (lottery) options are needed to guarantee a $(1-\varepsilon)$ fraction of optimal revenue? In particular: is $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ menu size enough for fixed $\varepsilon$, and what is the exact two-item exponent in $1/\varepsilon$?
full_statement: A monopolist sells $n$ items to a single additive, risk-neutral, quasilinear buyer whose item values are drawn from a product distribution $F=F_1\times\cdots\times F_n$. By the taxation principle a mechanism is a menu $\{(x_k,p_k)\}_k$ of lottery-price pairs, where $x_k\in[0,1]^n$ gives allocation probabilities and $p_k\in\mathbb{R}$ a price; the buyer picks a utility-maximizing entry. The menu size of a mechanism is its number of entries. Let $\mathrm{Rev}(F)$ be the optimal (unbounded-menu) revenue and define $$C(n,\varepsilon)=\min\{s:\ \forall F\ \exists\ \text{menu of size}\le s\ \text{with revenue}\ge(1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{Rev}(F)\}.$$ Known: $C(n,\varepsilon)$ is finite for all $n,\varepsilon>0$ (Babaioff, Gonczarowski, Nisan); exponential lower bounds are known in the regime $\varepsilon\sim 1/n$; for $n=2$, $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})\le C(2,\varepsilon)\le O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ (the upper bound under standard distributional assumptions; $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$ unconditionally). Open: (i) for fixed $\varepsilon$, does $C(n,\varepsilon)$ grow polynomially in $n$, or is it exponential? (ii) determine the exact exponent $c$ with $C(2,\varepsilon)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-c})$.
known_results: Foundational negatives: Hart, Nisan (EC 2013 / JET 2019) show optimal mechanisms for two independent items may require randomization, and for correlated items every finite menu can miss almost all revenue (infinite menu-size complexity), so finite-menu guarantees require independence. Constant factors are cheap: Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, Weinberg (FOCS 2014) show max(SRev, BRev) — a menu of $n+1$ entries — is a $6$-approximation (constant since improved). Near-optimality: Babaioff, Gonczarowski, Nisan (STOC 2017 / GEB 2022) prove $C(n,\varepsilon)$ is finite for every $n,\varepsilon$, with upper bounds exponential in $n$, and exponential lower bounds when $\varepsilon\approx 1/n$. For two items, Hart-Nisan gave $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$; Gonczarowski (STOC 2018) strengthened this to $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ under standard economic assumptions and proved the first lower bound $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})$, even for i.i.d. values from nice distributions; as a corollary the deterministic communication complexity of $(1-\varepsilon)$-optimal two-item mechanisms is $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon))$. Related strands: buy-many mechanisms have $\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon)$ menu-size complexity in some regimes (Chawla, Teng, Tzamos, EC 2020), symmetric menu complexity of i.i.d. items is quasi-polynomial (Kothari et al. 2019), and communication/quantum-communication analogues have been studied through ITCS 2025. As of mid-2026, both headline quantitative questions — polynomial-in-$n$ menu size for fixed $\varepsilon$, and the tight two-item exponent in $[1/4,2]$ — remain open.

where_posed.text: Menu size as a complexity measure and the approximation question were introduced in Hart, Nisan, 'The Menu-Size Complexity of Auctions', EC 2013 (published as 'Selling Multiple Correlated Goods: Revenue Maximization and Menu-Size Complexity', Journal of Economic Theory 2019); the quantitative open questions are stated in Babaioff, Gonczarowski, Nisan, 'The Menu-Size Complexity of Revenue Approximation', STOC 2017 / Games and Economic Behavior 2022, and Gonczarowski, STOC 2018.

background: Myerson's theory makes single-item revenue maximization simple: the optimal mechanism is a posted price (for one buyer) or a virtual-value auction. Multi-item revenue maximization is drastically different. By the taxation principle, any mechanism for a single buyer is equivalent to a menu of (lottery, price) options, and Hart and Nisan showed the revenue-optimal menu can be startlingly complex: even for two independent items, optimal mechanisms may need randomization, and for correlated items the optimal revenue may be infinite while every finite-menu mechanism earns only a negligible fraction — an infinite 'menu-size complexity'. This motivated menu size as a clean complexity measure for mechanisms, quantifying the 'simple versus optimal' tension at the heart of multidimensional mechanism design. Two regimes anchor the theory. First, constant-factor approximation is cheap: Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg showed the better of selling separately and grand bundling (a menu of $n+1$ options) achieves a constant fraction of optimal revenue for an additive buyer over independent items. Second, near-optimal approximation is subtle: Babaioff, Gonczarowski, and Nisan resolved the qualitative question by proving a finite menu of size $C(n,\varepsilon)$ always suffices for $(1-\varepsilon)$-optimal revenue, and Gonczarowski's optimal-transport-duality lower bound of $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})$ (two i.i.d. items from nice distributions) shows real growth is necessary. What is not known is the quantitative rate: whether $C(n,\varepsilon)$ can be polynomial in $n$ for fixed $\varepsilon$ (the known exponential lower bounds only kick in when $\varepsilon\approx 1/n$), and even the exact exponent of $1/\varepsilon$ for two items, where the bounds $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ leave a polynomial gap. These questions connect to communication complexity, mechanism descriptions in practice, and the buy-many literature.

progress.summary: No movement on the two core quantitative questions since Gonczarowski (STOC 2018): the two-item gap $[\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4}), O(\varepsilon^{-2})]$ and the poly-vs-exponential growth of $C(n,\varepsilon)$ in $n$ for fixed $\varepsilon$ both stand as of mid-2026. Activity has shifted to adjacent models: buy-many mechanisms (poly menu-size complexity in restricted settings), symmetric menus for i.i.d. items, and the communication and quantum-communication complexity of auctions (e.g. ITCS 2025), which refine but do not resolve the menu-size questions.

counterexample_rationale: Improved lower bounds are explicit constructions: one must exhibit a (family of) product distributions and prove every small menu loses more than an $\varepsilon$ fraction of revenue. Candidate distributions can be searched numerically (the optimal two-item mechanism is computable via convex programming for discretized instances), but converting numerical evidence into a proof requires duality certificates, so this is construction-friendly rather than purely finite-checkable.
alphaevolve_rationale: An evolutionary loop could search over two-item value distributions (e.g. parameterized densities or discrete grids), compute optimal revenue and best size-$s$ menu revenue via LP/convex optimization, and evolve instances maximizing the gap — directly attacking the $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})$-vs-$O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ question with candidate worst cases; optimal-transport duality then offers a route to certify the discovered gaps.

literature.synthesis: The upper-bound technology is 'nudge and round': Babaioff, Gonczarowski, Nisan (STOC 2017 / GEB 2022) discretize the menu of an optimal mechanism, rounding allocations and prices so the buyer's choice changes little and revenue loses only $\varepsilon\cdot\mathrm{Rev}$, giving finiteness of $C(n,\varepsilon)$ but with bounds exponential in $n$; their lower bounds show exponential size is genuinely necessary when the accuracy target scales as $\varepsilon\sim 1/n$. Gonczarowski (STOC 2018) introduced the main lower-bound tool at fixed $n$: the optimal-transport (Daskalakis-Deckelbaum-Tzamos) duality characterizing optimal two-item mechanisms, from which he extracted the $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})$ bound and, in the positive direction, an $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ menu under standard assumptions, plus the tight $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ communication complexity for fixed $n$. Hart and Nisan's JET 2019 paper delimits the whole program: with correlated items no finite menu achieves any constant fraction of optimal revenue, so product distributions are essential. Adjacent lines: Babaioff-Immorlica-Lucier-Weinberg's constant-factor 'SRev vs BRev' result shows tiny menus suffice for constant approximation; Chawla, Teng, Tzamos show buy-many mechanisms — a natural robustness restriction — have polynomial menu-size complexity, suggesting the exponential blowup is tied to exotic one-shot lotteries; Kothari, Mohan, Schvartzman, Singla, Weinberg bound symmetric menu complexity for i.i.d. items at quasi-polynomial. The two-item exponent gap persists because the lower-bound construction exploits only local behavior of the transport dual near a critical region, while the upper bound rounds globally; closing it likely requires either a sharper duality-based construction or a fundamentally better rounding that adapts menu density to the distribution.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: For the two-item lower bound: use the optimal-transport duality to construct distributions whose optimal menus have many 'essentially distinct' entries — a parameterized search over densities with numerical solution of the two-item screening problem (an infinite-dimensional LP, tractable after discretization) could locate candidates, then duality certificates make the bound rigorous. For upper bounds: adaptive rounding of menus (finer near high-curvature regions of the utility function) could plausibly beat $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$; for the $n$-item question, either extend nudge-and-round with dimension-free discretization (suggesting poly(n)) or lift the $\varepsilon\sim 1/n$ exponential lower bound to constant $\varepsilon$ via direct-sum-style constructions.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A lower-bound claim must exhibit distributions and prove EVERY menu of size $s$ loses $>\varepsilon\cdot\mathrm{Rev}$ — referees should check the argument covers randomized (lottery) entries, not just deterministic bundle prices, and that optimal revenue is certified from below (e.g. an explicit mechanism) while small-menu revenue is bounded from above (duality). An upper-bound claim must construct, for an arbitrary product distribution in the stated class, a small menu with certified revenue; check the distributional assumptions (bounded support? MHR?) match the claim's generality. Discretized instances are machine-checkable via LP, but the headline bounds are asymptotic statements requiring proof.

notes_for_maintainer: Verified July 2026: no resolution of either core question found. The two-item bounds are exactly as in the old record — $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})$ (Gonczarowski STOC 2018) vs $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ (same paper, under standard assumptions; Hart-Nisan's unconditional bound is $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$) — and I found no 2024-2026 paper improving them. Note the subtlety that $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ requires distributional assumptions; the old record stated it unconditionally. The poly(n)-for-fixed-$\varepsilon$ question likewise appears untouched; recent related activity is in buy-many mechanisms and (quantum) communication complexity of auctions (ITCS 2025), which I cite only as context.

title: Price of anonymity in multi-unit auctions
short_statement: For multi-unit auctions with non-identical regular buyers, sharpen the exact finite-$k$ revenue gap between optimal discriminating mechanisms and anonymous pricing/reserves.
full_statement: There are $n$ unit-demand buyers with independent, not necessarily identical, regular value distributions and a seller with $k$ identical units. Let $\mathrm{OPT}(F)$ be the optimal expected revenue over all Bayesian incentive-compatible mechanisms. Let $\mathrm{AP}(F)$ be the best anonymous posted-price revenue: the seller posts one common price $p$ to all buyers, buyers with value at least $p$ may purchase, and at most $k$ units are sold. Define $$\rho_k=\sup_F \frac{\mathrm{OPT}(F)}{\mathrm{AP}(F)},$$ where the supremum ranges over all independent regular distributions and all numbers of buyers. The single-item case $k=1$ has a tight constant about $2.62$. The open problem is to determine the sharp finite-$k$ constants $\rho_k$, identify extremal distribution families, and reconcile these constants with the known asymptotic gap structure among Myerson auctions, sequential posted pricing, anonymous reserves, and anonymous posted prices as $k$ grows.
known_results: Alaei, Hartline, Niazadeh, Pountourakis, and Yuan showed that anonymous pricing gives an $e$-approximation to the ex-ante relaxation for single-item auctions, improving earlier four-approximation bounds for anonymous reserves. Jin, Lu, Qi, Tang, and Xiao settled the single-item anonymous-pricing ratio at about $2.62$ and gave matching lower-bound examples. Jin, Jiang, Lu, and Zhang studied multi-unit revenue gaps among Myerson auctions, sequential posted pricing, anonymous reserves, and anonymous pricing. They proved asymptotically tight $1+\Theta(1/\sqrt{k})$ gaps within discriminating or anonymous groups and $\Theta(\log k)$ gaps across the two groups, depending on which mechanism classes are compared. These results give the right asymptotic scale for several comparisons, but they do not pin down the exact finite-supply constants $\rho_k$ for anonymous pricing versus the optimal auction.

where_posed.text: The single-item anonymous-pricing gap originates in Alaei et al.; finite multi-unit gaps are sharpened but not completely pinned down by Jin, Jiang, Lu, and Zhang.

background: The price of anonymity measures the revenue lost when a seller cannot discriminate among buyers. In Bayesian auction theory, Myerson's optimal auction may use distribution-specific reserve prices and allocation rules. Anonymous pricing is much simpler: post one common price and sell while supply lasts. The question is important both practically and conceptually because anonymous mechanisms are transparent, easy to implement, and often legally or institutionally preferable. For one item, the basic approximation gap is now essentially resolved: anonymous pricing loses a factor about $2.62$ relative to optimal discriminating auctions. Multi-unit environments are subtler. Supply $k$ changes the role of market thickness, and the gap between anonymous and discriminating mechanisms can depend on whether one compares exact finite-$k$ constants, asymptotic rates, or within-group versus cross-group mechanism classes.

progress.summary: The single-item constant is tight, and asymptotic multi-unit group gaps are known. Exact finite-supply constants and broader multi-item anonymity losses remain open.

counterexample_rationale: Hard instances are finite collections of distributions, often with few distributional shapes. Numerical optimization over discrete distributions can suggest tight examples for small $k$.
alphaevolve_rationale: The problem is well suited to computational search over distribution families and revenue-ratio certificates, followed by analytic proof of extremality.

literature.synthesis: The literature separates two questions: how well anonymous prices approximate optimal auctions, and how revenue gaps scale among broader mechanism classes. Alaei et al. showed that anonymous pricing is within an $e$ factor of an ex-ante benchmark for single-item settings. Jin et al. later solved the exact single-item constant at about $2.62$, showing the $e$ bound was not tight. Multi-unit work reveals that supply can either wash out or amplify anonymity losses depending on the comparison class. In particular, within anonymous mechanisms or within discriminating mechanisms the gap tends to one with growing $k$, while cross-group gaps grow like $\Theta(\log k)$. What remains is the exact finite-$k$ picture and the extension to richer feasibility constraints.

title: Maximum number of stable matchings in an n x n instance
short_statement: Determine the exponential growth base of the maximum possible number of stable matchings in an $n\times n$ stable-marriage instance.
full_statement: For an instance of the stable-marriage problem with $n$ men and $n$ women, each agent has a strict complete preference order over the opposite side. A perfect matching is stable if there is no blocking pair, meaning no man and woman who both prefer each other to their assigned partners. Let $s(I)$ be the number of stable matchings in instance $I$, and let $$f(n)=\max_I s(I),$$ where the maximum ranges over all strict complete $n\times n$ preference profiles. Determine the sharp asymptotic growth of $f(n)$. In particular, determine the exponential growth rate, or matching upper and lower exponential bounds. Equivalently, characterize the richest possible rotation posets that can arise from stable-marriage instances and the largest possible number of downsets they can have.
known_results: Irving and Leather proved that counting stable matchings is hard and gave early exponential lower-bound constructions. Later gadget constructions give lower bounds with base about $2.28$. Before 2018, the best general upper bounds were superexponential of the form $2^{n\log n-O(n)}$. Karlin, Oveis Gharan, and Weber gave the first simply exponential upper bound, proving $f(n)\le c^n$ for a universal constant $c$ by reducing to downsets of mixing posets. Palmer and Palvolgyi then improved the upper bound from the large Karlin-Oveis Gharan-Weber constant to $3.55^n+O(1)$ using an entropy formulation. This was the prior exponential gap. Ghorbani and Mnich, 'A 2.81^n upper bound on the number of stable matchings' (arXiv:2611.06494v1, November 4, 2026), Theorem 1, improve the upper bound to $f(n)<2.81^n$ for strict complete preferences. The lower bound is more precisely $2.28^n/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ for all n. The exact exponential base is not determined.

where_posed.text: First posed by Knuth and revisited in Karlin, Oveis Gharan, and Weber, 'A Simply Exponential Upper Bound on the Maximum Number of Stable Matchings'.

background: Stable matching is usually taught as an algorithmic existence theorem: Gale and Shapley guarantee at least one stable matching and find it efficiently. But a single instance can have many stable matchings, forming a distributive lattice. Counting them is computationally hard, and the extremal question asks how large this lattice can be as a function of market size. Knuth posed this in the 1970s. The problem is mathematically clean: preferences are strict and complete, stability has its standard blocking-pair definition, and the objective is just the largest possible number of stable matchings among all $n\times n$ instances. The answer is known to be exponential, but the base remains unknown despite major progress on both lower and upper bounds.

progress.summary: A November preprint lowers the upper base; no matching lower construction is supplied.

title: Existence threshold for stable matching with couples
short_statement: Find the sharp growth threshold for the number of couples in large random matching markets that still admit stable matchings with high probability.
full_statement: Consider a sequence of hospitals/residents markets with $n$ positions and applicants consisting of singles and couples. Singles rank individual positions; each couple ranks ordered pairs of positions, and hospitals have responsive preferences or priority orderings over individual residents. A matching is stable if there is no blocking single, blocking couple move, or hospital-side deviation under the standard hospitals/residents-with-couples definition. Fix a random large-market model: for example, bounded or slowly growing preference-list lengths, random acceptable positions or pairs, and hospital capacities scaled with $n$. Let $c(n)$ be the number of couples. Determine the sharp asymptotic boundary, including constants where meaningful, between regimes in which a stable matching exists with high probability and regimes in which nonexistence has probability bounded away from zero or tends to one. The formulation should specify whether couples may be a vanishing, polynomial, near-linear, or constant fraction of the market and how overlap among their acceptable pairs is generated.
known_results: Roth showed that stable matchings need not exist with couples, and Ronn showed that deciding existence is NP-complete. Kojima, Pathak, and Roth proved that stable matchings exist with high probability in large markets under assumptions motivated by residency markets when the fraction of couples is sufficiently small, and they connected the theory to observed NRMP behavior. Ashlagi, Braverman, and Hassidim gave a new algorithm and showed high-probability stability for a broad random-market class allowing the number of couples to grow at a near-linear rate. They also proved tightness in the sense that, when the number of couples grows linearly in their model, stable matchings can fail to exist with constant probability. What is still missing is a sharp threshold or phase diagram for concrete random market families, especially constants and intermediate regimes between positive near-linear results and negative linear-density constructions.

where_posed.text: Large-market threshold questions are developed by Kojima, Pathak, and Roth and by Ashlagi, Braverman, and Hassidim.

background: Couples are a central difficulty in real matching markets such as medical residency. A couple submits preferences over pairs of positions, creating complementarities that destroy the lattice and guaranteed existence properties of classical stable matching. Worst-case theory is bleak: stable matchings may fail to exist, and deciding existence is NP-complete. Yet large clearinghouses routinely find stable outcomes. This motivates average-case and large-market theory: if the market is large, preferences are random enough, and couples do not create too many conflicting complementarities, perhaps stable outcomes exist with high probability. The existing results show strong positive regimes and genuine negative regimes, but not a sharp boundary. The problem is clean once the random market model, list lengths, capacities, and couple-preference assumptions are fixed.

progress.summary: Existence is known with high probability under several sparse or near-linear random-market regimes, and failure can occur with constant probability in linear-couple regimes. The sharp threshold and constants for concrete models remain unresolved.

counterexample_rationale: Finite random-market simulations can reveal candidate threshold behavior and minimal obstruction patterns, but proving a sharp threshold requires probabilistic combinatorics.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can help identify small nonexistence gadgets and estimate scaling, but rigorous asymptotic threshold proofs are the main obstacle.

literature.synthesis: The couples problem highlights the gap between worst-case computational theory and observed market performance. Worst-case nonexistence and NP-completeness explain why no simple Gale-Shapley analogue exists. Large-market work shows that random structure and limited overlap among complementarities can restore stability with high probability. Kojima, Pathak, and Roth provide market-design conditions motivated by residency data. Ashlagi, Braverman, and Hassidim sharpen the average-case picture by proving positive results for a broad class of random markets with near-linear couples and by giving linear-couple regimes where nonexistence occurs with constant probability. The unresolved part is not whether sparse random markets can be stable, but where the exact phase boundary lies for specified random preference and capacity models.

title: Tight competitive ratio of the prophet secretary problem
short_statement: Determine the exact optimal competitive ratio for selecting one item from independent non-identical distributions arriving in uniformly random order.
full_statement: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent nonnegative random variables with known distributions. Nature draws all values, then reveals them one by one in a uniformly random permutation unknown to the gambler. After seeing a realized value and its identity, an online algorithm must irrevocably accept it and stop, or reject it forever; at most one value may be selected. The prophet benchmark is $\mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i]$. For a stopping rule $A$, write $\mathrm{CR}(A)=\inf_{(X_i)} \mathbb{E}[A(X_1,\ldots,X_n)]/\mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i]$, where the expectation includes both values and arrival order. The open problem is to determine $$\alpha^*=\sup_A \mathrm{CR}(A).$$ Equivalently, find matching lower and upper bounds for the best possible competitive ratio in the original random-order prophet-secretary model with independent non-identical distributions.
known_results: Esfandiari, Hajiaghayi, Liaghat, and Monemizadeh introduced the prophet-secretary model and proved that random order beats the classical adversarial-order $1/2$ barrier, with simple threshold methods reaching the $1-1/e$ scale and an early $0.75$ upper bound. Correa, Saona, and Ziliotto developed blind quantile strategies, proved a $0.665$ guarantee, showed blind strategies cannot exceed $0.675$, and gave a $0.732$ upper bound for arbitrary algorithms. Bubna and Chiplunkar improved the random-order hardness to about $0.7254$ and separated random order from order selection. Chen, Huang, Li, and Tang gave a $0.688$-competitive algorithm in 2024, breaking the blind-strategy barrier. Feng, Jin, Wu, and Xiang, 'Mean-only Prophet Inequalities' (arXiv:2610.24711), Theorem 1.2, improve the lower bound to $0.6902$ for every n using only the expected maximum and arrival count, hence also in the known-distribution model. Giambartolomei, Mallmann-Trenn, and Saona (arXiv:2304.04024), Theorem 1.1, bound the order-unaware ratio strictly below $0.7235$. Thus $0.6902\le\alpha^*<0.7235$ is supported by the reviewed papers.

background: Prophet secretary combines two classical optimal-stopping models. In prophet inequalities, distributions are known but arrivals may be adversarial; in secretary problems, order is random but values are often adversarial or unknown. Prophet secretary keeps known independent distributions and random arrival order. This is a minimal model for posted-price selling when buyer types are heterogeneous but arrive in random order. The exact constant matters because it quantifies the value of random order over adversarial order. The original result showed that random order beats the $1/2$ prophet-inequality barrier and approaches $1-1/e$ with simple nonadaptive thresholds. Later work improved both lower and upper bounds, but the exact worst-case ratio is still not known.

progress.summary: Both the algorithmic and impossibility summaries improve; neither paper determines the exact constant.

alphaevolve_rationale: The problem is well suited to numerical optimization over discrete distributions and threshold functions, with exact proof needed afterward.

literature.synthesis: The model began with simple threshold strategies that already showed a qualitative separation from adversarial-order prophet inequalities. Subsequent work introduced blind strategies, which choose acceptance probabilities as a function of time and value quantile rather than distribution identity, giving cleaner analyses and better constants. The hard examples are delicate because random order symmetrizes the instance, while non-identical distributions still allow rare high values to distort the prophet benchmark. Recent separations among random-order, i.i.d., and order-selection variants show that constants are genuinely model-specific. The remaining task is to identify the extremal distribution family and matching optimal stopping rule. The newer mean-only guarantee transfers to the full-information model, but its restricted-threshold hardness does not bound all known-distribution algorithms.

title: Tight competitive ratio of online bipartite matching under random arrival
short_statement: For unweighted online bipartite matching with uniformly random online arrival order, determine the optimal competitive ratio and the exact ratio of Ranking.
full_statement: Let $G=(L,R,E)$ be a bipartite graph. The offline side $L$ and the full set of possible online vertices $R$ are fixed by an adversary, but vertices of $R$ arrive in a uniformly random order. When $v\in R$ arrives, the algorithm observes its incident edges to $L$ and must either match $v$ irrevocably to an unmatched neighbor in $L$ or discard it forever. The objective is the expected cardinality of the final matching, compared with $\nu(G)$, the maximum matching size in $G$. Define $$\rho^*=\sup_A \inf_G \frac{\mathbb{E}[|A(G,\pi)|]}{\nu(G)},$$ where the supremum is over online algorithms without advance knowledge of the unrevealed graph and the expectation is over the random permutation $\pi$ and any internal randomness. Determine $\rho^*$. A second concrete target is to determine the exact worst-case random-arrival competitive ratio of the Ranking algorithm, which chooses a random priority order on $L$ and greedily matches each arrival to its highest-priority available neighbor. The new guarantee below assumes the number of online arrivals is known.
known_results: Karp, Vazirani, and Vazirani proved the tight $1-1/e$ ratio for adversarial arrival order. Mahdian and Yan showed that Ranking achieves at least $0.696$ in the random-order model using strongly factor-revealing LPs. Manshadi, Oveis Gharan, and Saberi gave a $0.823$ upper bound that applies to related known-distribution and permutation models. Chierichetti, Giacchini, Panconesi, and Vattani improved this impossibility to $1-e/e^e=0.82062\ldots$ in 2025. Peng and Tang revisited Ranking's primal-dual analysis and showed that within the current primal-dual framework Ranking is pinned between roughly $0.686$ and $0.703$, with the classical $0.696$ value essentially the limit of that analysis. The exact optimal ratio, and the exact ratio of Ranking, remain open. Peng and Tang, 'Harmonic Ranking for Edge-Weighted Oblivious Matching' (arXiv:2608.12176), Corollary 1.2, gives $0.698015475248$ in the vertex-weighted random-arrival model, hence also in this unweighted special case, assuming the number of arrivals is known. This is not a determination of ordinary Ranking's exact ratio.

background: Random-order online bipartite matching asks how much of the classical adversarial barrier is caused by worst-case order rather than irrevocability. The graph is still worst-case, but online vertices arrive in a uniformly random permutation. This model is relevant to ad allocation, recommendation, and platform matching when demand is not controlled by an adversary but the underlying compatibility graph may be highly structured. The canonical Ranking algorithm is optimal in adversarial order at $1-1/e$, but random order allows better performance. The exact optimal ratio is a long-standing constant-factor question: the updated lower bound is given below, while the strongest upper bounds are above $0.82$. Even the exact ratio of Ranking in this model is not fully pinned down.

title: Computing EF1 and Pareto-optimal allocations in polynomial time
short_statement: For indivisible goods with additive valuations, an allocation that is both EF1 (envy-free up to one good) and Pareto-optimal always exists, but the known general algorithms are only pseudo-polynomial. Can such an allocation be computed in time polynomial in the number of agents, the number of goods, and the bit-length of the values?
full_statement: There are $n$ agents with additive valuations $v_i:2^M\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$ over a set $M$ of $m$ indivisible goods, with the values $v_i(\{g\})$ given in binary. An allocation $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ partitioning $M$ is EF1 (envy-free up to one good) if for all agents $i,j$ with $X_j\ne\emptyset$ there exists $g\in X_j$ with $v_i(X_i)\ge v_i(X_j\setminus\{g\})$; it is Pareto-optimal (PO) if no other allocation makes some agent strictly better off without making another worse off, and fractionally Pareto-optimal (fPO) if no fractional allocation does so. EF1+PO allocations always exist (any maximum-Nash-welfare allocation is one; Caragiannis et al. 2016), and EF1+fPO allocations always exist (Barman–Krishnamurthy–Vaish 2018), so the question is purely computational: is there an algorithm running in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,\log V_{\max})$, where $V_{\max}=\max_{i,g}v_i(\{g\})$, that outputs an allocation that is simultaneously EF1 and PO (or the stronger EF1 and fPO)? The best general algorithms run in pseudo-polynomial time $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,V_{\max})$. The problem of computing an EF1+fPO allocation is in PLS and is not known to be NP-hard, PLS-hard, or in P. Determine whether a truly polynomial-time algorithm exists; as of mid-2026 this is open for general $n$, resolved affirmatively only when $n$ is constant or the agents have constantly many distinct values.
known_results: Existence: max-Nash-welfare allocations are EF1+PO (Caragiannis, Kurokawa, Moulin, Procaccia, Shah, Wang, EC 2016 / TEAC 2019); EF1+fPO allocations always exist (Barman, Krishnamurthy, Vaish, EC 2018, via a non-constructive perturbation/convergence argument). Upper bounds: Barman–Krishnamurthy–Vaish (2018) compute EF1+PO in pseudo-polynomial time $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,V_{\max})$; Garg and Murhekar (IJCAI 2021 / JAIR 2024, arXiv 2204.14229) strengthened this to a pseudo-polynomial algorithm for EF1+fPO, gave a strongly polynomial-time algorithm for $k$-ary instances (each agent has at most $k=O(1)$ distinct values for the goods), a polynomial-time algorithm for EF1+PO when the number of agents $n$ is constant, and showed the EF1+fPO problem is in PLS. The most notable recent progress is Mahara (arXiv 2411.01810, Nov 2024; SAGT 2025), who gave the first truly polynomial-time algorithm computing an EF1+fPO allocation for any FIXED number of agents (polynomial in $m$ and $\log V_{\max}$ for constant $n$), by sequentially inserting agents while maintaining EF1+fPO. Special valuation classes are also solved: binary valuations (EFX+PO in polynomial time; Halpern et al. 2020, Babaioff–Ezra–Feige 2021), bi-valued valuations (EF1/EFX+PO in polynomial time; Garg–Murhekar 2023, Bu et al. 2024). Lower bounds: none — the problem is not known to be NP-hard or PLS-hard, and no super-polynomial lower bound is known in any model. The headline question — $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,\log V_{\max})$ computation of EF1+PO (or EF1+fPO) for general $n$ — remains open as of July 2026.

where_posed.text: The computational question originates with Barman, Krishnamurthy, Vaish, 'Finding Fair and Efficient Allocations', EC 2018 (whose algorithm is pseudo-polynomial), is listed as an open problem in the Aziz–Li–Moulin–Wu survey (SIGecom Exchanges 2022), and is restated crisply in Mahara, 'A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for Fair and Efficient Allocation with a Fixed Number of Agents', arXiv 2411.01810 (SAGT 2025).
where_posed.quote: Nevertheless, the latter existence proof relies on a non-constructive convergence argument and does not directly yield an efficient algorithm for finding EF1 and fPO allocations. Whether a polynomial-time algorithm exists for finding an EF1 and PO (or fPO) allocation remains an important open problem.

additional_refs.title: The Unreasonable Fairness of Maximum Nash Welfare

background: A central theme in discrete fair division is whether fairness and economic efficiency can be achieved simultaneously, and at what computational cost. For indivisible goods with additive valuations, envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) — introduced by Budish (2011) and, implicitly, Lipton et al. (2004) — is the standard fairness relaxation: any envy an agent feels toward another must vanish after hypothetically removing some single good from the envied bundle. Pareto optimality (PO), and its strictly stronger fractional variant fPO (no fractional reallocation Pareto-dominates the allocation), are the standard efficiency notions. Each property is trivial to achieve alone (round-robin gives EF1; welfare maximization gives PO), but combining them is subtle. The landmark result of Caragiannis, Kurokawa, Moulin, Procaccia, Shah, and Wang (EC 2016) showed that any allocation maximizing Nash social welfare is simultaneously EF1 and PO — a striking existence proof, but computationally useless since maximizing Nash welfare is NP-hard (indeed APX-hard). Barman, Krishnamurthy, and Vaish (EC 2018) bypassed this via a market-based algorithm with price-rounding that computes an EF1+PO allocation in pseudo-polynomial time — polynomial in the magnitudes of the values rather than their bit-length — and proved (non-constructively, by a convergence argument) that EF1+fPO allocations always exist. Since then, the question of whether an EF1+PO (or EF1+fPO) allocation can be computed in truly polynomial time, with values given in binary, has become one of the best-known open computational problems in fair division, appearing in the Aziz–Li–Moulin–Wu survey and in the introductions of many follow-up papers. The problem is intriguing complexity-theoretically: existence is guaranteed, the problem lies in PLS (Garg–Murhekar), and no NP-hardness or PLS-hardness is known, so it sits in the same murky total-search territory as problems like computing a competitive equilibrium from equal incomes. A polynomial-time algorithm would make fair-and-efficient allocation practical in applications such as course allocation and public resource division; a hardness result would delineate a genuine computational price of combining fairness with efficiency.

progress.summary: The general question is still open as of July 2026, but there has been real movement on special cases since 2024: Mahara (arXiv 2411.01810, Nov 2024; published at SAGT 2025) gave the first truly polynomial-time algorithm for EF1+fPO with a fixed (constant) number of agents, strengthening Garg–Murhekar's constant-$n$ EF1+PO result to the stronger fPO guarantee, via a new agent-by-agent insertion technique. Garg and Murhekar's JAIR 2024 journal version (arXiv 2204.14229) consolidated the pseudo-polynomial EF1+fPO algorithm, strongly polynomial algorithms for constantly many distinct values ($k$-ary instances), and PLS membership. For general $n$ with values in binary, neither a polynomial-time algorithm nor any hardness result is known.

counterexample_rationale: Existence of EF1+PO allocations is already proven, so no counterexample can resolve the problem; the question is purely algorithmic/complexity-theoretic (design a polynomial-time algorithm or prove PLS-/NP-hardness), and neither direction is settled by a finite instance.
alphaevolve_rationale: An evolutionary search loop could plausibly help discover algorithmic ingredients — e.g., price-update or rounding rules for the Fisher-market framework that provably converge in polynomially many steps, or families of instances on which existing pseudo-polynomial algorithms exhibit exponential-in-bit-length behavior (evidence toward hardness or toward better potential functions) — but the final deliverable is a proof about all instances, which search alone cannot supply.

literature.synthesis: All known positive results flow from two techniques. The first is the Fisher-market / price-envy-freeness framework of Barman, Krishnamurthy, and Vaish (EC 2018): maintain an fPO allocation as a market equilibrium with item prices, and perform local swaps and price rises until price-EF1 (hence EF1) holds; a potential-function argument bounds the number of steps by $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,V_{\max})$, which is only pseudo-polynomial because the potential moves in value-magnitude increments. Garg and Murhekar (IJCAI 2021 / JAIR 2024) refined this machinery to reach the stronger EF1+fPO guarantee in pseudo-polynomial time, to run in strongly polynomial time when agents have constantly many distinct values (the price space collapses), and to place the problem in PLS — currently the only nontrivial complexity classification. The second technique, due to Mahara (2024, SAGT 2025), is incremental: insert agents one at a time, restoring EF1+fPO after each insertion; the analysis is polynomial for each fixed number of agents, giving the first $\mathrm{poly}(m,\log V_{\max})$ algorithm for constant $n$ and the strongest partial result to date. Restricted valuation classes (binary, bi-valued) admit polynomial-time algorithms even for the stronger EFX+PO combination (Halpern et al. 2020; Babaioff–Ezra–Feige 2021; Garg–Murhekar 2023; Bu et al. 2024). The remaining gap is stark: for general $n$ and binary-encoded additive values there is neither a polynomial-time algorithm nor any hardness evidence. New ideas seem needed either to make the market potential decrease geometrically (bit-scaling the prices is the obvious but so-far-unsuccessful route) or to prove PLS-hardness, which would be the first hardness result of its kind in fair division.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Most plausible routes: (1) bit-scaling or polynomial-step variants of the Barman–Krishnamurthy–Vaish market dynamics — design a price-rise/swap schedule whose potential decreases multiplicatively rather than additively, converting pseudo-polynomial to polynomial; (2) extend Mahara's agent-insertion technique from constant to general $n$ by finding a polynomially-bounded restoration procedure per insertion; (3) on the hardness side, attempt a PLS-hardness reduction (the problem is in PLS via Garg–Murhekar), which would explain the decade-long lack of progress; (4) exhaustive small-case experiments to map the behavior of existing algorithms on adversarial binary-encoded instances (exponentially large values) and locate worst-case families.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed algorithm must be verified on three axes: (a) EF1 — the $O(n^2)$ EF1 inequalities are directly checkable in polynomial time; (b) PO/fPO — verifying fPO of a given allocation is polynomial-time (via LP duality / market-equilibrium prices supporting the allocation), but verifying plain PO of an arbitrary allocation is coNP-hard in general, so proofs should certify fPO via explicit supporting prices; (c) running time — the analysis must be polynomial in $\log V_{\max}$, not $V_{\max}$; the classic failure mode is a potential-function argument whose step count secretly scales with value magnitudes (pseudo-polynomial), or an algorithm analyzed only for bounded/polynomially-large values. A hardness claim must reduce from a known PLS-hard or NP-hard problem and respect the promise that a solution always exists (so NP-hardness of the search problem must be argued carefully, e.g., via a decision variant).

title: Query complexity of envy-free cake cutting
short_statement: Determine the deterministic worst-case query complexity of complete exact envy-free cake cutting; newer randomized expected bounds are a distinct result.
full_statement: A cake is the interval $[0,1]$. Each of $n$ agents has a nonatomic additive valuation measure over subintervals. In the Robertson-Webb model, a protocol may ask evaluation queries $\mathrm{Eval}_i(x,y)$, returning agent $i$'s value for $[x,y]$, and cut queries $\mathrm{Cut}_i(x,\alpha)$, returning a point $y$ such that agent $i$ values $[x,y]$ at $\alpha$ when such a point exists. An allocation, possibly using disconnected pieces, is envy-free if every agent weakly prefers its own allocated piece to every other agent's piece. Let $Q(n)$ be the minimum worst-case number of Robertson-Webb queries required by a bounded deterministic protocol that always terminates and returns a complete exact envy-free allocation for every profile of nonatomic additive valuations. Determine the asymptotic growth of $Q(n)$, or give substantially tighter upper and lower bounds.
known_results: Aziz and Mackenzie established bounded exact protocols, and Procaccia proved a quadratic query lower bound. Ye and Bai, 'Cutting Down the Tower: Single-Exponential Envy-Free Cake Cutting' (arXiv:2609.05191v1), give a deterministic $n^{O(1)}2^n$ upper bound for complete exact envy-freeness with disconnected shares. Mackenzie and Suzuki, 'Exact Envy-Free Cake Cutting with Polynomial Expected Queries' (arXiv:2610.28535v1), Theorem 1, report a Las Vegas protocol with $\widetilde O(n^{30})$ expected Robertson-Webb queries, using independent uniform cake-point samples. It terminates almost surely and never outputs an incorrect allocation. Remark 1.1 extends the hungry-agent presentation to valuations with zero-valued intervals. This does not give a deterministic polynomial worst-case bound.

where_posed.text: The bounded-protocol breakthrough and enormous upper bound appear in Aziz and Mackenzie, 'A Discrete and Bounded Envy-Free Cake Cutting Protocol for Any Number of Agents'.

background: Cake cutting is a canonical fair-division model for divisible heterogeneous resources. Existence of envy-free allocations is classical, but algorithmic access to valuations matters: protocols cannot inspect arbitrary value measures directly. The Robertson-Webb model formalizes access through cut and evaluation queries. For decades, a major open question asked whether a bounded finite envy-free protocol exists for every number of agents. Aziz and Mackenzie answered yes, with a historical tower-of-exponentials query bound, subsequently improved as recorded below. The resulting problem is not whether envy-free cake cutting is possible; it is to understand the true information complexity of finding such allocations under the standard query model.

progress.summary: The deterministic upper bound is single-exponential; a separate randomized expected-polynomial result is reported. The deterministic target is not resolved.

The returned allocation must be exactly envy-free for arbitrary nonatomic additive valuations; approximate envy-freeness, free-disposal partial allocations, connected-piece relaxations, or special valuation classes do not solve this exact problem. A lower bound must be adversarial over valuation measures and query transcripts, not merely over a finite parametric family unless that family is rich enough to support the adversary argument.
