title: Best approximation ratio for maximum stable matching with ties
short_statement: In stable marriage with ties and incomplete lists (SMTI), weakly stable matchings can differ in size and finding a maximum one (MAX-SMTI) is NP-hard. The best polynomial-time algorithm achieves ratio $3/2$; the best lower bounds are $33/29$ (P $\ne$ NP), $4/3$ (UGC), and $3/2$ (Small Set Expansion Hypothesis / strong UGC). What is the optimal approximation ratio — in particular, can $3/2$ be beaten under standard assumptions?
full_statement: An SMTI instance consists of a bipartite set of men $U$ and women $W$, where each agent ranks a subset of the other side (incomplete lists) in a weak order (ties allowed); a pair $(m,w)$ is acceptable if each appears on the other's list. A matching $M$ (a set of disjoint acceptable pairs) is weakly stable if there is no acceptable pair $(m,w)\notin M$ such that $m$ is unmatched or strictly prefers $w$ to $M(m)$, AND $w$ is unmatched or strictly prefers $m$ to $M(w)$. Weakly stable matchings always exist but can differ in size by up to a factor of $2$. MAX-SMTI asks for a weakly stable matching of maximum cardinality; it is NP-hard (Iwama, Manlove, Miyazaki, Morita 1999). Let $\alpha^*$ be the infimum of ratios $\alpha$ such that a polynomial-time algorithm always outputs a weakly stable matching of size at least $|M_{\mathrm{OPT}}|/\alpha$. Known: $\alpha^*\le 3/2$ (McDermid 2009; linear-time versions by Paluch and Király); $\alpha^*\ge 33/29$ unless P $=$ NP and $\alpha^*\ge 4/3$ under the Unique Games Conjecture (Yanagisawa 2007; Halldórsson, Iwama, Miyazaki, Yanagisawa 2007); and $\alpha^*\ge 3/2$ assuming the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis or the strong UGC (via Dudycz, Lewandowski, Marcinkowski 2019). Open: determine $\alpha^*$ — equivalently, either give a polynomial-time $(3/2-\varepsilon)$-approximation for some $\varepsilon>0$ (which would refute SSEH and strong UGC), or prove a matching $3/2$ lower bound under P $\ne$ NP or standard UGC.
known_results: Upper bound: the best general polynomial-time approximation ratio is $3/2$, first achieved by McDermid (ICALP 2009), then by simpler linear-time algorithms of Paluch (WAOA 2011 / Algorithms 2014) and Király (MATCH-UP 2011 / Algorithms 2013). Csáji (arXiv:2304.02558; with Király and Yokoi, Mathematics of Operations Research 2025) gives a simple edge-duplication-based $3/2$-approximation covering many generalizations (free edges, critical vertices, matroid constraints, $\Delta$-stabilities) — still at exactly $3/2$. Lower bounds: NP-hard to approximate within $33/29\approx 1.1379$ (Yanagisawa 2007; Halldórsson, Iwama, Miyazaki, Yanagisawa, ACM Trans. Algorithms 2007), within $4/3$ under the Unique Games Conjecture, and — crucially — within $3/2-\varepsilon$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ assuming the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis or the strong UGC (follows from Dudycz, Lewandowski, Marcinkowski, IPCO 2019, via the connection between MAX-SMTI and minimum maximal matching). So $3/2$ is conditionally optimal, and the surviving open gap is $[4/3,\,3/2]$ under standard UGC and $[33/29,\,3/2]$ under P $\ne$ NP. Restricted variants do better: with ties on one side only, $25/17\approx 1.4706$ (Iwama, Miyazaki, Yanagisawa, Algorithmica 2014) and subsequently $1+1/e\approx 1.368$ (Lam and Plaxton, SODA 2019); with all ties of length at most $L$, $(3L-2)/(2L-1)$ (Koenemann, Pashkovich, Tofigzade, SAGT 2020), which is $4/3$ for $L=2$; and $1.25$ for the one-sided ties-at-the-end special case, matching its UGC lower bound. As of July 2026, no verified polynomial-time algorithm with ratio below $3/2$ for general MAX-SMTI exists; despite rumors of such claims, careful search of arXiv found none, consistent with the SSEH-conditional optimality of $3/2$.

where_posed.text: The approximation question was opened by the NP-hardness proof of Iwama, Manlove, Miyazaki, Morita (ICALP 1999) and became the field's benchmark open problem once McDermid, 'A 3/2-Approximation Algorithm for General Stable Marriage', ICALP 2009, set the current record; the state of the art including the conditional tightness of 3/2 is summarized in Csáji, 'A Simple 1.5-Approximation Algorithm for a Wide Range of Max-SMTI Problems', arXiv:2304.02558 (SAGT 2023; journal version with Király and Yokoi, Math. Oper. Res. 2025).
where_posed.quote: Since then, various algorithms have been proposed to improve the approximation ratio, e.g. Iwama et al. and Király, and the current best ratio is 3/2 by a polynomial-time algorithm of McDermid, where the same ratio is attained by linear-time algorithms of Pauluch and Király. [...] Yanagisawa and Halldórsson et al. showed that assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, there is no 4/3 − ε-approximation for any ε > 0. By a recent work by Dudycz et al. it follows that assuming the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis or the strong-UGC, there cannot even be a 3/2 − ε-approximation algorithm for Max-SMTI.

background: The stable marriage problem of Gale and Shapley (1962) is the founding model of matching under preferences: two sides rank each other, and a matching is stable if no pair would rather be together than with their assigned partners. In real deployments — hospital-resident matching (e.g., the Scottish Foundation Allocation Scheme), school choice, and labor markets — agents routinely submit preference lists that are both incomplete (they rank only acceptable partners) and contain ties (indifference among several partners). This combination, SMTI, changes the problem fundamentally. Under the standard notion of weak stability, stable matchings still always exist and one can be found by breaking ties arbitrarily and running Gale-Shapley, but different weakly stable matchings can have different sizes — up to a factor of two apart. Since leaving participants unmatched is costly in applications (an unmatched resident, an unfilled position), the natural objective is MAX-SMTI: find a maximum-cardinality weakly stable matching. Iwama, Manlove, Miyazaki, and Morita (1999) proved this NP-hard, and it was soon shown APX-hard even under severe restrictions (e.g., ties of length two on one side only). This launched a long approximation race — from the trivial factor 2 through 15/8, 5/3, and 8/5 — culminating in McDermid's 3/2-approximation at ICALP 2009, later simplified and made linear-time by Paluch and by Király, and recently extended by Csáji, Király, and Yokoi to a wide range of generalizations (matroid constraints, free edges, critical agents) still at ratio exactly 3/2. Meanwhile the hardness frontier advanced from 21/19 to Yanagisawa's 33/29 (assuming P ≠ NP) and 4/3 under the Unique Games Conjecture, and — importantly — Dudycz, Lewandowski, and Marcinkowski (IPCO 2019) showed that under the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis or a strong form of UGC, no $(3/2-\varepsilon)$-approximation exists at all. Determining the true approximation threshold, and in particular whether 3/2 can be beaten under only P ≠ NP or standard UGC, is one of the best-known open problems in the algorithmics of matching under preferences (it is highlighted in Manlove's monograph and recurs in the open-problem lists of the field).

progress.summary: The general ratio has been stuck at $3/2$ since McDermid (2009), and Dudycz, Lewandowski, Marcinkowski (IPCO 2019) showed $3/2$ is optimal assuming the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis or strong UGC, conditionally explaining the stall. Progress since then has been lateral: Csáji (SAGT 2023; with Király and Yokoi, Math. Oper. Res. 2025) extended the $3/2$-approximation to a broad framework of generalizations via a simple edge-duplication technique, and restricted variants (one-sided ties: $1+1/e$; bounded ties of size $L$: $(3L-2)/(2L-1)$) beat $3/2$. As of July 2026 no verified sub-$3/2$ algorithm for the general problem exists, and the gap $4/3$ vs $3/2$ under standard UGC (and $33/29$ vs $3/2$ under P $\ne$ NP) remains open.

counterexample_rationale: The question asks for an algorithm or a hardness proof, neither of which is a finite counterexample; explicit small instances only serve the secondary role of showing tightness of specific algorithms' analyses (e.g., instances where McDermid-type algorithms output exactly $2/3$ of optimum), which are already known.
alphaevolve_rationale: An evolutionary search loop could plausibly discover improved rounding/augmenting-path rules or tie-breaking heuristics whose worst case is then bounded via factor-revealing LPs, and could search for integrality-gap instances of the natural LP relaxations (Rothblum-type stable matching LPs) to map where $3/2$ is tight; however, since $3/2$ is optimal under SSEH/strong-UGC, a genuine general-case improvement is unlikely to be found by search, making restricted variants (one-sided or bounded ties) the realistic target.

literature.synthesis: Two lines of attack dominate. Algorithmically, all $3/2$-approximations descend from Gale-Shapley augmented with mechanisms to reduce the number of length-3 augmenting paths between the output and an optimal matching: McDermid (ICALP 2009) first achieved $3/2$, Paluch and Király gave linear-time versions, and Csáji, Király, and Yokoi (Math. Oper. Res. 2025; arXiv:2304.02558) distilled the approach into an edge-duplication technique that extends the ratio to matroid constraints, free edges, and critical agents — but every known charging argument saturates at $3/2$ because a stable matching can miss one vertex of each of $\mathrm{OPT}$'s length-3 alternating paths. On the hardness side, Halldórsson, Iwama, Miyazaki, and Yanagisawa (ACM Trans. Algorithms 2007) and Yanagisawa's 2007 thesis established $33/29$ NP-hardness and $4/3$ UGC-hardness, and Dudycz, Lewandowski, and Marcinkowski (IPCO 2019) leveraged the tight connection to minimum maximal matching to show that no $(3/2-\varepsilon)$-approximation exists under the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis or strong UGC — strong evidence that $3/2$ is the true threshold. The remaining gap is thus really a question about complexity assumptions: beating $3/2$ would refute SSEH, while confirming $3/2$-hardness under vanilla UGC or P $\ne$ NP needs new gadget constructions beyond the current $4/3$ and $33/29$ reductions. Restricted variants show the algorithmic frontier is not rigid everywhere: one-sided ties admit $1+1/e$ (Lam-Plaxton, SODA 2019) against a $(1+1/e)$-matching UGC lower bound conjectured tight, and ties of size $\le L$ admit $(3L-2)/(2L-1)$ (Koenemann-Pashkovich-Tofigzade, SAGT 2020). New ideas are most needed on the unconditional hardness side.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: For the algorithmic side (only promising for restricted variants, given SSEH-tightness of the general case): factor-revealing LPs over the structure of alternating paths between the algorithm's output and OPT; LP rounding of Rothblum-type stable-matching polytopes with tie-aware constraints; local-search algorithms whose ratio is certified by charging arguments. For the hardness side: new gadget reductions from vertex cover / minimum maximal matching aiming to lift the unconditional bound above $33/29$ or to derive $3/2-\varepsilon$ hardness from vanilla UGC rather than SSEH/strong-UGC. Exhaustive small-instance search is useful only to falsify proposed algorithms (find instances where a candidate algorithm's stable output is smaller than $\mathrm{OPT}/(3/2-\varepsilon)$).
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed $(3/2-\varepsilon)$-approximation must (i) always output a WEAKLY STABLE matching — check the stability definition used, since strong/super stability variants are polynomial and confusing them is a classic failure mode; (ii) prove the cardinality guarantee against the true maximum stable matching via a worst-case argument (numerics/experiments do not suffice); and (iii) run in polynomial time. Referees should be alert that such a result refutes the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis and strong UGC — an extraordinary consequence demanding extraordinary scrutiny; any paper claiming a general ratio below 3/2 (e.g., rumored '1.4986'-type claims) should be checked against the Dudycz-Lewandowski-Marcinkowski reduction and tested on minimum-maximal-matching-derived instances. A claimed hardness improvement must specify the exact complexity assumption and the reduction's completeness/soundness parameters.

Importantly, the batch record UNDERSOLD the hardness side: Dudycz-Lewandowski-Marcinkowski (IPCO 2019, arXiv:1811.08506, verified) implies no (3/2−ε)-approximation under the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis or strong UGC, so 3/2 is CONDITIONALLY TIGHT — this both explains the 17-year stall and makes any sub-3/2 claim tantamount to refuting SSEH. I added this to known_results/full_statement (the batch's '4/3 ≤ α* ≤ 3/2 under UGC' framing is still correct for vanilla UGC). title: Minimum subsidy for envy-freeness with monotone valuations
short_statement: For monotone valuations with item marginals at most one, determine the minimum subsidy needed to guarantee an envy-free allocation.
full_statement: There are $n$ agents and a finite set $M$ of indivisible goods. Each agent $i$ has a monotone valuation $v_i:2^M\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$ with bounded marginal increments: $v_i(S\cup\{g\})-v_i(S)\le 1$ for all $S\subseteq M$ and goods $g\notin S$. An allocation $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ partitions $M$. A subsidy vector $p\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n$ makes the allocation envy-free if $$v_i(X_i)+p_i\ge v_i(X_j)+p_j\quad\text{for all agents }i,j.$$ Let $S_{\mathcal V}(n)$ be the smallest number such that every instance in valuation class $\mathcal V$ admits some allocation and subsidies with $\sum_i p_i\le S_{\mathcal V}(n)$. The additive case has the tight value $S_{\mathrm{add}}(n)=n-1$. The open problem is to determine $S_{\mathrm{mon}}(n)$ for arbitrary monotone valuations with unit marginals: does the $n-1$ total-subsidy bound still suffice, or can complementarities/substitutabilities force asymptotically larger total or per-agent subsidies?
known_results: Halpern and Shah showed that subsidies can guarantee envy-freeness and conjectured a sharp $n-1$ total bound for additive valuations with unit marginal upper bounds. Brustle, Dippel, Narayan, Suzuki, and Vetta proved this additive conjecture: a total subsidy of $n-1$ suffices, equivalently at most one dollar per agent after normalizing one subsidy to zero, and this is tight. They also proved that for general monotone valuations an envy-free allocation always exists with subsidy at most $2(n-1)$ per agent, hence total subsidy $O(n^2)$ independent of the number of goods. Binary, identical, and other structured valuation classes admit stronger bounds in related work. The open gap is whether general monotone valuations require more than the additive $n-1$ total subsidy, and if so what the correct dependence on $n$ is.

where_posed.text: The monotone-valuations gap follows from Brustle et al., 'One Dollar Each Eliminates Envy', EC 2020.

background: Indivisible goods often do not admit envy-free allocations, but cash transfers can compensate agents and restore envy-freeness. The subsidy question asks how much money is always sufficient. This is a clean hybrid of fair division and quasi-linear utility: allocate indivisible goods, then add nonnegative payments so every agent prefers its own bundle plus payment. For additive valuations with each item worth at most one dollar marginally, Brustle, Dippel, Narayan, Suzuki, and Vetta proved the striking tight result that total subsidy $n-1$ suffices. For general monotone valuations with bounded marginals, envy can still be eliminated with bounded subsidy independent of the number of items, but the best known bounds are much larger. The main open question is whether the additive one-dollar-each phenomenon extends to monotone valuations.

progress.summary: The additive case is tight at total subsidy $n-1$. General monotone valuations have bounded subsidies independent of item count, but the optimal dependence on $n$ is open.

links.title: One Dollar Each Eliminates Envy

counterexample_rationale: A lower-bound improvement could be a finite valuation profile. Search over monotone set functions for small $n,m$ may reveal whether additive-style subsidies fail.
alphaevolve_rationale: Finite monotone valuations can be represented explicitly for small instances, and subsidy minimization can be solved by linear programming once an allocation is fixed.

literature.synthesis: The subsidy approach changes indivisible fair division from an impossibility-heavy setting into a quantitative compensation problem. Halpern and Shah initiated the systematic study and gave broad guarantees. Brustle et al. resolved the additive conjecture with an elegant tight $n-1$ total subsidy bound, showing that the necessary money can be very small and independent of the number of goods. Their monotone result shows boundedness survives without additivity, but the proof loses much more in $n$. The open issue is whether complementarity/substitutability inside monotone valuations truly forces larger payments or merely defeats current allocation methods.

A claimed upper bound must construct, or prove existence of, an allocation and nonnegative subsidies for arbitrary monotone valuations under the unit-marginal condition, with total subsidy measured after the usual normalization that at least one agent receives zero. Algorithmic claims should also state the valuation oracle model.

title: Optimal policy structure for lost-sales inventory with positive lead time
short_statement: For periodic-review lost-sales inventory with positive deterministic lead time, characterize the exact optimal policy. Uniform approximation results are available, including a 2026 capped-base-stock bound, but do not give an exact policy.
full_statement: Consider periodic-review lost-sales inventory with i.i.d. nonnegative demands $D_t$, $0<\mathbb E D_t<\infty$, deterministic lead time $L\ge1$, and holding/lost-sales costs $h,p>0$. Before arrivals in period $t$, the state is on-hand stock $I_t$ and pipeline $(x_{1,t},\ldots,x_{L,t})$. Receive $x_{1,t}$, choose a nonnegative order $q_t$ without seeing $D_t$, then meet demand up to available stock. Set $I_{t+1}=(I_t+x_{1,t}-D_t)^+$, shift $x_{i,t+1}=x_{i+1,t}$ for $i<L$, and set $x_{L,t+1}=q_t$. Start empty and minimize $$C(\pi)=\limsup_{T\to\infty}T^{-1}\mathbb E^\pi\sum_{t=1}^T[hI_{t+1}+p(D_t-I_t-x_{1,t})^+],\quad\mathrm{OPT}=\inf_\pi C(\pi).$$ The exact finite-lead-time policy structure is the target. Base-stock and constant-order policies are not generally exactly optimal. Uniform approximation is not wholly open: Xin's July 2026 preprint proves $\inf_{\pi\in\mathrm{CBS}}C(\pi)\le[1+4L^2/((L+1)(3L-1))]\mathrm{OPT}\le(7/3)\mathrm{OPT}$ for capped base-stock policies, including ordinary base stock as the infinite-cap case. Seek sharper bounds or exact structure beyond these guarantees.
known_results: The optimal policy can in principle be computed by dynamic programming on the $L$-dimensional pipeline state but is intractable for moderate $L$, and its structure is uncharacterized: Karlin and Scarf (1958) showed base-stock is already suboptimal at $L=1$, and Zipkin (Operations Research 2008) proved via $L^{\natural}$-convexity that the optimal policy is monotone with bounded sensitivity in the pipeline vector but neither base-stock nor constant-order is generally optimal. Asymptotic regimes are well understood: (i) order-up-to/base-stock policies are asymptotically optimal as the lost-sales penalty $p\to\infty$ (Huh, Janakiraman, Muckstadt, Rusmevichientong, Management Science 2009); (ii) the constant-order policy is asymptotically optimal as $L\to\infty$ (Goldberg, Katz-Rogozhnikov, Lu, Sharma, Squillante, Mathematics of OR 2016), with optimality gap decaying exponentially in $L$ (Xin and Goldberg, Operations Research 2016). Capped base-stock policies (a base-stock rule with an order cap) interpolate between the two extremes: Xin (Operations Research 2021) showed they converge exponentially fast in the base-stock level to constant-order policies and perform robustly, and Xin (Operations Research 2022) proved an asymptotic worst-case guarantee for a continuous-review lost-sales model — a capped base-stock policy has asymptotic ratio at most 1.79 for the continuous-review model with Poisson demand (via an asymptotic analysis jointly in large penalty and lead time). Projected-inventory-level (PIL) policies are asymptotically optimal in BOTH classical regimes: as $p\to\infty$ for general demand, and as $L\to\infty$ for exponential demand (van Jaarsveld and Arts, Operations Research 2024); Moradi, Arts, and Drent (arXiv:2504.10132, April 2025) extended large-$L$ asymptotic optimality of PIL to any demand with finite second moment provided the penalty is sufficiently large, via a Wiener-Hopf/ladder-process solution of the constant-order relative value function. On the learning side, Zhang, Chao, and Shi (Management Science 2020) gave a $O(\sqrt{T})$-regret algorithm against the best base-stock policy under censored demand, and Lyu, Zhang, and Xin (Operations Research 2024) gave UCB-type algorithms with Kaplan-Meier estimation that learn the best capped base-stock policy with regret whose lead-time dependence is linear rather than exponential. Xin's 'Capped Base-Stock Policies: A 2.33-Approximation' (July 2026 preprint), Section 2 and Theorem 1, gives the nonasymptotic periodic-review bound stated above for all positive finite-mean i.i.d. demand, all $L\ge1$, and $h,p>0$. It does not improve the earlier factor 2 for the different dual-balancing policy class. Separately, Hu (arXiv:2610.34576v1, October 2026), Theorem 4.1, claims a uniform $\sqrt2$ base-stock bound without setup costs and $(\sqrt2+\sqrt6)/2<1.932$ for an $(r,Q)$-or-no-order policy with setup costs, but only in continuous review with unit Poisson demand. Neither is an exact optimal-policy characterization.

where_posed.text: The model originates with Karlin and Scarf (1958); the modern structural framing and negative results are in Zipkin, 'On the Structure of Lost-Sales Inventory Models', Operations Research 56(4):937-944, 2008, which proves the optimal policy is neither base-stock nor constant-order. The problem is presented as the flagship open line in Goldberg, Reiman, and Wang, 'A Survey of Recent Progress in the Asymptotic Analysis of Inventory Systems', Production and Operations Management 30(6):1718-1750, 2021.

background: Periodic-review inventory theory with backlogged demand is one of the great success stories of operations research: for the backlog model the $L$-dimensional pipeline of outstanding orders collapses to the scalar inventory position, the dynamic program is convex, and a simple base-stock (order-up-to) policy is exactly optimal. Karlin and Scarf, in their foundational 1958 work, already observed that the seemingly innocuous change from backlogging to lost sales — unmet demand simply vanishes, as in brick-and-mortar and online retail, perishables, and spare parts, where customers walk or switch to a competitor — destroys this entire structure: even for lead time $L=1$ the optimal order is not a function of the inventory position alone, so base-stock optimality fails in general. Morton (1969) derived bounds relating the optimal policy to the backlog solution, but the exact dynamic program lives on the full $L$-dimensional pipeline vector and is intractable beyond very small lead times. Zipkin's influential 2008 papers revived the problem: using $L^{\natural}$-convexity he established monotonicity and bounded-sensitivity properties of the optimal order quantity, showed that neither base-stock nor constant-order is generally optimal, and showed numerically that base-stock policies can perform badly when the lead time is long and the penalty moderate. The problem then became the launching pad for the modern "asymptotic analysis of inventory systems" program surveyed by Goldberg, Reiman, and Wang (2021): if the exact optimum cannot be computed or described, prove that simple, interpretable policies are near-optimal in limiting regimes (large penalty, large lead time), and quantify the rate. Beyond its intrinsic role as perhaps the oldest unsolved structural question in inventory theory, the model is now a canonical benchmark for approximation guarantees in MDPs with high-dimensional states, for online learning with censored demand, and for deep-reinforcement-learning methods in operations, so any genuine structural characterization would reverberate well beyond inventory theory.

progress.summary: The 2026 periodic-review CBS guarantee removes the alleged absence of uniform nonasymptotic bounds for that class. Exact policy characterization and sharper worst-case factors remain separate targets; continuous-review improvements require different assumptions.

counterexample_rationale: The headline question asks for a positive structural characterization, which no single finite object can settle; the useful negative results (base-stock and constant-order are not optimal) are already known via small computed instances. Finite search can only refute candidate characterizations — e.g., exactly solving a small-$L$ discrete-demand DP to show that PIL or capped base-stock policies are not exactly optimal — which is genuine but secondary progress.
alphaevolve_rationale: An evolutionary loop over interpretable policy programs (functions of the pipeline vector) with fitness from simulation or exact small-$L$ value iteration could plausibly rediscover or beat PIL/capped-base-stock heuristics and suggest new conjecturable policy structures — exactly how PIL itself emerged from human insight plus numerics. However, the open problem as posed demands proofs (characterization or uniform gap bounds), which search alone cannot supply, and existing heuristics are already within a percent of optimal on benchmark instances, leaving little numeric headroom.

literature.synthesis: Three kinds of progress must be kept separate: structural properties of exact optima, asymptotic optimality in limiting regimes, and uniform approximation factors. The existing base-stock, constant-order and projected-inventory analyses remain relevant, but the statement that nothing is known at finite parameters is false. The new CBS theorem directly addresses the periodic-review model. Continuous-review Poisson guarantees are related results, not substitutes for it; nor does a guarantee for the best policy within a restricted class characterize the unrestricted optimum.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Plausible routes: (1) extend the Wiener-Hopf/ladder-process solution of relative value functions (Moradi-Arts-Drent 2025) from the constant-order policy to richer policy classes, aiming at sharper bounds beyond the existing CBS guarantee or new PIL bounds at finite $L$; (2) exploit $L^{\natural}$-convexity (Zipkin 2008) more aggressively to pin down the optimal policy on low-dimensional slices, combined with exact value iteration for discrete demand at $L=2,3,4$ to conjecture and then prove structural invariants; (3) LP/duality or information-relaxation lower bounds to certify small optimality gaps for candidate simple policies uniformly over parameters; (4) coupling arguments interpolating between the two proven asymptotic regimes.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed characterization must specify the policy class precisely and prove optimality (or an explicit gap bound) for the stated demand class and cost parameters under the long-run average criterion — check that the average-cost optimality equation or a vanishing-discount argument is handled rigorously, a classic failure point on unbounded state spaces. Numerical claims of exact optimality for a policy class can be refuted (but not confirmed) by exact value iteration on small discrete-demand instances ($L\le 4$, truncated support) with rigorous span-based error bounds; watch for discretization artifacts with continuous demand. Common failure modes: silently assuming backlog-style state collapse to inventory position, confusing asymptotic optimality with exact optimality, and heuristics validated only on the standard (geometric/Poisson demand) benchmark grid. Compare any claimed CBS improvement with Xin's 2026 theorem and keep periodic/continuous review assumptions separate.

title: Optimal policy structure for dual-sourcing inventory (fast/slow sources)
short_statement: A firm replenishes a single product from a cheap slow source and an expensive fast source under stochastic demand and full backlogging. When the lead-time gap is at least 2, the optimal ordering policy's structure is unknown and believed intractable; whether any simple policy (Tailored Base-Surge, dual-index, single-index) is optimal is open.
full_statement: A single item is reviewed each period over an infinite horizon (discounted or long-run average cost) with i.i.d. demands $D_t$. Two sources are available: a regular source with per-unit cost $c_r$ and deterministic lead time $L_r$, and an expedited source with cost $c_e > c_r$ and lead time $L_e$, where $L_r > L_e \ge 0$. In period $t$ the firm chooses order quantities $q^r_t, q^e_t \ge 0$; unmet demand is fully backlogged with holding cost $h$ and backorder penalty $b$. The state must encode both outstanding-order pipelines, of dimension $\sim (L_r - L_e)$, giving a high-dimensional MDP. A Tailored Base-Surge (TBS) policy fixes a constant regular order $q^r_t \equiv r$ and uses an order-up-to rule $q^e_t = (S - \widehat{IP}_t)^+$ at the expedited source, where $\widehat{IP}_t$ is the expedited inventory position. $$\textbf{Open:}\quad \text{characterize an optimal policy when the lead-time gap } L_r - L_e \ge 2.$$ For $L_r - L_e = 1$ the optimal expedited decision is a base-stock rule, but for $L_r - L_e \ge 2$ the optimal policy has no known simple structure and is conjectured intractable. What remains open: the exact structure of $\pi^\star$ for gap $\ge 2$; whether TBS, dual-index, or single-index policies are exactly optimal in any nontrivial case; and non-asymptotic guarantees for moderate $L_r - L_e$. Only an asymptotic result is known: TBS is asymptotically optimal as the regular lead time $L_r \to \infty$ with $L_e$ fixed.
known_results: For lead-time gap one, the state and dynamic program simplify enough to yield tractable structural results. For larger gaps, dual-index policies and Tailored Base-Surge policies have strong numerical performance. Xin and Goldberg prove that a simple Tailored Base-Surge policy is asymptotically optimal as the regular-source lead time tends to infinity with the express-source lead time fixed, giving a theoretical foundation for the heuristic in the regime where the dynamic program is most intractable. The exact optimal policy for fixed finite lead-time gaps at least two remains unknown. Later survey and inventory-asymptotics work clarifies why large-lead-time asymptotic optimality does not automatically provide a usable exact policy for moderate lead times.

where_posed.text: The long-standing finite-gap structural problem is discussed in the dual-sourcing inventory literature; Xin and Goldberg identify the model as having resisted exact solution for more than forty years while resolving the large-regular-lead-time TBS asymptotic question.

background: Dual sourcing is a classic supply-chain model where a firm can replenish from a slow cheap supplier and a fast expensive supplier. The model is simple to state but hard because orders placed today arrive after different deterministic lead times, so the state includes a multi-period pipeline from each supplier. When the lead-time difference is one, the dynamic program has much more tractable structure. When the gap is two or more periods, the exact optimal policy has resisted a clean characterization for decades. This makes the problem a good fit for ORdős Problems: the modelling choices are already settled, the objective is a standard infinite-horizon inventory cost, and there are strong heuristic and asymptotic policies. Xin and Goldberg gave theoretical support for Tailored Base-Surge policies by proving asymptotic optimality when the regular-source lead time grows while the express-source lead time is fixed. That result resolves an important large-lead-time question, but it does not characterize the exact finite-lead-time optimal policy. The remaining open problem is structural: describe the optimal policy, or prove sharp non-asymptotic guarantees for a simple policy class, when the two lead times differ by at least two.

progress.summary: Tailored Base-Surge is now known to be asymptotically optimal in a large-lead-time regime, but no exact finite-gap optimal-policy characterization is known for lead-time differences at least two.

counterexample_rationale: Small finite lead-time and finite-demand-support instances can refute conjectured threshold or index structures through dynamic programming. A full characterization must handle an unbounded inventory/pipeline state.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can map optimal actions in truncated dynamic programs, infer switching surfaces, and locate counterexamples to proposed structures. It is less suited to proving asymptotic or infinite-state optimality without analytic support.

literature.synthesis: Dual-sourcing inventory has a clean economic interpretation and an unusually difficult state space. Earlier work proposed dual-index and Tailored Base-Surge policies and demonstrated strong computational performance. Xin and Goldberg supplied the major theoretical advance by proving TBS asymptotically optimal as the regular lead time grows. Their result supports the intuition that a constant slow-source base flow plus a fast-source order-up-to correction becomes nearly optimal when the slow pipeline is long. The open finite-gap problem remains because optimality for $L_r \to \infty$ does not tell us the exact Bellman structure for fixed $L_r-L_e \ge 2$, where pipeline imbalances and expediting decisions interact. A successful solution would likely identify monotonicity, convexity, or low-dimensional sufficient statistics for the dynamic program, or else show that no simple threshold/index form can be exact.

title: Optimal policy for one-warehouse multi-retailer (distribution) inventory systems
short_statement: A single warehouse ships, with positive lead times, to several retailers each facing independent random demand. The optimal replenishment-and-allocation policy is unknown: echelon base-stock is optimal only under the artificial balance assumption (which permits negative allocations); without it, the true optimal structure is open.
full_statement: Consider a periodic-review, one-warehouse $N$-retailer distribution (divergent) system over an infinite horizon. Retailer $i$ faces i.i.d. demand $D_i$ per period, with deterministic lead times $L_0$ (supplier$\to$warehouse) and $L_i$ (warehouse$\to$retailer $i$). Unit holding costs $h_0 \ge 0$ at the warehouse and $h_i$ at retailer $i$, and unit backorder penalty $p_i$ at retailer $i$, are charged per period. Each period the warehouse orders $q_0 \ge 0$ and then allocates on-hand stock $y_0$ among retailers as shipments $q_i \ge 0$ subject to $\sum_{i=1}^N q_i \le y_0$ (no lateral transshipment, no return). Holding and backorder costs accrue at the retailers and holding cost at the warehouse. The objective is $\min \limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\,\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{t=1}^{T}(h_0 (y_0^t)^+ + \sum_{i=1}^N (h_i I_i^t + p_i B_i^t))\big]$ over admissible policies. Clark and Scarf (1960) proved echelon base-stock policies optimal for SERIAL systems, but here the difficulty is the allocation/imbalance problem: once stock is shipped down it cannot be moved sideways, so the warehouse cannot always achieve desired echelon positions. \textbf{Open:} Characterize the structure of an optimal policy, or prove none of a simple form exists. If the constraint $\sum_i q_i \le y_0$ is RELAXED to allow $q_i \in \mathbb{R}$ (the balance/allocation assumption), the problem decomposes and an echelon base-stock policy is optimal; under the true constraint $q_i \ge 0$, echelon base-stock is provably suboptimal and the optimal policy is unknown. Is there a polynomial-time-computable or closed-form characterization of the optimal (or a provably near-optimal, with explicit small constant) replenishment-and-allocation policy?
known_results: Structure under relaxation: echelon base-stock (order-up-to) policies are optimal for divergent systems ONLY under the balance assumption, which permits negative allocations to retailers (Eppen–Schrage 1981; Federgruen–Zipkin 1984; Diks–de Kok, EJOR 1998, for general $n$-echelon divergent networks). Under the true constraint $q_i \ge 0$ the problem does not decompose, echelon base-stock is suboptimal, and no well-structured optimal policy is known — de Kok, Grob, Laumanns, Minner, Rambau, Schade (EJOR 2018) state flatly that 'so far, it has been impossible to identify well-structured optimal policies for n-echelon divergent systems without this assumption,' and a mid-2026 check finds no paper overturning this. Asymptotic/approximation progress for the STOCHASTIC problem: Miao, Jasin, Chao (Operations Research 70(1):141–159, 2022) give Lagrangian-relaxation-based policies for one-warehouse (and multi-warehouse) multi-store systems with lost sales whose loss relative to optimal is sublinear in both the horizon $T$ and the number of stores $N$ — asymptotic optimality as the system grows, but no fixed-instance constant-factor guarantee, and for the lost-sales rather than backlog objective. Najy, Diabat, Elbassioni (Operations Research 73(3):1151–1164, 2025) give an FPTAS for the continuous relaxation of the stochastic OWMR under the $(S,T)$/power-of-two policy class (building on Chu–Shen's 2010 approximate cost model) with an improved rounding factor to power-of-two solutions — approximation within a restricted policy class of an approximate model, not the true optimum. For the DETERMINISTIC lot-sizing OWMR, the best general constant remains the 1.8-approximation of Levi, Roundy, Shmoys, Sviridenko (Management Science 54(4):763–776, 2008; incorporating the Levi–Sviridenko APPROX 2006 improvement); the JRP special case has a 1.791-approximation (Bienkowski, Byrka, Chrobak, Jeż, Nogneng, Sgall, SODA 2014), and Segev (Mathematics of Operations Research, 2025; arXiv:2408.05443) recently gave the first improvement over power-of-two-type guarantees for continuous-time joint replenishment. As of July 2026, neither an optimal-policy characterization nor a constant-factor approximation for the stochastic divergent system with the no-negative-shipment constraint is known.

where_posed.text: The serial foundation is Clark & Scarf, 'Optimal Policies for a Multi-Echelon Inventory Problem,' Management Science 6(4):475–490, 1960; the divergent-system obstruction is developed in Eppen–Schrage (1981), Zipkin (Math. OR 1984) and Federgruen–Zipkin (NRL 1984). The open problem is stated explicitly in the survey of de Kok, Grob, Laumanns, Minner, Rambau, Schade, 'A typology and literature review on stochastic multi-echelon inventory models,' European Journal of Operational Research 269(3):955–983, 2018.
where_posed.quote: However, this can only be shown under the assumption that negative shipment quantities to downstream stockpoints are allowed. This assumption was first proposed by Eppen and Schrage (1981). The implication is that echelon inventory positions after allocation can be lower than before the allocation, i.e., the option of free transshipments. As a consequence, the classical inventory balance equations for individual items may no longer hold. So far, it has been impossible to identify well-structured optimal policies for n-echelon divergent systems without this assumption.

background: Multi-echelon inventory theory began with Clark and Scarf's 1960 proof that for SERIAL supply chains — a single chain of stages, each feeding the next — the optimal policy has a beautifully simple structure: each stage follows an echelon base-stock policy, ordering up to a fixed target measured in echelon inventory position. The natural next topology, and by far the most common in practice, is the divergent (distribution) system: one warehouse replenishes from an outside supplier and ships to $N$ retailers, each facing its own random demand. Here the Clark–Scarf decomposition breaks. The culprit is the allocation problem: once stock is shipped to a retailer it cannot be moved sideways to a sister retailer, so when demands realize unevenly the system becomes imbalanced — one retailer is overstocked while another is starved — and the warehouse cannot simultaneously bring all echelon inventory positions to their desired levels. Eppen and Schrage (1981) and then Federgruen and Zipkin (1984) showed that if one relaxes the model to permit negative shipments (the so-called balance or allocation assumption, effectively free lateral transshipment), the problem decomposes and echelon base-stock policies become optimal; Diks and de Kok (1998) extended this to general $n$-echelon divergent networks. But the relaxation is a fiction, and Zipkin (1984) analyzed exactly how inventory imbalance degrades these approximations. Without the balance assumption, echelon base-stock policies are provably suboptimal, the dynamic program does not decompose, and after six decades no well-structured optimal policy is known — a gap flagged as a central open issue in every major survey of the field. The problem matters enormously in practice: essentially every retail and spare-parts distribution network is divergent, and the industry runs on heuristics (allocation rules like fair-share rationing, projected-inventory policies, Lagrangian decompositions) whose optimality gaps are typically assessed only numerically. A structural characterization, or a simple policy with a provable small constant-factor guarantee for the stochastic backlog objective, would close one of the oldest open questions in inventory theory.

progress.summary: No structural breakthrough as of July 2026: the optimal policy for divergent systems without the balance assumption remains uncharacterized. Recent progress is asymptotic and computational rather than structural: Miao–Jasin–Chao (Operations Research 2022) proved Lagrangian-relaxation policies asymptotically optimal (loss sublinear in horizon and number of stores) for one-/multi-warehouse multi-store systems with lost sales, and Najy–Diabat–Elbassioni (Operations Research 2025) gave an FPTAS-based method computing near-optimal power-of-two $(S,T)$ policies for an approximate stochastic OWMR model. On the deterministic side the 1.8-approximation of Levi–Roundy–Shmoys–Sviridenko (2008) is still the best general constant for OWMR; Segev (Math. OR 2025) improved continuous-time joint replenishment guarantees beyond power-of-two policies, suggesting the OWMR constant may also be improvable.

counterexample_rationale: The question asks for a positive structural characterization or a policy with a provable guarantee; the negative side is already settled (echelon base-stock is known to be suboptimal without the balance assumption, and imbalance examples are classical since Zipkin 1984), so no finite counterexample can resolve what remains open.
alphaevolve_rationale: An evolutionary search loop could plausibly discover interpretable replenishment-and-allocation policy templates (parametrized allocation rules, projected-inventory or Lagrangian-index policies) and score them against exact DP values on small instances (2–3 retailers, short lead times, discretized demand), potentially revealing structure worth proving; on the deterministic OWMR side, searching over LP-rounding parameters and shifted power-of-two schedules to beat the 1.8 constant is a concrete, factor-revealing-style target well-suited to automated search.

literature.synthesis: Work on divergent systems splits into three strands. (1) Structure under relaxation: Eppen–Schrage (1981) and Federgruen–Zipkin (1984) showed the balance assumption (allowing negative allocations) restores the Clark–Scarf decomposition, making echelon base-stock policies optimal; Diks–de Kok (1998) generalized this to $n$-echelon divergent networks, and Zipkin (1984) quantified how real imbalance erodes these approximations. This line has been essentially frozen since the 1990s: the de Kok et al. (2018) survey records that no well-structured optimal policy is known without the assumption. (2) Asymptotics for the true stochastic system: Miao–Jasin–Chao (OR 2022) is the state of the art, proving Lagrangian-relaxation policies for one-/multi-warehouse multi-store lost-sales systems have optimality loss sublinear in both the horizon and the number of stores — the first rigorous performance guarantee for the unrelaxed allocation dynamics, but asymptotic rather than uniform, and for lost sales rather than backlogging. (3) Approximation algorithms for the deterministic lot-sizing OWMR: Levi–Roundy–Shmoys–Sviridenko (MS 2008) hold the best general constant at 1.8 via LP rounding; JRP stands at 1.791 (Bienkowski et al., SODA 2014); and Segev (Math. OR 2025) broke the long-standing power-of-two barrier for continuous-time JRP, with Najy–Diabat–Elbassioni (OR 2025) contributing an FPTAS for computing power-of-two $(S,T)$ policies in an approximate stochastic OWMR model. The remaining gap is stark: nothing connects strands (2)–(3) to a fixed-instance constant-factor guarantee — let alone a structural optimality result — for the stochastic backlog divergent system with the no-lateral-transshipment constraint. New ideas seem needed either in coupling/cost-accounting arguments that tame imbalance directly, or in identifying a richer but still tractable policy class (state-dependent allocation indices) provably close to the DP optimum.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Plausible routes: (1) coupling/cost-accounting arguments in the style of recent asymptotic-optimality proofs (Lagrangian decomposition with per-retailer subproblems, then bounding the imbalance cost of reconciling the relaxed allocation with $q_i\ge 0$) aimed at a uniform constant-factor guarantee for the backlog objective; (2) restricted-policy-class optimization — prove that some tractable class (state-dependent allocation indices, projected-inventory-level rules, or balanced base-stock with rationing) is within a provable factor of the DP optimum, perhaps via an LP/factor-revealing analysis; (3) exact DP computation on tiny systems (2 retailers, lead times 0–2, discrete demand) to conjecture structural properties (monotonicity, weak decomposition) of the true optimal policy; (4) for the deterministic OWMR, LP-rounding parameter search to push below 1.8.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A structural claim must specify the policy class exactly and prove optimality against ALL admissible policies of the full-information DP with the non-negative-shipment constraint — the classic failure mode is silently reintroducing the balance assumption (negative allocations, free transshipment, or 'virtual' reallocation) somewhere in the induction; a referee should check every allocation step respects $q_i \ge 0$ and $\sum_i q_i \le y_0$. A constant-factor claim must state the benchmark (optimal DP cost, not a relaxation) and hold per instance, not asymptotically; verify that lower bounds used (e.g., Lagrangian or balance-relaxed cost) are proved to be valid bounds on the true optimum. Numerical DP comparisons on small instances can falsify structural conjectures but cannot substitute for proof; asymptotic results (regime $N\to\infty$ or $T\to\infty$) should not be reported as resolving the constant-factor question.

title: Tractable optimal control of assembly systems from arbitrary (imbalanced) initial inventory
short_statement: For stochastic assembly systems, the optimal balanced base-stock structure is known under broad conditions; can the time-varying levels be computed explicitly, and does comparable structure survive fixed ordering costs?
full_statement: Consider an assembly system in which $M$ components are procured with deterministic lead times, one unit of each component is required to assemble one finished product, demand for the finished product is stochastic over time, holding costs are linear at component or echelon levels, and unmet finished-good demand is backlogged or penalized. In the no-fixed-ordering-cost model, decisions are replenishment quantities for each component at each review epoch, subject to lead times and assembly balance. Rosling's serial reduction and Chen-Muharremoglu's extension imply that the optimal policy is a balanced echelon base-stock policy, possibly with base-stock levels that evolve dynamically from arbitrary imbalanced initial states. The open question is to give a closed-form or polynomial-time characterization of these dynamic levels without solving the full high-dimensional dynamic program, and to determine whether an analogous tractable optimal-policy structure exists when component orders incur fixed costs $K_j>0$ or when the assembly network is generalized beyond the in-tree case.
known_results: Clark and Scarf introduced the echelon-stock dynamic-programming structure for serial multi-echelon systems. Rosling proved that, under a long-run balance condition, an assembly system can be remodeled as an equivalent serial system and simple reorder policies are optimal. Chen and Muharremoglu completed the no-fixed-cost structural characterization for arbitrary initial states, showing that the optimal policy remains balanced echelon base-stock with dynamically evolving levels. Thus the broad qualitative structure for the classical in-tree no-fixed-cost model is no longer open. The unresolved part is the explicit computation or closed-form description of the evolving levels and the fixed-ordering-cost extension, where inventory control typically moves toward $(s,S)$-type regions and balanced base-stock optimality is not established.

where_posed.text: Residual gap following Rosling's assembly-system reduction and Chen-Muharremoglu's completion of the arbitrary-initial-state case.

background: Multi-echelon inventory theory asks how to coordinate replenishment across components, subassemblies, and finished goods when demand is random and lead times are positive. Assembly systems are especially difficult because one missing component can block a finished unit even when other components are abundant. Rosling's classic 1989 paper showed that, under a long-run-balance condition on the initial state, a stochastic assembly system can be transformed into an equivalent serial system, leading to optimal balanced echelon base-stock policies. Chen and Muharremoglu later removed the restrictive initial-condition assumption: from any starting state, the optimal policy remains a balanced echelon base-stock policy, but the base-stock levels evolve dynamically with time and state. This means the qualitative structural question is mostly solved. The remaining research-level gap is more computational and explicit: can the dynamic levels be characterized in a form that is usable without solving a large dynamic program, and what happens once fixed ordering costs or more general assembly topologies destroy the clean serial reduction?

progress.summary: The qualitative optimal-policy structure for the no-fixed-cost in-tree model is largely known. The remaining open part is narrower: efficient explicit computation from arbitrary initial states and fixed-cost/general-topology structure.

counterexample_rationale: Small assembly networks with fixed ordering costs could refute natural base-stock or $(s,S)$-type conjectures. The closed-form computation question itself is unlikely to be settled by one finite counterexample.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search over small dynamic programs can identify patterns in the evolving base-stock levels and fixed-cost policy regions. Any discovered structure would need exact proof through dynamic-programming convexity or lattice arguments.

literature.synthesis: The important correction for this record is that the main Rosling initial-imbalance issue has already been structurally resolved. Rosling established the serial-system equivalence under long-run balance and thereby reduced an assembly inventory problem to a tractable echelon base-stock policy. Chen and Muharremoglu showed that arbitrary starting states do not destroy balanced base-stock optimality, but they introduce time-varying levels. The open gap is therefore not whether a balanced policy exists in the no-fixed-cost model; it is whether the dynamic levels admit a parsimonious formula or polynomial-time description and whether similar structure survives fixed costs, where inventory control usually shifts from base-stock to $(s,S)$-type policies and coupling across components becomes more delicate.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Work from small component counts and exact dynamic programs, looking for monotone/lattice structure in the moving thresholds. For the fixed-cost case, test whether $K$-convexity or multimodularity survives the assembly coupling.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A valid solution must distinguish the already-solved no-fixed-cost structural theorem from the remaining computational or fixed-cost questions. A closed-form or polynomial-time characterization should state the input encoding, horizon or discounted/average-cost criterion, lead-time assumptions, demand model, and how the dynamic base-stock levels are computed. A fixed-cost theorem must specify whether fixed costs apply per component, per joint order, or per echelon and must prove the claimed policy structure globally, not only for two components or zero lead times. Finite examples should be checked by exact dynamic programming and should report lead times, costs, demand distributions, and boundary/truncation error if the state space is truncated.

open_problem: Develop an explicit, efficiently computable characterization of the time-varying balanced echelon base-stock levels for arbitrary initial imbalance, and characterize the optimal policy when fixed ordering costs are added to the same stochastic assembly model.

title: Whittle index asymptotic optimality and the global attractor condition (Weber-Weiss)
short_statement: For average-reward restless bandits, characterize when Whittle-index or LP-priority policies are asymptotically optimal, and determine the minimal assumptions for $O(N^{-1/2})$, $O(N^{-1})$, or exponentially small optimality gaps.
full_statement:
Consider $N$ arms, each a two-action ($a\in\{0,1\}$) MDP with common kernels $P^0,P^1$ and rewards $R^0,R^1$ on a finite state space, under the hard constraint that exactly $\alpha N$ arms are activated each time, with the long-run average-reward criterion. Let $V^{\mathrm{opt}}(N)$ be the optimal value and $V^{\mathrm{rel}}(N)=Nho^{\mathrm{rel}}$ Whittle's relaxation value (the per-period constraint replaced by its time-average), which upper-bounds $V^{\mathrm{opt}}(N)$. A bandit is $\emph{indexable}$ if the set of states where the passive action is optimal in the $
u$-subsidized single-arm MDP is monotone non-decreasing in the subsidy $
u$; the Whittle index $
u_i$ is the smallest $
u$ making passive optimal in state $i$, and the Whittle Index Policy (WIP) activates the $\alpha N$ highest-index arms. Let $\mathbf m(t)\in\Delta^d$ be the empirical state distribution; under WIP it follows, as $N	o\infty$, a piecewise-affine mean-field drift $\dot{\mathbf m}=\phi(\mathbf m)$ with fixed point $\mathbf m^*$. $	extbf{Whittle's conjecture: }$ $V_{\mathrm{WIP}}(N)/N	oho^{\mathrm{rel}}$. $	extbf{Weber-Weiss (1990): }$ if the bandit is indexable and $\mathbf m^*$ is a $\emph{global attractor}$, then $V_{\mathrm{WIP}}(N)/N	oho^{\mathrm{rel}}$; and there exists an indexable instance whose ODE has a stable limit cycle (no global attractor) for which WIP is $\emph{not}$ asymptotically optimal. $	extbf{Open: }$ (a) a checkable characterization of when the global-attractor / Uniform Global Attractor Property holds; (b) the tight minimal-assumption characterization of when the gap is $O(\sqrt N)$ vs $O(1)$ vs $O(e^{-cN})$, and whether non-degeneracy/local stability are necessary for the exponential rate for index/priority-type policies.
known_results: Weber and Weiss proved asymptotic optimality of Whittle's index policy under indexability plus a global-attractor condition for the mean-field ODE, and gave an indexable counterexample where the ODE cycles and the policy is not asymptotically optimal. Verloop extended priority-policy asymptotic optimality under related global-attractor assumptions. Gast, Gaujal, and Yan proved exponential convergence for Whittle's index policy under uniform global attraction plus nondegeneracy, and later gave necessary and sufficient conditions for LP-priority policies, including an LP-index policy with $O(N^{-1/2})$ gap in broad models and exponential rates under stronger assumptions. Hong, Xie, Chen, and Wang introduced simulation-based policies that remove the uniform global-attractor condition for $O(N^{-1/2})$ asymptotic optimality, and a two-set policy with exponential gaps under aperiodic-unichain, nondegeneracy, and local stability. What remains open is the practical structural characterization: when does the original Whittle-index or simple priority rule itself have the desired rate, and which assumptions are genuinely necessary rather than artifacts of the current proofs?

background: Restless bandits are one of the canonical hard dynamic-allocation models in Operations Research: many Markovian projects evolve whether or not they are served, but only a fixed fraction can receive service at each time. Whittle's relaxation replaces the hard per-period resource constraint by a time-average constraint and decomposes the problem into single-arm subsidy problems. When the arms are indexable, this produces the Whittle index policy, a remarkably simple priority rule used in queueing, machine maintenance, healthcare screening, web crawling, and communication scheduling. The mathematical difficulty is that indexability only makes the heuristic well defined; it does not by itself explain why the many-arm constrained process should track the relaxed optimum. Weber and Weiss showed that a mean-field global-attractor condition is enough and also showed that the condition is not cosmetic: without it, an indexable system can cycle and Whittle's policy can be asymptotically suboptimal. The resulting open problem is not a modelling question. The model is fixed and classical. The unresolved part is a structural theorem: identify checkable conditions under which the index or priority policy is asymptotically optimal, and determine the exact assumptions needed for the different possible gap rates.

progress.summary: Recent work has substantially narrowed the issue: there are now non-index simulation-based policies with $O(N^{-1/2})$ gaps without UGAP, and exponential-gap policies under local stability assumptions. The original Whittle-index/global-attractor characterization is still incomplete because UGAP is hard to verify and not implied by indexability.

counterexample_rationale: Finite-state restless-bandit instances can be enumerated and their mean-field dynamics simulated, so counterexamples to overly strong conjectures are plausible search targets. A positive characterization, however, requires proof about all finite-state models satisfying structural conditions.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can help discover small indexable examples with cycles, degenerate fixed points, or surprising gap rates, which may guide conjectures. It is less likely to prove the general global-attractor or exponential-rate theorem directly.

literature.synthesis: The literature has moved from Whittle's heuristic to a fine-grained mean-field theory. Weber and Weiss established the first clean theorem: indexability plus global attraction of the fluid fixed point implies asymptotic optimality, while an indexable cyclic example rules out indexability alone. Verloop broadened the priority-policy view. Gast, Gaujal, and Yan then refined the rate story: under uniform global attraction and nondegeneracy, Whittle-type policies can have exponentially small gaps, while degeneracy changes the rate; their Mathematics of Operations Research work gives a more general LP-priority certificate. The 2023-2024 Hong-Xie-Chen-Wang line changes the algorithmic landscape by showing that non-index, simulation-based policies can avoid UGAP, first at $O(N^{-1/2})$ scale and then exponentially under local stability. The remaining gap is therefore sharp and well formed: Whittle-index policies are attractive precisely because they are simple, local, and interpretable, but the known sufficient assumptions are hard to verify and not known to be necessary.

title: Optimal policy for the Bayesian multi-armed bandit with switching costs
short_statement: Switching costs destroy the classical Gittins-index decomposition; characterize the exact optimal policy or a provably near-optimal tractable policy.
full_statement: There are $n$ independent Markov reward processes, one for each arm. At each time $t$, the decision maker chooses an arm $a_t$, receives the reward from that arm, and only the chosen arm's state evolves. Future rewards are discounted by $\beta\in(0,1)$. If $a_t\ne a_{t-1}$, the decision maker pays a switching cost $c_{a_{t-1},a_t}\ge0$, often specialized to a constant cost or an arm-dependent matrix. The objective is to maximize expected discounted reward net of switching costs. Without switching costs, the Gittins-index theorem gives an optimal policy that computes an index for each arm separately and plays the arm with the largest index. With positive switching costs, the current arm becomes part of the state, arms are coupled through future switching opportunities, and ordinary separability fails. The open problem is to characterize the exact optimal policy for general finite-state discounted arms, or to prove a uniform approximation guarantee for a tractable continuation/switching-index policy.
known_results: Banks and Sundaram showed that positive switching costs destroy ordinary Gittins-index optimality: no index depending only on each arm's own state can be optimal in general. Asawa and Teneketzis introduced a pair of indices, a continuation index and a switching index, that partially characterize optimal policies and can be computed by reducing to a doubled-state Gittins-index problem. Nino-Mora developed a faster decoupled computation method for the Asawa-Teneketzis indices and reported near-optimal performance across many randomly generated two- and three-project instances. Related restless-bandit index theory supplies computational tools, but it does not yield a general exact optimality theorem for switching-cost Bayesian bandits. The remaining gap is a structural theorem or a worst-case approximation guarantee.

where_posed.text: The open structural issue follows from Banks-Sundaram's impossibility of a Gittins-style index and Asawa-Teneketzis's partial-index characterization.

background: The classical discounted Bayesian multi-armed bandit is one of the cleanest success stories in dynamic allocation: Gittins indices reduce a high-dimensional dynamic program to independent single-arm calculations. Switching costs are a tiny modeling change with large structural consequences. If moving from one project, treatment, or machine setting to another incurs a cost, then the value of an arm depends not only on its own posterior state but also on which arm is currently active and how expensive it will be to return. Banks and Sundaram showed that a standard per-arm Gittins index is not generally optimal once switching is costly. Asawa and Teneketzis introduced continuation and switching indices that partially characterize decisions. Nino-Mora later gave much faster computation for those indices and found strong empirical near-optimality. What is still missing is a theorem that either fully describes the optimal policy or explains, with worst-case guarantees, why an index-like approximation is the right tractable substitute.

progress.summary: Partial indices and efficient computations exist, and they perform well computationally. The gap is an exact general structural theorem or a rigorous approximation guarantee.

counterexample_rationale: Small finite-state bandits can refute proposed index rules or structural conjectures. Exact value iteration can verify optimal actions for small examples.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can generate small bandit instances that separate candidate policies from the optimum, or discover regularities in optimal switching regions. These examples are machine-checkable by dynamic programming.

literature.synthesis: This problem is a clean case where a classical solved model becomes hard under a minimal operational friction. Gittins indices rely on separability: the value of working on one arm can be compared to a retirement option independently of other arms. Switching costs couple arms through the currently active project, so optimality regions depend on relative states and past action. Asawa and Teneketzis recover part of the lost structure through continuation and switching indices, and Nino-Mora improves the computational side enough to make large numerical studies feasible. The unresolved gap is whether those partial indices can be elevated into a complete theorem, or whether the best possible general result is approximation rather than exact optimality.

title: Fine-grained regret for bandits with switching costs
short_statement: The headline minimax rates are known; the remaining problem is a sharp instance-dependent and cost-geometry theory for stochastic and best-of-both-worlds bandits with switching costs.
full_statement: A learner chooses arms $a_t\in[K]$ over $t=1,\ldots,T$, observes only the chosen reward or loss, and incurs a switching cost when $a_t\ne a_{t-1}$ or, more generally, a cost $c(a_{t-1},a_t)$ determined by an arm-pair cost matrix or graph. Performance can be measured by regret that includes switching penalties, or by ordinary reward regret subject to a hard budget on total switching cost. For unit switching costs, adversarial minimax rates and stochastic switch-budget phase transitions are largely understood. The open problem is to determine the exact instance-dependent and structure-dependent regret in the remaining regimes: dependence on the gaps $\Delta_i$, on nonuniform cost matrices or metric/graph structure, on the number and placement of switches, and on simultaneous best-of-both-worlds guarantees that remain adversarially robust while adapting optimally to stochastic instances.
known_results: Dekel, Ding, Koren, and Peres proved adversarial unit-cost minimax regret $\widetilde{\Theta}(T^{2/3})$. Simchi-Levi and Xu characterized minimax regret for stochastic bandits under switching-budget constraints and identified phase transitions in the optimal rate; they also showed that general switching-cost structures lead to graph-traversal subproblems such as shortest Hamiltonian path. Rouyer, Seldin, and Cesa-Bianchi gave an algorithm with both adversarial and stochastically constrained guarantees when a fixed switching penalty is paid. Amir, Azov, Koren, and Livni improved the stochastic side of the best-of-both-worlds tradeoff and proved lower bounds showing that adversarial robustness forces additional stochastic regret in some regimes. These results leave open a complete formula for instance-dependent regret under heterogeneous costs and a full characterization of which best-of-both-worlds tradeoffs are simultaneously achievable.

background: Switching costs capture a simple operational friction in bandit learning: changing suppliers, treatments, ads, prices, servers, or experimental configurations may be costly even when observations are otherwise standard bandit feedback. Dekel, Ding, Koren, and Peres showed that adversarial bandits with unit switching cost have minimax regret of order $T^{2/3}$ up to logarithmic factors, a qualitative change from the usual $\sqrt{T}$ scale. In stochastic bandits, the story is subtler because logarithmically many carefully batched switches can be enough for classical gap-dependent learning in some models, while hard switching budgets produce phase transitions. Simchi-Levi and Xu gave matching minimax bounds for stochastic bandits with switching constraints and showed that general switching costs connect to graph-traversal structure. Later best-of-both-worlds work improved simultaneous stochastic/adversarial guarantees and proved tradeoff lower bounds. This means the useful open problem is no longer the basic minimax exponent; it is the Lai-Robbins-style fine structure under switching frictions.

progress.summary: Adversarial minimax rates, stochastic switch-budget rates, and several best-of-both-worlds tradeoffs are known. The unresolved part is a sharp instance-dependent theory with exact dependence on switching-cost geometry and adversarial-robustness requirements.

counterexample_rationale: Small Bernoulli or Gaussian instances with two or three arms and carefully chosen switching-cost matrices can refute proposed gap-dependent formulas. Full lower bounds require asymptotic information-theoretic arguments.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can optimize small hard instances, switching graphs, or adaptive policies and compare empirical regret scalings. Proofs still need change-of-measure lower bounds and algorithm analysis.

literature.synthesis: The basic rate story is mostly settled, so this record should be read as a fine-grained open problem. The adversarial unit-cost case has the $T^{2/3}$ barrier; stochastic switching-budget models have phase transitions; and best-of-both-worlds algorithms now show that stochastic adaptation and adversarial robustness can coexist, but not for free. The missing theory is analogous to the gap-dependent theory of classical stochastic bandits, except that every sample path also has a switching geometry. The most useful resolution would identify the right complexity measure combining gaps and costs, prove an algorithm achieving it, and match it with lower bounds for both pure stochastic and robust-to-adversarial formulations.

open_problem: Develop tight instance-dependent regret bounds for bandits with switching costs, including nonuniform arm-pair costs and best-of-both-worlds constraints, with matching lower bounds that explain the exact dependence on gaps, horizon, arms, and switching-cost geometry.

title: Exact optimality of the cμ/θ index rule for multiclass queues with abandonment
short_statement: A server handles several customer classes that abandon while waiting. Without abandonment the $c\mu$ rule is exactly optimal; with abandonment the $c\mu/\theta$ rule is asymptotically optimal in heavy traffic. Open: whether $c\mu/\theta$ - or any static priority/index rule - is exactly optimal for the discounted or average-cost problem, and under what conditions.
full_statement: Consider a multiclass $M/M/1{+}M$ queue (or $M/M/N{+}M$ many-server system) with classes $i=1,\dots,K$. Class-$i$ arrivals are Poisson at rate $\lambda_i$, service is exponential at rate $\mu_i$, each waiting class-$i$ customer abandons (reneges) independently at rate $\theta_i>0$, and holding incurs cost rate $c_i$ per class-$i$ customer. A (preemptive or non-preemptive) policy $\pi$ chooses which class to serve. The objective is $$ \min_{\pi}\; \limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\,\mathbb{E}^{\pi}\!\left[\int_0^T \sum_{i=1}^K c_i Q_i(t)\,dt\right] \quad\text{(or discounted)}, $$ where $Q_i(t)$ is the number of class-$i$ customers. The $c\mu/\theta$ rule serves a customer of a class maximizing $c_i\mu_i/\theta_i$. \textbf{Open:} Is the $c\mu/\theta$ rule — or any static priority / index policy — the EXACT optimal policy (discounted or average cost), and if not, under what conditions on $(c_i,\mu_i,\theta_i)$ is a static priority rule exactly optimal? In contrast to the no-abandonment case ($\theta_i=0$), where the $c\mu$ rule (serve the class of largest $c_i\mu_i$) is provably exactly optimal, no exact index characterization is known when $\theta_i>0$, and the optimal policy is generally not a static priority rule.
known_results: Without abandonment, the $c\mu$ rule is exactly optimal in the classical single-server setting. Atar, Giat, and Shimkin prove asymptotic optimality of the $c\mu/\theta$ rule for many-server queues with abandonment in heavy traffic, including related ergodic-cost results. Down, Koole, and Lewis analyze the exact single-server abandonment problem and show that the ordinary priority-rule intuition does not hold without additional ordering assumptions; under special parameter orderings, static priority can be recovered. Larrañaga, Ayesta, and Verloop develop Whittle/index-style policies for abandonment queues with convex holding costs and prove asymptotic optimality in suitable regimes. A full exact optimal-policy characterization remains open.

where_posed.text: The $c\mu/\theta$ rule is introduced and justified asymptotically in Atar, Giat, and Shimkin, while the exact-control gap is clarified by Down, Koole, and Lewis.

background: The classical $c\mu$ rule is one of the cleanest exact scheduling results in queueing: in a multiclass single-server queue with linear holding costs and exponential service, serve the class with largest $c_i\mu_i$. Abandonment changes the economics. A class with high abandonment rate may leave soon if ignored, so serving it is less valuable than its holding cost alone suggests. The $c\mu/\theta$ rule emerged as a heavy-traffic prescription for many-server queues with impatient customers and has strong asymptotic justification. But exact optimality outside the heavy-traffic limit is much less settled. Down, Koole, and Lewis show that simple priority structure can fail in general with abandonment, while special order conditions recover static priorities. The open problem is a precise structural characterization of the exact Markov decision problem: when, if ever, is $c\mu/\theta$ or another static index rule exactly optimal?

progress.summary: The heavy-traffic theory is strong, and exact static-priority optimality is known under special orderings. The general finite-system discounted or average-cost policy remains uncharacterized.

literature.synthesis: The no-abandonment $c\mu$ result provides a rare exact index theorem. Abandonment introduces an additional time scale, and heavy-traffic analysis suggests the $c\mu/\theta$ index. Atar, Giat, and Shimkin show that this is the right asymptotic rule in many-server abandonment queues. Down, Koole, and Lewis then demonstrate that exact finite-system control is subtler: static priority is not generally valid, but can be proved under special parameter orderings. The Whittle-index literature gives powerful asymptotic and heuristic tools for more general convex costs. The remaining open problem is to bridge these views: either find an exact index/threshold characterization for the original Markov control problem, or prove that no simple static index form can cover the general case.

title: Optimal dispatching to heterogeneous parallel servers (JSQ optimality fails)
short_statement: For identical exponential servers, Join-the-Shortest-Queue is provably optimal. When servers have different service rates, JSQ is no longer optimal and no simple policy is known to exactly minimize mean response time. Characterizing the optimal dispatching policy for heterogeneous parallel servers is open.
full_statement: Consider $N$ parallel single-server queues with a central dispatcher. Jobs arrive as a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$; upon arrival a job is irrevocably routed to one queue based on the observed queue-length vector $\mathbf{Q}(t)=(Q_1,\dots,Q_N)$ (full information). Server $j$ works at rate $\mu_j$ (exponential service), FCFS. \textbf{Homogeneous ($\mu_j\equiv\mu$):} JSQ — route to $\arg\min_j Q_j$ — stochastically minimizes $\mathbf{Q}(t)$ in an appropriate order and minimizes $\mathbb{E}\sum_j f(Q_j)$ for increasing convex $f$, hence mean response time (Winston 1977; Weber 1978). \textbf{Open (heterogeneous, $\mu_j$ distinct):} determine the policy minimizing long-run mean response time $$ \min_{\pi}\; \limsup_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{T}\,\mathbb{E}^{\pi}\!\left[\int_0^T \sum_{j=1}^N Q_j(t)\,dt\right] $$ (equivalently mean sojourn time by Little's law). JSQ is provably NOT optimal when the $\mu_j$ differ; the exact optimal routing policy is unknown and conjectured to have a complicated, non-index threshold structure. A clean stated-open variant: is JSQ (or any explicit policy) optimal for minimizing mean response time with GENERAL (non-exponential) i.i.d. service even for identical servers?
known_results: Winston proved optimality of the shortest-line discipline for homogeneous exponential queues, and Weber extended related assignment optimality results. Power-of-$d$ and JSQ($d$) policies have a mature mean-field theory, including double-exponential queue tails and asymptotic JSQ equivalence when $d(N)$ grows. Eschenfeldt and Gamarnik established heavy-traffic limits for JSQ with many servers. For heterogeneous servers, JSQ is not optimal, and SED/JSED, speed-aware JSQ, and redundancy/replication variants have asymptotic guarantees in specific regimes. The exact finite-system average-cost optimal dispatching policy for distinct service rates remains uncharacterized; even the cleanest two-server cases lead to nontrivial threshold regions.

where_posed.text: The homogeneous optimality benchmark is Winston's 1977 paper; the heterogeneous-server gap is highlighted in modern load-balancing surveys and the dispatching literature.
where_posed.location: Winston 1977 for the solved homogeneous case; van der Boor et al. survey for modern asymptotic context.

background: Dispatching to parallel queues is one of the oldest and cleanest stochastic-control problems in queueing theory. With identical exponential servers and full queue-length information, Join-the-Shortest-Queue has strong stochastic optimality properties: routing to the shortest line minimizes a broad class of queue-length costs. That theorem is often treated as folklore, but it is delicate and does not survive many natural perturbations. Heterogeneous service rates are the most basic perturbation. If one server is faster, the dispatcher must trade off a longer line at the fast server against a shorter line at a slow server. Simple policies such as SED or weighted JSQ work well asymptotically and in simulations, but the exact average-cost optimal policy is not characterized even in small heterogeneous systems. This is a well-defined OR open problem: the CTMC model and objective are fixed, JSQ's identical-server solution is known, and the missing theorem is a structural characterization or a proof that no simple index/threshold structure can work.

progress.summary: Large-system asymptotics are well developed, but they do not settle finite heterogeneous optimality. Modern surveys explain how JSQ-like policies become asymptotically optimal in many regimes, while exact dynamic-programming structure remains unresolved.
