alphaevolve_rationale: Computational search can map optimal-action regions for two- and three-server systems, infer threshold surfaces, or find counterexamples to conjectured monotonicity. It can provide evidence but not a full proof unless paired with symbolic or Lyapunov arguments.

literature.synthesis: The identical-server theory is unusually clean: shortest-queue routing has stochastic monotonicity and convex-order optimality. The many-server literature then shows that even partial information can recover JSQ-like asymptotic performance, motivating scalable policies. Heterogeneous servers break the symmetry that powers these results. The dispatcher must compare workload, queue length, and service-rate effects, and the optimal policy depends on the global queue vector. Heavy-traffic and mean-field approximations suggest good speed-aware policies, but they are approximation theorems rather than exact finite-system optimality. The open question asks for a structural theorem for the original Markov decision problem, or a rigorous impossibility result ruling out the common simple policy classes.

title: Tight regret of LP-relaxation policies for network revenue management: degenerate and choice-based cases
short_statement: In network revenue management, the deterministic LP upper-bounds optimal revenue and re-solving heuristics achieve $O(1)$ regret under non-degeneracy in the independent-demand case. For choice-based NRM, no policy is known to achieve constant ($T$-independent) regret without a non-degeneracy assumption, and the tight relaxation gap and best simple-policy regret are uncharacterized.
full_statement: Quantity-based NRM: $T$ periods, $m$ resources with integer capacities $c \in \mathbb{Z}_{+}^m$, $n$ products; product $j$ consumes bundle $A_{\cdot j} \in \{0,1\}^m$ and yields revenue $r_j$; demand is stochastic. In the choice-based model, at each period the firm offers an assortment $S \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}$ and an arriving customer chooses $j \in S$ with probability $P_j(S)$ (e.g. MNL). Let $V^*$ be the optimal DP value and $V^{\mathrm{CDLP}} = \max_{\lambda \geq 0} \sum_S \lambda_S (\sum_j P_j(S) r_j)$ s.t. $\sum_S \lambda_S \sum_j P_j(S) A_{ij} \leq c_i\ \forall i$, $\sum_S \lambda_S \leq T$, so $V^{\mathrm{CDLP}} \geq V^*$ (the choice-based deterministic LP). Define the regret of policy $\pi$ as $V^* - V^\pi$ under fluid scaling $c \to k c$, $T \to kT$, $k \to \infty$. $$\textbf{Open: } \text{Is there a tractable policy } \pi \text{ (e.g. CDLP-based re-solving/decomposition) with regret } O(1) \text{ (independent of } k,T\text{) for } \textit{all} \text{ choice-based instances, including degenerate CDLP?}$$ Equivalently, characterize $\inf_\pi \sup_{\text{instances}} \mathrm{Regret}(\pi)$ and the tightest bound on $V^{\mathrm{CDLP}} - V^*$ as a function of $m,n,T$ without a non-degeneracy assumption. For independent demand, re-solving achieves O(1) regret under non-degeneracy, and recent work removes non-degeneracy for continuous-value models.
known_results: Talluri and van Ryzin introduced deterministic LP and randomized linear-programming methods for NRM. Liu and van Ryzin developed the choice-based deterministic linear program for assortment-based revenue management. Bumpensanti and Wang prove that for canonical quantity-based NRM, a carefully timed re-solving heuristic with probability thresholds has uniformly bounded loss independent of horizon and capacities. Jiang, Ma, and Zhang show that degeneracy is not fatal in a continuous-value quantity-based NRM model: they obtain $O(\log^2 T)$ regret without nondegeneracy assumptions and $O(\log T)$ under second-order growth. These results do not yet give a general $O(1)$ regret theorem for choice-based NRM under degenerate CDLP structure.

where_posed.text: The quantity-based bounded-loss benchmark is Bumpensanti and Wang; the remaining degenerate and choice-based gap is visible from the contrast with Liu-van Ryzin choice-based CDLP and the Jiang-Ma-Zhang degeneracy results.
where_posed.location: NRM re-solving and degeneracy literature; open synthesis as of July 2026.

background: Network revenue management is a foundational model for selling products that consume shared limited resources, such as airline itineraries, hotel stays, or ad inventory. The exact dynamic program is usually intractable, so much of the theory compares online policies against deterministic linear-program relaxations and asks for small regret as the horizon and capacities scale. In quantity-based NRM with accept/reject decisions, re-solving and bid-price policies now have strong guarantees, including uniformly bounded loss in important nondegenerate settings. Degeneracy matters because the deterministic LP can have multiple optimal bases or flat directions; then small demand noise can change the right acceptance mix. Choice-based NRM adds another difficulty: the decision is an assortment or offer set, and customers choose according to a demand model, so the CDLP may be nonlinear or have a more complicated feasible structure. The open problem is clean: obtain $O(1)$ regret, or prove it impossible, for general choice-based NRM including degenerate instances.

progress.summary: Quantity-based NRM has bounded-loss and logarithmic-regret guarantees in increasingly broad settings. General choice-based NRM with degenerate CDLP remains the unresolved frontier.

alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can generate small degenerate CDLP instances where re-solving, bid-price, or assortment heuristics incur growing regret. It may also discover factor-revealing examples for lower bounds.

literature.synthesis: The NRM literature has made sharp progress by understanding when deterministic relaxations are accurate enough for online control. Bumpensanti and Wang show that naive frequent re-solving is not enough, but a sparse re-solving schedule plus thresholding can obtain bounded loss in canonical NRM. Jiang, Ma, and Zhang weaken nondegeneracy requirements for continuous-value quantity-based NRM and introduce tools such as semi-fluid relaxations and dual-convergence bounds. Choice-based NRM is structurally harder because decisions alter a customer's substitution set rather than accept or reject a fixed request, and CDLP degeneracy can interact with substitution in ways not covered by quantity-based analyses. The live problem is to decide whether the bounded-loss paradigm survives this combination.

title: Optimal policy for stochastic single-machine weighted completion time with release dates or precedence
short_statement: On a single machine with random processing times, WSEPT is optimal for minimizing expected total weighted completion time with no release dates or precedence (Rothkopf 1966). With release dates and/or precedence, the optimal non-anticipative policy is uncharacterized even for exponential jobs; only constant-factor LP-based approximations are known.
full_statement: Single machine, jobs $j = 1,\dots,n$ with independent random processing times $P_j$ and weights $w_j > 0$; $C_j$ is the policy-dependent random completion time. A policy $\pi$ must be non-anticipative (decisions at time $t$ depend only on information available by $t$). Objective: $$\min_{\pi \in \Pi_{\mathrm{non\text{-}ant}}} \ \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{j=1}^n w_j C_j^{\pi}\Big].$$ Baseline (Rothkopf 1966): with all $r_j = 0$ and no precedence, the static list policy WSEPT (process in non-increasing order of $w_j / \mathbb{E}[P_j]$) is optimal. $$\textbf{Open (release dates): } \text{with release dates } r_j \ (1\,|\,r_j\,|\,\mathbb{E}\sum w_j C_j), \text{ characterize an optimal non-anticipative policy, even when } P_j \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\mu_j).$$ $$\textbf{Open (precedence): } \text{with precedence constraints (e.g. series-parallel) and } P_j \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\mu_j), \text{ characterize the optimal policy for } 1\,|\,\mathrm{prec}\,|\,\mathbb{E}\sum w_j C_j.$$ No closed-form optimal priority policy is known in either case; the gap between best-known approximation guarantees and optimality is open. (The deterministic special cases $1\,|\,r_j\,|\,\sum w_j C_j$ and $1\,|\,\mathrm{prec}\,|\,\sum w_j C_j$ are already strongly NP-hard.)
known_results: Rothkopf proves WSEPT optimal for independent stochastic processing times on a single machine when all jobs are initially available and there is no precedence. Möhring, Schulz, and Uetz show the power of LP-based priority policies and obtain constant-factor approximation guarantees for stochastic scheduling with release dates, precedence, and related constraints. Skutella, Sviridenko, and Uetz extend approximation results to unrelated machines under stochastic processing times. Moseley, Pruhs, Uetz, and Zhou prove in 2026 that minimizing expected completion times of stochastic jobs on parallel machines is #P-hard even for two-point processing-time distributions and unit weights, and even evaluating WSEPT can be #P-hard. The exact single-machine release-date and precedence policy structure remains open.

where_posed.text: The solved WSEPT baseline is Rothkopf 1966; the release-date and precedence gap is implicit in the LP-priority approximation literature and sharpened by recent stochastic scheduling hardness results.

background: Stochastic scheduling asks for nonanticipative policies when processing times are random but their distributions are known. In the cleanest single-machine setting with all jobs available at time zero and no precedence constraints, Rothkopf's stochastic analogue of Smith's rule, WSEPT, is optimal: sequence jobs by decreasing $w_j/\mathbb{E}P_j$. Release dates and precedence constraints are the next natural modelling features, and they fundamentally change the problem. The controller must decide whether to process an available job now, wait for a future release, or respect precedence while learning processing completions. LP-based priority policies give constant-factor approximations, but they do not characterize the optimal nonanticipative policy. Recent hardness work for stochastic completion-time scheduling on parallel machines confirms that stochasticity itself creates computational difficulty, not just the deterministic special case.

progress.summary: Approximation algorithms are known, and recent #P-hardness results rule out naive optimism in broader machine environments. The exact single-machine stochastic release-date/precedence structure is still not characterized.

alphaevolve_rationale: Search can identify small instances where WSEPT-like, release-date-adjusted, or precedence-adjusted priority rules fail. It may also help infer candidate policies for restricted precedence classes.

literature.synthesis: Rothkopf's theorem gives a rare exact solution in stochastic scheduling: expected processing times are enough when all jobs are available and independent. LP-based priority-policy work shows that once release dates or precedence enter, exact optimality is elusive but good approximations remain possible. The 2026 hardness result demonstrates that stochastic scheduling has intrinsic computational complexity, including hardness of evaluating common greedy policies in broader settings. What remains unsettled for the single-machine release-date and precedence variants is whether there is hidden structure in the nonanticipative policy space, or whether even these clean special cases are computationally intractable in a way not yet formally captured.

title: The 4/3 Conjecture for the Subtour LP Integrality Gap (Metric TSP)
short_statement: For metric TSP, the integrality gap of the subtour-elimination (Held-Karp) LP relaxation is conjectured to be exactly $4/3$. Examples force it to be at least $4/3$, but the best proven upper bound is only barely below $3/2$.
full_statement: Let $I=(V,c)$ be a finite metric TSP instance: $c_{uv}=c_{vu}\ge 0$, $c_{uu}=0$, and $c_{uv}\le c_{uw}+c_{wv}$ for all vertices $u,v,w$. A tour is a Hamiltonian cycle, or equivalently a connected Eulerian multigraph whose shortcutting gives a Hamiltonian cycle, and $\operatorname{OPT}(I)$ is its minimum cost. The subtour-elimination, or Held-Karp, relaxation has variables $x_e$ for unordered pairs $e\in {V\choose 2}$, degree constraints $x(\delta(v))=2$ for every $v\in V$, subtour constraints $x(\delta(S))\ge 2$ for every nonempty proper $S\subset V$, and $x_e\ge0$. Let $\operatorname{LP}(I)$ be the minimum cost of this relaxation and define $\gamma=\sup_I \operatorname{OPT}(I)/\operatorname{LP}(I)$ over all finite metric instances. The $4/3$ conjecture asserts that $\gamma=4/3$. The lower bound comes from explicit families whose optimal tours cost asymptotically $4/3$ times the subtour LP value. The open problem is to prove a universal rounding theorem that converts every feasible subtour solution into a tour of cost at most $(4/3)\,c\cdot x$, or to exhibit and certify a metric instance whose gap is strictly larger than $4/3$.
known_results: Families of metric TSP instances give subtour-LP integrality gap approaching $4/3$, so the conjectured value would be tight. Christofides-Serdyukov gives a $3/2$ tour relative to the optimum, and the same ratio was the best known general upper bound for the subtour LP for roughly forty years. Karlin, Klein, and Oveis Gharan proved that the gap is at most $3/2-\epsilon$ for an absolute $\epsilon>10^{-36}$, the first general improvement below $3/2$. Half-integral instances, often conjectured to be extremal, have seen incremental progress: Karlin-Klein-Oveis Gharan obtained $1.49993$, later work improves special half-integral classes, and exact computational verification now supports the $4/3$ conjecture for small subtour-polytope instances. The full gap remains open between $4/3$ and just below $3/2$.

where_posed.text: Long-standing subtour LP integrality-gap conjecture surveyed in Traub and Vygen, 'Approximation Algorithms for Traveling Salesman Problems'.

background: The metric traveling-salesman problem is one of the central problems in combinatorial optimization. The subtour-elimination LP, also called the Held-Karp relaxation, is the standard relaxation behind both exact TSP solvers and approximation algorithms. The famous $4/3$ conjecture says that every feasible subtour LP solution can be rounded to a tour of cost at most $4/3$ times the LP value, and this would be tight. For decades the best general upper bound was the $3/2$ Christofides-Serdyukov ratio. Karlin, Klein, and Oveis Gharan finally broke the $3/2$ barrier by an extremely small amount using maximum-entropy tree sampling, but the result is still nowhere near $4/3$. This makes the problem a clean benchmark for whether modern probabilistic rounding can fully capture the structure of the subtour polytope.

progress.summary: The general upper bound is now strictly below $3/2$, but only by a tiny constant. Special half-integral and cycle-cut cases have stronger results, and exact small-instance computations support the conjecture.

counterexample_rationale: A refutation could be a finite metric instance with subtour LP gap exceeding $4/3$. Such a candidate can be checked by solving the LP and TSP exactly for moderate sizes.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search over small metrics, graph metrics, and subtour-polytope extreme points can find hard instances or support structural conjectures. Positive progress still requires a proof of a rounding theorem.

literature.synthesis: The main lines of attack are probabilistic tree rounding, structure of subtour extreme points, and reductions to half-integral or graph-like instances. Christofides-style arguments naturally stop at $3/2$ because they build a spanning tree and then pay for a parity-correction matching that can be charged by half the LP. The maximum-entropy approach perturbs this charge in favorable cases and gives the first nonzero improvement, but its constants are far from the $4/3$ target. Half-integral instances remain central because many hard examples and conjectural extremal structures live there, and exact computations suggest that small extreme points do not violate the conjecture. The gap is therefore not a lack of examples; it is a missing structural theorem showing that every subtour solution has enough negative dependence, parity slack, or decomposability to support $4/3$ rounding. A counterexample would have to beat decades of half-integral and graph-metric searches with a rigorously certified LP/tour gap.

title: Exact Integrality Gap of the Held-Karp LP for Asymmetric TSP
short_statement: The asymmetric metric TSP Held-Karp integrality gap lies between $2$ and $17$; its exact value remains open.
full_statement: Let $(V,d)$ be a finite directed metric: $d(u,u)=0$ and $d(u,w)\le d(u,v)+d(v,w)$, but $d(u,v)$ need not equal $d(v,u)$. The asymmetric traveling salesperson problem asks for a minimum-cost directed Hamiltonian cycle. The Held-Karp relaxation has variables $x_{uv}\ge0$ for ordered pairs $u\ne v$, imposes one unit of outgoing and incoming flow at each vertex, and enforces subtour-elimination constraints $x(\delta^+(S))\ge1$ and $x(\delta^-(S))\ge1$ for every nonempty proper $S\subset V$. Its value is at most the optimum tour cost. The integrality gap is $$\sup_{(V,d)} \frac{\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(V,d)}{\mathrm{HK}(V,d)}.$$ Determine this supremum exactly. Current evidence leaves a broad interval: explicit directed metrics give gap at least $2$, while the best general rounding/approximation analysis gives gap at most $17$.
known_results: Charikar, Goemans, and Karloff constructed ATSP instances with Held-Karp integrality gap at least $2$, establishing the main lower-bound benchmark. Before 2018, general ATSP had only logarithmic approximation guarantees, and it was unknown whether the Held-Karp relaxation had any constant gap. Svensson, Tarnawski, and Vegh gave the first constant-factor approximation for general ATSP, implying a constant Held-Karp gap; their analysis yields an integrality-ratio upper bound of $319$ and an approximation factor $506$. Traub and Vygen simplified and strengthened the framework, improving the approximation ratio to $22+\epsilon$ and the Held-Karp integrality-gap upper bound to $22$. Traub and Vygen's 2024 book strengthens this to gap at most $17$ (Corollary 8.26), via a $(17+\epsilon)$-approximation relative to the LP (Theorem 8.25). The remaining interval is $[2,17]$.

where_posed.text: Exact-value gap left by Svensson, Tarnawski, Vegh and Traub-Vygen constant-factor analyses of the Held-Karp relaxation for ATSP.

background: Asymmetric TSP replaces undirected metrics by directed metrics, and this destroys the parity structure that makes Christofides' algorithm work. The standard Held-Karp LP is still the central relaxation: it enforces one unit of in-flow and out-flow at each vertex plus subtour-elimination constraints. For many years it was not even known whether this relaxation had a constant integrality gap. Svensson, Tarnawski, and Vegh proved the breakthrough constant-factor approximation, analyzed against the LP, thereby establishing a bounded gap. Traub and Vygen improved the bound first to $22$ and then to $17$ in their 2024 book. The lower bound remains only $2$. The exact integrality gap is therefore a major open quantitative question in directed network design.

progress.summary: The published Held-Karp gap interval is $[2,17]$; boundedness is resolved but the exact constant is not.

The gap may reflect inefficiency in the decomposition/augmentation framework, or it may indicate missing lower-bound gadgets with much larger ratio than $2$. Progress likely requires either a sharper rounding of thin directed structures or a new family of directed metrics that exposes limitations of Held-Karp.

title: Integrality Gap of the Bidirected-Cut Relaxation for Steiner Tree
short_statement: For the Steiner tree problem, the integrality gap of the bidirected-cut relaxation is conjectured to be close to $1$; the best known lower bound is $6/5 = 1.2$ and the best upper bound is $1.9988$ (only shown below $2$ in 2024).
full_statement: In the graph Steiner tree problem, the input is an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with nonnegative edge costs $c_e$ and a terminal set $R\subseteq V$. The goal is to find a minimum-cost connected subgraph containing all terminals; nonterminals may be used as Steiner vertices. The bidirected cut relaxation fixes a root terminal $r\in R$, replaces every undirected edge $uv$ by arcs $(u,v)$ and $(v,u)$ of cost $c_{uv}$, and has variables $x_a\ge0$ for arcs. For every cut $U\subseteq V$ with $r\notin U$ and $U\cap R\ne\emptyset$, it imposes $x(\delta^-(U))\ge1$, so each terminal side of a root-separating cut has one unit of incoming directed capacity. The integer version chooses an arborescence-like directed connection from $r$ to all terminals and corresponds to a Steiner tree. The open problem asks for the supremum, over all finite Steiner tree instances, of $\operatorname{OPT}_{ST}/\operatorname{OPT}_{BCR}$.
known_results: When all vertices are terminals, the relaxation reduces to Edmonds-style arborescence/spanning-tree structure and is integral. For proper Steiner instances it can be fractional. The classical general upper bound was $2$, matching standard undirected cut-relaxation reasoning and leaving open whether the directed formulation was theoretically stronger. Vicari constructed simplex-based instances showing gap at least $6/5$, improving the earlier $36/31$ lower bound. Byrka, Grandoni, and Traub proved the first nontrivial general upper bound below $2$, namely $1.9988$. Paschmanns and Traub later improved the upper bound to $1.898$. For the special case in which a terminal minimum spanning tree is an optimal Steiner tree, they prove an upper bound $12/7$ and show that a broad class of moat-growing algorithms cannot certify a bound below $12/7$. Thus the exact general gap remains open in the interval $[1.2,1.898]$, and current evidence suggests that closing it will require either stronger lower-bound gadgets or rounding methods beyond the known moat-growth framework.

where_posed.text: Long-standing gap question highlighted and advanced in Byrka, Grandoni, and Traub, 'The Bidirected Cut Relaxation for Steiner Tree has Integrality Gap Smaller than 2'.

background: The bidirected cut relaxation is one of the most natural LP relaxations for graph Steiner tree. It orients every undirected edge both ways, selects a root terminal, and requires one unit of directed capacity across every cut separating another terminal from the root. The relaxation is compact and performs well computationally, but for decades its theoretical integrality gap was stuck at the trivial upper bound $2$, the same as the undirected cut relaxation. This changed only recently: Byrka, Grandoni, and Traub proved the first upper bound below $2$, and Paschmanns and Traub later improved it substantially. The lower bound, however, is only $6/5$. The question is now a clean LP-strength problem: how powerful is this canonical directed relaxation really?

progress.summary: The gap is now known to be below $2$ and at most $1.898$, while the best lower bound is $6/5$. Moat-growing methods alone appear limited.

literature.synthesis: The old $2$ upper bound came from generic Steiner tree approximations and did not use enough structure of the directed relaxation. The new upper bounds use dual growth, terminal-moat structure, and refined accounting of how fractional directed cuts can be converted into an integral connecting subgraph. These methods prove that BCR is genuinely stronger than the undirected cut relaxation, but the improvement is still numerically modest compared with the best lower bound. Paschmanns and Traub's moat-growing barrier is especially informative: within a broad algorithmic template, one cannot certify a gap below $12/7$ even in an important special case. The remaining gap can therefore be attacked from two directions. Lower-bound work can search for terminal-rich or simplex-like gadgets with BCR value much smaller than the integral tree. Upper-bound work likely needs rounding ideas that use global structure not visible to moat growth, or comparisons to stronger relaxations such as the hypergraphic relaxation.

title: Best Approximation Ratio for Steiner Tree (1.39 vs. hardness)
short_statement: For graph Steiner tree, the best polynomial-time algorithm achieves ratio $\ln 4 \approx 1.39$, while the best hardness only rules out ratios below $96/95 \approx 1.01$. Closing this gap - and pinning down the hypergraphic-LP integrality gap - is open.
full_statement: In the graph Steiner tree problem, the input is an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with nonnegative edge costs and a terminal set $R\subseteq V$. The goal is to find a minimum-cost connected subgraph spanning all terminals; nonterminals may be used as Steiner vertices. Let $\alpha^*$ be the best polynomial-time approximation ratio achievable for general graph Steiner tree, assuming $P\ne NP$. Let $\gamma_{\mathrm{hyp}}$ be the integrality gap of the hypergraphic relaxation, whose variables correspond to full components connecting subsets of terminals and whose constraints encode terminal connectivity. Determine $\alpha^*$ and $\gamma_{\mathrm{hyp}}$, or at least close the current gap between the best algorithmic guarantee $\ln4+\epsilon$, the best known hypergraphic-LP lower bound around $8/7$, and the best NP-hardness threshold $96/95$. A solution should specify whether the hypergraphic LP is the right barrier or whether stronger algorithms/hardness reductions move the true threshold elsewhere.
known_results: Byrka, Grandoni, Rothvoss, and Sanita give a $(\ln4+\epsilon)$-approximation via iterative randomized rounding of the hypergraphic relaxation, and Goemans, Olver, Rothvoss, and Zenklusen later gave a deterministic analysis proving a matching $\ln4$ upper bound on the hypergraphic integrality gap. Chlebik and Chlebikova prove NP-hardness of approximation below $96/95$. Known lower-bound instances for the hypergraphic relaxation give a gap at least $8/7$, far below $\ln4$. Recent work has improved the related bidirected-cut relaxation below $2$, but that does not resolve the stronger hypergraphic relaxation or the true approximation threshold. Thus algorithmic, LP-gap, and hardness bounds remain widely separated.

background: Graph Steiner tree asks for the cheapest connected subgraph spanning a specified terminal set and is a foundational network-design problem. The approximation landscape has an unusually large gap: sophisticated LP rounding gives a ratio of $\ln 4\approx1.386$, while NP-hardness only rules out ratios below $96/95$. The best algorithm uses the hypergraphic relaxation and iterative randomized rounding, which captures full components connecting terminals through Steiner vertices. Despite the strength of this relaxation, known lower bounds for its integrality gap are much smaller than $\ln4$. The open problem is therefore both algorithmic and polyhedral: identify the true approximation threshold for Steiner tree and the true power of the hypergraphic LP.

literature.synthesis: The hypergraphic relaxation was a major advance because it reasons about full components rather than individual edges, enabling iterative randomized rounding below earlier combinatorial ratios. The remaining gap may be due to a loose analysis of that rounding, an actual gap in the relaxation, or a much stronger hardness construction still unknown. Bidirected-cut developments are related but not identical: BCR is compact and practical, while hypergraphic relaxations are stronger but component-heavy. A resolution likely needs either a new rounding theorem for components or a better understanding of hard instances for terminal-connectivity relaxations.

title: Integrality Gap of the Configuration LP for Restricted Santa Claus
short_statement: Determine the restricted Santa Claus configuration-LP gap, currently between $2$ and $53/15\approx3.5333$.
full_statement: In the restricted max-min fair allocation problem, let $P$ be a set of players and $R$ a set of indivisible resources. Each resource $r$ has a value $v_r\ge 0$, and each player $p$ either desires $r$ and values it at $v_r$, or does not desire it and values it at $0$. An allocation partitions resources among players and has value $\min_{p\in P}\sum_{r\in A_p} v_r$. For a target $T$, the configuration LP has one variable $x_{p,C}$ for every player $p$ and every subset $C\subseteq R_p$ with $\sum_{r\in C}v_r\ge T$; it requires each player to receive one unit of configurations and each resource to be used fractionally at most once. Let $T_{LP}$ be the largest feasible target and $T_{INT}$ the optimal integral allocation value. Determine the smallest universal constant $\gamma$ such that $T_{LP}\le \gamma T_{INT}$ for every restricted instance. Equivalently, close the gap between the best known lower-bound instances and the best known rounding/existence analyses for this canonical configuration LP.
known_results: Bansal and Sviridenko introduced the configuration-LP approach for Santa Claus-type allocation and showed why weaker assignment relaxations are inadequate. Asadpour, Feige, and Saberi proved that the restricted configuration LP has constant integrality gap at most $4$ using hypergraph matching and local-search ideas, but their existence proof did not by itself yield a polynomial-time $4$-approximation. Jansen and Rohwedder gave a shorter analysis improving the upper bound to $3+5/6$, and Cheng and Mao later improved it to $3+21/26\approx 3.808$ while also developing stronger constructive algorithms. On the lower-bound side, explicit instances show an integrality gap of at least $2$. The remaining gap interval is $[2,53/15]$. Haxell and Szabo (SODA 2023; Combinatorica 2025), Theorem 1.1, improve the restricted configuration-LP gap to $53/15$. This is existential, not a polynomial-time allocation algorithm.

background: Restricted Santa Claus, also called restricted max-min fair allocation, is the max-min analogue of scheduling and fair division. There are players and indivisible resources; each resource has a value and is acceptable only to some players. The goal is to allocate resources so that the least-valued player bundle is as large as possible. The configuration LP is the standard relaxation: for a guessed target value $T$, each player may fractionally choose configurations of resources whose total value is at least $T$. The LP is strong enough to certify constant-factor existence results, but rounding it constructively is difficult because feasible configurations form a hypergraph matching problem. The exact integrality gap of this LP is a central structural question: it measures the true power of the canonical relaxation independently of the current limitations of algorithms.

progress.summary: The restricted configuration-LP gap lies in $[2,53/15]$; the upper bound is existential.

alphaevolve_rationale: Search over hypergraph allocation instances may find stronger LP gaps or patterns suggesting a tight family.

literature.synthesis: The restricted Santa Claus literature separates three questions: estimating the optimum via the configuration LP, proving existential integrality-gap bounds, and finding polynomial-time algorithms that construct allocations. The configuration LP is the natural relaxation for the first two questions, but its rounding is tied to difficult hypergraph matching local search. The historical $4$ and $3.808$ upper bounds, now improved to $53/15$, show substantial structure, while the lower bound $2$ leaves room for either sharper rounding or stronger gap constructions. A tight answer would clarify whether the algorithmic $4+\delta$ frontier is close to intrinsic LP limitations or mostly a constructive artifact.

title: Beating the 2-Approximation for Makespan on Unrelated Machines (R||Cmax)
short_statement: For makespan minimization on unrelated machines, the classic Lenstra-Shmoys-Tardos algorithm gives a $2$-approximation and it is NP-hard to beat $3/2$. Whether a ratio below $2$ (ideally $3/2$) is achievable has been open since 1990.
full_statement: In unrelated parallel-machine makespan minimization, an instance consists of machines $i\in[m]$, jobs $j\in[n]$, and processing times $p_{ij}\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\}$ specifying the time required if job $j$ is assigned to machine $i$. A schedule assigns every job to one machine with finite processing time, and the load of machine $i$ is $\sum_{j\mapsto i}p_{ij}$. The objective is to minimize $C_{\max}=\max_i\sum_{j\mapsto i}p_{ij}$. Lenstra-Shmoys-Tardos gave a polynomial-time $2$-approximation and proved NP-hardness below $3/2$. The open problem is to determine whether there is a polynomial-time $(2-\epsilon)$-approximation for some universal $\epsilon>0$, or conversely to prove hardness of approximation strictly above $3/2$ for general unrelated processing matrices. The approximation must be with respect to the optimal integral makespan for the same processing-time matrix, not a relaxation value.
known_results: Lenstra, Shmoys, and Tardos gave the classic polynomial-time $2$-approximation and proved NP-hardness of any ratio below $3/2$. Their algorithm rounds the assignment LP after discarding assignments longer than a guessed makespan. The configuration LP has gap $2$ for full unrelated machines, even for unrelated graph balancing, by Verschae and Wiese, so this strongest standard LP does not by itself beat the barrier in full generality. Important special cases behave better: restricted assignment has configuration-LP gap below $2$, and graph balancing admits nonconstructive/local-search estimates below $1.75$. None of these results gives a polynomial-time approximation below $2$ for general unrelated machines, and no stronger hardness has closed the gap.

background: Scheduling on unrelated machines is the most general classical parallel-machine makespan model: each job has an arbitrary processing time on each machine. Lenstra, Shmoys, and Tardos gave a $2$-approximation in 1990 by rounding a natural assignment LP after guessing the makespan, and proved NP-hardness below $3/2$. The $[3/2,2]$ gap has survived for decades. Many special cases, such as restricted assignment and graph balancing, have seen progress below $2$ in LP estimation or quasi-polynomial algorithms, but the full unrelated-machines problem has resisted any polynomial-time ratio strictly below $2$. This is one of the cleanest approximation gaps in scheduling and a central test of whether stronger configuration relaxations or local-search methods can beat assignment-LP rounding.

progress.summary: The general problem remains at $2$ versus $3/2$. Configuration-LP and local-search progress applies to special cases but not to full unrelated machines.

literature.synthesis: The assignment-LP rounding of Lenstra-Shmoys-Tardos is tight for its relaxation, and configuration-LP gaps show that simply strengthening to configurations cannot solve the full problem. The special-case successes suggest that restricted processing structure enables local-search or hypergraph-matching style arguments, but arbitrary unrelated processing times can encode much more complex conflicts. The remaining gap is therefore not only quantitative; it asks what relaxation or algorithmic structure can see beyond the known $2$ barrier for arbitrary matrices.

title: Beck-Fiala Conjecture (Discrepancy of Bounded-Degree Set Systems)
short_statement: The dimension-free $O(\sqrt t)$ Beck-Fiala bound is claimed by September 2026 Komlos preprints. Status: solution claimed, not independently verified here.
full_statement: Let $\mathcal S=\{S_1,\ldots,S_m\}$ be a set system on ground set $[n]$, and suppose every element belongs to at most $t$ sets. Equivalently, let $A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$ be an incidence matrix whose columns have at most $t$ ones. A signing $x\in\{-1,+1\}^n$ colors the elements red and blue, and its discrepancy is $\|Ax\|_\infty=\max_{r\le m}|\sum_{j\in S_r}x_j|$. Beck and Fiala proved discrepancy at most $2t-1$. The Beck-Fiala conjecture asks whether there is a universal constant $C$ such that every degree-$t$ set system has a signing with discrepancy at most $C\sqrt t$, independent of $m$ and $n$. The historically open problem is to prove this dimension-free $O(\sqrt t)$ bound for every relation among $t,m,n$, or to construct a family of degree-$t$ set systems with discrepancy $\omega(\sqrt t)$. Results that work only when $t$ is large compared with $n$, or that retain a residual $\sqrt{\log n}$ term, are partial progress but do not settle the conjecture. Status at 2026-11-09: Guo, Fang, and Lu's September 2026 preprint claims the full Beck-Fiala conjecture via its Komlos theorem and Corollary 1.2. This record flags a claimed resolution, pending verification.
known_results:
Historical context before the 2026 full-resolution claims: Beck and Fiala proved the original $2t-1$ bound. Bukh slightly improved the linear bound to $2t-O(\log^*t)$, but this remains far from square-root behavior. Banaszczyk's vector-balancing theorem implies $O(\sqrt{t\log n})$, which has the conjectured dependence on $t$ but retains a dimension factor. Bansal-Dadush-Garg made Banaszczyk-type bounds algorithmic. Bansal and Jiang recently improved the landscape: they resolve Beck-Fiala for $t\ge\log^2 n$ and give bounds of the form $\widetilde O(\sqrt t+\sqrt{\log n})$ in the remaining regime, improving on $O(\sqrt{t\log n})$. These results also provide efficient algorithms for the colorings they guarantee. The dimension-free $O(\sqrt t)$ statement for every $t$, especially small and intermediate $t$ relative to $n$, was not settled by those earlier results. Status at 2026-11-09: Guo, Fang, and Lu's September 2026 preprint claims the full Beck-Fiala conjecture via its Komlos theorem and Corollary 1.2.

Algorithmic follow-up: Guo, Fang, and Lu, arXiv:2609.23540v2, Corollary 1.2, report a deterministic real-RAM algorithm with discrepancy below $16544\sqrt t$. Xiaoyu Li, arXiv:2609.30044v1, Corollary 1.2, improves this to below $99\sqrt t$, with a polynomial-bit implementation on rational inputs. These are algorithmic square-root guarantees for all degree regimes, not only existential or high-degree results. The full proofs have not been independently certified here.

background: Historical context before the 2026 full-resolution claims: Combinatorial discrepancy asks whether a set system can be two-colored so that every set sees nearly the same number of red and blue elements. Beck-Fiala studies the sparse case where each element appears in at most $t$ sets. The original theorem gives discrepancy at most $2t-1$, while the conjecture predicts the much smaller bound $O(\sqrt t)$ independent of the number of sets and elements. This is a central problem because it sits between sparse set systems, vector balancing, rounding, and discrepancy algorithms. It is also implied by the more general Komlos conjecture. Recent work by Bansal and Jiang goes beyond the Banaszczyk bound and resolves the conjecture for high-degree regimes such as $t\ge \log^2 n$, but the full range of $t$ was not settled by those earlier results. Status at 2026-11-09: Guo, Fang, and Lu's September 2026 preprint claims the full Beck-Fiala conjecture via its Komlos theorem and Corollary 1.2.

title: Komlos Conjecture (O(1) Discrepancy of Unit-Norm Vectors)
short_statement: The dimension-free constant Komlos bound is claimed in September 2026 preprints. Status: solution claimed, not independently verified here.
full_statement: Let $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^m$ be vectors with Euclidean norms $\|v_j\|_2\le 1$. Equivalently, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ be a real matrix whose columns have $\ell_2$ norm at most $1$. A signing $x\in\{-1,+1\}^n$ has discrepancy $\|Ax\|_\infty$, the largest absolute coordinate of the signed vector sum. The Komlos conjecture asks whether there is a universal constant $K$ such that every such matrix admits a signing with $\|Ax\|_\infty\le K$, independent of the number of rows $m$ and columns $n$. The conjecture implies Beck-Fiala after scaling each degree-$t$ incidence column by $1/\sqrt t$: a constant Komlos bound would give $O(\sqrt t)$ discrepancy for degree-$t$ set systems. The historically open problem is the full dimension-free constant bound for arbitrary real unit-column matrices, with no distributional, smoothed-input, bounded-rank, or sparsity assumption. An algorithmic solution would additionally find the signing in polynomial time. Status at 2026-11-09: Guo, Fang, and Lu's September 2026 preprint claims the full Komlos conjecture (Theorem 1.1); Karingula and Lovett give a subsequent elementary-proof preprint. This record flags a claimed resolution, pending verification.
known_results:
Historical context before the 2026 full-resolution claims: Banaszczyk proved that unit-column matrices admit discrepancy $O(\sqrt{\log n})$, and Bansal, Dadush, and Garg gave an efficient algorithm matching that bound. The conjectured answer is $O(1)$. Bansal, Jiang, Meka, Singla, and Sinha proved Komlos in a smoothed-analysis setting when the input vectors are perturbed and sufficiently numerous relative to the dimension. Bansal and Jiang recently improved the pre-September-2026 worst-case general dependence to $\widetilde O(\log^{1/4}n)$ using affine spectral-independence constraints in an SDP-guided random walk. They also obtain improved Beck-Fiala consequences. Lower bounds show that the optimal universal constant, if the conjecture holds, cannot be too small, but no superconstant lower bound is known. The pre-September-2026 gap was between constant and about a fourth-root logarithm. Status at 2026-11-09: Guo, Fang, and Lu's September 2026 preprint claims the full Komlos conjecture (Theorem 1.1); Karingula and Lovett give a subsequent elementary-proof preprint.

Algorithmic follow-up: Guo, Fang, and Lu, arXiv:2609.23540v2, Theorem 1.1, report a deterministic polynomial-time real-RAM algorithm with discrepancy at most $8272$. Xiaoyu Li, arXiv:2609.30044v1, Theorem 1.1, reduces this to below $99$ and proves polynomial bit complexity for rational inputs. Emile Anand and Peter Chen, arXiv:2610.20995v1, Theorem 1.1, report the same discrepancy in $\widetilde O(L_{\mathrm{in}}+n^\omega)$ expected bit operations. Thus algorithmic constant discrepancy is also addressed by current preprints, not left wholly unresolved. These statements were checked, not their full proofs.

background: Historical context before the 2026 full-resolution claims: The Komlos conjecture is a central vector-balancing problem. Given vectors of Euclidean norm at most one, choose signs so that every coordinate of the signed sum is bounded by a universal constant. It generalizes Beck-Fiala because the incidence columns of a degree-$t$ set system can be scaled to unit length, and a constant Komlos bound would imply $O(\sqrt t)$ Beck-Fiala discrepancy. The conjecture is also a benchmark for algorithmic discrepancy, convex geometry, and rounding. Banaszczyk's theorem gives the best classical asymptotic bound $O(\sqrt{\log n})$, and recent work of Bansal and Jiang improves this to roughly $\widetilde O(\log^{1/4} n)$, but the desired dimension-free constant was not settled by those earlier results. Status at 2026-11-09: Guo, Fang, and Lu's September 2026 preprint claims the full Komlos conjecture (Theorem 1.1); Karingula and Lovett give a subsequent elementary-proof preprint.

title: Matrix Spencer Conjecture
short_statement: For $n$ real symmetric $n\times n$ matrices of operator norm at most one, the $O(\sqrt n)$ signing conjecture has a full-resolution preprint. Status: solution claimed, not independently verified here.
full_statement: Let $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ be real symmetric $n\times n$ matrices, and assume $\|A_i\|_{op}\le 1$ for every $i$. Choose signs $x_i\in\{-1,+1\}$ and measure the discrepancy of the signing by the spectral norm $\|\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i\|_{op}$. The Matrix Spencer conjecture asks whether there is a universal constant $C$ such that, for every such family of $n$ matrices, some signing satisfies $\|\sum_i x_iA_i\|_{op}\le C\sqrt n$. When the matrices are diagonal this is exactly the classical Spencer theorem for $n$ sets on $n$ elements, after encoding set incidence in the diagonal entries. The historically open problem is the noncommutative full-rank case: prove the $O(\sqrt n)$ bound without assuming that the matrices commute, have low rank, or share an eigenbasis. The desired theorem is purely existential but algorithmic signings with the same guarantee would also resolve the record. Status at 2026-11-09: Akbas and Sra's August 2026 preprint claims the full square Matrix Spencer conjecture and an efficient signing algorithm (Theorem 1.2). This record flags a claimed resolution, pending verification.
known_results: Historical context before the 2026 full-resolution claims: The conjectured bound is $O(\sqrt n)$ and is tight up to constants in the diagonal Spencer setting. Standard random signing plus matrix concentration gives dimension-dependent logarithmic behavior, which is not enough. Bansal, Jiang, and Meka prove the $O(\sqrt n)$ bound for matrices of rank at most $n/\log^3 n$, giving the strongest general partial result and an efficient algorithm in that regime. Their proof uses refinements of noncommutative Khintchine inequalities due to Bandeira, Boedihardjo, and van Handel. The low-rank theorem also has consequences for quantum random access codes. For arbitrary full-rank matrices, known matrix concentration and discrepancy tools did not remove extra logarithmic or rank-dependent losses. The case left by those earlier results was full rank with only operator-norm boundedness. Status at 2026-11-09: Akbas and Sra's August 2026 preprint claims the full square Matrix Spencer conjecture and an efficient signing algorithm (Theorem 1.2).

background: Historical context before the 2026 full-resolution claims: Spencer's theorem says that $n$ sets on $n$ elements can be signed with discrepancy $O(\sqrt n)$. The Matrix Spencer conjecture asks for a noncommutative analogue: sign $n$ bounded symmetric matrices so that the spectral norm of the signed sum is $O(\sqrt n)$. The diagonal case recovers Spencer, but general matrices do not commute, so scalar discrepancy arguments do not apply directly. This problem connects discrepancy theory, matrix concentration, free probability, and quantum information, where signed sums of observables and matrix-valued concentration inequalities naturally appear. Bansal, Jiang, and Meka proved the conjectured bound for matrices of rank at most $n/\log^3 n$ using refined noncommutative Khintchine tools. The full-rank case was not settled by those earlier results. Status at 2026-11-09: Akbas and Sra's August 2026 preprint claims the full square Matrix Spencer conjecture and an efficient signing algorithm (Theorem 1.2).

title: Approximability of Unit-Demand Capacitated Vehicle Routing
short_statement: In capacitated vehicle routing, the classic iterated tour partitioning gives ratio $\alpha+1$ ($\alpha$ = best TSP ratio). A 2021 breakthrough shaved off a tiny amount; whether the $+1$ can be reduced - ideally to match TSP - is open.
full_statement: In unit-demand capacitated vehicle routing, the input is a finite metric space with a distinguished depot $r$, a set of customers $C$, and an integer vehicle capacity $Q$. Each customer has demand one. A feasible solution is a collection of tours, each starting and ending at $r$, such that every customer is visited by some tour and each tour visits at most $Q$ customers. The objective is to minimize total tour length. Let $\alpha$ denote the best approximation ratio known or achievable for metric TSP. Classical iterated tour partitioning gives ratio $\alpha+1$ by building a TSP tour through all customers and cutting it into capacity-feasible routes. Determine the optimal approximation ratio for unit-demand CVRP in arbitrary metrics. In particular, decide whether one can substantially beat the tour-partitioning barrier, perhaps approaching the TSP ratio plus a smaller capacity-overhead term, or prove that a large additive loss over TSP is inherent.
known_results: Haimovich and Rinnooy Kan's iterated tour partitioning gives an $\alpha+1$ approximation for unit-demand CVRP, where $\alpha$ is the approximation ratio for metric TSP; Altinkemer and Gavish obtained related partitioning guarantees. This was the benchmark for about 35 years. Blauth, Traub, and Vygen prove the first improvement, obtaining $\alpha+1-\epsilon$ for an explicit positive constant, and their result applies to unit-demand CVRP, splittable CVRP, and general CVRP variants in arbitrary metrics. Hardness is much weaker and largely inherited from metric TSP, so the true threshold could be near $\alpha$, near $\alpha+1$, or somewhere between. Recent work improves other unsplittable CVRP variants, but the clean unit-demand approximability threshold remains open.

background: Capacitated vehicle routing is a fundamental routing model in operations research. In the unit-demand version, a depot and customers lie in a metric space, every customer has demand one, and each vehicle tour may visit at most $Q$ customers before returning to the depot. The classical iterated tour partitioning algorithm starts with a TSP tour and cuts it into capacity-feasible pieces, yielding ratio roughly $\alpha+1$, where $\alpha$ is the best metric-TSP approximation ratio. That guarantee stood for decades. Blauth, Traub, and Vygen gave the first improvement, shaving a fixed constant from the $\alpha+1$ bound for general, unit-demand, and splittable variants. The resulting open problem is how much of the extra $+1$ capacity loss is inherent, and whether CVRP approximability can be pushed much closer to TSP.

progress.summary: The classical $\alpha+1$ barrier has been beaten by a small constant, but no near-tight algorithmic or hardness threshold is known.

literature.synthesis: The $\alpha+1$ guarantee separates routing cost into a TSP backbone plus depot-return/capacity overhead. The Blauth-Traub-Vygen improvement shows that this decomposition is not tight in the worst case, but the improvement is small. A major challenge is to integrate capacity decisions into the tour construction rather than partition after the fact. Lower bounds are also underdeveloped: known hardness does not explain an additive $+1$ loss. Progress may come from stronger route-covering relaxations, better randomized partitioning, or hard metric families where depot-distance and intercustomer-distance terms conflict.

title: Metric Uncapacitated Facility Location: 1.463 vs. 1.488
short_statement: For metric uncapacitated facility location, the best known algorithm achieves $1.488$ while it is NP-hard to beat $1.463$. This $\approx 0.025$ gap has stood for over a decade and is one of the cleanest open problems in approximation.
full_statement: An instance of metric uncapacitated facility location has a finite set $F$ of candidate facilities, a finite set $C$ of clients, nonnegative opening costs $f_i$ for facilities $i\in F$, and connection costs $d(i,j)$ between facilities and clients. The costs are induced by a metric on $F\cup C$, so triangle inequalities hold after including facility-facility and client-client distances. A feasible solution opens a subset $S\subseteq F$ and assigns every client $j\in C$ to some open facility $i(j)\in S$, paying $\sum_{i\in S} f_i+\sum_{j\in C} d(i(j),j)$. Facilities are uncapacitated: an open facility can serve any number of clients. The open problem is to determine the exact polynomial-time approximation threshold for this standard metric UFL problem. The best known general approximation ratio is $1.488$, while the best known NP-hardness threshold is $1.463$. Closing the gap means either improving the algorithmic ratio below $1.488$, proving stronger hardness above $1.463$, or identifying a matching threshold.
known_results: Guha and Khuller established the standard $1.463$ approximability lower bound for metric facility location. Algorithmically, a long sequence of primal-dual, local-search, greedy, LP-rounding, and bifactor algorithms reduced the upper bound. Jain, Mahdian, and Saberi developed influential primal-dual and bifactor tradeoff tools; Mahdian, Ye, and Zhang improved the ratio to about $1.52$. Byrka and Aardal then gave a $1.5$ approximation by combining a modified Chudak-Shmoys LP-rounding algorithm with another bifactor algorithm and by touching the Jain-Mahdian-Saberi limit curve for connection-cost-dominated instances. Shi Li improved the guarantee to $1.488$ through a randomized scaling/bifactor combination, which remains the best known ratio for the standard centralized metric UFL problem in the sources checked here. Later work improves related variants, such as distributed, multi-level, capacitated, or penalty versions, but no source in this sweep improved the $1.488$ versus $1.463$ window for ordinary metric UFL.

background: Metric uncapacitated facility location is a foundational clustering and network-design model. Facilities have opening costs, clients must be assigned to open facilities, and connection costs form a metric. The problem is simple to state and has been a testing ground for primal-dual, LP-rounding, greedy, and bifactor approximation techniques. The best known general approximation ratio is Shi Li's $1.488$, while the best hardness is $1.463$. This narrow numerical gap has persisted for more than a decade. Its appeal is that the remaining problem is not one of modelling or asymptotics: determine the exact polynomial-time approximability threshold for a clean metric optimization problem.

progress.summary: Best known algorithmic ratio is $1.488$ and best hardness is $1.463$. No later improvement was found in this sweep.

literature.synthesis: Facility location approximation is driven by tradeoffs between opening-cost and connection-cost guarantees. A bifactor algorithm with guarantee $(\lambda_f,\lambda_c)$ controls the facility-opening part and connection part separately, and many of the best single-factor algorithms arise by combining algorithms that perform well in different regions of this two-dimensional cost plane. Byrka and Aardal's $1.5$ result shows the power of this viewpoint: their LP-rounding algorithm touches the known bifactor limit curve in the connection-cost-dominated regime and is balanced with a complementary algorithm. Shi Li's $1.488$ algorithm pushes the same broad strategy further using randomized scaling. The remaining gap is small but conceptually important. It is unclear whether the bifactor/LP-rounding framework still has room, or whether a new hardness construction can move the $1.463$ barrier upward toward $1.488$.

title: Metric k-Median: 1.736 Hardness vs. 2+epsilon Algorithm
short_statement: A 2026 research-release manuscript claims the metric $k$-median threshold $1+2/e$, via algorithms at every fixed factor above it; not independently verified here.
full_statement: In metric $k$-median, the input is a finite metric space containing a set of clients $C$, a set of candidate facilities $F$, distances $d$, and an integer $k$. The goal is to open at most $k$ facilities $S\subseteq F$ and minimize $$\sum_{j\in C} d(j,S),\qquad d(j,S)=\min_{i\in S} d(j,i).$$ Determine the optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for this problem in arbitrary metrics. The original barrier question was whether there is a $(2-\epsilon)$-approximation for some fixed $\epsilon>0$, or prove hardness approaching $2$. The standard LP relaxation has an integrality gap near $2$, so a below-$2$ algorithm would likely need a stronger relaxation or a method that escapes the usual LP barrier. OpenAI's September 24, 2026 research-release manuscript claims a deterministic $(1+2/e+\epsilon)$ approximation for each fixed $\epsilon>0$, in polynomial binary-input time, opening at most $k$ specified candidate facilities. Under $P\ne NP$, it claims the infimum is $1+2/e$, not attainment of the exact endpoint. This record flags a claimed resolution.
known_results: Historical context before the September 2026 claim: Jain, Mahdian, and Saberi prove NP-hardness below $1+2/e\approx1.736$ through the facility-location approximation framework. The natural LP relaxation has integrality gap at least $2-o(1)$, limiting direct LP rounding and Lagrangian-relaxation approaches. Before 2025, the best exactly-$k$ approximation ratio was $2.613$, with progress bottlenecked by bi-point rounding after facility-location-style algorithms. Cohen-Addad, Grandoni, Lee, Schwiegelshohn, and Svensson give a $2+\epsilon$ approximation, improving the previous best ratio by avoiding the old bi-point rounding loss and combining a phased greedy modification with a stable-instance algorithm. Thus the pre-September-2026 gap was between hardness $1.736$ and algorithms arbitrarily close to $2$, with the LP barrier suggesting but not proving that $2$ may be tight. OpenAI's September 24, 2026 research-release manuscript claims a deterministic $(1+2/e+\epsilon)$ approximation for each fixed $\epsilon>0$, in polynomial binary-input time, opening at most $k$ specified candidate facilities.

The question left by the 2025 result was whether the true threshold was near the hardness bound, near the LP barrier at $2$, or exactly at $2$. title: Graph Balancing (Restricted Two-Machine Makespan)
short_statement: Graph balancing is unrelated-machine scheduling where each job can go on only two machines (same time on either). It is NP-hard to beat $3/2$ and the best ratio is below $1.75$, but the exact threshold is open.
full_statement: Given an undirected weighted multigraph $G=(V,E)$ with edge weights $w_e\ge 0$, orient every edge toward one of its two endpoints. The load of a vertex is the total weight of edges oriented into it, and the objective is to minimize the maximum vertex load. Equivalently, each job has exactly two eligible machines, its endpoints, and processing time $w_e$ on either endpoint. Determine the best polynomial-time approximation ratio for this graph-balancing problem. In particular, does there exist a polynomial-time algorithm with guarantee strictly below $7/4$, can the nonconstructive configuration-LP/local-search bound around $1.749$ be made constructive, or is there hardness above the known $3/2$ threshold?
known_results: Ebenlendr, Krcal, and Sgall established the classical picture: graph balancing is NP-hard to approximate within any factor below $3/2$, and there is a polynomial-time $7/4$ approximation based on LP rounding and structural handling of large and small edges. This left the interval between $3/2$ and $7/4$ open. Verschae and Wiese studied configuration-LP behavior for broader unrelated-machine scheduling settings and showed that some natural relaxations still have significant gaps. Jansen and Rohwedder later proved that, for graph balancing, a configuration-LP/local-search analysis obtains an integrality-gap or estimation bound of about $1.749$, strictly below $7/4$. However, they explicitly note that polynomial-time termination of the local search is unclear, so this does not settle the existence of a polynomial-time sub-$7/4$ approximation. The open problem is to convert this evidence into an efficient algorithm, improve hardness above $3/2$, or identify the exact threshold.

background: Graph balancing is a clean special case of unrelated-machine scheduling. Jobs are edges of a weighted multigraph, machines are vertices, and assigning a job to one of its two allowed machines is orienting the edge toward that vertex. The load of a machine is the total weight of incoming edges, and the goal is to minimize maximum load. This model captures restricted two-machine choices while retaining enough structure for graph-theoretic methods. Ebenlendr, Krcal, and Sgall gave a $7/4$ approximation and $3/2$ hardness. Jansen and Rohwedder later showed that a configuration-LP/local-search approach can beat $1.75$ at the level of integrality gap or estimation, but polynomial constructive status and exact approximability remain unresolved.

The sub-$1.75$ local-search result suggests the configuration LP is stronger than earlier relaxations for this special case, but the lack of polynomial termination leaves a constructive gap. Closing the problem likely requires either a polynomial implementation of the local-search ideas or a stronger hardness construction above $3/2$.

title: Restricted Assignment Makespan (Polynomial-Time Below 2)
short_statement: In restricted-assignment makespan, each job has a fixed size and a set of allowed machines. The general $2$-approximation applies and the configuration LP estimates the optimum within $\approx 1.94$, but producing an actual schedule below $2$ in polynomial time is open.
full_statement: In restricted-assignment makespan minimization, there are machines $M$ and jobs $J$. Each job $j$ has a processing time $p_j$ and an eligibility set $M_j\subseteq M$; assigning $j$ to a machine outside $M_j$ is forbidden, equivalently $p_{ij}=\infty$, while assigning it to any eligible machine takes time $p_j$. A schedule assigns every job to one eligible machine and has makespan $\max_{i\in M}\sum_{j\text{ assigned to }i}p_j$. The Lenstra-Shmoys-Tardos rounding gives a polynomial-time factor $2$ approximation even for general unrelated machines. The open restricted-assignment problem is to construct, in polynomial time, a schedule with approximation ratio $2-\varepsilon$ for some absolute $\varepsilon>0$, or to prove that no such algorithm exists under standard assumptions. The problem remains open even though the configuration LP can estimate the optimum below factor $2$ and quasi-polynomial rounding is known.
known_results: The Lenstra-Shmoys-Tardos algorithm gives a polynomial-time $2$-approximation for unrelated-machine makespan and therefore for restricted assignment. The standard hardness barrier is $3/2$: no polynomial-time approximation below $3/2$ exists unless $P=NP$. Svensson proved that, for restricted assignment, the configuration LP has integrality gap at most $33/17\approx1.9412$, so the LP value estimates the optimum below factor $2$. Jansen and Rohwedder simplified and strengthened this analysis to $2-1/6=11/6\approx1.8333$, and their extended work gives a constructive $1.8334$-approximation in quasi-polynomial time. These results leave a precise open issue: sub-$2$ structure is present in the relaxation, but no general polynomial-time algorithm is known to turn it into a schedule. Closing this constructive gap, or proving that it cannot be closed, is the core open problem.

background: Restricted assignment is the special case of unrelated-machine makespan where each job has one processing time $p_j$ and can run on a specified subset of machines; it is forbidden elsewhere. This model captures eligibility constraints in scheduling and is much more structured than arbitrary unrelated machines. The general $2$-approximation of Lenstra-Shmoys-Tardos applies, and the problem is hard below $3/2$. Svensson showed that the configuration LP estimates the optimum within $33/17<2$, later improved and simplified by Jansen and Rohwedder to $11/6$. They also gave a quasi-polynomial constructive approximation with that ratio. What remains open is a genuinely polynomial-time algorithm that constructs a schedule with ratio below $2$.

title: Best Polynomial-Time Approximation for Restricted Santa Claus
short_statement: Restricted Santa Claus has a $4+\delta$ polynomial-time algorithm and an existential configuration-LP bound $53/15$; close the constructive gap.
full_statement: Given players $P$, resources $R$, resource values $v_r$, and desire sets $R_p\subseteq R$, find a polynomial-time algorithm that allocates every resource to at most one player and maximizes, up to approximation, $\min_{p\in P}\sum_{r\in A_p\cap R_p}v_r$. The restricted case means every acceptable resource has the same value $v_r$ for all players who desire it; unacceptable resources have value $0$. Let $OPT$ be the maximum possible minimum bundle value. Determine the infimum constant $\alpha$ for which there is a polynomial-time $\alpha$-approximation for all restricted instances. In particular, can one beat the current $4+\delta$ polynomial-time guarantee, match the best known configuration-LP existence bound $53/15$, or prove that no polynomial-time algorithm below some larger threshold exists under standard complexity assumptions?
known_results: Feige and Asadpour-Feige-Saberi established constant-factor existence results for restricted max-min allocation through configuration-LP and hypergraph-matching methods. Annamalai, Kalaitzis, and Svensson gave a polynomial-time $13$-approximation, introducing lazy updates and other devices to make local search terminate efficiently. Cheng and Mao subsequently improved polynomial-time guarantees, first to $6+\delta$ and then to $4+\delta$ for every fixed $\delta>0$; their 2019 paper also proves the stronger existential configuration-LP integrality-gap upper bound $3+21/26\approx3.808$. The lower-bound side includes the basic hardness barrier of factor $2$ for related max-min allocation formulations and the known configuration-LP lower bound of $2$. The remaining open problem is the constructive threshold: whether the $4+\delta$ algorithm can be improved, whether the newer $53/15$ existence bound can be made algorithmic, or whether a new hardness or algorithmic barrier separates efficient algorithms from the LP gap. Haxell and Szabo (SODA 2023; Combinatorica 2025), Theorem 1.1, improve the restricted configuration-LP gap to $53/15$. This is existential, not a polynomial-time allocation algorithm.

background: The restricted Santa Claus problem has two related but distinct open questions. One asks for the integrality gap of the configuration LP; the other asks for the best polynomial-time approximation algorithm. These are not the same because the strongest LP-gap proofs rely on local-search or hypergraph-matching arguments whose polynomial-time convergence is difficult. The best current polynomial-time guarantee is Cheng and Mao's $4+\delta$ approximation. Their same work improved the LP integrality-gap upper bound to about $3.808$; Haxell and Szabo subsequently reached $53/15$, showing that better allocations exist relative to the LP than current efficient algorithms can necessarily find. The open problem is to close this constructive-versus-existential gap.

title: Monotonicity in T of the tight k-unit IID prophet ratio
short_statement: For the i.i.d. prophet inequality accepting up to $k$ of $T$ values, an LP captures the tight online-to-offline ratio. Numerically the ratio decreases in $T$; the conjecture is to prove this monotonicity for general $k$, which would fully characterize the tight $k$-unit IID prophet guarantee.
full_statement: Consider the IID prophet inequality with $T$ values and capacity $k$: T values arrive i.i.d. from a distribution $\mathbf F$, and the gambler may accept up to $k$ of them online, comparing against the offline optimum. Let $\mathrm{val}(k,T)=\inf_{\mathbf F}\mathrm{ONL}/\mathrm{OFF}$ be the tight competitive ratio (online versus offline) for given $k$ and $T$, captured by a known LP (the LP of the notes without the normalization constraint). \textbf{Open:} Show that for each fixed $k$, $\mathrm{val}(k,T)$ is decreasing in $T$ (more arrivals make the gambler's task relatively harder). For $k=1$ this monotonicity was established by Correa et al. (2017); the general $k$ case is open. Proving it would fully characterize the tight $k$-unit IID prophet guarantee.
known_results: For $k=1$, Hill and Kertz identified the limiting i.i.d. prophet constant and later work by Correa, Foncea, Hoeksma, Oosterwijk, and Vredeveld gave the tight finite-horizon interpretation used in posted-price mechanisms. Jiang, Ma, and Zhang characterize the tight multi-unit ratio relative to the standard LP/fluid relaxation and show that Alaei's widely used $1-1/\sqrt{k+3}$ guarantee is not tight for $k>1$. The open monotonicity question is about the online-to-offline finite-horizon ratio captured by the LP from Will Ma's notes: numerical evidence suggests $\mathrm{val}(k,T)$ decreases in $T$ for every fixed $k$, but no proof is known beyond $k=1$.

background: The i.i.d. prophet inequality is one of the cleanest models in online selection. A decision maker observes $T$ independent draws from a known common distribution and must decide online which values to keep. In the $k$-unit version, at most $k$ values may be accepted, so the model interpolates between the classical single-choice prophet inequality and online resource allocation with a homogeneous capacity. The benchmark is the offline prophet, who sees all $T$ draws and keeps the best $k$. For $k=1$, the tight i.i.d. ratio is the Hill-Kertz constant, approximately $0.745$, and the underlying finite-horizon values are known to decrease to that limit. For larger $k$, Jiang, Ma, and Zhang show that the relevant tight ratio can be represented by an LP, but a simple structural fact remains missing: for fixed $k$, does the worst-case ratio decrease as the number of periods $T$ grows? A proof would turn a computationally defined finite-horizon family into a clean characterization of the tight $k$-unit i.i.d. prophet guarantee.

progress.summary: No general-$k$ proof of monotonicity is known in the site sources. The problem remains a finite-dimensional inequality/LP-structure question rather than a modelling question.

counterexample_rationale: For fixed small $k$ and $T$, the conjecture can be stress-tested by solving the finite LPs and searching for a monotonicity violation. A counterexample would likely be a finite certificate.
alphaevolve_rationale: An evolutionary or symbolic-search loop could look for dual certificates, reductions between adjacent horizons, or finite counterexamples. A final proof would still need a rigorous LP or coupling argument.

literature.synthesis: The single-item i.i.d. prophet inequality has a long optimal-stopping history, with the Hill-Kertz constant giving the limiting worst-case ratio and later algorithmic work connecting the same constant to posted prices. Multi-unit prophet inequalities became central because they are used as subroutines for ad allocation, appointment scheduling, and revenue-management relaxations. Jiang, Ma, and Zhang show that the tight multi-unit guarantee in Alaei's LP setting is strictly better than the classical bound, and their analysis supplies the LP objects behind Will Ma's course-note open problem. What is missing is a monotonicity theorem in the horizon $T$. Such a theorem would let one identify the worst case by passing to the infinite-horizon limit, rather than treating each $T$ separately.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Good attack routes include deriving an explicit dual for the finite-horizon LP, proving a horizon-extension coupling from $T$ to $T+1$, or finding a total-positivity/majorization property of the worst-case distribution. A computational agent should first reproduce small-$k$ LP values and inspect dual variables for a pattern.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A correct proof must compare the exact worst-case ratios for adjacent horizons at fixed $k$, not just show monotonicity for a particular policy or distribution family. A counterexample must include enough numerical precision and preferably rational LP data so the strict violation can be independently certified.

title: Online-vs-offline ratio for k-unit prophet under adversarial order (k>1)
short_statement: For adversarial-order $k$-unit prophet inequalities, determine the tight online-to-offline ratio for $k>1$, even for weighted Bernoulli distributions.
full_statement: There are $T$ independent nonnegative values $V_1,\ldots,V_T$ drawn from known distributions and revealed one by one in an adversarial order. An online algorithm may accept at most $k$ values and receives the sum of accepted values. Let $\mathrm{ONL}(F,k)$ be the value of the best online policy in the worst arrival order, and let $\mathrm{OFF}(F,k)=\mathbb{E}[\sum_{j=1}^k V_{(j)}]$ be the expected sum of the largest $k$ realized values. Jiang, Ma, and Zhang characterize tight guarantees in Alaei's multi-unit prophet framework relative to a fluid or LP benchmark, but Will Ma's open problem asks for the true online-to-offline ratio $\inf_F \mathrm{ONL}(F,k)/\mathrm{OFF}(F,k)$ for every fixed $k>1$. The problem remains open even when each $V_t$ is weighted Bernoulli, taking value $w_t$ with probability $p_t$ and $0$ otherwise. This restriction keeps the offline benchmark nontrivial, because it is the expected weighted top-$k$ value among random successes, while making the instance space discrete enough for exact search.
known_results: For $k=1$, classical prophet inequalities give tight constant-factor guarantees against the offline maximum. For $k>1$, Alaei's framework and the Jiang-Ma-Zhang refinement characterize tight ratios relative to an LP/fluid benchmark, and the paper explicitly treats multi-unit prophet inequalities as a core online allocation primitive. The same Jiang-Ma-Zhang work also gives tight LP-relative results for online stochastic knapsack. None of these LP-relative theorems automatically yields the desired online-to-offline ratio, because $\mathrm{OFF}$ is a nonlinear order-statistic benchmark, not an ex-ante capacity relaxation. The weighted-Bernoulli restriction remains open in Will Ma's notes and is a natural place to search for the exact constant or a separating example, since the offline benchmark is explicit but still captures the correlation among top-$k$ realized successes.

background: In multi-unit prophet inequalities, the benchmark matters. A fluid or ex-ante LP benchmark is often easier to analyze and composes well with downstream resource-allocation reductions, but the true offline benchmark is the expected value of the best feasible set after all random values are revealed. For one item, many of these distinctions collapse or are well understood: the classical adversarial-order prophet inequality has the tight $1/2$ flavor. For $k>1$, the offline optimum contains correlations induced by selecting the top $k$ realized values, while LP/fluid relaxations decouple ex-ante selection probabilities. Jiang, Ma, and Zhang show that the tight Alaei-style guarantees are better than the older $1-1/\sqrt{k+3}$ bound, but those guarantees do not identify the true online-to-offline constant. Will Ma's formulation asks for this missing benchmark conversion in the most basic multi-unit setting.

progress.summary: The site sources do not contain a tight bound for the online-to-offline ratio when $k>1$. The weighted-Bernoulli special case is explicitly called out as open.

links.title: Jiang, Ma, Zhang, Tight Guarantees for Multi-unit Prophet Inequalities and Online Stochastic Knapsack

counterexample_rationale: Small weighted-Bernoulli instances can be enumerated or optimized to produce upper-bound examples. Such examples would be directly useful for guessing the correct constant.
alphaevolve_rationale: This is well suited to automated search: an agent can generate small adversarial-order Bernoulli instances, solve dynamic programs for the optimal online policy, and compare to offline top-$k$ value.

literature.synthesis: The main line of progress uses LP or ex-ante relaxations to obtain clean ratios for multi-unit prophet problems, with Jiang, Ma, and Zhang giving tight guarantees in the Alaei-style setting. Those ratios are powerful for algorithms but do not automatically answer the online-to-offline question. The offline optimum is nonlinear in the realized values; for Bernoulli-valued instances it becomes a stochastic top-$k$ weighted selection problem. A plausible path is to identify the worst Bernoulli instance and prove that arbitrary distributions reduce to it by threshold decomposition, convex-order arguments, or factor-revealing LP duality. No such reduction is currently part of the site evidence.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Start with the weighted-Bernoulli case. For each small instance, compute the exact optimal online dynamic program under the worst arrival order and the exact expected offline top-$k$ value, then search for extremal patterns. For proofs, try threshold decomposition, convex-order reduction to Bernoulli distributions, or a factor-revealing LP whose dual certifies a ratio. Track carefully whether the adversarial order is fixed before or after realization.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed lower bound must be against the true offline optimum, not the fluid benchmark. A claimed upper-bound instance must specify distributions, order model, capacity $k$, and exact computations of both online and offline values. If an argument passes through the LP relaxation, it must include a separate bound relating the LP to $\mathrm{OFF}$ in the relevant direction.

open_problem: Determine the tight value of $\inf_F \mathrm{ONL}(F,k)/\mathrm{OFF}(F,k)$ for adversarial-order $k$-unit prophet inequalities when $k>1$, or prove nontrivial upper and lower bounds. Resolve the weighted-Bernoulli special case if the full distributional problem is too hard.

title: Overcoming the correlation gap for k-unit prophet under random order (k>1)
short_statement: For random-order $k$-unit prophet inequalities, beat the correlation-gap/static-threshold constant $c_k^{CG}$ for some $k>1$, or prove it is a true barrier.
full_statement: In the $k$-unit prophet secretary problem, independent values are drawn from known distributions and then presented in a uniformly random order. The online algorithm may accept at most $k$ values. Arnosti and Ma show that static threshold policies achieve the guarantee $c_k^{CG}=1-e^{-k}k^k/k!$ against the offline optimum, and that this is tight for the class of static thresholds. For $k=1$, random-order prophet inequalities can beat the corresponding static-threshold baseline $1-1/e$. In free-order variants, where the algorithm can choose the order, correlation-gap constants can also be exceeded. Will Ma's open problem asks whether random order plus adaptive decision making can beat $c_k^{CG}$ for any fixed $k>1$, or whether the static-threshold/correlation-gap value is the true optimal online-to-offline ratio for multi-unit random-order prophet inequalities.
known_results: Arnosti and Ma prove that an appropriate static threshold achieves $c_k^{CG}$ and that this guarantee is tight within the static-threshold class. Their result gives the best-known guarantee for prophet secretary with $k>1$ in the site sources, and their proof reduces the worst static-threshold behavior to extremal Bernoulli-sum calculations. For $k=1$, the static-threshold value $1-1/e$ is not optimal for random-order prophet inequalities; later work obtains better constants using more refined stopping rules. In free-order prophet settings, controlling the arrival order can also beat correlation-gap-style barriers. No general $k>1$ random-order policy with guarantee above $c_k^{CG}$, and no impossibility theorem for all adaptive policies, is recorded in the current sources.
