background: The correlation-gap constant $c_k^{CG}=1-e^{-k}k^k/k!$ appears throughout online allocation because it measures the loss from independent ex-ante rounding under a $k$-unit constraint. Static-threshold prophet-secretary policies achieve exactly this benchmark in random order, and Arnosti and Ma show that no static threshold can guarantee more. The conceptual question is whether random order contains additional power beyond this correlation-gap barrier. For $k=1$, refined random-order and sample-driven stopping techniques beat the basic $1-1/e$ threshold. For $k>1$, however, the best general guarantees in the current site sources remain pinned at $c_k^{CG}$. The difficulty is that accepting one value changes both remaining capacity and the conditional distribution of future opportunities, so single-item arguments do not lift directly.

progress.summary: Static-threshold policies are fully understood, and the conjectural barrier is known to be beatable in neighboring models such as $k=1$ random order and free order. The $k>1$ random-order case remains open.

links.title: Arnosti and Ma, static threshold guarantees

counterexample_rationale: Upper-bound instances can be searched computationally, but proving that no policy beats $c_k^{CG}$ would require quantifying over adaptive policies.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated policy search may find small improvements over static thresholds for small $k$, or evidence that simple dynamic policies fail. Certifying a universal ratio remains proof-heavy.

literature.synthesis: Arnosti and Ma isolate static thresholds as a tractable and surprisingly powerful family for prophet secretary problems. Their guarantee $c_k^{CG}$ matches the correlation-gap expression and is tight for static thresholds. The open question is whether adaptivity to the random order can exploit more information than a single fixed threshold. Single-item random-order prophet inequalities and free-order prophet inequalities show that correlation-gap constants are not always ultimate barriers. The challenge is that for $k>1$, accepting one value changes both remaining capacity and the distribution of future order statistics, making direct reductions from the $k=1$ case ineffective.

Search for factor-revealing finite distributions where every natural adaptive threshold collapses to $c_k^{CG}$. For proof attempts, look for martingale or balance identities that separate the correlation-gap loss from the random-order information gain.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed improvement must be a policy with a rigorously proved worst-case ratio above $c_k^{CG}$ for some fixed $k>1$. Numerical evidence alone is not enough, but it can guide a finite-dimensional factor-revealing proof. A lower bound must apply to all adaptive online policies, not only static thresholds.

open_problem: For some fixed $k>1$, design a random-order $k$-unit prophet policy with worst-case ratio strictly larger than $c_k^{CG}=1-e^{-k}k^k/k!$, or prove that no online policy can beat this constant.

title: The stockout-probability static-threshold conjecture
short_statement: For the $k$-unit IID prophet problem, Arnosti and Ma conjecture (and verify numerically) that setting a single static threshold so the stockout probability $\Pr[D \ge k]$ equals $\Pr[\mathrm{Pois}(k) \ge k]$ achieves the tight correlation-gap guarantee. The open problem is to prove this or find a counterexample.
full_statement: In the $k$-unit prophet secretary problem, independent nonnegative values $V_1,\ldots,V_n$ are drawn from known distributions and then revealed in a uniformly random order. A policy may accept at most $k$ realized values and seeks expected accepted value compared with the expected sum of the largest $k$ realized values. A static threshold policy fixes a number $\tau$ before arrivals and accepts the first $k$ values exceeding $\tau$. For a chosen threshold, let $D(\tau)=\sum_i \mathbf 1\{V_i\ge\tau\}$ be the random number of threshold exceedances. Arnosti and Ma prove the best possible guarantee for the class of static thresholds is $c_k^{\mathrm{CG}}=1-e^{-k}k^k/k!$. The open problem is the stronger operational conjecture from Will Ma's notes: prove or disprove that there is always an optimal static threshold satisfying the stockout-probability calibration $\mathbb P(D(\tau)\ge k)=\mathbb P(\mathrm{Pois}(k)\ge k)$, or the appropriate boundary/interpolation version when no threshold attains equality. Equivalently, show that this Poisson-stockout rule always achieves the tight $c_k^{\mathrm{CG}}$ guarantee, or give an explicit instance where it falls short.
known_results: Arnosti and Ma prove that some static threshold achieves $c_k^{\mathrm{CG}}$ and that no static threshold can guarantee more. They give two simple threshold-setting prescriptions: one chooses a threshold so that the expected number accepted is $k c_k^{\mathrm{CG}}$ and gives the optimal guarantee for every $k$; another chooses a threshold with expected exceedance count equal to $k$, which is optimal for $k>4$ but suboptimal for small $k$. Their proof relies on a Bernoulli-sum extremal inequality extending Hoeffding's 1956 theorem. The stockout-probability rule is more refined: instead of calibrating the expectation of $D(\tau)$ or the expected number accepted, it calibrates the tail event that capacity is exhausted. This rule is supported by numerical Bernoulli-optimization evidence in Will Ma's notes and is operationally appealing, but a general proof that it always attains the tight static-threshold guarantee is not known from the site sources. The problem is therefore not to recover the known existence of an optimal threshold; it is to prove that this particular stockout-tail calibration is always sufficient.

additional_refs.title: Tight Guarantees for Static Threshold Policies in the Prophet Secretary Problem

background: Static thresholds are attractive in prophet secretary problems because they are simple, distribution-aware, and robust to limited information. In the $k$-unit setting, a threshold induces a random demand $D$: the number of arrivals whose values exceed the threshold. If too few values exceed the threshold, the policy leaves capacity unused; if too many exceed it, the policy stocks out and loses some high values. Arnosti and Ma analyze this tradeoff and identify the correlation-gap constant $c_k^{\mathrm{CG}}=1-e^{-k}k^k/k!$ as the exact best guarantee attainable by static thresholds. Will Ma's course-note conjecture asks for a sharper structural statement: a particular stockout-probability rule should achieve the tight guarantee. Namely, choose the threshold so that $\mathbb{P}(D\ge k)$ matches the Poisson benchmark $\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Pois}(k)\ge k)$. This rule is natural from revenue-management intuition: tune the threshold so the chance of exhausting inventory matches the canonical Poissonized $k$-unit load. The conjecture is appealing because it would turn an optimization over threshold-induced Bernoulli sums into a one-line operational prescription.

progress.summary: The optimal static-threshold value is known, but the specific stockout-probability threshold rule remains conjectural.

links.title: Arnosti and Ma, Tight Guarantees for Static Threshold Policies

counterexample_rationale: The conjecture can be tested by finite Bernoulli-sum optimization for fixed $k$ and discretized exceedance probabilities. A counterexample would likely be explicit.
alphaevolve_rationale: This is a good target for automated inequality discovery: search over Bernoulli vectors, inspect extremizers, and try to infer a Schur-convexity or majorization certificate.

literature.synthesis: The static-threshold literature reduces a prophet-secretary policy question to understanding sums of independent Bernoulli indicators above a threshold, plus the expected excess value above the threshold. Arnosti and Ma's contribution is to optimize this reduction tightly for all $k$, recovering the correlation-gap expression $1-e^{-k}k^k/k!$. Their theorem already proves that static thresholds are fully characterized in value, so the live conjecture must be stated carefully: it is about a simple rule for choosing the threshold, not about the existence of some good threshold. The stockout conjecture asks whether the optimal threshold can be selected by matching the tail probability of filling all $k$ slots to the Poissonized benchmark. This resembles classical extremal results for Poisson-binomial sums, including Hoeffding-style theorems, but tail calibration is subtler than mean calibration. A solution likely needs an inequality showing that, among threshold-induced Bernoulli vectors with a fixed stockout probability, the reward loss is maximized by the Poisson or another explicitly controlled extremal vector.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Focus on the induced Bernoulli variables above the threshold. Search for majorization, log-concavity, or Poisson-binomial extremal inequalities that imply the reward lower bound when the stockout probability is fixed.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A proof must show the stockout-probability threshold works for every distribution and every $k$, not merely that some static threshold achieves $c_k^{\mathrm{CG}}$. The verifier should check how the proof handles thresholds at atoms, cases where $\mathbb P(D(\tau)\ge k)$ jumps over the Poisson target, and randomized/interpolated thresholds if they are allowed. A counterexample should give the value distributions or an equivalent finite-support threshold decomposition, compute the exceedance probabilities, compute the stockout-calibrated threshold, and compare its expected accepted value with the offline expected top-$k$ value. Numerical counterexamples need certified error bounds because the conjectured constant can be close to the computed ratio.

title: Guarantee 1/2 with a static threshold without randomization or cardinal values
short_statement: In the single-item prophet inequality, the $1/2$ guarantee is achievable by a deterministic static threshold, and separately knowing only ordinal (median) information. Open: can both restrictions hold at once - a static threshold guaranteeing $1/2$ using neither randomization nor cardinal values?
full_statement: Consider the single-choice prophet inequality with independent nonnegative random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_T$ and benchmark $E[\max_t X_t]$. In the classical known-distribution model, a deterministic static value threshold can guarantee one half of this benchmark. In the ordinal version from Will Ma's notes, the algorithm is given only ordered rank information, represented by a probability vector or ordered list of ranks, not the cardinal values that those ranks will later take. The algorithm must commit before seeing the online values to a deterministic static threshold specified only by an index $J$ in that rank order, with any tie-breaking rule also deterministic. After the index is chosen, the actual cardinal values consistent with the order may be set adversarially. The open problem is whether such a nonrandomized ordinal static-threshold policy can still guarantee $E[ALG]\ge \frac12 E[\max_t X_t]$ for every instance.
known_results: Samuel-Cahn proved the classic threshold comparison theorem giving the $1/2$ prophet guarantee for independent nonnegative random variables. Deterministic threshold rules can achieve $1/2$ when cardinal distributional information is available. Rubinstein, Wang, and Weinberg showed that sample-based information can recover the optimal $1/2$ guarantee in the single-choice case, while later work on sample and ordinal static thresholds shows that natural ordinal threshold classes can fall below $1/2$ in related sample models. The unresolved part of Will Ma's formulation is the simultaneous restriction: one deterministic static threshold, no randomization, and no cardinal values, under the precise adversarial cardinal-realization model in the notes. The current source sweep found neither a construction meeting all three requirements nor a separating counterexample.

additional_refs.authors: Ester Samuel-Cahn
additional_refs.title: Comparison of Threshold Stop Rules and Maximum for Independent Nonnegative Random Variables

background: The classical single-choice prophet inequality says that a gambler observing independent nonnegative values online can secure at least half of the expected maximum. This $1/2$ guarantee is robust in several separate ways. With full distributional knowledge, a deterministic static threshold suffices. With less cardinal information, median-style or ordinal approaches can also recover the half guarantee in related formulations. Will Ma's problem asks whether these two kinds of simplicity can coexist. The algorithm should commit to a deterministic threshold described only by an index in an ordered list of possible ranks, without using the actual cardinal values and without randomization. After that index is chosen, an adversary may assign the actual values consistent with the order. This matters for data-poor posted-pricing settings, where a seller may trust quantile ranks more than exact valuations. This is a small-looking question, but it probes what information the prophet inequality really needs: is the half guarantee fundamentally cardinal, fundamentally randomized, or can it be obtained by a purely ordinal deterministic threshold?

progress.summary: The separate ingredients are classical, but the combined ordinal-deterministic-static version remains open in the site sources.

counterexample_rationale: A negative answer may be witnessed by a finite ordered support and adversarial cardinal assignment. Such examples are suitable for exhaustive search over small supports.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can alternate between candidate threshold-index rules and adversarial cardinal assignments, producing either counterexamples or patterns for a proof.

literature.synthesis: Prophet inequalities often look cardinal because thresholds are expressed as values, but many proofs ultimately use quantiles, medians, or exceedance probabilities. Samuel-Cahn's threshold rule is the classical benchmark for the half guarantee. Sample-based prophet inequalities show that surprisingly little distributional information can suffice in some models, but Ezra's 2024 sample-threshold result warns that natural ordinal static threshold classes can have ratios below one half in adjacent formulations. Will Ma's formulation strips the model down to an ordinal minimax decision: pick a rank-index threshold before the actual values are known. A proof would likely identify an ordinal threshold index whose worst cardinal realization is balanced; a disproof would find a finite family where every deterministic index can be exploited.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Model the problem as a minimax game over finite ordered supports. Search for small counterexamples using linear programming over cardinal values, or try to prove that a median-like index equalizes the adversary's two failure modes.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A positive solution must use neither randomization nor actual value magnitudes and must work for every admissible ordered cardinal realization in Will Ma's model. A counterexample must show that every deterministic ordinal threshold index falls below $1/2$ after an adversarial cardinal assignment; evidence against sample-based ordinal thresholds is relevant but does not automatically settle this exact formulation.

open_problem: Decide whether a deterministic ordinal static threshold can guarantee the tight $1/2$ single-choice prophet ratio without using cardinal values or randomization.

title: Is unknown uniformly random order ever worse than worst-case known order?
short_statement: Intuitively, an algorithm facing values in unknown uniformly random order should do at least as well as facing an adversary's worst order that it is told in advance. The open question: can this ever fail for some product distribution? Resolving that it never does would derive random-order prophet inequalities from fixed-order analysis.
full_statement: Fix independent nonnegative random variables with product distribution $F=F_1\times\cdots\times F_T$ and a single-choice stopping objective. For each deterministic arrival order $\sigma$, let the algorithm know $\sigma$ in advance and choose the best policy adapted to that revealed order. This gives the value $\sup_\pi E_{V\sim F}[ALG^\pi(\sigma(V))]$. Compare this with the model in which the arrival order is a uniformly random permutation unknown to the algorithm before it commits to a policy, giving $E_\sigma E_{V\sim F}[ALG^\pi(\sigma(V))]$ optimized over order-unaware policies $\pi$. Will Ma's question asks whether unknown random order can ever be strictly worse than the worst revealed deterministic order, i.e. whether the order of $\sup_\pi$, $E_\sigma$, and $\min_\sigma$ in Equation (C.1) can create a real gap. The open problem is to prove no such product distribution exists, or exhibit a finite product distribution with a certified strict gap.
known_results: Prophet-secretary work shows that random order can improve competitive ratios relative to adversarial order in standard prophet models, with threshold-based guarantees above $1/2$ in several settings. Ezra, Feldman, Gravin, and Tang formalize the value of knowing the arrival order through the order-competitive ratio and prove tight bounds for several prophet settings and algorithm classes. Their results show that order-awareness can matter, but they do not directly settle Will Ma's sharper minimax comparison: can the expectation over unknown uniformly random order be strictly worse than the minimum over revealed deterministic orders? No counterexample or general theorem for Equation (C.1) is recorded in the current site sources.

additional_refs.title: On the Significance of Knowing the Arrival Order in Prophet Inequalities

background: Arrival order is one of the main axes along which prophet inequalities vary. In a fixed-order model, the algorithm knows the order and can tailor thresholds to it. In an adversarial-order model, a malicious order is chosen. In the random-order or prophet-secretary model, the order is uniformly random but unknown in advance. Intuition says that an unknown random order should not be worse than the worst deterministic order revealed to the algorithm: randomness should average over bad permutations rather than create a new disadvantage. Will Ma's problem asks whether this intuition is actually true for single-choice product distributions. The subtlety is that the known-order benchmark may choose a different optimal policy for each permutation, whereas the random-order algorithm must commit to one strategy before seeing the permutation. This is an interchange-of-information question rather than a new stochastic model. If the inequality always holds, random-order prophet analyses could sometimes be reduced to simpler fixed-order arguments.

progress.summary: Related order-awareness losses have been characterized in other formulations, but the exact minimax comparison in Equation (C.1) remains open.

links.title: Ezra et al., significance of knowing arrival order

counterexample_rationale: A counterexample would likely be a finite product distribution with a certified gap between two dynamic programs. Small-support search is feasible.
alphaevolve_rationale: This is a direct computational game: generate finite product distributions, compute order-aware and order-unaware optimal policies exactly, and search for a strict inequality.

literature.synthesis: Prophet-secretary results show that random arrival order can be algorithmically helpful, but they optimize a standard competitive ratio and do not compare against a worst revealed order. Recent work on arrival-order knowledge shows that order information can matter, yet Will Ma's formulation asks a more surgical minimax question. The known-order side optimizes after seeing the permutation; the random-order side optimizes before the permutation is drawn. This creates a nontrivial interchange of min, expectation, and sup. A positive result might come from convexity or a symmetrization argument showing that a randomized mixture of known-order policies can be implemented order-unaware. A negative result would identify a product distribution where policy specialization across permutations is essential.

title: Are ex-ante prophet inequalities and OCRS equivalent under oblivious adversarial order?
short_statement: Online contention resolution schemes (OCRS) and ex-ante prophet inequalities give equivalent guarantees under random and fixed order. The open question is whether the same equivalence holds under oblivious adversarial order: prove it for a general feasibility family and polytope relaxation, or give a counterexample.
full_statement: Let $N$ be a ground set and let $\mathcal F\subseteq2^N$ be a downward-closed feasibility family, such as a matroid. An ex-ante fractional point $x\in P_{\mathcal F}$ specifies activation probabilities: each element $i$ is active independently with probability $x_i$, and active elements are revealed online. An online contention resolution scheme must decide immediately whether to accept each revealed active element while maintaining an accepted set in $\mathcal F$. A scheme is $c$-selectable if every element $i$ is accepted with probability at least $c x_i$, possibly under assumptions on the arrival order. An ex-ante prophet inequality instead assigns independent values to elements and compares an online selection policy with an ex-ante relaxation that maximizes expected value subject to marginal probabilities in $P_{\mathcal F}$. Lee and Singla show that, in fixed-order and random-order models, optimal ex-ante prophet inequalities can be converted into optimal OCRSs. The open problem is whether this equivalence continues to hold when the order is chosen adversarially but obliviously to the active set and values: for every feasibility family and every target guarantee, does an ex-ante prophet inequality in the oblivious-adversarial-order model imply an OCRS with the same guarantee, and conversely?
known_results: Feldman, Svensson, and Zenklusen introduced OCRSs and showed their broad applicability to Bayesian selection, posted pricing, stochastic probing, and submodular objectives. Lee and Singla proved optimal OCRS guarantees via reductions to ex-ante prophet inequalities, including an optimal $1/2$ OCRS for matroids and a $(1-1/e)$ random-order contention-resolution scheme for matroids. Their work answers a conceptual question: prophet inequalities can be used to design optimal OCRSs, not just the other way around. However, their reductions are order-sensitive. Fixed orders and uniformly random orders are covered, while the course-note problem identifies the oblivious-adversarial-order case as unresolved. In this model the adversary chooses the order before seeing activations or values, so it is weaker than an adaptive adversary, but it can still arrange elements to stress the rounding scheme. No source-checked theorem was found that either extends the Lee-Singla equivalence to this intermediate model or gives a separating feasibility system.

additional_refs.title: Optimal Online Contention Resolution Schemes via Ex-Ante Prophet Inequalities

background: Online contention resolution schemes (OCRS) are rounding procedures for random active sets subject to feasibility constraints. They were introduced as a generic way to convert fractional solutions into online feasible selections, and they now form a bridge between prophet inequalities, stochastic probing, posted pricing, and submodular optimization. A parallel viewpoint is the ex-ante prophet inequality, where the benchmark is a relaxation that constrains each element's selection probability before values are realized. Lee and Singla showed that, in random and fixed arrival orders, optimal ex-ante prophet inequalities can be used to design optimal OCRSs. Will Ma's problem asks whether this equivalence survives under an oblivious adversarial order. This adversary chooses the order without seeing realizations, so it is weaker than an adaptive adversary but stronger than random order. The question is structural: are OCRSs and ex-ante prophet inequalities still the same object in this intermediate model, or can their guarantees diverge?

progress.summary: Equivalence is known for random and fixed orders. The oblivious-adversarial-order model remains the missing intermediate case.

links.title: Lee and Singla, ex-ante prophet inequalities and OCRS

counterexample_rationale: A separation might be witnessed by a small feasibility system and fractional point, but proving optimality of both sides for that example may be nontrivial.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can test small set systems and orders for gaps between OCRS and ex-ante values. General proofs likely require structural reductions.

literature.synthesis: OCRSs began as online analogues of offline contention resolution schemes and quickly became a unifying tool for Bayesian selection. Their role is to round independent activations while preserving marginal acceptance probabilities under online feasibility constraints. Ex-ante prophet inequalities use a value objective, but after conditioning on quantiles they often expose the same marginal-rounding structure. Lee and Singla's key insight was that ex-ante prophet inequalities can be used to obtain optimal OCRSs, reversing the earlier direction where OCRSs implied prophet inequalities. The open problem asks whether this symmetry is robust to an oblivious adversarial order. The difficulty is that ex-ante prophet policies may use value thresholds and distributional information in a way that is harder to translate into value-free selectability when the element order is worst-case but fixed independently of realizations. A positive solution would unify the two objects across the main order models. A negative solution would identify a genuinely new separation between value-aware selection and contention-resolution rounding.

Computational searches over small set systems should report exact LPs or dynamic programs for both quantities; simulation alone is not enough because small gaps may be artifacts of discretization.

title: Rank-1 OCRS selectability against an almighty adversary
short_statement: Distinguish the optimal greedy rank-1 guarantee from the broader almighty-adversary online-rule question.
full_statement: Fix a rank-1 matroid on ground set $N$, so the online algorithm may select at most one active element. Given an ex-ante feasible vector $x\in[0,1]^N$ with $\sum_i x_i\le 1$, each element $i$ is active independently with probability $x_i$. An online contention resolution scheme (OCRS) observes active elements in an order chosen by an adversary and must irrevocably decide whether to select each active element, selecting at most one. In the almighty-adversary model, the adversary sees the entire realized active set before choosing the order. A $c$-selectable OCRS must select every element $i$ with probability at least $c x_i$, or equivalently select it with conditional probability at least $c$ given that it is active. Livanos' greedy OCRS below gives a stronger guarantee than the historical $1/4$. Its optimality theorem is restricted to greedy schemes; it must not be interpreted as a lower bound against every history-dependent randomized online rule. Any broader formulation must additionally specify whether the adversary sees the algorithm's random seed or only the active set.
known_results: Livanos, 'Simple and Optimal Greedy Online Contention Resolution Schemes' (NeurIPS 2022), Theorem 1.1, gives a $1/e$-selectable greedy OCRS for rank one, improving $1/4$. Theorem 1.3 makes this optimal among greedy OCRSs. These schemes tolerate an almighty adversary; the upper bound is not stated for all history-dependent OCRSs. The familiar $1/2$ result in weaker order models must not be transferred to this model without proof.

title: An explicit k-unit OCRS achieving the correlation-gap guarantee under random order
short_statement: A new explicit random-order uniform-matroid contention-resolution scheme attains the correlation-gap guarantee.
full_statement: Consider the uniform matroid of rank $k$: each element $i$ is active independently with probability $x_i$, where $x\in[0,1]^N$ and $\sum_i x_i\le k$, and active elements arrive in uniformly random order. A random-order online contention resolution scheme must irrevocably accept or reject each active element while accepting at most $k$ elements in total. The target selectability constant is $c_k^{CG}=1-e^{-k}k^k/k!$, the same correlation-gap expression appearing in $k$-unit prophet-secretary and uniform-matroid contention resolution. Existence of a scheme at this constant can be inferred indirectly from ex-ante prophet-inequality/CRS machinery, and explicit constructions are known in special cases such as $k=1$ or offline CRS variants. The historical question asks for a direct, explicit online random-order OCRS for every $k>1$ that is $c_k^{CG}$-selectable for all feasible $x$. The new construction below reports an affirmative answer.
known_results: Dughmi, Livanos, and Nuti, 'Optimal Contention Resolution from Samples' (arXiv:2611.08673v1, November 5, 2026), Algorithm 4 and Theorem 4.1, give the explicit Almost-Greedy ROCRS attaining $c_k^{CG}=1-e^{-k}k^k/k!$. It accepts the first k-1 active elements; at the kth, a single independent Bernoulli sample controls a randomized acceptance test, otherwise the next active element is accepted. Known activation probabilities permit generating these samples internally. Theorem 4.1 states total activation mass k; Appendix C.5 handles mass at most k. Corollary 5.1 shows ordinary greedy already suffices for k>=5.

title: Tight guarantee for online knapsack (unit-density / IID): is it (1-e^{-2})/2?
short_statement: In online knapsack, items must be irrevocably accepted or rejected. For the unit-density (reward = size) and IID special cases, the best known guarantee relative to the fluid benchmark is $\approx 0.355$ and no policy beats $\approx 0.432$. The conjecture is that the tight guarantee equals $(1 - e^{-2})/2 \approx 0.432$.
full_statement: A capacity-one knapsack faces independent requests $S_t\in[0,1]$ from known, possibly heterogeneous distributions in a fixed order. On observing $S_t$, a policy accepts or rejects it irrevocably, keeping total accepted size at most one. Reward equals accepted size. Define the standard ex-ante relaxation $$UP=\sup_{0\le x_t(s)\le1}\left\{\sum_t\mathbb E[S_t x_t(S_t)]:\sum_t\mathbb E[S_t x_t(S_t)]\le1\right\}.$$ For positive UP, determine the largest universal ratio of expected online reward to UP. The reviewed lower and upper bounds are $0.3557$ and $(1-e^{-2})/2$. This is not the ratio to the expected offline integral optimum.
known_results: Jiang, Ma, and Zhang, arXiv:2107.02058v4, Section 5.2, give the $0.3557$ unit-density guarantee relative to the standard ex-ante LP. Proposition 3 bounds that LP-relative guarantee by $(1-e^{-2})/2$. Their Section 2.5 explicitly distinguishes a $1/2$ guarantee against offline packing for a single knapsack. Thus the quoted smaller constants concern LP rounding, not an IID-only model or the offline benchmark. The broader arbitrary reward/size model has the separate tight LP-relative constant $1/(3+e^{-2})$.

title: An L-sparse network revenue management guarantee interpolating in starting capacity
short_statement: Find a competitive guarantee for $L$-sparse network revenue management that degrades like $1/(1+L)$ at unit capacity but tends to $1$ as the minimum capacity grows.
full_statement: Consider an online network revenue management instance with resources $i=1,\ldots,m$, integer starting capacities $b_i\ge k$, and customer types arriving over a finite horizon in an adversarially chosen order from known independent distributions. Serving type $t$ yields reward $r_t\ge 0$ and consumes a vector $a_t\in\{0,1\}^m$ with support size at most $L$. Decisions are irrevocable and must respect the remaining capacities. Let $\mathrm{FLU}$ be the standard fluid/ex-ante LP relaxation that chooses expected acceptances subject to expected resource consumptions at most $b_i$. Determine the best possible function $\gamma(L,k)$ such that every $L$-sparse instance admits an online policy with expected reward at least $\gamma(L,k)\,\mathrm{FLU}$. The desired bound should recover the known small-capacity scale $\gamma(L,1)=\Omega(1/(1+L))$ and satisfy $\gamma(L,k)\to 1$ as $k\to\infty$ for each fixed $L$.
known_results: For adversarial arrival order and small capacities, a $1/(1+L)$-type guarantee is known from the prophet-inequality/online-rounding analysis in Will Ma's notes, and a folklore upper bound of order $2/(1+L)$ indicates that linear dependence on $L$ cannot be avoided at unit capacity. Amil, Makhdoumi, and Wei prove asymptotically optimal guarantees for related multi-item order-fulfillment and network revenue-management models when the retailer has sufficiently large inventory; their SSRN abstract states that the method gives new asymptotically optimal bounds for NRM. The open gap is non-asymptotic: no sharp finite-capacity expression is known that smoothly connects the $1/(1+L)$ regime with the asymptotic ratio $1$.

background: Network revenue management is one of the standard places where prophet-inequality ideas enter operations research. A firm has several reusable or consumable resources, customer types arrive online, and accepting a request consumes a vector of capacities. The usual fluid relaxation is tractable and often gives the right first-order benchmark, but online rounding loses value because accepting one customer can block future customers that need overlapping resources. The $L$-sparse case is a clean structural restriction: every product uses at most $L$ resources. It interpolates between single-resource stochastic knapsack and genuinely networked allocation, while still retaining a simple combinatorial parameter. In adversarial order, the canonical guarantee scales like $1/(1+L)$, and examples show that dependence on $L$ is not an artifact when capacities are small. On the other hand, large-capacity asymptotics are much more favorable. Amil, Makhdoumi, and Wei connect multi-item order fulfillment and network revenue management to prophet inequalities and prove asymptotic optimality once the minimum starting capacity is large. The open problem is to bridge these regimes with a single bound depending on both sparsity $L$ and minimum capacity $k$.

progress.summary: The endpoint regimes are understood: a sparse adversarial-order guarantee exists at the $1/(1+L)$ scale, and large-capacity asymptotic optimality is known. The missing result is a finite-capacity guarantee with explicit dependence on both $L$ and $k$.

literature.synthesis: This problem sits between single-resource online stochastic knapsack and high-dimensional online resource allocation. Classical NRM policies often analyze asymptotic regimes in which capacities scale, while prophet-inequality and OCRS methods give non-asymptotic constants relative to fluid relaxations. The $L$-sparse model is attractive because the resource interaction graph is limited by support size rather than by the number of resources. Existing guarantees establish the two natural endpoints: for small capacities, online rounding loses a factor depending linearly on $L$; for large capacities, Amil, Makhdoumi, and Wei's method-based formulation and prophet-inequality connection yields asymptotic optimality for multi-item fulfillment and new NRM bounds. The missing theorem would likely require a capacity-aware contention-resolution scheme that tracks not only whether a resource is scarce but how many sparse conflicts remain.

Coupling to independent per-resource contention schemes is tempting, but the main difficulty is preserving joint feasibility across overlapping supports.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed guarantee must specify the arrival-order model, the benchmark $\mathrm{FLU}$, and a policy that is implementable online. A verifier should check that the proof works for all $m$, all $L$-sparse incidence patterns, and finite $k$, not just under asymptotic scaling.

title: Any nonzero guarantee for the most general L-sparse knapsack
short_statement: For online stochastic knapsack where each request consumes fractional amounts of at most $L$ resources, obtain any positive adversarial-order guarantee relative to the fluid relaxation.
full_statement: There are resources $i=1,\ldots,m$, each with normalized capacity $1$. Request $t$ arrives online in an adversarially chosen order. Conditional on arrival, its reward $r_t\ge0$ and consumption vector $s_t\in[0,1]^m$ are drawn from known distributions, with support size $|\{i:s_{ti}>0\}|\le L$. The algorithm observes the realized reward and consumption vector and must irrevocably accept or reject the request; accepted requests must satisfy $\sum_{t\in A}s_{ti}\le1$ for every resource $i$. Let $\mathrm{FLU}$ be the ex-ante fluid LP that fractionally accepts types or realizations subject to expected capacity constraints. For every fixed sparsity $L$, does there exist a constant $c_L>0$ and an online policy with expected reward at least $c_L\mathrm{FLU}$ for all such instances? The target would ideally recover the tight single-resource constant $c_1=1/(3+e^{-2})$ from Jiang, Ma, and Zhang and degrade gracefully with $L$.
known_results: For $L=1$, Jiang, Ma, and Zhang give the tight LP-relative guarantee $1/(3+e^{-2})\approx0.319$ for general online stochastic knapsack. Their best-fit magician selects feasible sample paths with the most capacity already used and maintains a utilization invariant; they also prove an upper bound showing the constant is tight for the standard LP. For unit-density and other special cases, better or different constants are known, and multi-resource appointment-scheduling applications can exploit additional structure. For binary or unit-demand sparse allocation models, guarantees depending on sparsity can be obtained by other prophet/OCRS techniques. These results do not cover arbitrary fractional consumption vectors supported on up to $L$ resources, where one request may be best-fit for one resource and damaging for another. No positive constant for the full $L>1$ model is recorded in the current site sources.

background: The most general $L$-sparse online knapsack model allows each accepted request to consume fractional amounts of several resources. This is much harder than unit-demand or binary sparse network revenue-management models, because a request can partially fill several capacities and thereby create many different residual-capacity states. The case $L=1$ is already the online stochastic knapsack problem: requests arrive online, sizes are realized from known distributions, and the algorithm must decide immediately whether to accept. Jiang, Ma, and Zhang resolved the best possible LP-relative guarantee for this single-resource benchmark by giving a best-fit magician with ratio $1/(3+e^{-2})\approx0.319$ and proving tightness with respect to the standard LP relaxation. The multi-resource $L>1$ version is a clean next step: the model is formal, the fluid benchmark is standard, and sparsity is the only structural handle.

progress.summary: The single-resource case is tight at $1/(3+e^{-2})$. No comparable nonzero guarantee is known for arbitrary fractional $L$-sparse consumptions when $L>1$.

links.title: Jiang, Ma, Zhang, tight online stochastic knapsack guarantee

counterexample_rationale: If a proposed constant or policy is wrong, small discretized multi-resource knapsack instances may expose it. Exhaustive dynamic programming can evaluate optimal online policies for small state spaces.
alphaevolve_rationale: This is a strong candidate for automated search: residual-capacity states are finite after discretization, and both hard instances and policy rules can be optimized computationally before proof.

literature.synthesis: Jiang, Ma, and Zhang show that the single-resource setting has a clean best-fit structure: to preserve enough room for future large items, the policy deliberately fills capacity on selected paths as much as possible, and the tight constant follows from a utilization invariant. Moving to $L$-sparse fractional consumptions breaks the one-dimensional ordering of residual capacity. A request can be best-fit on one resource and worst-fit on another, and scarce resources may be correlated through shared requests. Known sparse NRM guarantees handle binary resource incidence, while general online stochastic knapsack handles fractional sizes for one resource. The open problem asks for a synthesis of these two theories: a multi-dimensional contention-resolution scheme that maintains enough residual slack across all sparse supports to obtain any LP-relative constant.

A claimed algorithm that assumes unit-density, binary sizes, independent resource decomposition, or random arrival order does not solve this problem. A counterexample must compare against the fluid LP used in the statement.

open_problem: Prove that every fixed $L$ admits a positive constant $c_L$ for adversarial-order online stochastic knapsack with arbitrary fractional $L$-sparse consumptions, or construct instances showing that no such LP-relative constant is possible.

title: Does the 1-1/e matroid random-order guarantee extend to abstract online resource allocation?
short_statement: Does the optimal $(1-1/e)$ random-order matroid CRS guarantee extend from matroids to the abstract online resource-allocation model used in stochastic allocation and NRM?
full_statement: Let an online resource-allocation instance have a finite horizon $T$, request types arriving either IID from a known distribution or as a uniformly random permutation of a known multiset, and for each realized request type a finite set of feasible actions. Taking an action yields reward and consumes a vector of resources with capacities $B_1,\ldots,B_d$; the online policy observes the request and must choose an action or reject irrevocably while keeping realized resource consumption feasible. Let $\mathrm{FLU}$ be the natural ex-ante/fluid LP that fractionally assigns type-action pairs subject to expected capacity constraints and obtains the corresponding expected reward. In the special case where the feasible accepted sets form a matroid, Lee and Singla's random-order contention-resolution scheme gives the optimal guarantee $1-1/e$ relative to the ex-ante benchmark. The open problem asks whether every instance in the broader abstract online resource-allocation model admits an online policy with expected reward at least $(1-1/e)\mathrm{FLU}$ under IID or random arrival order. If the answer is no, determine the best universal constant and identify the structural property separating matroid-like instances from harder resource-allocation instances.
known_results: Kleinberg and Weinberg introduced matroid prophet inequalities with constant guarantees, and OCRSs were later developed as a general online rounding framework for stochastic selection problems. Lee and Singla designed optimal OCRSs via ex-ante prophet inequalities: an optimal $1/2$ OCRS for adversarial-order matroids and an optimal $(1-1/e)$ random-order contention-resolution scheme for matroids. The $1-1/e$ constant is best possible even for rank one, so the matroid random-order theory is tight. Online stochastic knapsack and multi-unit prophet problems show that LP-relative constants can be characterized for some resource-allocation subcases, but those models do not cover arbitrary type-action systems with multiple resources and non-matroid feasibility. No source checked here proves or refutes the full extension from random-order matroids to Will Ma's abstract resource-allocation model.

background: Random-order contention resolution is one of the places where matroid structure gives an unusually clean constant. In a matroid, an ex-ante feasible fractional vector can be rounded online while preserving feasibility as elements arrive. Lee and Singla prove an optimal $1/2$ OCRS for adversarial order and an optimal $(1-1/e)$ random-order contention-resolution scheme for matroids. This constant is tight already for rank one, so the matroid theory is, in that sense, complete. Online resource allocation is broader: a request can consume a vector of resources, may have several feasible assignment options, and the feasible family is not necessarily a matroid even though it is still described by a clean ex-ante relaxation. Will Ma's notes isolate an abstract online resource-allocation model that includes several NRM and stochastic matching formulations. The open problem asks whether the random-order $1-1/e$ phenomenon is really a matroid artifact or a more general consequence of IID/random arrivals plus ex-ante feasibility.

progress.summary: The matroid version is tight at $1-1/e$, and the adversarial-order matroid OCRS is tight at $1/2$. No published result found extends the random-order $1-1/e$ guarantee to the full abstract resource-allocation model.

counterexample_rationale: A negative answer could plausibly be witnessed by a small resource-allocation instance whose optimal online value is below $(1-1/e)$ times the fluid LP. Such instances are finite and searchable after discretization.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can compare optimal online dynamic programs against the fluid LP for small non-matroid resource-allocation systems and test whether $1-1/e$ is plausible beyond matroids.

literature.synthesis: The strongest existing theorem is matroid-specific. Lee and Singla reduce optimal OCRSs to ex-ante prophet inequalities and obtain the optimal $1/2$ adversarial-order matroid OCRS plus the optimal $(1-1/e)$ random-order CRS. The proof exploits matroid exchange and rank structure. In broader online resource allocation, ex-ante LPs are still central, but feasibility comes from capacities and assignment options rather than a hereditary matroid family. Single-resource stochastic knapsack results show that even one-dimensional capacity can have tight constants below $1-1/e$ in adversarial order; random/IID order may help, but it is unclear whether it restores the matroid constant. The open problem is therefore structural: either find a resource-allocation CRS with the same correlation-gap-style behavior, or construct a non-matroid allocation instance where the fluid LP overstates what random-order online policies can achieve.

agent_guidance.verification_notes: A proof must define the abstract resource-allocation model precisely: request process, known distributions or random-order multiset, action sets, reward/consumption feedback, resource capacities, and stopping rule when a resource is exhausted. The guarantee must be relative to the same ex-ante/fluid LP benchmark used in the statement, not a weaker prophet benchmark or an LP with additional valid inequalities. A positive result must handle general action-resource systems, not only matroids, rank-one constraints, single-resource knapsack, or independently activated elements. A negative result should give a finite instance, compute or certify $\mathrm{FLU}$, and upper-bound the value of every online policy under the stated IID/random-order model. Claims for adversarial order should be labeled separately because the constant can be different.

title: A strongly polynomial algorithm for linear programming (Smale's 9th problem)
short_statement: Does every linear program admit a strongly polynomial algorithm, with operation count bounded polynomially in only the number of variables and constraints?
full_statement: Given a rational linear program, for example $\min\{c^\top x: Ax \ge b\}$ with $A \in \mathbb{Q}^{m \times n}$, $b \in \mathbb{Q}^m$, and $c \in \mathbb{Q}^n$, decide feasibility and, when bounded, return an optimal solution. Is there an algorithm whose number of arithmetic operations is bounded by $\operatorname{poly}(m,n)$ and whose intermediate numbers have bit length polynomial in the input bit length? Equivalently, can general LP be solved in strongly polynomial time rather than merely weakly polynomial time?
known_results: Khachiyan's ellipsoid method and Karmarkar/interior-point methods give weakly polynomial algorithms. Tardos (1986) gave strongly polynomial algorithms for LPs whose constraint matrix has small integral entries, covering many combinatorial optimization problems. Fixed-dimensional LP and several structured network and matrix classes are also strongly polynomial. Modern work by Dadush, Huiberts, Natura, and Vegh gives scaling-invariant algorithms whose complexity depends on geometric condition measures of the constraint matrix, which is important progress but still not a general strongly polynomial bound. As of 2026, the unrestricted problem remains open.

where_posed.text: Listed as Smale's ninth problem in Steve Smale, 'Mathematical Problems for the Next Century', The Mathematical Intelligencer, 1998.

background: Linear programming is one of the core algorithmic models of Operations Research: production planning, flows, matching, auctions, statistical estimation, and many relaxations for hard discrete problems are all expressed as LPs. The ellipsoid method and interior-point methods show that LP is solvable in time polynomial in the input bit length, but this is a weakly polynomial guarantee. A strongly polynomial algorithm would use a number of arithmetic operations polynomial only in the numbers of variables and constraints, and would keep intermediate numbers under polynomial bit control. This distinction matters because LP is also the canonical test case for whether continuous optimization admits a genuinely combinatorial complexity theory. Many special LP families have strongly polynomial algorithms, and Tardos's framework explains why bounded-coefficient combinatorial LPs behave better than arbitrary rational LPs. Smale listed the general problem as one of his mathematical problems for the next century. Despite decades of progress in scaling, conditioning, and interior-point methods, no algorithm is known whose worst-case complexity removes all dependence on coefficient magnitudes or condition numbers.

progress.summary: Special structured LPs have strongly polynomial algorithms, and recent condition-based algorithms reduce the role of data scaling. The remaining open problem is the fully general LP with no condition-number or coefficient-size dependence in the arithmetic count.

links.title: A scaling-invariant algorithm for linear programming whose running time depends only on the constraint matrix

counterexample_rationale: This is an algorithm-existence problem for an infinite class of LP instances. A finite counterexample can refute a proposed algorithm or pivot rule, but cannot by itself resolve the general existence question.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search might discover hard families for candidate algorithms, improved scaling rules, or low-dimensional geometric gadgets. A full solution would still require a proof of a global polynomial bound or a formal lower-bound framework.

literature.synthesis: The main positive line is to identify LP families whose arithmetic complexity is controlled by combinatorial structure rather than coefficient size. Tardos's bounded-coefficient framework remains the most influential strongly polynomial theorem for broad combinatorial LP classes. Interior-point and ellipsoid algorithms solve general LP in weakly polynomial time, but their iteration and bit-complexity analyses still depend on input encoding or conditioning. Dadush, Huiberts, Natura, and Vegh developed a scaling-invariant approach whose running time depends on the constraint matrix through geometric condition measures; this clarifies why some numerical instances are tractable, but it does not eliminate all instance-geometry dependence. The remaining gap is therefore very crisp: no known method gives a $\operatorname{poly}(m,n)$ arithmetic bound for arbitrary rational LP, and no lower-bound theory rules such an algorithm out.

The open part is not polynomial-time solvability of LP, but the removal of all dependence on numerical magnitudes, encoding length, or condition measures from the iteration count.

title: A polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method
short_statement: Is there a simplex pivot rule that always reaches an optimal LP vertex in polynomially many pivots?
full_statement: Consider a linear program $\max\{c^Tx:Ax=b,x\ge0\}$, or an equivalent inequality form, with $m$ constraints and $n$ variables. Assume first that the feasible polyhedron is nondegenerate, so every basic feasible solution is a vertex and every simplex pivot moves along one improving edge to an adjacent vertex. A pivot rule is an efficiently computable rule that, from the current basis/tableau and the input data, chooses an entering variable and a leaving variable whenever the current basis is not optimal. The question is whether there exists a deterministic pivot rule with worst-case pivot count $\operatorname{poly}(m,n)$ for every linear program, or a randomized pivot rule with expected pivot count $\operatorname{poly}(m,n)$ against an appropriate adversarial model. A complete answer must also handle degeneracy, either directly or through a perturbation/lexicographic rule whose bit complexity and pivot count remain polynomial. The open problem is about simplex paths and pivot rules, not about linear programming solvability by ellipsoid or interior-point methods.
known_results: Klee and Minty showed exponential behavior for Dantzig's rule on deformed cubes, establishing that the practical success of simplex is not explained by the most classical worst-case rule. Bland's rule prevents cycling, but it is not polynomial and belongs to a family of rules for which exponential lower bounds are known. Random-Facet and the Kalai/Matousek-Sharir-Welzl line of randomized simplex algorithms achieve subexponential expected bounds, roughly of the form $\exp(O(\sqrt{n\log n}))$, which is the strongest general positive evidence for pivoting but still far from polynomial. A long sequence of lower-bound constructions now covers many deterministic, randomized, and history-based rules, including Zadeh's least-entered rule and combinations of classical rules; some earlier claimed Random-Facet lower-bound transfers required errata, so the precise rule model matters. Santos disproved the original Hirsch conjecture, showing that linear diameter is false, but polynomial diameter and polynomial pivot-rule complexity are distinct questions. As of the source check, no efficiently computable pivot rule is known with a polynomial worst-case or expected number of pivots for all linear programs.

where_posed.text: The modern problem traces to Klee-Minty worst-case examples and the subsequent simplex complexity literature; it is commonly posed as the question of a polynomial-time simplex variant.

background: The simplex method is the workhorse algorithm of linear programming in practice. It moves along vertices of the feasible polyhedron, improving the objective at each pivot until an optimum is reached. Its practical speed contrasts sharply with worst-case examples: the Klee-Minty cubes show that natural pivot rules can take exponentially many steps. The open question is not whether LP is polynomial-time solvable, since ellipsoid and interior-point methods already establish that, but whether the simplex method itself has a pivot rule with a worst-case polynomial number of pivots. This sits between geometry and algorithms. A polynomial pivot rule would imply that every LP has a short efficiently navigable monotone path to optimality under that rule; conversely, lower bounds for many rules show that local improvement can be trapped by carefully constructed polyhedra. The problem is also tied to polytope diameter questions: small diameter is necessary but not sufficient, because the simplex path must be found by a rule using local information.

progress.summary: Many natural pivot rules have exponential or superpolynomial lower bounds, while randomized rules give subexponential upper bounds. These results narrow the plausible rule families but leave the central polynomial-pivot question open.

links.title: Random-Facet simplex algorithms on combinatorial cubes

counterexample_rationale: For any proposed concrete pivot rule, a finite family of LPs can refute a claimed polynomial bound. Search over small polytopal gadgets may help construct lower-bound instances for candidate rules.
alphaevolve_rationale: Evolutionary search can explore LP/tableau gadgets that force long paths for a proposed rule, or discover potentials for new rules. It is especially useful for refuting candidate rules before attempting a proof.

literature.synthesis: The literature has two complementary strands. Lower-bound constructions start with Klee-Minty cubes and now cover many natural deterministic, randomized, and history-based pivoting strategies, showing that local improvement rules can be forced into very long monotone paths. Modern constructions often pass through unique-sink orientations, parity games, or policy-iteration gadgets before translating back to linear programs. Upper-bound work shows that randomization helps: Random-Facet and related algorithms obtain subexponential pivot counts, far better than exponential but still not polynomial. Geometric diameter results provide necessary background, but the simplex question is sharper because a pivot rule must identify a good monotone path using information available along the run. The remaining gap is not a missing polynomial-time LP algorithm; it is the absence of either a polynomial pivoting rule or a lower-bound theorem broad enough to explain why all efficiently computable simplex rules must fail.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: For lower bounds, encode pivot dynamics as games or gadgets and search for compositions that force long paths. For positive work, look for nonlocal pivot rules with a potential that falls by an inverse-polynomial fraction per pivot, possibly borrowing interior-point geometry.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A lower-bound submission must define the pivot rule exactly, specify whether the construction is an actual linear program, an oriented matroid, or an abstract unique-sink orientation, and prove the claimed path length on an infinite family. A lower bound for an abstract cube or for a restricted implementation of a rule should not be advertised as a lower bound for all LP pivot rules unless the reduction is explicit. A positive submission must prove that the rule is efficiently computable, that it chooses valid improving pivots, and that its pivot count is polynomial for all inputs. Degeneracy cannot be ignored: either prove the result for degenerate LPs or supply a perturbation/lexicographic implementation with controlled bit complexity and no hidden exponential sequence of degenerate pivots.

open_problem: Find a polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method, or prove that no rule in a well-defined broad class can have a polynomial worst-case pivot bound. The unresolved part is the existence of any efficiently computable rule with polynomial pivot count, not the polynomial-time solvability of LP by other methods.

title: The Polynomial Hirsch Conjecture
short_statement: Santos disproved the original linear Hirsch bound, but it remains open whether every polytope has graph diameter bounded by a polynomial in its facets and dimension.
full_statement: Let $P\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a convex polytope described by $n$ facet inequalities, and let $G(P)$ be its vertex-edge graph. The combinatorial diameter $\delta(P)$ is the maximum, over pairs of vertices of $P$, of the shortest-path distance between them in $G(P)$. Hirsch's original conjecture asserted the linear bound $\delta(P)\le n-d$, and Santos disproved it. The polynomial Hirsch problem asks for the surviving qualitative version: does there exist an absolute constant $c$ and a polynomial $p(n,d)$, for example $(nd)^c$ or $n^c d^c$, such that every $d$-dimensional polytope with $n$ facets satisfies $\delta(P)\le p(n,d)$? Equivalently, can the current quasipolynomial/subexponential upper bounds be improved to polynomial, or can one construct an explicit family of polytopes whose graph diameters grow superpolynomially in the natural input parameters?
known_results: Santos disproved the original Hirsch conjecture with a 43-dimensional polytope having 86 facets and diameter larger than $n-d$, and his construction also yields linear-factor violations in related families. Kalai and Kleitman proved the foundational quasipolynomial upper bound for polyhedron diameter; Todd improved the form to approximately $(n-d)^{\log_2 d}$, and later refinements improve exponents in some ranges without reaching polynomial. Polynomial or linear bounds are known for special classes, including low dimension, some 0/1-polytopes, and other structured families. General lower bounds remain only linear or mildly super-Hirsch, far below quasipolynomial. Thus both sides are open: no polynomial upper bound is known, and no superpolynomial lower-bound family is known.

where_posed.text: The polynomial version is the surviving form of the Hirsch diameter problem after Santos's counterexample to the linear bound.

additional_refs.title: An improved Kalai–Kleitman bound for the diameter of a polyhedron

background: The graph of a polytope is the state space traversed by simplex-type algorithms: vertices are basic feasible solutions, and edges are pivots. Warren Hirsch conjectured in 1957 that a $d$-dimensional polytope with $n$ facets has graph diameter at most $n-d$. Such a bound would have been a clean geometric explanation for short paths through feasible regions of linear programs. Santos disproved the original conjecture by constructing a 43-dimensional polytope with 86 facets and diameter exceeding $n-d$. That counterexample is fundamental, but it does not imply long simplex paths of superpolynomial length, nor does it rule out a larger polynomial diameter bound. The polynomial Hirsch conjecture is therefore the key residual geometric question: are all polytope graphs polynomial-diameter objects, or can high-dimensional polyhedral geometry force truly superpolynomial shortest paths?

progress.summary: The original linear Hirsch conjecture is false. The best general upper bounds remain quasipolynomial/subexponential, while known lower bounds do not approach superpolynomial growth. The polynomial gap remains fully open.

links.title: A counterexample to the Hirsch conjecture

counterexample_rationale: A superpolynomial explicit family would refute the conjecture, and finite high-diameter candidates can be searched and verified computationally. Proving asymptotic superpolynomial growth, or a general polynomial upper bound, remains a mathematical proof task.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can explore spindle constructions, wedge operations, oriented matroids, and small polytope families with unusually large graph diameter. Candidate families still require rigorous realization and asymptotic diameter proofs.

literature.synthesis: The linear Hirsch conjecture failed, but known counterexamples are still far from refuting polynomial diameter. The upper-bound side descends from the Kalai-Kleitman recurrence and its improvements: these bounds are dramatically better than exponential but remain quasipolynomial in the relevant parameters. The lower-bound side has not produced a superpolynomial family; known constructions show that the Hirsch constant is false, not that polytope graphs can be extremely long. A solution therefore needs either a new global geometric/combinatorial argument giving polynomial diameter, or a construction method that amplifies local non-Hirsch behavior into genuine superpolynomial diameter while preserving realizability as convex polytopes.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: For a disproof, search for structured families of spindles, wedge constructions, abstract polytopes, or oriented matroids with provably growing graph diameter, then verify realizability. For a proof, study separator-type arguments, recurrence inequalities stronger than Kalai-Kleitman, randomized shadow-vertex geometry, expansion properties of polytope graphs, and special classes that might admit bootstrapping.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A counterexample to the original Hirsch bound is not enough; a disproof must give an infinite family with superpolynomial diameter in the chosen parameters and prove the family is realizable as convex polytopes. A positive proof must apply to arbitrary convex polytopes or state a restricted class. Claims about simplex pivot rules do not by themselves settle polynomial Hirsch, because graph diameter and algorithmic pivot length are related but not identical.

open_problem: Prove a polynomial upper bound on the graph diameter of every convex polytope in terms of facets and dimension, or construct an explicit superpolynomial-diameter family of polytopes that disproves the polynomial Hirsch conjecture.

title: A strongly polynomial algorithm for Markov decision processes
short_statement: Is there a strongly polynomial algorithm for general finite discounted MDPs when the discount factor is part of the input?
full_statement: Let an MDP have finite state set $S$, finite action sets $A(s)$, rational rewards $r(s,a)$, rational transition probabilities $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$, and discount factor $\gamma\in(0,1)$ given as part of the input. A stationary deterministic policy chooses one action in each state, inducing a value vector $v^\pi$ satisfying $v^\pi=r^\pi+\gamma P^\pi v^\pi$; an optimal policy maximizes $v^\pi$ componentwise and can be found by solving the associated Bellman optimality equations or an LP. Weakly polynomial algorithms exist through linear programming and dynamic programming. The open problem asks for a strongly polynomial algorithm: an algorithm whose number of arithmetic operations is bounded by a polynomial in the number of states $n=|S|$ and total actions $m=\sum_s |A(s)|$, independent of the bit lengths of rewards/probabilities and independent of the numerical size of $1/(1-\gamma)$, with intermediate numbers controlled in the usual strongly-polynomial sense. Equivalently, can the special LP structure of discounted stochastic MDPs be exploited to avoid any pseudo-polynomial dependence as $\gamma\to1$?
known_results: Ye (2011) proved polynomial iteration bounds for Howard policy iteration and the simplex method for discounted MDPs with a fixed discount factor; more precisely, the bounds scale polynomially in $n,m$ and in quantities such as $1/(1-\gamma)$, so they are strongly polynomial only when the discount factor is treated as a fixed constant. Hansen, Miltersen, and Zwick improved and extended fixed-discount strategy-iteration analysis to two-player turn-based stochastic games, again with explicit dependence on $1/(1-\gamma)$. Post and Ye proved a genuinely strongly polynomial simplex bound for deterministic MDPs independent of the discount factor, using layered progress/milestone arguments; their result covers deterministic transitions, not general stochastic transition matrices. General finite discounted MDPs with stochastic transitions and input discount factor remain open. The average-reward/undiscounted limiting regime is closely related because hard behavior may appear as $\gamma$ approaches one.

where_posed.text: Explicitly discussed in Ye's work on simplex and policy iteration for MDPs, where the fixed-discount result is contrasted with the open input-discount case.

background: Finite Markov decision processes are the dynamic-programming analogue of linear programming: a finite set of states, a finite set of actions, transition probabilities, and rewards define an optimal control problem. Discounted MDPs can be solved by value iteration, policy iteration, or LP formulations, and these methods are fundamental in OR, reinforcement learning, and stochastic control. Complexity becomes delicate when the discount factor $\gamma$ approaches one. A bound polynomial in $1/(1-\gamma)$ is useful for fixed discount, but it is not strongly polynomial when $\gamma$ is part of the input. Ye proved a strong polynomiality result for fixed $\gamma$, and Post and Ye later obtained strongly polynomial simplex bounds for deterministic MDPs independent of the discount factor. The general stochastic case remains unresolved and is closely connected to whether special LP structure can be exploited more deeply than in arbitrary linear programming.

progress.summary: The deterministic case is strongly polynomial, and fixed-discount stochastic MDPs have polynomial iteration bounds. The unresolved gap is stochastic transitions with discount factor encoded in the input or average-reward limiting behavior.

links.title: The simplex method is strongly polynomial for deterministic Markov decision processes

counterexample_rationale: Finite MDPs can refute proposed policy-iteration bounds or reveal exponential behavior for a specific rule. They cannot by themselves rule out all possible strongly polynomial algorithms.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search over small stochastic MDPs is well suited for finding hard instances for policy iteration, value-iteration variants, and LP pivot rules. Candidate counterexamples can be verified exactly using rational arithmetic.

literature.synthesis: Known results show a sharp divide between fixed-discount or deterministic structure and the fully stochastic input-discount case. Ye's analysis gives polynomial iteration bounds for Howard policy iteration and simplex when the discount factor is fixed, but the dependence on $1/(1-\gamma)$ is exactly what prevents a strongly polynomial theorem for input discounts near one. Post and Ye remove the discount dependence for deterministic MDPs by exploiting the structure of deterministic transitions: the induced policy graph has cycles and paths whose primal/dual values move through a polynomial number of layers or milestones. In stochastic MDPs, transition matrices mix states, values can change gradually, and the deterministic graph-layer argument no longer applies. A solution could come from a new progress measure for policy iteration, a different combinatorial algorithm for the Bellman inequalities, or a reduction to a special LP class with known strongly polynomial algorithms. A negative result for a specific policy-iteration rule would be useful but would not rule out all strongly polynomial algorithms.

agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed algorithm must handle arbitrary rational stochastic transition probabilities and discount factors supplied as part of the input. The operation count must be polynomial in state/action counts and not merely polynomial in $1/(1-\gamma)$ or the input bit length. If the result is for a pivot rule or policy-iteration rule, verify that the rule is exactly specified and that the proof bounds policy changes uniformly over all reward and transition encodings. Counterexamples to a named rule should distinguish exponential dependence on $1/(1-\gamma)$ from exponential dependence on $n,m$; such counterexamples refute that rule but not the existence of some other strongly polynomial algorithm. Average-reward or deterministic-transition results should be clearly labeled as special cases.

open_problem: Give a strongly polynomial algorithm for general discounted MDPs with input discount factor, or prove that policy iteration/simplex-type algorithms cannot be strongly polynomial in a precise model. The open issue is the regime $\gamma \to 1$ for stochastic MDPs, not fixed-discount MDPs.

title: The exact value of the Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley TSP constant
short_statement: Determine the exact Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley constant for the random Euclidean TSP, or close the large gap between rigorous upper and lower bounds.
full_statement: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent uniform random points in $[0,1]^2$, and let $L_n$ be the length of the shortest Euclidean traveling-salesman tour through those points. Beardwood, Halton, and Hammersley proved that $L_n/\sqrt n$ converges almost surely to a universal constant $\beta_{TSP}$, now called the planar Euclidean TSP constant. The theorem proves existence but not the exact value. Simulations place the constant near $0.71$, while the best rigorous bounds remain much wider: recent lower bounds are around $0.6277$ and recent upper bounds are around $0.9037$. The open problem is to determine $\beta_{TSP}$ exactly, or at least to produce substantially sharper certified upper and lower bounds with rigorous asymptotic error control. Natural variants ask the same question in other dimensions or for related Euclidean functionals, but this record focuses on the two-dimensional TSP constant.
known_results: Beardwood, Halton, and Hammersley proved almost-sure convergence and gave early bounds. Later computational experiments, including the Concorde-era numerical study by Applegate, Bixby, Chvatal, and Cook, estimate the constant near $0.712$. Gaudio and Jaillet improved the rigorous lower bound to $0.6277$ by building on geometric lower-bound ideas. Carlsson and Yu improved the rigorous upper bound to about $0.9038$ using a computer-aided band construction. Gaudio and Guan improved the upper bound slightly to $0.90367$ using band crossovers and also gave evidence that the current band-traversal paradigm may not go much below about $0.88$. The exact constant remains unknown, and the rigorous bounds are still far from the simulated value.

where_posed.text: Implicit in Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley's theorem, which proves existence of the constant without identifying it.
where_posed.location: Asymptotic constant in the main theorem

background: The Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley theorem is a foundational result in probabilistic combinatorial optimization. It says that the optimal tour length through many random planar points has a deterministic first-order growth constant, so random Euclidean TSP is asymptotically governed by geometry rather than arbitrary instance details. This constant matters as a benchmark for Euclidean optimization, vehicle routing, stochastic routing approximations, and subadditive Euclidean functionals. The difficulty is that the existence proof relies on subadditivity and coarse geometric partitioning, while the value of the constant depends on fine local structure of optimal tours. Lower bounds must certify that every tour has enough length, and upper bounds must construct tours with rigorously bounded expected length. Existing proof templates have moved slowly, and the newest band-crossover upper-bound work suggests that one well-developed band-traversal approach has limited headroom.

progress.summary: Recent certified bounds improved slightly, with the best 2026 upper bound reported as $0.90367$. The gap to numerical estimates remains large.

counterexample_rationale: The problem asks for an asymptotic constant, not a universal conjecture refutable by one finite instance. Computations can improve candidate bounds but do not themselves determine the limit.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can discover better constructive tour templates, partitions, local crossing patterns, or lower-bound certificates. Computer-aided proof is already part of the best upper-bound literature.

literature.synthesis: The BHH theorem converts random Euclidean TSP into the study of a universal constant. The lower-bound side uses geometric inequalities that every tour must satisfy, while the upper-bound side constructs tours by partitioning the square and bounding expected connection costs. Both approaches have improved slowly. The 2026 band-crossover work is useful because it both nudges the upper bound and diagnoses limitations of the current band-traversal method. The main remaining gap is methodological: existing certified bounds are far from the simulated value, so progress likely needs new local geometric inequalities, richer constructive schemes, or a computer-assisted proof architecture with much tighter certified error.

For lower bounds, look for local constraints on degrees, crossings, matching structure, or transport that every TSP tour must satisfy. Poissonization and subadditive Euclidean-functional techniques are likely necessary to pass from finite computation to asymptotic constants.

Numerical estimates near $0.71$ are evidence but are not a proof of the constant.

title: Complexity and approximability of two-stage stochastic programming
short_statement: General compactly represented two-stage stochastic programming is #P-hard even approximately in broad settings; the open task is to classify the exact tractable boundary.
full_statement: Consider a two-stage stochastic program of the form $\min_{x\in X} c^\top x+\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[Q(x,\xi)]$, where $x$ is chosen before the random vector $\xi$ is observed and $Q(x,\xi)$ is the optimal recourse value, for example $Q(x,\xi)=\min\{q(\xi)^\top y: W(\xi)y\ge h(\xi)-T(\xi)x, y\ge0\}$. The distribution of $\xi$ is part of the input and may be represented compactly, such as by independent random variables or other succinct descriptions rather than by explicitly listing all scenarios. Broad general formulations are known to be #P-hard, including high-accuracy approximate solution in corrected fixed-recourse settings. The open problem is to draw the sharp boundary: identify the largest natural restrictions on $X$, recourse structure, distributional representation, dimension, separability, and sampling access that admit polynomial-time approximation or an FPRAS, and prove matching hardness outside those regimes. In the positive regimes, also determine tight nonasymptotic sample sizes for sample-average approximation to output an $\varepsilon$-optimal first-stage decision with high probability.
known_results: Dyer and Stougie proved #P-hardness for two-stage stochastic programming under compact independent distributions and PSPACE-hardness for certain multistage variants, although the two-stage proof later required correction. Hanasusanto, Kuhn, and Wiesemann identified the flaw and proved that even approximate solution of linear two-stage stochastic programs with fixed recourse is #P-hard for sufficiently high accuracy; they also gave evidence that random recourse can be still more difficult. Kleywegt, Shapiro, and Homem-de-Mello developed SAA convergence and finite-sample theory for stochastic discrete optimization, while Shapiro and Nemirovski studied complexity phenomena for stochastic programming more broadly. Swamy and Shmoys and subsequent approximation work show that many named two-stage stochastic optimization problems do admit useful approximation algorithms under specific structural assumptions. The open part is not the existence of worst-case hardness; it is the sharp classification of which assumptions buy tractability and which still hide #P-hard expectation computation. Buchheim's May 2026 preprint refines the boundary for fixed recourse with coefficients affine in a uniformly distributed box vector. Strong #P-hardness persists with one random coordinate, or with one standard-form second-stage constraint; fixing the number of second-stage variables leaves weak #P-hardness and pseudopolynomial high-accuracy algorithms. Fixing both random dimension and the number of second-stage constraints permits polynomial-time approximation to arbitrary accuracy, with logarithmic dependence on $1/\varepsilon$.
