background: Two-stage stochastic programming is a standard framework for decisions under uncertainty: choose a first-stage decision now, observe random data later, and then pay an optimal recourse cost. If all scenarios are explicitly listed, the deterministic equivalent may be large but conceptually ordinary. The deeper algorithmic issue appears when uncertainty is represented compactly, since the expectation can encode an exponentially large sum or integral. Dyer and Stougie gave a foundational complexity analysis for two-stage and multistage stochastic programs. Hanasusanto, Kuhn, and Wiesemann later showed that part of the original two-stage proof was incorrect and supplied a stronger corrected result: approximate solution is still #P-hard at sufficiently high accuracy for important linear two-stage models. Therefore the broad question 'is there a general FPRAS?' should not be presented as open. The research-level question is now a taxonomy problem: which structural assumptions genuinely remove the counting hardness, and how do those assumptions interact with SAA, decomposition, and approximation algorithms used in OR practice?

progress.summary: Broad compactly represented formulations are known to be #P-hard, including high-accuracy approximation in corrected two-stage fixed-recourse settings. Many structured stochastic optimization models have approximation or SAA guarantees. The remaining problem is a boundary theorem aligning hardness, distributional representation, and positive approximation/SAA conditions. A 2026 preprint supplies a finer fixed-dimension/second-stage-size classification; this is not a universal SAA or FPRAS result.

counterexample_rationale: Compact distributions or recourse matrices can refute proposed tractability claims by embedding a counting problem. A full classification, however, requires asymptotic reductions and algorithms rather than one finite counterexample.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search may find small hard distributions, bad SAA examples, or structural decompositions that suggest tractable subclasses. Formal complexity reductions and sample-complexity proofs remain essential.

literature.synthesis: The right open problem is a classification theorem, not a rediscovery of general hardness. The Dyer-Stougie paper established the complexity agenda, and the Hanasusanto-Kuhn-Wiesemann correction shows that compactly represented linear two-stage programs remain #P-hard even approximately at high accuracy. On the other hand, the OR literature contains many positive results for named stochastic optimization problems and SAA consistency under regularity assumptions. These two facts coexist because the input model matters: explicit scenarios, sampling oracles, fixed recourse, random recourse, bounded dimension, separability, and distributional succinctness are different computational regimes. A useful resolution would state, for each natural regime, whether the barrier is expectation evaluation, first-stage optimization, sample complexity, or all three. Buchheim's May 2026 preprint refines the boundary for fixed recourse with coefficients affine in a uniformly distributed box vector. Strong #P-hardness persists with one random coordinate, or with one standard-form second-stage constraint; fixing the number of second-stage variables leaves weak #P-hardness and pseudopolynomial high-accuracy algorithms. Fixing both random dimension and the number of second-stage constraints permits polynomial-time approximation to arbitrary accuracy, with logarithmic dependence on $1/\varepsilon$.

title: Exact optimality of the generalized cμ rule for convex delay costs
short_statement: For scheduling a multiclass queue with convex delay costs, the generalized $c\mu$ rule is optimal in heavy traffic; is it (or some clean index policy) exactly optimal outside the heavy-traffic limit?
full_statement: Consider a multiclass single-server or flexible-server Markovian queue. Class $i$ jobs arrive according to a renewal or Poisson input process, have exponential or otherwise specified service requirements with rate parameter $\mu_i$ at the relevant server, and incur holding cost $C_i(q_i)$ when $q_i$ class-$i$ jobs are present, where $C_i$ is increasing and convex. A scheduling policy observes the queue-length vector and chooses which nonempty class to serve, possibly subject to server-compatibility constraints. The classical linear-cost case $C_i(q_i)=c_iq_i$ is solved by the $c\mu$ rule: serve a class maximizing $c_i\mu_i$. The generalized rule serves a class maximizing a marginal-cost index such as $\mu_i(C_i(q_i)-C_i(q_i-1))$ or its smooth analogue $\mu_i C_i'(q_i)$. Heavy-traffic theory proves this rule is asymptotically optimal in important regimes. The open problem is to determine whether a generalized $c\mu$-type marginal index is exactly optimal for finite stochastic systems with convex holding costs, and if not, to characterize the exact optimal policy or the smallest additional state/lookahead information needed.
known_results: For linear holding costs and exponential service, the classical $c\mu$ rule is exactly optimal in the standard multiclass single-server setting. Van Mieghem introduced the generalized $c\mu$ rule for convex delay costs and proved heavy-traffic asymptotic optimality: after diffusion scaling, the policy minimizes the limiting Brownian control problem and is asymptotically optimal for the original queueing system. Mandelbaum and Stolyar extended the heavy-traffic optimality picture to flexible-server systems with convex delay costs. These results do not prove Bellman optimality for a fixed finite system away from heavy traffic. Exact optimality for general strictly convex queue-length or age-based costs is known only in special cases. Gurushankar, Li, Harchol-Balter, and Scheller-Wolf's 2026 LookAhead paper shows how delicate the nonasymptotic question is: even in a two-class M/M/1 model with one age-dependent cost class and one constant-cost class, no prior nonasymptotic optimality result was known; their optimal nondecreasing index looks ahead by an exponential amount rather than simply using current holding cost. This supports the view that generalized $c\mu$ may need refinement for exact finite-system optimality.

where_posed.text: The asymptotic-vs-exact gap originates from Van Mieghem's generalized $c\mu$ heavy-traffic theorem and subsequent scheduling literature.

background: The generalized $c\mu$ rule is the convex-cost analogue of the classical priority rule for multiclass queues. When holding costs are linear, a fixed priority index $c_i\mu_i$ is exactly optimal in the single-server Markovian model. With nonlinear delay costs, the natural index becomes state dependent: serve the class with largest marginal holding cost times service rate, $C_i'(Q_i)\mu_i$. Van Mieghem proved that this generalized rule is asymptotically optimal in heavy traffic, and Mandelbaum and Stolyar extended the heavy-traffic picture to flexible-server systems. These theorems are powerful but asymptotic. The exact finite-system stochastic control problem remains open in general, and recent work on time-varying holding costs underscores that nonasymptotic optimal index structure is still hard even in seemingly simple two-class special cases.

progress.summary: Heavy-traffic optimality is established for single and flexible-server settings. Exact nonasymptotic index optimality is only known in special cases, with recent progress for a two-class time-varying holding-cost model.

counterexample_rationale: Small two-class finite-state truncations can test whether the generalized $c\mu$ action violates Bellman optimality. Counterexamples to exact optimality are plausible and machine-verifiable.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can discover convex cost functions and rate parameters where the marginal-cost rule fails, or infer lookahead/index forms that repair it.

literature.synthesis: The generalized $c\mu$ literature shows how far heavy-traffic analysis can go: state-space collapse and Brownian control problems lead naturally to marginal-cost priority rules. In a diffusion limit, serving the largest marginal holding-cost rate is the right local action because the system state is close to a lower-dimensional workload manifold. Exact dynamic programming in the original Markov chain is more demanding. A service decision changes the future queue-length vector, and with convex costs the value of reducing one class now depends on how quickly that class's marginal cost will grow relative to other classes. The 2026 LookAhead paper makes this issue concrete in a related time-varying holding-cost model: the optimal nondecreasing index uses future cost rather than current cost. That does not disprove generalized $c\mu$ for queue-length convex costs, but it shows why current marginal cost alone may be insufficient outside asymptotic regimes. The remaining task is to determine whether there is an exact finite-system index theorem, a class of convex costs where generalized $c\mu$ is exactly optimal, or explicit counterexamples showing that Bellman-optimal policies require richer state dependence.

agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed exact theorem must define the queueing model precisely: arrivals, service distributions, preemption, cost criterion, stability assumptions, and whether costs depend on queue length, waiting time, or age. It must prove Bellman optimality inequalities for all states of the original Markov chain, not just a Brownian or fluid limit. A counterexample should state arrival rates, service rates, cost functions, discount or average-cost criterion, and a state where the generalized $c\mu$ action is strictly suboptimal; value comparisons should be certified by exact dynamic programming on a truncated chain with error bounds or by analytic inequalities. Heavy-traffic optimality, simulation, or optimality within a restricted index class should not be reported as exact global optimality unless the restriction is part of the problem statement.

notes_for_maintainer: This is adjacent to, but distinct from, the abandonment $c\mu/\theta$ problem.
open_problem: Determine whether the generalized $c\mu$ rule, or another explicit state-dependent index policy, is exactly optimal for multiclass queues with convex delay costs outside heavy traffic; if not, characterize the exact optimal policy.

title: Optimality of smallest-variance-first sequencing in appointment scheduling
short_statement: SVF is not universally optimal, but it performs well; determine its tight approximation ratio and the exact regimes where variance-order sequencing is optimal.
full_statement: There are $n$ jobs with independent service times $S_1,\ldots,S_n$ and known distributions. A policy chooses a permutation $\pi$ and appointment times $a_1\le\cdots\le a_n$ for the ordered jobs. Given a sequence and appointment schedule, the induced single-server recursion determines each customer's waiting time, server idle time, and possibly overtime at the end of the session. The objective is a weighted sum of expected waiting time, expected idle time, and possibly expected overtime. For a fixed sequence, define $C(\pi)$ as the minimum achievable expected cost over appointment times. Let $\pi_{\mathrm{SVF}}$ be the sequence ordering jobs by increasing service-time variance. The open problem is to determine the tight worst-case ratio $\sup C(\pi_{\mathrm{SVF}})/\min_\pi C(\pi)$ over natural distribution and cost classes, and to characterize the distributional or cost conditions under which SVF is exactly optimal.
known_results: Weiss introduced dispersion-based sequencing ideas and showed that simple dispersion orderings can fail for three jobs. Wang studied stochastic-server sequencing and proved SVF-type optimality in special exponential cases while motivating broader optimality claims. de Kemp, Mandjes, and Olver showed that SVF is not always optimal, but proved quantitative approximation guarantees and asymptotic optimality as the number of jobs grows under broad conditions. Their results reframe SVF as an approximation algorithm rather than a universal optimum rule. The remaining open problem is the tight finite-$n$ worst-case performance, the exact extremal examples, and the largest natural distribution classes where variance ordering is truly optimal.

background: Appointment sequencing is a clean stochastic scheduling problem that often appears in healthcare operations but is not itself a modelling question: the service-time distributions, appointment-time optimization problem, and cost criterion are fixed. A single server must process a known set of jobs with independent random durations. For any chosen sequence, the optimal appointment times can be computed by a newsvendor-like dynamic program or convex optimization routine, so the difficult combinatorial part is the ordering of service distributions. The smallest-variance-first rule, or SVF, orders customers from least variable to most variable service time. Earlier work suggested SVF as a robust sequencing principle and proved it in small or special cases. Later work by de Kemp, Mandjes, and Olver clarified that SVF is not universally optimal, but also proved that it has strong approximation and asymptotic performance guarantees. Thus the right open problem is no longer the bare conjecture that SVF is always optimal. The sharper question is to determine the exact worst-case performance and the structural regimes in which SVF, or a small modification of it, is genuinely optimal.

progress.summary: The original universal-optimality conjecture is too strong. SVF is known to be near-optimal in several senses, but the exact worst-case ratio and exact optimality classes remain open.

literature.synthesis: This record needed a correction. The interesting current question is not whether SVF is always optimal, because later work says it is not. The value of SVF is that it is simple, operationally interpretable, and provably close to optimal under broad assumptions. de Kemp, Mandjes, and Olver move the literature toward approximation-style guarantees, which is a better fit for a clean open-problem repository than a healthcare-specific modelling question. The remaining finite-sample theory is still incomplete: tight approximation constants, exact extremal instances, and exact conditions for optimality are not settled. A sharp answer would also clarify whether variance alone is the right statistic or whether higher moments and cost-weight asymmetry must enter any optimal sequencing rule.

title: Best approximation ratio for constrained assortment under the Markov-chain choice model
short_statement: For capacity-constrained assortment under Markov-chain choice, close the gap between constant-factor algorithms and APX-hardness.
full_statement: There are products $1,\ldots,n$ with revenues $r_i$, initial arrival probabilities $\lambda_i$, and Markov transition probabilities $\rho_{ij}$ among products and the no-purchase state $0$. Given an offered set $S$, a customer purchases the first offered product hit by the chain or leaves at state $0$, producing expected revenue $R(S)$. Under a feasibility constraint such as $|S|\le k$ or $\sum_{i\in S}w_i\le W$, choose $S$ maximizing $R(S)$. Determine the best possible polynomial-time approximation ratio for this constrained Markov-chain assortment problem.
known_results: Blanchet, Gallego, and Goyal introduced the Markov-chain choice model and showed that the unconstrained assortment problem has tractable structure, making the model attractive for revenue-management applications. The constrained setting is much harder: Desir, Goyal, Segev, and Ye prove that cardinality- and capacity-constrained Markov-chain assortment is APX-hard even in restricted uniform-price cases, so a PTAS is impossible unless $P=NP$. They also give constant-factor approximation algorithms based on externality adjustment and reductions to better-behaved surrogate objectives. What remains open is the exact approximation threshold: the known APX-hardness does not match the algorithmic constants, and no tight integrality-gap or inapproximability result is known for the natural constrained variants.

background: Assortment optimization asks which products to offer when customers substitute among unavailable items. The Markov-chain choice model of Blanchet, Gallego, and Goyal represents substitution by a Markov chain: a customer begins at an initial product and, if that product is unavailable, transitions among alternatives until purchasing an offered item or exiting. The unconstrained revenue-maximization problem has favorable structure, but practical assortments often face cardinality, shelf-space, or capacity constraints. Desir, Goyal, Segev, and Ye showed that the constrained version is algorithmically much harder: the revenue function is nonlinear, nonsubmodular, and nonmonotone, yet constant-factor approximations are possible through an externality-adjustment framework. They also prove APX-hardness, so a PTAS is impossible unless $P=NP$. The current open problem is the approximation threshold: how close can polynomial-time algorithms get to optimal revenue under cardinality or knapsack constraints, and can hardness be strengthened to match the best achievable constants?

progress.summary: Constant-factor approximation and APX-hardness are known. The remaining gap is the optimal approximation ratio for cardinality and knapsack/capacity constraints.

literature.synthesis: The constrained Markov-chain assortment problem has the right shape for this repository: the model is fixed and clean, the unconstrained baseline is understood, and the hard part is a precise approximation gap. The revenue function lacks monotonicity and submodularity, so standard constrained-submodular tools do not apply directly. Desir, Goyal, Segev, and Ye's externality adjustment gives a way to linearize marginal effects enough to obtain constant approximations, while their APX-hardness result rules out arbitrarily close approximation. The missing theorem is either a stronger algorithmic idea that improves the constant or a reduction showing that the current constant is essentially best possible.

title: A simple optimal policy for perishable inventory with fixed lifetime ≥ 3
short_statement: For periodic-review inventory of a product that expires after a fixed number of periods ($\ge 3$), is any simple ordering policy exactly or asymptotically optimal?
full_statement: Consider a single item under periodic review whose units perish exactly $m$ periods after arrival (fixed shelf life), with i.i.d. demand, FIFO issuance, and linear holding, outdating (expiry), and shortage (or lost-sales) costs. The state needed for the dynamic program is the age profile of on-hand stock — the vector $(x_1,\dots,x_{m-1})$ of quantities with $1,\dots,m-1$ periods of remaining life — so the optimal order quantity is a function of this whole vector. For $m\ge 3$ the optimal policy is not of base-stock/order-up-to form and is computationally intractable (curse of dimensionality). Question: does there exist a simple, tractable policy (e.g. an order-up-to rule in total inventory, or a critical-number policy) that is exactly optimal for $m\ge 3$, or that is provably asymptotically optimal with explicit performance guarantees?
known_results: Nahmias and Pierskalla solve important two-period perishability cases, and Nahmias's 1982 review records how quickly the dynamic program becomes difficult for longer lifetimes. For $m \ge 3$, the optimal order quantity depends on the full age vector, and no general base-stock, critical-number, or low-dimensional exact policy is known. Zhang, Ayer, and White prove 2-approximation guarantees for marginal-cost dual-balancing and truncated-balancing policies when FIFO is optimal, under general stochastic demand. These approximation guarantees are useful but leave a large gap between known tractable policies and exact optimality. Later asymptotic inventory-control work gives additional insight in special regimes, but it does not resolve the finite-lifetime exact policy structure.

background: Perishable inventory is a classical operations-management model for blood products, pharmaceuticals, food, and other goods with fixed shelf lives. The model is not hard because the business setting is vague; it is hard because the exact dynamic program has a high-dimensional age-profile state. If units expire after $m$ periods, the controller must track how many units have each remaining lifetime, because ordering too much creates future outdating while ordering too little creates shortages or lost sales. For $m=2$, the state is essentially one-dimensional and classical structure is available. For $m \ge 3$, simple base-stock or order-up-to rules do not describe the optimal policy in general, and exact dynamic programming scales poorly. Approximation algorithms and heuristics exist, including myopic/critical-number ideas and later dual-balancing policies with constant-factor guarantees under FIFO optimality. The central open problem is therefore structural and algorithmic: find a simple exact policy class, or a sharper provably near-optimal policy, for the fixed-lifetime model beyond the two-period case.

progress.summary: The two-period case is classical, and modern approximation algorithms give worst-case factor-2 guarantees under FIFO optimality. General exact structure for $m \ge 3$ remains open.

counterexample_rationale: Small finite-support demand instances with $m=3$ or $4$ can refute proposed base-stock, total-inventory, or critical-number structures through exact dynamic programming. A positive theorem must handle the unbounded age-profile state.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can map optimal actions for truncated MDPs and find counterexamples to conjectured monotonicity or low-dimensional policies. It can also optimize candidate heuristic parameters, but proofs need dynamic-programming or convexity arguments.

literature.synthesis: The perishable inventory literature has a long split between exact dynamic programming and usable policies. Classical work resolves special short-lifetime models, while Nahmias's review explains that fixed lifetime $m \ge 3$ creates a multidimensional state and destroys the simplicity of ordinary inventory base-stock rules. Approximation work by Zhang, Ayer, and White provides a robust positive result: when FIFO issuing is optimal, dual-balancing-style policies are within a factor of two of the optimal ordering policy. This is meaningful operationally but still far from a structural characterization. The open gap is to decide whether the general model admits a clean policy description, whether stronger approximation ratios are possible, and which assumptions on demand, issuing, or costs recover simple optimality.

title: Optimal policy in dynamic matching markets with stochastic arrivals and departures
short_statement: Characterize exact optimal policies and loss rates in dynamic matching markets beyond the homogeneous sparse random-graph model.
full_statement: Consider a dynamic matching market in continuous or discrete time. Agents of finitely many types, or agents with random compatibility edges, arrive according to stochastic processes, wait for random or deterministic patience times, and abandon if unmatched. A policy observes the current market state and possibly partial departure information, chooses compatible pairs or chains to match, and removes matched agents. The objective may be long-run loss, perish probability, waiting cost plus match value, or regret against an online optimum, fluid benchmark, or clairvoyant benchmark. The open problem is to characterize exact optimal policies and sharp performance constants in clean stochastic models beyond the homogeneous sparse random-graph benchmark: for which compatibility networks is greedy optimal or constant-regret, when does patience or priority strictly improve performance, and when does global matching structure beat local immediate matching?
known_results: Akbarpour, Li, and Oveis Gharan introduced a benchmark stochastic network model and showed that waiting to thicken the market can be far more valuable than speeding transactions; they also showed that naive timing policies can be close to optimal without departure information, while even partial information about departures can substantially improve outcomes. Ashlagi, Burq, Jaillet, and Saberi studied finite-patience dynamic matching under adversarial arrivals and gave a $1/4$-competitive algorithm, with no online algorithm beating $1/2$ in their model and a $1/8$ guarantee for certain random departure times. Ashlagi, Burq, Jaillet, and Manshadi analyzed heterogeneous dynamic markets and showed that market composition changes whether bilateral matching, chains, and priorities help. Recent work by Kerimov, Yang, and Yu gives constant regret for state-independent greedy policies under general-position-type conditions, while Arnosti and Simon prove tight $1/2$ competitive guarantees for LP-guided greedy policies in several abandonment models. The remaining gap is a unified exact optimal-policy theory for heterogeneous stochastic compatibility networks.

background: Dynamic matching markets create a basic operational dilemma: match agents quickly to reduce waiting and abandonment, or hold them to thicken the market and improve match quality. Akbarpour, Li, and Oveis Gharan gave a benchmark random-graph model where agents arrive and depart stochastically and compatibility edges are sparse. Their main message is that information about imminent departures is extremely valuable: without it, greedy is near optimal, while with it, patient policies can achieve much lower loss. Later work studies heterogeneous types, adversarial arrivals, finite patience, constant-regret policies, and competitive policies. These papers make clear that there is no single universal 'always wait' or 'always greedy' principle. The remaining clean problem is to characterize optimal dynamic policies and exact losses in concrete stochastic graph models beyond the original homogeneous sparse setting, while distinguishing what is solved by greedy, what needs patience, and what needs global matching structure.

progress.summary: Several regimes now have near-optimal greedy, patient, competitive, or constant-regret policies. A general exact optimal-policy characterization for heterogeneous stochastic compatibility remains open.

literature.synthesis: The field has moved from a single homogeneous random graph model to a collection of typed, adversarial, and abandonment models. The main resolved lesson is qualitative: greediness is often surprisingly strong, but departure information and patient matching can matter a great deal. Recent constant-regret and LP-guided greedy results narrow particular gaps, yet they usually require structural assumptions such as common departure rates, bipartite symmetry, or nondegenerate fluid relaxations. The remaining problem is to identify the right general theorem: a policy class with exact or sharp asymptotic performance across heterogeneous compatibility networks.

title: Greedy dynamic matching with heterogeneous departure rates
short_statement: In dynamic matching with Poisson arrivals, exponential abandonment and rewards, does the LP-selected greedy policy of Arnosti and Simon always achieve the tight $1/2$ ratio against the omniscient benchmark without any homogeneous-departure-rate assumption?
full_statement: There is a finite set of types $T$. Type $i$ agents arrive according to an independent Poisson process with rate $\lambda_i$, abandon if unmatched after an independent exponential time with rate $\mu_i$, and matching an earlier type-$i$ agent to an arriving type-$j$ agent earns reward $r_{ij}$. The objective is the long-run steady-state reward rate. The benchmark $\mathrm{OMN}(I)$ is an omniscient policy that knows the full arrival and departure sequence. A greedy policy fixes, for each arriving type, an ordered list of acceptable waiting types and immediately matches to the best present acceptable type if one exists. Arnosti and Simon define an LP-based procedure that selects a greedy policy $\mathrm{ALG}(I)$. They prove $V(\mathrm{ALG}(I),I) \ge \frac12\mathrm{OMN}(I)$ when all departure rates are equal, and in bipartite instances when departure rates are equal within each side; they also prove the two-type heterogeneous case. The open problem is to prove or disprove the same guarantee for arbitrary heterogeneous departure rates $\mu_i$ and rewards $r_{ij}$: $$ V(\mathrm{ALG}(I),I) \ge \frac12\mathrm{OMN}(I) \quad \text{for every instance } I. $$ Equivalently, determine whether a well-chosen deterministic greedy policy always obtains the best possible $1/2$ competitive ratio against the omniscient benchmark in the general dynamic matching-with-abandonment model.
known_results: Collina, Immorlica, Leyton-Brown, Lucier, and Newman proved a $1/8$-competitive algorithm for dynamic weighted matching with heterogeneous arrivals and departures. Aouad and Saritac developed an LP-based approach for dynamic stochastic matching under limited time in Operations Research. Arnosti and Simon introduce $LP^{ALG}$ to select a greedy policy and prove that its value lower-bounds the greedy policy in two main cases: equal departure rates for all types, and bipartite instances with equal departure rates on each side. They also prove $LP^{ALG}$ is at least half of the omniscient benchmark, yielding a tight $1/2$ guarantee in those settings, and show no online policy can do better than $1/2$. They prove the heterogeneous-departure conjecture for two types and report no computational counterexample, but the arbitrary heterogeneous-rate case remains open.

background: Dynamic matching with abandonment is a clean model for markets where compatibility is valuable but delay risks losing agents: kidney exchange pools, labor platforms, freight exchanges, rideshare pooling, and peer-to-peer barter markets all have this shape. A planner sees agents arrive over time, can match compatible agents currently in the system, and loses agents who depart unmatched. The fundamental tension is whether to match greedily or wait for market thickness. In full generality, the offline optimum is too strong because it knows future arrivals and departure times, but it is a useful benchmark for competitive analysis. The Arnosti-Simon paper is important because it asks a very sharp question inside this fixed stochastic model: can a deterministic greedy policy, chosen by an LP, always get the optimal possible $1/2$ of the omniscient benchmark? They prove this in equal-departure and certain bipartite settings, and no online policy can beat $1/2$ there. The missing theorem is exactly the kind this site should track: extend or refute the $1/2$ guarantee for heterogeneous departure rates.

progress.summary: The 2025 Arnosti-Simon paper improves the general state of knowledge from a $1/8$ guarantee to a tight $1/2$ theorem in homogeneous-departure settings and proves the conjecture for two types. The heterogeneous many-type case is the remaining gap.

alphaevolve_rationale: This is a strong target for automated search: generate small heterogeneous-rate instances, solve $LP^{ALG}$, compute or simulate the greedy steady-state reward, and compare against upper bounds on the omniscient benchmark. Search may find the first obstruction or suggest the invariant needed for a proof.

literature.synthesis: Earlier dynamic matching theory established that greedy and patient policies can be dramatically different depending on information and market thickness, but heterogeneous weighted models resisted sharp guarantees. Collina et al. handled arbitrary heterogeneous arrival and departure rates with a $1/8$ competitive ratio against an omniscient benchmark. Aouad and Saritac gave an Operations Research LP framework for limited-time dynamic stochastic matching. Arnosti and Simon sharpen the model by studying deterministic greedy policies selected through $LP^{ALG}$ and prove the best possible $1/2$ ratio in homogeneous-departure cases. Their proof hinges on a lemma relating the probability that some agent in a set is present to the expected number of such agents. The open problem is whether an analogous inequality or replacement argument survives heterogeneous departure rates, where fast-departing and slow-departing types create asymmetric inventory effects.

title: Optimal dynamic policy for kidney exchange with heterogeneous cycles and chains
short_statement: Greedy clearing is near optimal in homogeneous dynamic barter; characterize optimality and guarantees under heterogeneous kidney-exchange structure, chains, failures, and finite pools.
full_statement: Consider a dynamic kidney-exchange or barter pool. Patient-donor pairs arrive over time. A directed compatibility edge $i\to j$ means the donor of pair $i$ can donate to the patient of pair $j$. At a clearing time, the platform may select vertex-disjoint directed cycles of length at most $L$, and possibly chains initiated by altruistic donors or non-directed donors. Cleared pairs leave; unmatched pairs wait and may depart or fail depending on the model. The objective may be to maximize expected transplants, minimize average waiting time, minimize patient loss, or optimize a weighted fairness objective. In homogeneous sparse random barter graphs, greedy clearing is near optimal for several exchange technologies. The open problem is to characterize the optimal policy, or tight approximation/asymptotic guarantees, in heterogeneous type-based kidney-exchange models with hard-to-match patients, finite pool sizes, stochastic edge failures, and mixed cycle-chain technologies.
known_results: Unver introduced dynamic kidney exchange and early timing principles. Anderson, Ashlagi, Gamarnik, and Kanoria prove that in a homogeneous random barter model, greedy policies are near optimal for two-way cycles, two/three-way cycles, and chains, and that allowing three-way cycles or chains can sharply reduce waiting when compatibility is sparse. Ashlagi, Jaillet, and Manshadi analyze dynamic sparse heterogeneous pools with highly sensitized patients and show that the value of waiting depends strongly on whether only two-way cycles are allowed, whether three-way cycles are allowed, and whether even one non-simultaneous chain is available. Ashlagi, Nikzad, and Strack show that in large imbalanced dynamic exchange markets, greedy can beat batching by giving shorter waits and at least as many matches. These papers leave open a unified finite, heterogeneous, failure-aware policy theory with sharp guarantees.

background: Dynamic kidney exchange is a canonical operational matching problem with a clean mathematical core. Static exchange already involves difficult cycle-packing constraints, while dynamics add the choice of whether to clear immediately or wait for a thicker market. Anderson, Ashlagi, Gamarnik, and Kanoria studied a homogeneous sparse random-graph barter model and found a striking conclusion: for two-way cycles, for two- and three-way cycles, and for chains initiated by altruistic agents, the cost of waiting to thicken the market outweighs the benefit, so greedy clearing is near optimal for average waiting time. Real kidney-exchange pools, however, are not homogeneous. They include easy- and hard-to-match pairs, blood/tissue compatibility structure, logistical cycle caps, edge failures after crossmatch, and fairness constraints for highly sensitized patients. Later work on sparse heterogeneous pools and imbalanced markets shows that these features can change the value of waiting, chains, and batching. The remaining problem is to retain clean policy theorems while moving beyond the homogeneous random graph.

progress.summary: The homogeneous sparse random barter model is largely understood: greedy is near optimal and chains/three-way cycles reduce waiting. Heterogeneous, finite, failure-aware, and weighted variants still lack a unified optimal-policy theory.

literature.synthesis: The initial homogeneous model gives a strong positive benchmark: delay to thicken the market often costs more than it helps, and greedy clearing is near optimal. That lesson is not automatically universal. Kidney exchange pools are heterogeneous, hard-to-match patients create bottlenecks, chains are operationally different from cycles, and compatibility edges can fail after screening. Sparse heterogeneous-pool results and imbalanced-market results show that these details affect waiting and match rates. The remaining gap is to preserve the clean model-based style while incorporating enough heterogeneity to obtain robust policy theorems and finite-pool guidance.

title: Cost of the greedy algorithm for dynamic spatial matching
short_statement: Determine the exact expected cost scaling of nearest-neighbor greedy in balanced dynamic spatial matching.
full_statement: Supply and demand points are sampled independently in $[0,1]^d$, usually uniformly, and matching cost is Euclidean distance. In the semi-dynamic model, $N$ supply points are initially present and $N$ demand points arrive sequentially; each demand must be matched irrevocably to an unmatched supply point. In the fully dynamic model, supply and demand both arrive over time and unmatched agents may wait subject to the model's queue-size or market-thickness assumptions. The standard greedy policy matches each arriving agent to the nearest currently available compatible opposite-side agent. Kanoria characterizes near-optimal achievable cost scaling using hierarchical greedy policies, but the ordinary nearest-neighbor greedy policy is not sharply understood in balanced markets. The open problem is to determine the expected average cost of standard greedy as a function of $N$ and dimension $d$, including possible logarithmic factors and constants, and to compare this scaling with the optimal achievable cost.
known_results: Kanoria determines the optimal achievable cost scaling in major static, semi-dynamic, and fully dynamic random spatial matching regimes and gives concrete hierarchical matching algorithms. In almost all cases, the optimal dynamic scaling is close to the static benchmark or nearest-neighbor distance; one explicit remaining gap in that paper is a logarithmic factor for $d=1$ in the fully dynamic model. Akbarpour, Alimohammadi, Li, and Saberi show that in one-dimensional spatial markets, a small amount of excess supply can make a simple greedy algorithm perform very well. These results do not give a sharp analysis of standard nearest-neighbor greedy under balanced supply and demand, nor do they determine whether greedy suffers avoidable logarithmic losses in the key low-dimensional dynamic regimes.

background: Dynamic spatial matching is a stripped-down model of platforms that match supply and demand in metric space: ride-hailing, delivery, labor platforms, and service dispatch all face the tension between immediate local matching and preserving future options. In random spatial models, supply and demand locations are iid in $[0,1]^d$, and static optimal matching already has dimension-dependent behavior governed by Ajtai-Komlos-Tusnady and Talagrand-type results. Kanoria showed that in many dynamic regimes the platform can achieve cost nearly as low as if future arrivals were known, using policies that deliberately preserve balance across spatial scales. Standard nearest-neighbor greedy is the more obvious operational rule, but it is myopic. It may consume nearby supply in a way that creates holes and causes later long matches. Excess supply can repair greedy in one-dimensional settings, but the balanced case and the fully dynamic case remain much less clear.

progress.summary: Optimal scaling is known via hierarchical greedy-style algorithms, and excess-supply one-dimensional results explain some greedy behavior. Balanced standard nearest-neighbor greedy remains poorly understood.

counterexample_rationale: Finite simulations can reveal bad greedy configurations and plausible exponents, but the question is asymptotic for random inputs. Constructed finite patterns may guide lower-bound proofs.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated simulation and search over arrival sequences can estimate exponents, identify bottleneck configurations, and test coupling hypotheses. Proof still needs probabilistic scaling arguments.

literature.synthesis: The optimal-cost story is substantially clearer than the greedy-cost story. Kanoria's hierarchical algorithms deliberately preserve spatial balance across scales, avoiding the local myopia of nearest-neighbor matching. Standard greedy lacks that multiscale control; it can consume nearby supply in ways that create later long matches. Excess supply can mitigate this problem in one dimension, as Akbarpour et al. show, but that does not settle balanced markets or fully dynamic arrivals. The remaining open problem is a sharp stochastic-process analysis of greedy's spatial imbalance over time, potentially requiring tools from discrepancy, random allocation, transport, and queueing.

title: Parameterized complexity of single-machine throughput scheduling with release dates
short_statement: For single-machine throughput scheduling with release dates, are the unweighted and weighted tardy-job objectives W[1]-hard when parameterized by the maximum processing time?
full_statement: In $1|r_j|\sum U_j$ and $1|r_j|\sum w_jU_j$, each job $j$ has processing time $p_j$, release date $r_j$, due date $d_j$, and in the weighted case weight $w_j$. A nonpreemptive single-machine schedule chooses start times $S_j\ge r_j$ with no overlap; $U_j=1$ iff $C_j=S_j+p_j>d_j$. The objective is to minimize the number, or total weight, of tardy jobs. Let $p_{\max}=\max_j p_j$. The open problem asks whether these problems are W[1]-hard parameterized by $p_{\max}$, or instead fixed-parameter tractable (or even in XP) for this parameter. A positive FPT result would move toward polynomial-time algorithms for bounded-processing-time throughput scheduling; a hardness result would explain why this regime resists classical algorithms.
known_results: Without release dates, $1||\sum U_j$ is polynomial-time solvable by the Moore-Hodgson algorithm, while $1||\sum w_jU_j$ is weakly NP-hard but pseudo-polynomial. With release dates and arbitrary processing times, throughput scheduling is hard. Sgall asked whether the unweighted release-date case is polynomial for every fixed processing-time bound $c$, and whether the weighted case is NP-hard for fixed $c$. Mnich and van Bevern state the parameterized version as Open Problem 3 and note that, at the time, even containment in XP for parameter $p_{\max}$ was open. Hermelin et al. give FPT algorithms when two of three diversity parameters are simultaneously bounded: distinct due dates, distinct processing times, and distinct weights. The single-parameter $p_{\max}$ question remains the clean gap.

background: Throughput scheduling asks which jobs can be completed by their due dates when the machine cannot process everything on time. In the single-machine model with release dates, each job has an availability time, a processing requirement, and a deadline; the algorithm chooses a feasible nonpreemptive schedule and maximizes the number or total weight of on-time jobs. The case without release dates has classical polynomial or pseudo-polynomial algorithms, but release dates make the geometry much harder because feasible intervals for jobs interact over time. Sgall highlighted the constant-processing-time regime as a natural open frontier: if every job has processing time at most a fixed constant $c$, is the problem polynomial? Mnich and van Bevern reframed this as a parameterized-complexity question in $p_{\max}$. This formulation is useful because an FPT or XP algorithm would be evidence for tractability at every fixed $c$, while W-hardness would explain why even bounded processing times do not tame release-date throughput scheduling.

progress.summary: The problem is understood for no release dates and for combinations of multiple diversity parameters, but not for $p_{\max}$ alone. The parameterized classification remains open in the dataset.

counterexample_rationale: This is a complexity-classification problem. Search may find reductions or algorithmic patterns, but a finite counterexample cannot resolve it.
alphaevolve_rationale: Program search can test dynamic-programming state compressions for small $p_{\max}$ and discover reduction gadgets. The final result needs a proof of FPT/XP membership or parameterized hardness.

literature.synthesis: The key difficulty is that small processing times do not obviously bound the number of relevant time configurations once release dates and due dates are arbitrary. Classical pseudo-polynomial algorithms exploit total processing time or integer time horizons, but FPT in $p_{\max}$ would require compressing the schedule without depending exponentially on horizon length or the number of distinct release/deadline values. Hermelin-style diversity-parameter algorithms show that the problem becomes tractable when more structure is bounded, but they do not isolate $p_{\max}$. The open problem therefore sits exactly at the boundary between numerical boundedness and combinatorial time-window complexity.

title: FPT approximation scheme for job-shop makespan parameterized only by machines
short_statement: Does job-shop makespan minimization admit a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation running in $f(m,\epsilon)\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time, with dependence exponential only in the number of machines and accuracy?
full_statement: In the job-shop makespan problem $J||C_{\max}$, the input consists of $m$ machines and $n$ jobs. Job $j$ is a sequence of operations $(o_{j1},\ldots,o_{j\ell_j})$; operation $o_{jh}$ must be processed nonpreemptively for processing time $p_{jh}$ on a specified machine $\mu_{jh}$, and operation $o_{j,h+1}$ may start only after $o_{jh}$ completes. A machine can process at most one operation at a time, and a job can process at most one operation at a time through its prescribed route. The objective is to minimize $C_{\max}$, the completion time of the last operation. The open problem asks whether, for every $\epsilon>0$, there is an algorithm returning a schedule with makespan at most $(1+\epsilon)C^*_{\max}$ in time $f(m,\epsilon)\operatorname{poly}(N)$, where $N$ is the ordinary input length and the non-polynomial factor is independent of $n$, the processing-time magnitudes, and especially $n_{\max}=\max_j\ell_j$, the maximum route length.
known_results: Three-machine flow shop and three-machine open shop are already strongly NP-hard, so exact polynomial algorithms are not expected even for very small fixed shop environments. Nevertheless, approximation behaves better. Sevastianov and Woeginger give a fixed-parameter approximation scheme for open-shop makespan with dependence $f(m,\epsilon)+O(n\log n)$, and Hall gives an analogous approximation scheme for flow-shop makespan. For job shop, Jansen, Solis-Oba, and Sviridenko give a $(1+\epsilon)$ approximation in time depending on $m$, $\epsilon$, and $n_{\max}$, plus linear or near-linear input dependence. Mnich and van Bevern pose Open Problem 13: remove the dependence on $n_{\max}$. The usual route to a negative answer is not straightforward, because showing W-hardness parameterized by $C_{\max}+m$ cannot work: with both $C_{\max}$ and $m$ bounded, the number of operation slots is bounded and the problem is trivially fixed-parameter tractable.

background: Job-shop scheduling is one of the canonical hard models in operations research. Each job has its own ordered route through machines, and the scheduler must interleave all routes while respecting both machine capacity and within-job precedence. The model captures a standard manufacturing abstraction, but the open question here is purely algorithmic: the routes, processing times, and makespan objective are already fully specified. For a fixed number of machines, approximation schemes are known for open shop and flow shop, and job shop also has approximation schemes when the maximum number of operations in a job is treated as an additional parameter. Mnich and van Bevern isolate the sharper question of whether that route-length parameter is genuinely necessary. A positive answer would say that a small number of machines is enough to obtain a true fixed-parameter approximation scheme for arbitrary job routes; a negative answer would identify a rare barrier for approximation schemes in a fixed-machine shop model.

progress.summary: Approximation schemes are known with extra dependence on route length or related job-structure parameters. A machine-only FPT approximation scheme remains open.

literature.synthesis: The positive results for open shop and flow shop show that fixed-machine shop scheduling is not automatically hostile to FPT approximation schemes. The obstruction in job shop is route complexity: a single job may revisit machines many times, so the schedule is not just an ordering of jobs on each machine but an interleaving of many route segments. Existing approximation schemes control this by including $n_{\max}$ in the parameter dependence. The open problem asks whether long routes can be compressed after rounding, perhaps by aggregating repeated visits or by proving that only a bounded set of critical operations matters for a $(1+\epsilon)$ schedule. A lower bound would need a subtler framework than standard EPTAS impossibility through optimum-parameter hardness, because bounded makespan and bounded machines already bound the number of operations that can appear in a yes-instance.

title: Open-shop scheduling with sequence-dependent batch setup times
short_statement: Is unit-time open-shop makespan scheduling with sequence-dependent batch setup times fixed-parameter tractable in the number of batches?
full_statement: In $O|p_{ij}=1,ST_{sd,b}|C_{\max}$, there are $m$ machines and jobs partitioned into $g$ batches. Each job has one unit-time operation on every machine. A machine may process at most one operation at a time, a job may be processed by at most one machine at a time, and the order of a job's operations is not fixed. If a machine switches from processing a job of batch $p$ to a job of batch $q$, it incurs a sequence-dependent setup time $s_{pq}$. The objective is to minimize the makespan. The open problem is whether this problem can be solved in $f(g)\mathrm{poly}(n,m,\log S)$ time when parameterized only by the number $g$ of batches, preferably even under high-multiplicity encoding where the number of jobs in each batch is written in binary rather than expanded job by job.
known_results: The model is NP-hard already for one machine because sequence-dependent setup times generalize routing/TSP-style sequencing. Van Bevern and Pyatkin showed that if each batch contains more jobs than the number of machines, the problem is solvable in time roughly exponential only in $g$ plus near-linear input handling, and they also obtained polynomial-time solvability when both the number of machines $m$ and the number of batches $g$ are constants. Mnich and van Bevern state the remaining question as Open Problem 14: FPT in $g$ alone. Their discussion emphasizes high-multiplicity encoding, because an algorithm that expands all jobs may be pseudo-polynomial in the batch counts rather than truly efficient for compact instances.

background: Setup times are a major source of scheduling complexity: changing from one batch or product family to another may require cleaning, tooling, calibration, or travel. In open-shop scheduling, every job has one operation on each machine and the operation order is not prescribed. The batch setup variant groups jobs into batches and charges sequence-dependent setup time whenever a machine switches batch. Even with unit processing times, the model combines shop-scheduling constraints with a sequencing problem resembling TSP on batch labels. Van Bevern and Pyatkin obtained algorithms for important restricted cases, including settings where every batch is larger than the number of machines and settings where both the number of machines and number of batches are constants. Mnich and van Bevern ask for the clean parameterized classification by the number of batches alone. This is a natural OR question because product families may be few while the number of jobs and machines is large.

progress.summary: Restricted large-batch and constant-$(m,g)$ cases have algorithms, and high-multiplicity computation is understood for those restricted makespan calculations. The single-parameter dependence on the number of batches remains unresolved.

counterexample_rationale: The question asks for FPT algorithms or parameterized hardness. Small instances can suggest canonical batch sequences or disprove proposed dominance rules, but they cannot decide the classification.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can explore normal forms for machine schedules as words over $g$ batch labels and look for bounded-state descriptions. It can also generate compact bad instances for natural dynamic programs, but formal proof is still required.

literature.synthesis: The number of batches is a plausible practical parameter because batch families are often few, but the open-shop constraints allow many interleavings across machines. The known large-batch algorithm suggests that once each batch has enough jobs, machine schedules can be regularized; the unresolved case is where small batches create scarcity and synchronization effects. A positive result would need to show that all relevant setup patterns can be represented by a bounded object depending only on $g$, even while $m$ and the job counts vary. A high-multiplicity result would be stronger: it must reason about counts arithmetically rather than by expanding every job. A negative result would likely need a reduction in which the number of batch labels stays small but their transition matrix and counts encode a hard selection problem.

title: Instance-dependent complexity of fixed-budget best-arm identification
short_statement: Fixed-budget best-arm identification has no universally optimal instance-wise error exponent in general. The remaining issue is a sharp achievable tradeoff or a meaningful restricted algorithm class, not a universal analogue of Track-and-Stop.
full_statement:
Fix a known one-parameter reward family and $K$ independent arms with unknown mean vector $\mu$ and a unique best arm $i^*(\mu)$. An algorithm family $A=(A_T)_{T\ge1}$ adaptively allocates exactly $T$ observations and returns $\widehat i_T$. Write $p_{\mu,T}(A)=\Pr_\mu(\widehat i_T\ne i^*(\mu))$ and $\Gamma_A(\mu)=\liminf_{T\to\infty}T^{-1}\log(1/p_{\mu,T}(A))$. Consistency means $p_{\mu,T}(A)\to0$ for every admissible instance.

The historical question asked for an instance-dependent complexity attained simultaneously by one algorithm across all instances. That cannot hold in general: Degenne's COLT 2023 impossibility theorem already covers two Bernoulli arms for algorithm classes containing all fixed-proportion rules. Thus the previous formulation asking unconditionally for a uniformly optimal exponent was stale.

A distinct residual problem, identified in Degenne's conclusion, is whether a meaningful restricted class admits such a complexity. The class must be specified before optimization; restricting to a singleton makes the question vacuous. Alternatively one can fix a benchmark and seek a minimax ratio across instances, rather than a pointwise optimum. These alternatives must not be reported as the original unrestricted conjecture.

The separate question of dominating uniform sampling also depends on the reward family: the two-arm Bernoulli case is settled negatively by Wang, Ariu, and Proutiere, while Imbens, Qin, and Wager give a positive Gaussian equal-variance result for $K\ge3$.
known_results:
Degenne (COLT 2023, Theorem 10) rules out a common attainable complexity for two-arm Bernoulli identification in classes containing all static-proportion algorithms; the paper also establishes an obstruction for sufficiently many Gaussian arms. Its conclusion asks about meaningful restricted algorithm classes. Wang, Ariu, and Proutiere (ICML 2024) show that uniform allocation is undominated in error-exponent performance for two Bernoulli arms.

Imbens, Qin, and Wager (2025 preprint, Assumption 1 and Theorem 5) construct batched elimination rules improving the exponent over uniform allocation for $K\ge3$ Gaussian arms with common variance. For a fixed unique-best instance, expected simple regret and error probability differ by fixed positive gap factors, so they have the same exponential rate.

Goldberger's July 2026 preprint, Theorems 3.2 and 4.3, reports nonexistence of a complexity for every $K\ge3$ in regular one-parameter natural exponential families. This is a preprint result, not a proof independently certified by this repository. The unresolved work is on restricted classes or alternative tradeoffs, not the original unrestricted existence claim.

background:
A fixed experimental budget is natural in simulation optimization and ranking and selection: the experiment ends after a predetermined number of samples, rather than when a confidence threshold is reached. The asymptotic question concerns rare erroneous recommendations. This is different from fixed-confidence sample complexity and from Bayesian posterior concentration. A sampling rule whose proportions converge almost surely to an oracle allocation need not inherit that allocation's frequentist error exponent: atypical trajectories can dominate errors.

Qin's COLT 2022 note separated the existence of a common instance-wise optimum from the weaker question of improving on uniform allocation. The two questions now have substantial answers. This entry retains the historical question and its limitations, rather than continuing to advertise an unrestricted optimal algorithm as an unsolved target.

progress.summary: Corrected on 2026-11-09: unrestricted complexity is impossible in general; uniform-sampling admissibility is settled for two-arm Bernoulli and equal-variance Gaussian K>=3 models. Broader restricted-class questions remain separate.

The newer Gaussian admissibility construction does not contradict the impossibility of uniformly matching a more powerful instance-specific oracle.

title: Best competitive ratio for Adwords with unknown budgets
short_statement: Determine the optimal randomized competitive ratio for Adwords when advertiser budgets are initially unknown.
full_statement: Advertisers have hidden budgets $B_i>0$. On each adversarially ordered query t, bids $b_{it}$ are revealed and the algorithm irrevocably assigns it to one advertiser or discards it. An assigned advertiser pays the bid truncated at its remaining budget; exhaustion is revealed, but budgets are not available upfront. The benchmark is the integral offline optimum knowing all bids and budgets. Let $\gamma=\max_{i,t}b_{it}/B_i$. Determine the optimal randomized competitive ratio in the small-bids limit $\gamma\to0$, for inputs fixed independently of the algorithm's random choices. This is not a failed-allocation model requiring the entire bid to fit.
known_results: Udwani, arXiv:2110.00504v5, Theorem 1, bounds deterministic budget-oblivious algorithms by $1/2$. Theorems 2-3 and Corollary 1 give GPG at least $0.522/(1+\gamma)$, hence $0.522$ in the small-bids limit. The general upper benchmark is $1-1/e$. Liang, Tang, Xu, Zhang, and Zhou, arXiv:2210.10370v2, Theorem 2, bound all Perturbed-Ranking perturbation functions by $1-1/e-0.0003$; the canonical perturbation has upper bound $0.624$. These are framework restrictions, not upper bounds for every randomized budget-oblivious algorithm.

title: Efficient robust policies for heterogeneous data-driven decisions
short_statement: In the heterogeneity-ball framework for data-driven decisions, can one efficiently compute or approximate general robust policies that retain rate-optimal worst-case regret guarantees?
full_statement: Consider the Besbes-Ma-Mouchtaki heterogeneity-ball framework. A decision $x\in\mathcal{X}$ is evaluated under a future distribution $\mu$, while historical observations are independent but may come from different unknown distributions $\nu_1,\dots,\nu_n$ lying in a radius-$\epsilon$ ball around $\mu$ under a specified metric such as Kolmogorov distance, Wasserstein distance, total variation, or another integral probability metric. A data-driven policy maps historical samples into a decision, and performance is measured by asymptotic worst-case expected regret relative to the oracle decision optimal for $\mu$. Sample-average approximation is rate-optimal for some problem/metric pairs but is provably suboptimal for others, including canonical pricing and ski-rental variants under natural heterogeneity metrics. The open problem is to design computationally efficient policies, or approximation schemes for the robust prescriptions such as RDRO/DRO, that preserve rate-optimal worst-case regret over broad OR/MS decision classes. A satisfactory solution should specify the metric, loss geometry, decision-set structure, finite-sample or asymptotic guarantee, and computational model.
known_results: Besbes, Ma, and Mouchtaki define the heterogeneity-ball framework and prove general regret upper bounds for broad policy classes. They analyze SAA under integral probability metrics and introduce an approximation parameter explaining when SAA succeeds or fails. They prove rate-optimal robust policies for illustrative problems including newsvendor, pricing, and ski rental, and they provide initial steps toward general rate-optimal algorithms. Their contextual-newsvendor follow-up gives an exact worst-case regret characterization for weighted empirical risk minimization policies on any fixed context configuration, reducing an infinite-dimensional distributional problem to a tractable one-dimensional search. Kumar and Mouchtaki later give an exact finite-dimensional reduction for worst-case regret of classical data-driven newsvendor policies under censored demand observations. These papers substantially sharpen exact performance analysis in special newsvendor-style models, but they do not settle the general open problem: efficient, broadly applicable robust policies with rate-optimal guarantees for general heterogeneous OR/MS decision classes, finite-sample settings, and unknown heterogeneity radii.

background: Most data-driven OR theory assumes that historical samples and the future deployment environment are iid draws from one distribution. Besbes, Ma, and Mouchtaki study a cleaner and more pessimistic model for the common case where historical data come from related but different environments: each historical distribution lies in a heterogeneity ball around the future distribution, and performance is measured by worst-case regret relative to the future oracle. This is not an open-ended modelling request; the heterogeneity-ball model, metrics, and benchmark are already defined. The paper shows that sample-average approximation can be rate-optimal in some problem/metric pairs and badly suboptimal in others, motivating robust policies such as RDRO and DRO variants. The remaining problem is algorithmic and structural: can one design broadly applicable policies that are computationally efficient and retain the rate-optimal guarantees, rather than proving problem-by-problem robust prescriptions?

progress.summary: The framework and several problem-specific rate-optimal policies are known. Follow-up work gives exact worst-case regret reductions for contextual and censored newsvendor variants. The broad efficient-algorithm question remains open for general losses and decision sets where the robust policy is not a simple scalar prescription.

literature.synthesis: The Beyond-IID paper builds a formal bridge between distributionally robust optimization and statistical rates under heterogeneous data. Its key contribution is not just that heterogeneity hurts, but that the interaction between metric, loss geometry, and decision class determines whether SAA is rate-optimal. The contextual and censored-data follow-ups show that exact worst-case analysis is possible in carefully structured newsvendor models, and they supply useful reduction templates for finite-dimensional certification. The open gap is that these templates are not yet a general computational theory. For a repository of open problems, this is a good candidate because the model is parsimonious and the missing object is precise: an efficient policy or approximation scheme with rate guarantees under heterogeneity balls, ideally covering broad convex losses and operational decision sets.

title: Talagrand's decomposition conjecture for empirical processes
short_statement: Does every bounded empirical process decompose into a non-cancellation part plus a generic-chaining part, as predicted by Talagrand's program?
full_statement: Let $(X_i)_{i\le N}$ be i.i.d. random variables on a measurable space and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a countable class of measurable functions. Define the empirical-process supremum $$S_N(\mathcal{F})=\mathbb{E}\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left|\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_{i\le N}(f(X_i)-\mathbb{E}f(X_i))\right|.$$ There are two basic mechanisms for controlling $S_N(\mathcal{F})$: a pointwise/no-cancellation bound through $\sum_i |f(X_i)|$, and a cancellation/chaining bound involving $\gamma_2(\mathcal{F},d_2)$ and $\gamma_1(\mathcal{F},d_\infty)$, where $d_p(f,g)=\|f-g\|_p$. Talagrand's conjecture asks whether these are the only mechanisms: can one always find a decomposition $\mathcal{F}\subset \mathcal{F}_1+\mathcal{F}_2$ such that $$\mathbb{E}\sup_{f_1\in\mathcal{F}_1}\sum_{i\le N}|f_1(X_i)|\le \sqrt N\,S_N(\mathcal{F}),$$ $$\gamma_2(\mathcal{F}_2,d_2)\le L S_N(\mathcal{F}),\qquad \gamma_1(\mathcal{F}_2,d_\infty)\le L\sqrt N\,S_N(\mathcal{F})$$ for a universal constant $L$? A related selector-process version asks for an analogous decomposition for Bernoulli selectors $\delta_i$.
known_results: Talagrand's majorizing-measure theorem characterizes Gaussian-process suprema. Bednorz and Latała prove the Bernoulli conjecture, giving a decomposition theorem for Bernoulli processes and resolving a major piece of Talagrand's program. Their paper explicitly discusses related open problems, including selector-process and empirical-process decomposition conjectures. These conjectures remain distinct from the solved Bernoulli case because empirical processes include sampling randomness and function-class geometry beyond independent signs.

background: Talagrand's majorizing-measure program asks for structural explanations of why stochastic-process suprema are bounded. For Gaussian processes, generic chaining gives an exact answer. Bernoulli and empirical processes are harder because large coordinates can contribute without cancellation, while the remaining part may behave like a chaining process. Bednorz and Latała solved the Bernoulli conjecture by proving that bounded Bernoulli processes decompose into an $\ell^1$ no-cancellation component and a Gaussian/chaining component. They also recorded broader Talagrand-style conjectures for selector and empirical processes. The empirical-process version is a clean applied-probability problem: given a bounded empirical-process supremum, can one always decompose the function class into a part controlled by pointwise absolute mass and a part controlled by $\gamma_2$ and $\gamma_1$ chaining functionals?

progress.summary: The Bernoulli analogue is solved by Bednorz and Latała. The empirical-process and selector-process decompositions remain open as broader Talagrand-program questions.

literature.synthesis: Gaussian processes are governed by generic chaining, but Bernoulli and empirical processes have an additional sparse-coordinate mechanism. Talagrand conjectured that the correct theory should decompose these mechanisms rather than bound them separately with loose estimates. Bednorz and Latała's solution of the Bernoulli conjecture proves exactly this type of decomposition for Bernoulli signs. The empirical-process conjecture asks for an analogous structural statement for sampled function classes, with a no-cancellation term and $\gamma_2/\gamma_1$ chaining terms. Existing Bernoulli machinery is suggestive but does not directly handle empirical-process symmetrization, selectors, and the interaction between $L_2$ and $L_\infty$ geometries.

title: Efficient recovery at the random graph matching threshold
short_statement: Can polynomial-time algorithms recover the hidden matching in correlated Erdos-Renyi graphs down to the information-theoretic threshold?
open_problem: Close the computational gap for unseeded correlated Erdos-Renyi graph matching: either design polynomial-time exact/almost-exact recovery algorithms matching the information-theoretic thresholds, or prove a computational barrier under a standard average-case hardness framework.
full_statement: Let $G_0\sim G(n,p)$ be a parent Erdos-Renyi graph. Generate two observed graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ by independently retaining parent edges so that their marginal edge density and edge-correlation parameter are $q$ and $\rho$, then relabel $G_2$ by an unknown uniform permutation $\pi$. Given only the unlabeled pair $(G_1,G_2)$, recover $\pi$ exactly, recover all but $o(n)$ vertices, or recover a positive fraction of vertices, depending on the regime. Information-theoretic thresholds are known sharply in dense models and increasingly sharply in sparse models, often by maximum-likelihood achievability and second-moment lower bounds. The open problem is to determine the polynomial-time threshold for unseeded correlated Erdos-Renyi graph matching: can an efficient algorithm succeed down to the information-theoretic boundary, including the sparse regimes below existing chandelier/tree-count guarantees, or is there a principled computational gap?
known_results: Wu, Xu, and Yu established sharp reconstruction thresholds for dense correlated random graph matching and sparse thresholds up to constant factors; their positive results are information-theoretic and rely on maximum-likelihood-type arguments rather than efficient algorithms. Ding and Du sharpened the positive-overlap recovery threshold in sparse correlated Erdos-Renyi graphs. Wu, Xu, and Yu also characterized testing thresholds for unlabeled graph correlation in dense settings and within constant factors in sparse settings. On the algorithmic side, Mao, Wu, Xu, and Yu introduced chandelier-count statistics and obtained a polynomial-time algorithm that almost exactly matches when $nq\to\infty$ and $\rho^2$ exceeds Otter's tree-counting constant $\alpha\approx0.338$, with exact recovery under an additional information-theoretically necessary condition. Seeded and structured variants are better understood. The unresolved gap is whether unseeded efficient algorithms can reach the full information-theoretic recovery boundary.

background: Graph matching asks whether two observed networks have the same hidden vertex labels. In the correlated Erdos-Renyi model, two graphs are generated from a common random parent graph and then independently subsampled, with one graph's labels permuted. The statistical question is whether the hidden permutation can be recovered exactly or approximately; the algorithmic question is whether this can be done in polynomial time at the same parameter values where recovery is information-theoretically possible. This model captures a clean version of entity resolution, network alignment, and average-case inference. Wu, Xu, and Yu determined sharp reconstruction thresholds in dense regimes and near-sharp thresholds in sparse regimes using information-theoretic and maximum-likelihood arguments. Subsequent work sharpened sparse thresholds and designed polynomial-time algorithms based on trees and chandeliers in some regimes. The central remaining issue is whether efficient algorithms can match the information-theoretic thresholds, or whether there is a genuine statistical-computational gap.

progress.summary: Information-theoretic thresholds are now sharp or nearly sharp in major regimes, and polynomial-time motif/tree algorithms succeed in some parameter ranges. The full efficient recovery threshold for unseeded matching remains unresolved.

counterexample_rationale: Finite simulations can disprove overly optimistic algorithms or reveal hard regimes, but the threshold question is asymptotic and probabilistic. Explicit counterexamples are less central than rigorous average-case lower bounds.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can explore graph statistics, motif families, and message-passing updates that correlate with the hidden permutation near threshold. Candidate algorithms can be tested extensively before proof.

literature.synthesis: The statistical side of correlated graph matching has advanced rapidly. Wu, Xu, and Yu used mutual-information and second-moment methods to locate reconstruction thresholds in dense models and approximate sparse thresholds, while maximum likelihood gives information-theoretic achievability. Ding and Du sharpened sparse recovery thresholds. Algorithmically, seeded matching and motif-counting methods provide efficient procedures in favorable regimes, and chandelier/tree statistics show that local structures carry exploitable correlation. The remaining gap is to determine whether such efficient statistics can be pushed to the full information-theoretic boundary, or whether low-degree or other average-case evidence points to inherent computational hardness.

title: Sharp computational thresholds for planted structures
short_statement: Make the statistical-computational thresholds for canonical planted dense-subgraph and submatrix models sharp.
open_problem: Close the remaining statistical-computational gaps for planted dense subgraph, planted clustering, and submatrix localization by matching efficient algorithms with sharp conditional lower bounds in the unresolved sparse/growing regimes.
full_statement: Fix a canonical planted-structure model such as planted dense subgraph, planted clustering, or submatrix localization. Under the null, the observation is an Erdos-Renyi graph, a random matrix with independent noise, or a related product distribution. Under the alternative, an unknown subset, community partition, or submatrix of size parameters such as $k$ and $r$ receives elevated edge probability, mean shift, or correlation. For each model and asymptotic regime, define the information-theoretic threshold as the smallest signal at which detection, weak recovery, exact recovery, or localization is possible by any estimator, and define the polynomial-time threshold as the smallest signal at which an algorithm running in $n^{O(1)}$ time succeeds with high probability. Determine the sharp polynomial-time threshold, including constants where meaningful, or prove a matching conditional lower bound under a standard average-case assumption such as planted clique or the low-degree-polynomial framework. The target is a precise threshold theorem for one unresolved sparse or growing planted model, not a new modeling variant.
known_results: Chen and Xu partitioned planted clustering and submatrix-localization parameter spaces into impossible, hard, easy, and simple regions, with tight results up to constants in several growing-cluster regimes. Wu and Xu surveyed the now-standard toolkit: first- and second-moment analyses for information-theoretic limits, mutual-information and interpolation methods for impossibility, and randomized reductions from planted clique for conditional computational lower bounds. Hajek, Wu, and Xu developed planted-clique-based lower bounds for community detection, showing how average-case reductions can explain algorithmic barriers. The low-degree framework has since become a second major source of evidence, and recent work on planted hypergraphs and tensor PCA identifies sharp low-degree thresholds in some regimes and turns matching upper bounds into algorithms above the threshold. Still, for several planted dense-subgraph, clustering, and submatrix regimes, the best algorithms, planted-clique reductions, and low-degree predictions do not yet form a single sharp boundary.

background: Planted-structure problems are clean average-case models for statistical-computational gaps. One observes a random object, such as an Erdos-Renyi graph or a noisy matrix, into which a hidden clique, dense subgraph, community, or elevated submatrix has been planted. Information theory may allow recovery at very low signal levels, while all known polynomial-time algorithms require much stronger signal. Wu and Xu survey a general toolkit for proving information-theoretic thresholds and conditional computational lower bounds, often by reductions from planted clique. Chen and Xu give a detailed four-region picture for planted clustering and submatrix localization with growing numbers of clusters. Since then, low-degree polynomial methods have sharpened evidence for computational thresholds in several planted models. The open problem is to turn this evidence into exact algorithmic thresholds or matching conditional lower bounds in canonical regimes where current constants and boundaries do not line up.

progress.summary: Information-theoretic thresholds, convex-algorithm guarantees, planted-clique reductions, and low-degree evidence cover many regimes. Sharp polynomial-time thresholds remain open in several sparse and growing planted-structure models.

alphaevolve_rationale: Search can find statistics, spectral matrices, message-passing rules, or low-degree features that improve algorithms near threshold. It can also generate hard instances for heuristics.

literature.synthesis: The core gap is now well formalized. The information-theoretic side often follows from likelihood, second-moment, or interpolation arguments. The algorithmic side includes spectral methods, semidefinite programming, message passing, and low-degree polynomials. Conditional lower bounds via planted clique and low-degree calculations provide evidence for gaps, but exact thresholds and constants are not universally known. Recent low-degree results sharpen the picture for planted hypergraphs and tensor PCA, suggesting that similarly precise analyses may be possible for other planted dense-subgraph and submatrix settings.
