title: The CTCS(infinity) limit and the beta(2,1) coalescent
short_statement: Characterize the infinite critical beta-splitting CTCS limit and its exact relation to the beta$(2,1)$ coalescent.
open_problem: Give a complete probabilistic description of $\mathrm{CTCS}(\infty)$ and identify the exact mathematical relationship, if any, between its exchangeable partition dynamics and the beta$(2,1)$ coalescent.
full_statement: In the critical beta-splitting model, a clade of size $m$ splits into subclades of sizes $i$ and $m-i$ with probability proportional to $1/(i(m-i))$, independently down the tree. Aldous and Janson embed this discrete Markov-branching tree in a continuous-time consistent splitting model $\mathrm{CTCS}(n)$ with real edge lengths. The family $\{\mathrm{CTCS}(n):n\ge2\}$ is consistent under deleting a uniformly random leaf and pruning degree-two vertices, which leads to an infinite exchangeable limit $\mathrm{CTCS}(\infty)$ represented through nested exchangeable partitions. The open problem is to give a complete probabilistic description of this infinite object and its partition-valued dynamics. In particular, determine whether the genealogy or time-reversal of $\mathrm{CTCS}(\infty)$ is exactly the beta$(2,1)$ coalescent, a deterministic time change of that coalescent, a projection or size-biased transform of it, or merely shares some marginal split-size asymptotics.
known_results: Aldous and Janson constructed the consistent finite $\mathrm{CTCS}(n)$ family, proved detailed results for leaf heights and fringe distributions, and formulated an exchangeable infinite limit. Their Part III paper develops the exchangeable partition representation and fringe tree more explicitly, giving a concrete framework in which finite restrictions of $\mathrm{CTCS}(\infty)$ can be studied. Part IV gives sharper Mellin analysis of leaf heights and normal/large-deviation estimates. Kolesnik supplied contraction-method proofs for related height central limit theorems. These advances clarify many one-dimensional and fringe statistics, but they do not fully identify the partition dynamics with, or separate it from, the beta$(2,1)$ coalescent.

background: Aldous's beta-splitting family is a fundamental model for random rooted binary trees, motivated in part by phylogenetic tree shapes. The critical beta-splitting case has splitting probabilities proportional to $1/(i(m-i))$ for a clade of size $m$, producing unusually balanced logarithmic phenomena and a rich connection between recursive tree structure, Markov chains, and exchangeable partitions. Aldous and Janson developed a continuous-time consistent splitting model $\mathrm{CTCS}(n)$ whose finite-$n$ trees are consistent under deletion of a uniform leaf. This consistency suggests an infinite exchangeable limit $\mathrm{CTCS}(\infty)$, analogous in spirit to continuum random tree limits but with different merger/splitting structure. Their later papers formalize exchangeable partition representations and fringe-tree limits. The remaining conceptual question is the exact relationship between this infinite critical splitting object and the beta$(2,1)$ coalescent.

progress.summary: The exchangeable partition representation and fringe tree have been developed further in later papers, but the exact beta$(2,1)$ coalescent relationship remains unresolved.

counterexample_rationale: Finite-dimensional distributions of $\mathrm{CTCS}(n)$ can refute a proposed exact coalescent identity. A complete positive result needs exchangeable-partition process convergence.
alphaevolve_rationale: Symbolic and simulation search can compare finite merger rates and suggest time changes. The main work is probabilistic identification of an infinite exchangeable process.

literature.synthesis: The finite critical beta-splitting model is explicit, but its infinite limit is subtle because consistency is expressed through deletion and pruning rather than a simple forward growth rule. The CTCS construction gives a natural continuous-time object, and later exchangeable-partition work makes the limit more concrete. The beta$(2,1)$ coalescent appears as the plausible coalescent-side analogue, but equality of finite-dimensional transition rates, time changes, and projections must be pinned down. The open problem is a structural identification, not just another asymptotic estimate.

title: Sharp cover times for random growing balls
short_statement: Develop sharp cover-time asymptotics for sequentially arriving randomly centered growing balls on compact metric spaces.
open_problem: Determine sharp cover-time laws for specified asymptotic families in the deterministic-birth model above. Separate this target from established Poisson, linear-growth results, and specify assumptions ensuring finite cover times.
full_statement: Let $(S,d)$ be a compact metric space with Borel probability measure $\mu$. At integer times $i=1,2,\ldots$, centers $X_i$ are sampled iid from $\mu$. A ball born at time $i$ has radius $r(t-i)$ at time $t\ge i$, where $r:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is deterministic, nondecreasing, and $r(0)=0$. The cover time is $$T=\inf\left\{t:S\subseteq \bigcup_{1\le i\le t} B(X_i,r(t-i))\right\}.$$ Aldous's weak-concentration theorem instead concerns Poisson birth times and linear growth; it is not a theorem for this entire deterministic-birth, arbitrary-growth model. Asymptotic questions must specify a sequence of spaces, arrival scalings, or growth scalings, and conditions ensuring finite cover times. The open problem is to determine sharp first-order constants, second-order corrections, and limiting distributions for $T$ in natural families of spaces: intervals, circles, flat tori, compact manifolds, fractals, finite metric spaces approaching a continuum, and irregular measures with nonuniform local dimension. A satisfactory answer should identify which geometric quantities, such as metric entropy, small-ball probabilities, boundary effects, and bottleneck sets, determine the cover-time law.
known_results: Aldous (2022), Section 3, equation (3.1) and Proposition 3.1, treats Poisson births of rate $\lambda$, iid centers, and radius $v(t-\tau_i)$, proving $\operatorname{Var}(C/\mathbb EC)\le c^*/\mathbb EC$, where $c^*=\sup_s\mathbb EC(s)$. This is not a result for arbitrary $r$ or deterministic birth times. Penrose and Higgs (2026), Theorems 2.2-2.3, give sharp centering and limiting laws for Poisson seeds restricted to $A\times[0,\infty)$ with linear unit growth: planar polygons and compact smoothly bounded domains in dimensions $d\ge2$. In dimension two the limit has both area and boundary contributions, not a single Gumbel term. Transferring such laws to this record's schedule requires a separate argument.

where_posed.text: Related Poisson, linear-growth questions occur in Aldous; the deterministic-birth, arbitrary-growth formulation here is an editorial extension, not his exact model.

title: Oracle-efficient agnostic contextual bandits
short_statement: Offline-regression reductions already tolerate misspecification in important stochastic models. The remaining scope must separate that solved case from fully agnostic best-policy regret and large-action oracle limitations.
open_problem: The finite-action misspecification-tolerant reduction is known. A narrower residual question about fully agnostic policy regret or large-action exploration must first fix its oracle model and exact guarantee; the previous blanket open claim is withdrawn.
full_statement:
There are two different contextual-bandit targets. In the finite-action stochastic model, $(x_t,r_t)$ are iid, $a_t\in[K]$, and only $r_t(a_t)\in[0,1]$ is observed. An offline squared-loss regression oracle fits a reward class $\mathcal F$. If its prediction error under every relevant sampling kernel is bounded by $B+\xi(n,\delta)$, Safe-FALCON already provides regret to the optimal policy of the form $\widetilde O(T\sqrt{KB}+T\sqrt{K\xi(T,\delta)})$, under its stated oracle assumptions. Asking only for an offline-regression algorithm that degrades gracefully with misspecification is therefore not open.

A fully agnostic best-in-class policy target is different: define $\Pi_\mathcal F=\{x\mapsto\arg\max_a f(x,a):f\in\mathcal F\}$ with fixed tie-breaking, and compare to $\max_{\pi\in\Pi_\mathcal F}\mathbb E\sum_t r_t(\pi(x_t))$ without assuming small reward-prediction error. Cost-sensitive policy optimization and square-loss regression are different oracle models. For large action spaces, finding exploration distributions also has a computational cost beyond fitting a predictor.

This record currently combines those directions. A proposed residual theorem must specify the comparator, oracle interface, query budget, and structural assumptions. The broad request for a 'canonical agnostic theorem' is not yet a sufficiently precise verified open conjecture.
known_results:
Krishnamurthy, Hadad, and Athey (ICML 2021, Assumption 1 and Theorem 1) establish the Safe-FALCON guarantee displayed above; their Theorem 2 gives a misspecification lower bound for policies in the convex hull of their kernel class $\mathcal K(\mathcal F)$, not for every conceivable use of a regression oracle. Thus robustness beyond realizability is already established without an online or constrained regression oracle.

Qin and Zhang (COLT 2026, arXiv v2) extend offline-regression reductions to large action spaces via DOEC and exploration-design conditions. Appendix D.1, Corollary 8, gives $\widetilde O(\sqrt{TD\log(|\mathcal F|/\delta)}+T\sqrt{BD})$ under uniform squared misspecification $B$ and the stated design assumptions. Its exploration parameter uses $B$. These results do not establish an unrestricted best-policy guarantee from a bare regression oracle.

title: Limited-switch contextual bandits with knapsacks
short_statement: What are the optimal regret rates for contextual bandits with knapsack constraints when the policy is allowed only a limited number of switches?
open_problem: Characterize the minimax regret of contextual bandits with knapsacks under a switching budget, including the correct dependence on horizon, budgets, resource dimension, policy-class complexity, and number of allowed switches.
full_statement: Consider a contextual bandits-with-knapsacks problem over horizon $T$. At each round $t$, a context $x_t$ is observed, the learner chooses an action $a_t$, receives stochastic reward $r_t(a_t,x_t)$, and consumes a vector $c_t(a_t,x_t)\in\mathbb R_+^d$ of resources from budgets $B_1,\ldots,B_d$. The learner competes with a benchmark class $\Pi$ of policies mapping contexts to actions, subject to the same resource budgets, and the process stops or must choose null actions when a budget is exhausted. Add a switching constraint: one may count either changes of realized actions or changes of the deployed context-to-action mapping. These are different models, not equivalent conventions. Under mapping switches, at most $S+1$ epochs can use fixed deployed policies even though actions vary with contexts. The open problem is to characterize the minimax regret as a function of $T$, the budgets, resource dimension $d$, policy-class complexity or oracle access, and switch budget $S$. The result should recover known contextual BwK rates when switching is unconstrained and known limited-switch BwK rates when there are no contexts.
known_results:
Simchi-Levi, Xu, and Zhao prove matching upper and lower bounds for blind network revenue management and bandits with knapsacks under limited switches. Their optimal regret rate is governed by a piecewise-constant function of the switch budget and the number of resource constraints. Agrawal, Devanur, and Li give efficient algorithms for contextual bandits with knapsacks without switching constraints. These results motivate asking whether the noncontextual switch-budget structure survives in a specified contextual model. The search conducted for this audit did not establish a sharp theorem for the combined setting, but that absence is not evidence that every such variant is open.

Audit caveat (2026-11-09): changing the realized action and changing a mapping from contexts to actions are not equivalent switching constraints. A fixed mapping can choose different actions on successive contexts. This record needs one explicit switching convention, context process, and benchmark before its combined open-status claim can be considered verified.

background: Bandits with knapsacks capture online allocation with learning and finite resources: each action earns stochastic reward and consumes one or more budgeted resources. Contextual versions are central in pricing, ad allocation, and revenue management because customer covariates change the reward and consumption distributions. Separately, limited-switch models impose a practical operational constraint: prices, assortments, or allocation rules cannot be changed every period. Simchi-Levi, Xu, and Zhao recently give a sharp limited-switch theory for blind network revenue management and bandits with knapsacks, showing a piecewise-constant dependence of regret on the switching budget and the number of resources. A possible research direction is their intersection with contextual BwK. However, combining the frameworks does not uniquely specify a model: the switching convention, context process, and comparator must first be fixed. This entry is provisional, not a verified clean open problem.

progress.summary: The cited sources treat the noncontextual limited-switch case and contextual BwK without switching. The status of a combined target is unverified because this entry has not fixed a unique switching convention and benchmark.

counterexample_rationale: Lower-bound instances can be finite contextual distributions with a small number of resources and switches. Counterexamples to proposed regret rates are plausible through constructed hard instances, but full minimax lower bounds require information-theoretic proof.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can help discover hard finite instances and test algorithm schedules for limited switches. Evolutionary methods could optimize adversarial context distributions or switch budgets against candidate policies.

literature.synthesis: The noncontextual limited-switch results and contextual BwK results supply useful starting points, but do not by themselves establish an open problem at their intersection. A fixed context-to-action policy can change realized actions on every round, so counting policy changes and counting action changes yield different feasible sets. Before asserting a remaining minimax gap, specify the context process, switching convention, comparator, resource-feasibility convention, and oracle access, then check the literature for that exact model. This audit did not complete that model-specific verification.

Lower bounds should adapt limited-switch price-learning constructions while embedding covariate uncertainty. A useful first target is finite policy classes with stochastic iid contexts and linear resource consumptions.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed rate must specify whether it is minimax, instance-dependent, Bayesian, or oracle-class dependent, and it must define the benchmark policy class. It must state exactly what counts as a switch: changing the concrete action, changing a mapping from contexts to actions, changing randomized mixture weights, or changing posted prices can lead to different models. Resource feasibility must hold for realized play, not only in expectation, unless the benchmark is also expectation-constrained. A positive theorem should reduce to the Simchi-Levi-Xu-Zhao limited-switch rate in the noncontextual case and to contextual BwK rates when $S$ is large. A lower bound should separate the contribution of switching scarcity from ordinary contextual learning and knapsack scarcity.

title: Optimal two-sided flexibility allocation for random bipartite matching
short_statement: In a two-sided platform where a fixed flexibility budget can be split between the two sides of a random bipartite graph, is the expected maximum matching always optimized by either the fully one-sided or the balanced allocation?
open_problem: Prove or refute that, in the Freund-Martin-Zhao random bipartite flexibility model, the expected maximum matching is always maximized by either a fully one-sided flexibility allocation or a balanced allocation, and characterize the boundary between the regimes.
full_statement: Consider the heterogeneous random bipartite-graph model of Freund, Martin, and Zhao. There are two sides of a matching market, a fixed budget $B$ of flexible agents, and an allocation decision specifying how much flexibility is placed on each side. Flexible nodes have a higher probability of being compatible with nodes on the opposite side, while the model normalizes edge probabilities so that changes in performance come from how compatibility is distributed rather than simply from adding more expected edges. The main performance metric $\mu$ is the asymptotic expected size of a maximum matching. Numerical evidence using the Karp-Sipser-based approximation $\mu_{KS}$ and empirical simulations $\mu_{EMP}$ suggests that $\mu$ is always maximized either by the one-sided allocation or by the balanced allocation. The open problem is to prove this extremal principle, or find a counterexample, and then give an analytical boundary in $(B,p_n,p_f)$ space separating the one-sided-optimal and balanced-optimal regimes.
known_results: Freund, Martin, and Zhao fully analyze a simpler isolation-based performance metric and derive partial comparisons for the maximum-matching objective in edge regimes. For the actual expected maximum matching size, their Karp-Sipser approximation and simulations suggest a striking dichotomy: optimal allocations appear to be either one-sided or balanced, not intermediate. The paper identifies flexibility cannibalization and flexibility abundance as drivers of the two regimes, but a proof of the extremal dichotomy and an analytical phase boundary remain open.

background: Process flexibility is a central operations-management idea: a little flexibility in who can serve whom can recover much of the value of full flexibility. Traditional models usually allocate flexibility on one side of a bipartite system, such as plants to products or servers to demand classes. Two-sided platforms complicate this because compatibility can be improved on either side: drivers may become able to serve more rider types, or riders may become willing to accept more provider types. Freund, Martin, and Zhao propose a parsimonious random bipartite-graph model where a fixed flexibility budget can be split across sides and performance is the expected maximum matching size. Their analysis shows that optimizing each side separately can be badly misleading, and that two forces, flexibility cannibalization and flexibility abundance, help explain when one-sided or balanced allocations are good. The unresolved part is a sharp structural theorem for the true matching objective.

progress.summary: Isolation-based metrics are analytically characterized and maximum-matching edge regimes are partially understood. The full expected-matching extremal principle is still conjectural.

links.title: Freund, Martin, Zhao, Two-Sided Flexibility in Platforms

counterexample_rationale: A counterexample would be a finite or asymptotic parameter setting where an intermediate split beats both one-sided and balanced allocations. Expected matching sizes can be estimated or computed for finite graphs.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search over random-graph parameters and finite-size exact matching computations can stress-test the dichotomy and suggest phase-boundary formulas.

literature.synthesis: The classical process-flexibility literature shows that sparse flexibility designs can be nearly as valuable as full flexibility, but it usually treats flexibility as located on one side. The two-sided model introduces a new allocation dimension: flexibility on the two sides can substitute for or cannibalize each other. Freund-Martin-Zhao's analytical isolation metric gives intuition, while the maximum-matching metric is the operationally central objective. The remaining gap is mathematical: prove that the observed one-sided/balanced dichotomy is inherent to the random matching model, or find a parameter regime where an interior split is strictly optimal.

title: Optimal type-dependence in contextual dynamic pricing with heterogeneous buyers
short_statement: For contextual dynamic pricing with an unknown finite mixture of buyer types, what is the optimal regret dependence on the number of latent types, and can it be achieved by a computationally efficient algorithm?
open_problem: Determine the optimal dependence on the latent type count $K_\star$ for contextual dynamic pricing with heterogeneous buyers, and achieve it with a computationally efficient algorithm.
full_statement: A seller repeatedly observes a $d$-dimensional context, posts a price, and observes only a binary purchase decision. The buyer's valuation type is drawn from an unknown distribution $D_\star$ with finite support size $K_\star$, so heterogeneity creates a context-dependent, non-i.i.d. demand curve even when the type distribution is fixed. Lykouris, Nietert, Okoroafor, Podimata, and Zimmert give an optimistic posterior sampling approach whose regret scales as $\widetilde O(K_\star\sqrt{dT})$ in the general contextual setting, with a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{K_\star dT})$ for sufficiently large horizons. In the non-contextual case they improve the type dependence to $\widetilde O(\sqrt{K_\star T})$ using a variance-aware zooming algorithm. The open problem is to obtain the right $K_\star$ dependence in the full contextual model, and to do so with an efficient algorithm rather than one whose runtime is exponential in $K_\star$ and $d$. The contextual lower bound in Theorem 3.8 assumes $K_\star>1$ and $T\ge 8dK_\star^3\log(2d)$. The stronger rate with ex-post valuation-vector feedback is a different feedback model, not a resolution under binary purchase feedback.
known_results: Lykouris et al. give an optimistic posterior sampling algorithm with regret $\widetilde O(K_\star\sqrt{dT})$ in the contextual model, tight in $d$ and $T$ up to logarithmic factors. They prove a lower bound of order $\Omega(\sqrt{K_\star dT})$ for sufficiently large horizons, leaving a gap between linear and square-root dependence on $K_\star$. In the non-contextual case, their variance-aware zooming algorithm achieves the optimal $\widetilde O(\sqrt{K_\star T})$ dependence, showing that linear $K_\star$ is not inevitable without context. The algorithmic efficiency question is also open because the posterior-sampling approach can have exponential dependence on model-class discretization.

background: Dynamic pricing with binary purchase feedback is a canonical revenue-management learning problem. Classical models usually assume a homogeneous valuation response after conditioning on observable context. Lykouris, Nietert, Okoroafor, Podimata, and Zimmert add a clean form of latent heterogeneity: each arriving buyer's type is drawn from an unknown finite distribution with support size $K_\star$, and the seller sees context but not type. This creates a mixture demand curve and makes exploration harder because the same price/context observation is informative about multiple latent valuation components. Their paper gives the first regret bounds for this contextual heterogeneous model, but leaves a sharp dependence on the number of latent types unresolved. This is a well-posed learning-theoretic gap inside a specified pricing model: the open question is about regret exponents and computational efficiency, not about choosing a better demand model.

progress.summary: The first contextual upper and lower bounds are known, and the non-contextual $K_\star$ dependence is resolved. The full contextual type-dependence and efficient implementation remain open.

counterexample_rationale: Finite mixture instances can test proposed algorithms and lower-bound constructions, but a tight minimax theorem requires asymptotic regret analysis.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can generate hard finite mixtures and evaluate pricing policies in simulation, especially to distinguish $K$ versus $\sqrt K$ behavior. Formal regret proofs are still required.

literature.synthesis: The known bounds show that context dimension and horizon dependence are essentially understood for the proposed heterogeneous model, while type dependence is not. The non-contextual solution suggests that variance-aware localization can exploit the finite mixture structure more efficiently than naive posterior sampling. The contextual difficulty is that context partitions interact with latent type learning, and price feedback is censored to a binary purchase decision. A plausible positive route would combine metric-bandit zooming with mixture estimation or variance-sensitive confidence bounds; a lower-bound route would need instances where contexts force repeated relearning across type components.

title: Optimal exploration of new products with heterogeneous priors
short_statement: For assortment-based exploration of new products, characterize the optimal ordering/grouping policy when entrants have heterogeneous priors rather than a common prior.
open_problem: Characterize the optimal assortment-exploration policy for heterogeneous entrant priors under the MNL social-learning model, or prove an optimal index/priority rule for deciding which entrants to explore and whether to group them.
full_statement: A platform repeatedly offers an assortment $S_t$ of at most $c$ products. Incumbent products have known MNL attraction parameters, while entrant products begin with cold-start attraction parameters and independent prior distributions over their true attraction parameters. If a customer purchases entrant $i$, a review reveals $i$'s true attraction parameter; otherwise no information about that entrant is learned. Rewards are generated by MNL purchase probabilities, and regret is measured relative to the assortment that would be optimal if all attraction parameters were known. Baek, Dinev, and Lykouris solve the homogeneous-prior case, where all entrants have the same prior, and show that the optimal EFA policy pairs entrants with top incumbents and chooses the number of entrants to explore through a threshold rule. The open problem is to characterize the optimal policy when entrants have heterogeneous priors: which entrants should be explored first, when should multiple heterogeneous entrants be grouped, and does there exist an index or low-dimensional priority rule that is provably optimal beyond the two-entrant special case?
known_results: Baek, Dinev, and Lykouris show that with one entrant it is optimal to include that entrant with the $c-1$ most attractive incumbents. With multiple homogeneous-prior entrants, they characterize the optimal number of entrants to explore simultaneously and show the threshold depends on entrant potential rather than individual purchase probabilities. They also prove that UCB and Thompson sampling can be arbitrarily suboptimal in opposite directions, and that simple heuristics such as always exploring all entrants or exploring one at a time can fail. For heterogeneous priors, they analyze a class with two entrants, two incumbents, and capacity two: the optimal policy is one of exploring entrant 1 first, entrant 2 first, or both together, and the best choice can depend subtly on prior tails. They explicitly leave open whether there is a prior-based index whose ordering is optimal in the general heterogeneous case.

background: Platforms constantly decide how much scarce display capacity to allocate to new products whose quality is unknown. The Baek-Dinev-Lykouris model is deliberately parsimonious: incumbents have known qualities, entrants require purchases and reviews to reveal quality, and assortment capacity creates a direct opportunity cost. This is not the same as an MNL bandit with unknown choice parameters, because before a review arrives the current choice model is common knowledge; the uncertainty concerns a future change in the choice model after social learning reveals a product's quality. Their homogeneous-prior result is structural rather than merely algorithmic. It explains why a new product should be paired with strong incumbents despite a lower purchase probability, and why the number of entrants explored simultaneously follows a threshold based on entrant potential. Heterogeneous priors remove the symmetry that makes EFA clean: the platform must rank entrants with different upside probabilities, cold-start attractions, and effects on future assortment value.

progress.summary: The homogeneous-prior model is solved by EFA, and a two-entrant heterogeneous special case is characterized. General heterogeneous-prior ordering and grouping remain open.

links.title: Optimal Exploration of New Products under Assortment Decisions

counterexample_rationale: Small heterogeneous-prior instances can refute proposed index, ordering, or threshold rules by exact dynamic programming or symbolic regret comparison.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search over two-, three-, and four-entrant finite-prior instances can map optimal policy regions and discover whether any scalar priority statistic survives.

literature.synthesis: The homogeneous-prior result shows that this is not a generic bandit question: assortment substitution and social learning create a specific exploration externality. The two-entrant heterogeneous analysis is especially useful because it demonstrates why a naive ordering by upside, mean, or UCB-like optimism is insufficient. The remaining problem is to identify whether the messy prior dependence still collapses to an index or threshold in larger instances, or whether optimal policies need genuinely history-dependent grouping. A positive result would give a clean operational rule for marketplace experimentation; a negative result would be equally valuable if it identifies the smallest heterogeneous-prior instance where every scalar-index policy fails.

title: Optimal contest design beyond quasiconvex gradient structure
short_statement: Characterize optimal rank-prize structures for contest objectives whose gradient patterns fall outside the quasiconvex regimes currently understood.
open_problem: Develop a general theory mapping objective-gradient patterns to optimal rank-prize structures, especially beyond the quasiconvex/nonconvex classes already covered.
full_statement: There are $n$ strategic contestants. A rank-prize mechanism chooses prizes $p_1\ge p_2\ge\cdots\ge p_n\ge0$ with budget $\sum_i p_i=B$, where $p_r$ is paid to the contestant ranked $r$ by realized quality. Contestants choose costly effort, the effort profile induces an equilibrium distribution or deterministic vector of qualities, and the designer maximizes a smooth objective $\Phi(q_1,\ldots,q_n)$ of the induced quality vector. Golrezaei, Hajiaghayi, and Shin connect the number of transitions in an optimal prize vector to sign/shape patterns in gradient sequences of $\Phi$ and prove that broad nonconvex objective classes have an optimal prize vector of the form $$p_1\ge p_2=\cdots=p_{n-1}\ge p_n=0.$$ The open problem is to classify what happens for objectives outside the covered gradient-pattern regimes: which patterns imply one, two, or finitely many prize levels, and which force genuinely high-dimensional or instance-specific prize vectors?
known_results: Classical contest-design work identifies simple structures such as winner-take-all, uniform-but-last, or hard-max prizes for special objectives and cost functions. Chawla, Hartline, and Sivan gave influential algorithmic contest-design results for crowdsourcing settings. Golrezaei, Hajiaghayi, and Shin extend structural characterization beyond convexity: for convex combinations of user welfare and average quality, arbitrary posynomials over quality, and related nonconvex objectives, the optimal mechanism has possibly larger first prize, equal intermediate prizes, and zero last prize. Their reduction from high-dimensional nonconvex optimization to one-dimensional optimization yields an FPTAS with a value oracle. The proof uses Schur-convexity, Bernstein basis polynomials, total positivity, variation diminishing properties, and restrictions on gradient-sequence transition patterns. General gradient patterns remain unclassified.

background: Rank-based contests are mechanisms for eliciting effort when direct contracting on effort is impossible. A designer allocates a prize budget across ranks, contestants choose costly effort, and the induced equilibrium quality profile determines the designer's objective. Classical contest-design results often focus on simple objectives such as maximum quality, total quality, or welfare and yield simple prize structures. Golrezaei, Hajiaghayi, and Shin study much broader nonconvex objectives motivated by recommender systems and content platforms. Their main insight is that the pattern of gradients of the designer objective can force a simple optimal prize structure even when the objective is nonconvex. The open frontier is structural: which gradient patterns still imply low-dimensional prize rules, and which require genuinely complex prize vectors?

progress.summary: A broad class of nonconvex objectives now has a simple optimal prize form and an FPTAS. General gradient patterns remain unclassified.

alphaevolve_rationale: The structural question is well suited to automated optimization over synthetic objectives and gradient patterns, followed by exact proof of candidate examples.

literature.synthesis: Contest design has a long tradition of simple rank-prize rules arising from special objectives. The recent nonconvex work shows that simplicity is not limited to convex objectives: gradient structure can imply a uniform-middle prize vector and reduce computation dramatically. This suggests a broader classification program. The unresolved question is whether more complicated gradient sign/curvature patterns lead to a finite menu of prize-vector templates, or whether the optimization problem becomes genuinely high-dimensional. A resolution would clarify both contest theory and algorithm design for platform incentives.

title: Second-order gap for online selection of a monotone subsequence
short_statement: The optimal online expected length is $v_n=\sqrt{2n}-(1/12)\log n+O(1)$; the second-order deficit is logarithmic (Seksenbayev, 2021).
open_problem: Resolved: the deficit has logarithmic growth with coefficient $1/12$.
full_statement: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. observations from a continuous distribution, reduced to uniform observations on $[0,1]$ by the probability integral transform. An online nonanticipating policy irrevocably accepts an increasing subsequence. Write $v_n=\sup_\pi\mathbb E[L_n^\pi]$ for its optimal expected length and $g(n)=\sqrt{2n}-v_n$. The historical question asked whether $g(n)$ is bounded or diverges and, if it diverges, at what rate. Seksenbayev (2021), Theorem 1, answers it: $$v_n=\sqrt{2n}-\frac{1}{12}\log n+O(1),\qquad g(n)=\frac{1}{12}\log n+O(1).$$ This is a fixed-sample-size result, not just a Poissonized approximation.
known_results: Samuels and Steele established the first-order scale; Arlotto, Wei, and Xie gave an adaptive policy with logarithmic additive guarantees. Seksenbayev, Acta Applicandae Mathematicae 174, article 6 (2021), Theorem 1, proves the expansion in full_statement directly for fixed $n$. Section 2.2 compares trial functions with the discrete Bellman recursion and bounds the remainder. Section 2.3 also proves an $O(1)$ gap for the adaptive square-root-window policy. These results settle this record's stated target, without identifying a limit for the bounded remainder.

background: Online monotone subsequence selection is a clean sequential-selection problem at the boundary of applied probability, optimal stopping, and online algorithms. A sequence of iid continuous observations arrives one at a time, and the decision maker must irrevocably select an increasing subsequence. The offline longest increasing subsequence has famous $2\sqrt n$ first-order behavior; the online constrained version has first-order constant $\sqrt{2}$. The first-order law is classical. The later second-order analysis resolves the bounded-versus-divergent question formerly posed here.

title: Tight ratio for known-i.i.d. online stochastic matching
short_statement: A recent paper reports the optimal asymptotic ratio for unweighted known-i.i.d. stochastic matching; polynomial-time attainment is separate.
open_problem: Verify the reported asymptotic resolution for the basic unweighted arbitrary-rate model. Exact finite-horizon performance, polynomial-time attainment, and any separate integral-rate optimum are not certified by this audit.
full_statement: Let $G=(Y,Z,E)$ be a bipartite graph. Vertices in $Z$ are offline bins/resources and can be matched at most once. Vertices in $Y$ are online types. A horizon $b$ and arrival rates $r_y\ge0$ are known in advance, with $\sum_y r_y=b$; at each time $t=1,\ldots,b$, a type $y$ is sampled independently with probability proportional to $r_y$. When a ball/customer of type $y$ arrives, the algorithm may irrevocably match it to one currently unmatched neighbor $z\in N(y)$ or discard it. The unweighted objective is the expected number of matched offline vertices; weighted variants attach edge or vertex weights. The benchmark is the expected value of the offline optimum that observes the entire realized sequence $\omega=(y_1,\ldots,y_b)$ and then computes a maximum matching. The competitive ratio is $\mathbb E[\mathrm{ALG}]/\mathbb E[\mathrm{OPT}]$. Determine the optimal asymptotic competitive ratio for the basic unweighted known-i.i.d. model with arbitrary rates, and clarify whether the integral-rate case has a different tight constant. The basic unweighted asymptotic target has the reported solution in the What Is Known section; weighted variants and the separate integral-rate comparison are not resolved by this audit.
known_results: Duetting, Feldman, and Molina, 'Optimal Online Stochastic Matching' (arXiv:2610.19866v1), Theorem 1.1 and Section 5, report the exact Poisson-arrival ratio $1-e/e^e\approx0.8206$ and $1-e/e^e-O(n^{-1/2})$ for exactly n IID arrivals from a known law, with arbitrary rates. The benchmark is expected offline maximum cardinality. The policy is not polynomial-time. This matches the asymptotic impossibility bound and supersedes the older $0.702$-$0.823$ summary. Weighted offline equivalence in the paper does not itself establish the same online weighted ratio.

title: Joint queue-length transform for gated/one-limited polling
short_statement: In the two-queue polling system where one queue has gated service and the other has one-limited service, determine the joint queue-length probability generating function at polling instants.
open_problem: Determine the joint queue-length probability generating function, or an equivalent exact transform characterization, for the two-queue polling system with one gated queue and one one-limited queue.
full_statement: Consider a stable two-queue cyclic polling system with one server. Customers arrive to queue $i$ according to independent Poisson processes with rates $\lambda_i$, service times at queue $i$ have known distributions with finite means, and switch-over times between queues are included as in the standard polling formulation. The server alternates between queue 1 and queue 2. Queue 1 uses gated service: during a visit, the server serves exactly those queue-1 customers present when the visit began, while arrivals during the visit wait for the next cycle. Queue 2 uses one-limited service: during a visit, the server serves at most one queue-2 customer, if any are present. Let $(N_1,N_2)$ be the stationary queue-length vector at an agreed embedded polling epoch, and let $P(z_1,z_2)=\mathbb E[z_1^{N_1}z_2^{N_2}]$ be its joint probability generating function. The open problem is to obtain an exact expression, boundary-value characterization, or other complete transform solution for this joint PGF and the associated stationary queue-length or waiting-time transforms.
known_results: Branching-type polling systems and several mixed two-queue disciplines have exact transform solutions. Classical polling theory gives product-form or recursive PGF equations for gated, exhaustive, globally gated, and other branching-type disciplines. Boon, Boxma, and Winands explain that the corresponding exhaustive/one-limited two-queue model can be handled, but the gated/one-limited case resists the usual approach even though gated and exhaustive service often have comparable analytic complexity. They derive the relevant functional equation and show why the natural substitution that solves the exhaustive/one-limited case does not close the unknown transform. As of their open-problems paper and the source sweep here, the exact joint PGF for the gated/one-limited case remains open.

background: Polling systems are queueing networks in which one server visits several queues cyclically. They model communication protocols, manufacturing cells, traffic signals, and service systems. Many polling disciplines are exactly solvable because their queue-length transforms satisfy branching-type recursions or boundary-value problems. The mixed gated/one-limited two-queue system is striking because it is small, concrete, and still unresolved. Queue 1 uses gated service, so all customers present at the start of a visit are served; queue 2 uses one-limited service, so at most one customer is served per visit. Boon, Boxma, and Winands isolate this as an open problem: the functional equation for the joint queue-length probability generating function is known, but standard substitutions do not close it. This is a crisp applied-probability target, not a modelling exercise.

progress.summary: The functional equation and related solvable models are known, but no exact joint transform for the gated/one-limited system is known in the cited open-problems paper.

counterexample_rationale: This asks for an exact transform solution of a specified stochastic model, not for proving or refuting a finite conjecture.
alphaevolve_rationale: Symbolic computation may help discover substitutions, invariants, or kernel factorizations for the functional equation. Numerical transform inversion can test candidate formulas.

literature.synthesis: Polling-system analysis often succeeds when the service discipline has a branching property: each customer present at a visit beginning can be replaced by an independent offspring population generated during service. Gated service has this property, but one-limited service does not fit the same branching template because a visit removes at most one customer regardless of queue length. The mixed gated/one-limited system therefore has just enough structure to write a functional equation, but not enough for the usual recursive PGF closure. Boon, Boxma, and Winands present it as a benchmark open problem because it is minimal, concrete, and analytically resistant. A solution may require a boundary-value problem on the bidisk, a kernel-canceling substitution not yet identified, or a regenerative representation that bypasses the missing branching property.

title: Large switch-over limit for polling with renewal arrivals
short_statement: Prove the large switch-over deterministic-cycle limit for branching-type polling systems with renewal arrivals.
open_problem: Prove or disprove that cyclic branching-type polling systems with general renewal arrivals have the same large deterministic switch-over-time limit as the corresponding Poisson-arrival systems.
full_statement: Consider an $N$-queue cyclic polling system. A single server visits queues in the fixed order $1,2,\ldots,N,1,\ldots$; queue $i$ has iid service times with finite mean, a branching-type service discipline such as gated or exhaustive service, and renewal arrivals with rate $\lambda_i$. Switch-over time from queue $i$ to queue $i+1$ is deterministic and equals $r s_i$, where $s_i>0$ is fixed and $r\to\infty$. Assume the usual stability condition that total load is less than one. For Poisson arrivals, the scaled waiting-time and queue-length processes converge to a deterministic fluid cycle plus a residual-cycle term. The open problem asks whether the same large-switch-over limit holds for independent renewal arrivals, and if not, to identify the additional renewal-age or residual-life terms that change the limit.
known_results: For branching-type polling systems with Poisson arrivals, Winands proves the large deterministic switch-over-time asymptotics: as switch-over times grow proportionally, waiting times and queue lengths converge after scaling to a deterministic cyclic limit with a residual-cycle component. Boon, Boxma, and Winands identify the renewal-arrival extension as an open problem, because the Poisson proof uses branching and independence identities that are not available for general renewal processes. Approximation work for renewal-arrival polling systems combines light-traffic, heavy-traffic, and interpolation ideas, giving useful formulas but not a rigorous exact large-switch-over limit. The open question is therefore whether renewal variability washes out at the large-switch-over scale, or whether residual-life effects can change the limiting cycle.

background: Polling systems model a single server cycling among several queues, with applications in manufacturing, communication systems, maintenance, and traffic control. Many exact polling results rely heavily on Poisson arrivals, because Poisson arrivals interact cleanly with branching-type service disciplines and switch-over periods. Boon, Boxma, and Winands highlighted a clean open problem where the model is already fixed: keep the cyclic polling structure and branching-type disciplines, let deterministic switch-over times become large, and replace Poisson arrivals by general renewal arrivals. For Poisson arrivals, the large switch-over-time limit is well understood and the system behaves like a deterministic fluid cycle plus a simple residual-cycle effect. The conjecture is that the same deterministic-cycle limit should survive renewal arrivals. The challenge is that renewal arrivals break the branching and independence identities used in the Poisson proof.

progress.summary: The Poisson-arrival large switch-over limit is solved. Renewal-arrival approximations exist, but the exact deterministic-cycle limit remains open.

counterexample_rationale: A renewal-arrival distribution with persistent scaled fluctuations could disprove the conjecture. Finite simulations may suggest such distributions but cannot prove the asymptotic behavior alone.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can test renewal distributions with high variability, lattice effects, or long-range residual-life behavior. The proof likely needs renewal-process functional laws of large numbers and polling fluid limits.

literature.synthesis: The Poisson model benefits from distributional identities that make queue lengths at polling epochs behave like a branching process with immigration. Renewal arrivals remove that exact structure because counts in future intervals depend on the current renewal age. On the other hand, when switch-over times scale like $r$, each cycle contains many renewals, so a law-of-large-numbers fluid picture should dominate local renewal variability. The conjecture is plausible but not automatic: a proof must control renewal ages, visit lengths, and service-generated cycle-length randomness uniformly over the whole cycle. The remaining gap is to replace Poisson branching machinery with renewal-fluid or regenerative arguments strong enough to produce the same deterministic-cycle limit.

title: Exact stability region for adaptive limited-service polling
short_statement: Characterize the exact stability region of adaptive limited-service polling systems, including whether full primitive distributions are unavoidable.
open_problem: Find the exact stability criterion for adaptive polling systems with general limited-service disciplines, and determine the minimal distributional information needed to state it.
full_statement: Consider a cyclic polling system with a single server and finitely many queues. Arrivals, service times, and switch-over times are generated by specified renewal or iid primitive sequences. The server normally visits queues cyclically, but follows an adaptive rule: if it finds a queue empty during a cycle, it may skip that queue in the next cycle. Under a limited-service discipline, at most a fixed number of customers are served per visit, so work can remain behind even after service. The stochastic process of interest is the queue-length vector observed in continuous time or at polling epochs. The open problem is to determine necessary and sufficient conditions for positive recurrence for the general adaptive limited-service class. In particular, decide whether the stability region can be expressed using finitely many moments of the primitives or whether transforms, exponential moments, or the entire service/interarrival distributions are unavoidable.
known_results: Chernova, Foss, and Kim derived stability and instability conditions for several adaptive polling models, but for general limited-service disciplines the sufficient conditions leave a gap. They conjectured that the exact condition may depend on entire primitive distributions. In a follow-up paper they constructed a polling system whose stability region depends on an exponential moment of a service-time distribution, showing that finite moment summaries can be insufficient in related adaptive polling models. Broader polling-system work gives exact transforms, heavy-traffic approximations, and open problems for gated, exhaustive, and mixed disciplines, but those classical tools do not directly close the adaptive limited-service stability gap. The unresolved issue is a full positive-recurrence/transience classification for the adaptive rule.

background: Stability of queueing networks is often summarized by a traffic-intensity condition, but adaptive polling systems can be more subtle. In the model of Chernova, Foss, and Kim, a single server cycles among queues and may skip a queue in the next cycle if it found that queue empty in the current cycle. Under limited service, each visit serves only a bounded number of customers. The natural fluid-limit approach gives sufficient stability and instability conditions in some cases, but the conditions do not always meet. The authors conjectured that this is not merely a proof artifact: for some adaptive limited-service polling systems, stability may depend on the full primitive distributions, not on a finite collection of moments. A follow-up example supports this view by showing dependence on an exponential moment of the service-time distribution. The open problem is to turn these partial criteria and examples into an exact stability characterization.

progress.summary: Evidence now shows that whole-distribution dependence can occur in adaptive polling. The exact stability region for the original broader limited-service class remains open.

alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search may find distributions that break candidate stability criteria. Formal proof requires Lyapunov, fluid-limit, or regenerative analysis.

literature.synthesis: The key difficulty is that adaptive skipping changes future server availability based on past emptiness events, and those events can encode more than average arrival and service rates. Standard fluid limits may wash out details that still affect whether the system empties often enough to skip queues. Chernova, Foss, and Kim's later example strengthens the original conjectural picture: stability can depend on an exponential moment, not just finitely many power moments. General polling-system theory provides transform and heavy-traffic methods for classical service disciplines, and Boon-Boxma-Winands document nearby open polling problems. The open task is to decide whether a general exact condition can be written in terms of transforms/regeneration quantities, or whether only model-by-model criteria are possible.

title: Exact threshold for random k-SAT
short_statement: Determine the exact satisfiability threshold for random $k$-SAT at small fixed $k$, especially $k=3$.
open_problem: Prove the exact random $k$-SAT satisfiability threshold for fixed small $k$, in particular $k=3$. The open part is not sharpness of the transition in a qualitative sense, but the rigorous identification of the threshold value for these small $k$.
full_statement: Let $F_k(n,m)$ be a uniformly random $k$-CNF formula on variables $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, formed by choosing $m=\lfloor \alpha n\rfloor$ clauses independently and uniformly from the $2^k\binom n k$ possible $k$-clauses with distinct variables. A satisfiability threshold value $\alpha_k$ would satisfy the following: for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, $F_k(n,\lfloor(\alpha_k-\varepsilon)n\rfloor)$ is satisfiable with probability tending to one, while $F_k(n,\lfloor(\alpha_k+\varepsilon)n\rfloor)$ is unsatisfiable with probability tending to one. Friedgut's theorem gives sharp-threshold behavior but does not identify a limiting value for each small $k$. The open problem is to prove the exact threshold for fixed small $k\ge3$, especially $k=3$, either as an explicit constant or as a rigorous variational characterization matching the statistical-physics prediction, and to establish both the satisfiable and unsatisfiable sides of the transition at that same value.
known_results: The $k=2$ threshold is exactly $1$. Friedgut proved that random $k$-SAT has a sharp threshold for each fixed $k$, but the theorem allows the threshold location to vary with $n$ and does not identify the limiting constant. Achlioptas, Moore, Coja-Oghlan, Panagiotou, and others developed increasingly sharp rigorous upper and lower bounds and established the correct asymptotic order in $k$. Ding, Sly, and Sun proved the satisfiability conjecture for all sufficiently large $k$, matching the one-step replica-symmetry-breaking prediction. For small $k$, especially $k=3$, the best rigorous numerical bounds are close to the predicted value, but the exact threshold and the full finite-$k$ condensation/satisfiability analysis are still not proved.

background: Random $k$-SAT is a central model at the boundary of combinatorics, probability, statistical physics, and computational complexity. A formula on $n$ Boolean variables is formed by drawing $m=\lfloor \alpha n\rfloor$ random clauses, each containing $k$ literals. For small clause density $\alpha$, the formula is satisfiable with high probability; for large $\alpha$, it is unsatisfiable with high probability. Physics predicts a detailed sequence of phase transitions, and the satisfiability threshold is the most basic one. For $k=2$, the exact threshold is $1$. For every fixed $k\ge3$, Friedgut proved sharp-threshold behavior, but this theorem does not identify a clean limiting threshold value. Ding, Sly, and Sun proved the predicted threshold for all sufficiently large $k$, a major breakthrough. The historically famous remaining case is small fixed $k$, especially random 3-SAT, where rigorous upper and lower bounds are close numerically but the exact limiting threshold is still unknown.

progress.summary: The exact threshold is known for $k=2$ and for all sufficiently large $k$. The small fixed cases such as 3-SAT remain open despite extensive rigorous and physics-based work.

links.title: Proof of the satisfiability conjecture for large k

counterexample_rationale: Finite formulas can test conjectured bounds or algorithms, but the threshold is an asymptotic probability statement. Search is more useful for finding obstructions to proof strategies than for a direct counterexample.
alphaevolve_rationale: Computational search may identify finite-size structures, interpolation inequalities, or survey-propagation-inspired certificates. A resolution requires rigorous asymptotic control of the random formula distribution.

literature.synthesis: The qualitative transition picture is well established: below the threshold solutions exist with high probability and above it they do not. Friedgut's theorem supplies sharpness but not a usable formula for the threshold. The large-$k$ breakthrough of Ding, Sly, and Sun validates the physics prediction in a regime where the one-step replica-symmetry-breaking calculations can be made rigorous. Small $k$ is harder because error terms, local dependencies, and condensation effects cannot be hidden in asymptotic large-$k$ expansions. The concrete gap is to convert the physics prediction for $k=3$ and other small values into a rigorous threshold theorem.

The verifier should check that the claimed value is not merely a sequence-dependent sharp threshold from Friedgut's theorem and that all error terms are uniform enough for the specific small $k$ under discussion. Numerical estimates, survey propagation, or finite-size simulations of random 3-SAT are useful evidence but do not resolve the problem without rigorous asymptotic probability bounds.

title: Higher-order capacity expansion for the deletion channel
short_statement: Find higher-order terms in the small-deletion expansion of binary deletion-channel capacity and characterize the near-optimal input process.
open_problem: Determine the higher-order small-$d$ capacity expansion for the binary deletion channel and the structure of capacity-achieving or asymptotically capacity-achieving input processes. The unresolved part is the exact expansion and optimizer beyond the currently proved leading orders.
full_statement: For deletion probability $d\in(0,1)$, the binary deletion channel takes an input bit string and independently deletes each bit with probability $d$; undeleted bits are received correctly and in order, but neither sender nor receiver observes the deletion positions. Let $C(d)$ be the Shannon capacity, optimized over stationary input processes in the usual information-spectrum/limit sense. As $d\downarrow0$, determine the asymptotic expansion of $C(d)$ beyond the terms already proved by Kanoria and Montanari. Their work computes the leading small-deletion terms and constructs input processes achieving capacity to that order. The open problem is to rigorously compute further coefficients and characterize the structure of asymptotically optimal input processes, for example whether finite-memory or run-length-modified perturbations of iid Bernoulli$(1/2)$ inputs remain optimal at higher orders.
known_results: Mitzenmacher surveyed the broad deletion-channel literature and emphasized that exact capacity is unknown for nontrivial deletion probabilities. Kanoria and Montanari initiated the small-deletion expansion program, first computing the two leading terms and showing that iid Bernoulli$(1/2)$ input is optimal to that order. Their later IEEE Transactions paper computes three leading terms of the expansion and gives an input distribution that achieves capacity up to that order, providing the first optimal coding result for the deletion channel in this asymptotic regime. These results strongly support a perturbative picture around iid Bernoulli input, but they do not determine all higher-order coefficients or the complete structure of capacity-achieving processes for small positive $d$.

background: The binary deletion channel is one of the simplest communication channels with synchronization errors. Each transmitted bit is independently deleted with probability $d$, and the receiver observes only the surviving subsequence, without knowing where deletions occurred. Unlike the binary erasure channel, where erasure positions are marked and capacity is elementary, the deletion channel has unknown capacity for every nontrivial deletion probability. The small-deletion regime offers a controlled asymptotic route: start at $d=0$, where capacity is $1$ and iid Bernoulli input is optimal, and ask how capacity changes as rare deletions are introduced. Kanoria and Montanari developed a systematic expansion and identified leading terms and near-optimal input processes. The remaining challenge is to push this perturbative program far enough to obtain exact higher-order terms and a structural description of optimal input distributions. This is a clean, well-defined open problem in information theory with strong probabilistic content.

progress.summary: The leading terms and near-optimal input processes are known for small deletion probability. The exact higher-order expansion and a complete optimizer characterization remain open.

alphaevolve_rationale: Search over finite-state stationary input processes, run-length constraints, and entropy-rate estimators may reveal better asymptotic candidates or disprove conjectured structures. Exact verification still requires analytic bounds.

literature.synthesis: Deletion-channel capacity is difficult because synchronization uncertainty couples distant input bits through random subsequence alignment. The small-$d$ expansion program isolates rare deletion events and studies how runs of identical bits create ambiguity. Kanoria and Montanari showed that iid Bernoulli input is optimal to leading order and that carefully modified input processes achieve sharper approximations. The remaining gap is a rigorous perturbation theory beyond the established orders: one needs matching achievability and converse bounds and a principled description of the finite-memory or run-length-biased processes that attain them.

Achievability should specify the input process, prove existence of the relevant entropy-rate limits, and control truncation or finite-memory approximations uniformly in small $d$. A converse must apply to all stationary or otherwise admissible input processes, not only iid or renewal inputs. Simulated mutual-information estimates, finite-block Blahut-Arimoto-style computations, or symbolic expansions for a candidate process are useful evidence but do not resolve the record unless accompanied by rigorous error bounds. Results for insertion channels or deletion-substitution channels should be treated as related progress unless they specialize back to the binary deletion channel capacity expansion.

title: Samuels' conjecture for sums of independent nonnegative random variables
short_statement: For independent nonnegative variables with prescribed means, determine the smallest probability that their sum falls below a fixed threshold. A general proof of Samuels' proposed formula has been reported.
open_problem: Ling (2026), Theorem 1.1, claims the full lower-tail infimum formula and attainment in the model below. Han and Nie (2026) give a refinement; this is a reported general resolution, not merely a special case. The catalogue has not independently certified the proofs.
full_statement: Let $0\le\mu_1\le\cdots\le\mu_n$ and $\lambda>\sum_i\mu_i$. Over independent nonnegative random variables with $\mathbb E X_i=\mu_i$, Samuels' formula is $$\inf\Pr\!\left[\sum_iX_i<\lambda\right]=\min_{1\le i\le n}\prod_{j=i}^n\left(1-\frac{\mu_j}{\lambda-\sum_{k<i}\mu_k}\right).$$ The infimum is attained: for a minimizing i, take $X_k=\mu_k$ for k<i and independent $X_j\in\{0,D_i\}$ for j>=i, with $D_i=\lambda-\sum_{k<i}\mu_k$ and $\Pr(X_j=D_i)=\mu_j/D_i$. Weighted mean-one formulations follow by absorbing weights into the variables. The lower-tail infimum, not supremum, is the nontrivial quantity.
known_results:
Zhi Ling, 'On Samuels' Conjecture' (arXiv:2608.18392v1, 2026), Theorem 1.1, reports the full formula and attainment for arbitrary ordered nonnegative means and thresholds above their sum.

Yanjun Han and Zipei Nie, 'A Sharp Refinement of Samuels' Inequality via Cap Moves' (arXiv:2608.22816v2, October 30, 2026), Theorem 1.1, restate Ling's result and prove a refinement in Theorem 1.2. Their paper is a follow-up, not independent certification of Ling's proof.

The original conjecture therefore has a reported full resolution. This catalogue checked the statements and model, not complete proof correctness, and does not assert a new remaining conjecture.

title: Tight prophet inequality with cancellation costs for small buyback cost
short_statement: In prophet inequalities with linear cancellation cost $f$, the optimal competitive ratio is known for $f\ge 1$ and asymptotically understood as $f\downarrow0$. Determine the exact tight ratio for every $0<f<1$.
open_problem: Determine the exact optimal prophet-inequality competitive ratio with buyback/cancellation cost $fX$ in the unresolved regime $0<f<1$.
background: Classical prophet inequalities force irrevocable decisions: once a value is accepted, the online decision maker stops or is committed. Many allocation markets are less rigid. A platform may tentatively allocate inventory, a seller may accept an offer and later cancel at a penalty, or an online algorithm may replace a current solution by paying a buyback cost. Prophet inequalities with cancellation costs formalize this recourse in the cleanest one-item model. The algorithm sees independent nonnegative random variables sequentially. It may hold one accepted value at a time, replace it later, and pays a linear penalty $f$ times the discarded value whenever it cancels. The payoff is the final kept value minus all cancellation costs. Ekbatani, Niazadeh, Nuti, and Vondrak solve the regime $f\ge1$ exactly and show that small $f$ has ratio $1-\Theta(f\log(1/f))$. The remaining interval $0<f<1$ is a precise constant-factor problem, not a modeling issue: the benchmark, policy class, and penalty rule are all fixed.
full_statement: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent nonnegative random variables with known distributions, revealed one by one to an online algorithm. At each time the algorithm may reject the current value, accept it if it holds no value, or replace the currently held accepted value $Y$ by the new value $X_t$, paying cancellation cost $fY$. At the end, the algorithm receives the value of its final held item minus the sum of cancellation costs paid. Let $\mathrm{OPT}=\mathbb{E}[\max_t X_t]$ be the offline prophet benchmark that sees all values and keeps the maximum without cancellation costs. For a fixed $f\in(0,1)$, determine the largest constant $\alpha(f)$ such that for every finite independent instance there is an online policy with expected net reward at least $\alpha(f)\mathrm{OPT}$. Equivalently, characterize the exact minimax competitive ratio for prophet inequalities with linear buyback cost in the small-cost regime.
known_results: Ekbatani, Niazadeh, Nuti, and Vondrak prove the exact optimal ratio $(1+f)/(1+2f)$ when $f\ge1$. For $0<f<1$, their paper explicitly states that the problem is still open. They give partial results for this regime, including almost matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds showing that as $f\downarrow0$, the optimal ratio is $1-\Theta(f\log(1/f))$. Classical prophet inequalities solve the no-recourse irrevocable case with ratio $1/2$, while secretary/buyback and online matching recourse models give related techniques but not this exact independent-values prophet benchmark. Thus the qualitative small-cost behavior is known, but the exact function $\alpha(f)$ for fixed $f\in(0,1)$ is not.

where_posed.text: Explicitly stated in Ekbatani, Niazadeh, Nuti, and Vondrak, 'Prophet Inequalities with Cancellation Costs', 2024.

progress.summary: The high-cost regime $f\ge1$ is solved exactly. The low-cost endpoint is understood asymptotically up to constant factors in the loss term $f\log(1/f)$, but the exact minimax curve for fixed $0<f<1$ remains open.

alphaevolve_rationale: For fixed $f$, discretized instances can be evaluated by dynamic programming. Search can discover extremal distributions, candidate threshold/flow policies, and dual certificates.

literature.synthesis: The cancellation-cost model interpolates between irrevocable prophet selection and near-free recourse. The source paper develops two complementary proof styles: threshold arguments inspired by classical prophet inequalities, and combinatorial-optimization methods based on LP duality, flows, and cuts. The exact $f\ge1$ ratio suggests a clean minimax structure, while the small-$f$ asymptotics show that very cheap cancellation nearly recovers the prophet but pays a logarithmic penalty. The unresolved regime is the interpolation between these behaviors. A solution likely needs either an exact factor-revealing program whose dual can be solved for every $f$, or a family of hard instances proving that a candidate policy is tight.

A theorem for $f\ge1$, asymptotic $f\downarrow0$, secretary arrivals, adversarial values, or multi-item buyback does not resolve the fixed-$0<f<1$ prophet benchmark unless an explicit reduction is given.

title: Exact stationary performance of the $M/G/k$ queue
short_statement: Find a tractable exact stationary characterization for the classical FCFS $M/G/k$ queue with $k\ge2$ and arbitrary service distribution.
open_problem: Give a computationally tractable exact characterization of stationary performance for the FCFS $M/G/k$ queue with arbitrary service-time distribution and $k\ge2$, or prove a rigorous obstruction under a natural computational model.
background: The $M/G/k$ queue is one of the oldest and most natural unsolved models in queueing theory. Poisson arrivals are routed to the first available one of $k$ identical FCFS servers, and service times have a general distribution. When $k=1$, the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula gives a classical exact transform for waiting time. When service times are exponential, the $M/M/k$ birth-death chain is exactly solvable. But for $k\ge2$ and general service times, the Markov state must include residual service times of all busy servers, destroying the one-dimensional transform structure of $M/G/1$. Decades of work provide approximations, special cases, phase-type numerical methods, continuity results, bounds, and heavy-traffic formulas, but no broadly tractable exact characterization comparable to the single-server formula. This is a clean mathematical open problem, not a modelling gap: the model is fixed and classical.
full_statement: Consider a stable first-come-first-served $M/G/k$ queue with $k\ge2$ identical servers. Arrivals form a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$, service times are iid with distribution $G$ and finite mean $1/\mu$, and the traffic intensity is $\rho=\lambda/(k\mu)<1$. Let $Q$ be the stationary number in system, $W$ the stationary waiting time, and let the full Markov state record the queue length together with residual service times of busy servers. The open problem is to find an exact representation or algorithm that computes the stationary distribution, transforms, or basic performance measures of $(Q,W)$ for arbitrary $G$ with provable finite error and complexity guarantees. The target is a theory comparable in generality to Pollaczek-Khinchine for $M/G/1$, Erlang formulas for $M/M/k$, or matrix-analytic methods for phase-type service, but without replacing $G$ by an approximation. A weaker but still meaningful resolution would prove a rigorous obstruction: for a natural input model for $G$, exact stationary performance cannot be represented or computed within a specified tractable class.
known_results: Exact formulas are known for $M/M/k$, $M/G/1$, $D/M/k$, $M/D/k$, and many phase-type or rational-transform special cases. For $M/G/2$, integral-equation and transform methods exist in special settings, and phase-type approximations convert the problem to large finite Markov chains. Tijms, van Hoorn, and Federgruen developed steady-state approximations and explicitly questioned whether computationally tractable exact methods for general $M/G/k$ steady-state probabilities are likely. Gupta, Harchol-Balter, Dai, and Zwart showed that two service-time moments are insufficient for universally accurate approximation, while Gupta and Osogami used Markov-Krein theory to obtain tight mean-waiting-time bounds under moment information. Sigman and Connor-Kendall developed exact or perfect simulation methods for stationary $M/G/c$ queues, but simulation of samples is not the same as a closed stationary characterization. The broad exact-performance problem remains open.

alphaevolve_rationale: Search can discover transform identities, numerical patterns, and hard service-time distributions for approximations. A resolution likely needs analytic queueing theory or a formal computational-complexity obstruction.

literature.synthesis: The obstruction in $M/G/k$ is residual-service dimensionality. In $M/G/1$, a departure or workload recursion collapses the system to one dimension. With multiple FCFS servers, the vector of residual service times matters, and arrivals see a correlated configuration of server ages. Phase-type approximations convert the problem to a finite Markov chain but can grow rapidly and do not constitute a closed-form exact solution for arbitrary $G$. Moment-based approximations are useful operationally, but impossibility results for two-moment approximations show that distributional detail can matter. The open gap is an exact representation that is both mathematically general and computationally usable.

title: Constructive constant-factor prophet inequalities for subadditive combinatorial auctions
short_statement: For Bayesian combinatorial auctions with independent subadditive buyers, a constant-factor prophet inequality is now known nonconstructively. Is there a constructive constant-factor posted-price prophet inequality, and what is the tight factor?
open_problem: Design a polynomial-time computable posted-price/order-online policy with a constant-factor prophet inequality for subadditive combinatorial auctions, or prove that no such constructive pricing guarantee exists.
background: Subadditive combinatorial auctions are a central model for allocation without complementarities. There are $m$ items and buyers arrive online with independently drawn subadditive valuations over bundles. The offline benchmark is the welfare-maximizing allocation after seeing all valuations. A prophet inequality asks whether a sequential allocation rule, ideally implementable by posted item prices, can obtain a constant fraction of this offline welfare in expectation. This is exactly the online-allocation analogue of simple truthful mechanisms for rich valuation classes. For XOS valuations, constant posted-price prophet inequalities are known, but subadditive valuations are substantially harder because there may be no compact additive support representation. Dütting, Kesselheim, and Lucier improved the constructive guarantee from $O(\log m)$ to $O(\log\log m)$ and explicitly conjectured that $O(1)$ should be possible with unequal-marginal dual prices. Later work resolved the existence of a constant-factor subadditive prophet inequality nonconstructively, but the survey by Saha and Parashar emphasizes that this approach cannot be implemented using prices. The remaining question is therefore clean: close the gap between existence and a constructive posted-price mechanism.
full_statement: There is a set $M$ of $m$ indivisible items and buyers $i=1,\ldots,n$ arrive sequentially in an arbitrary or fixed order. Buyer $i$ has a valuation function $v_i:2^M\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$ drawn independently from a known distribution over monotone subadditive valuations, meaning $v_i(S)+v_i(T)\ge v_i(S\cup T)$ for all $S,T\subseteq M$. When buyer $i$ arrives, the mechanism observes $v_i$ and irrevocably allocates a subset of the remaining items to that buyer. Let $\mathrm{OPT}$ be the expected welfare of the offline allocation maximizing $\sum_i v_i(S_i)$ over disjoint item bundles after all valuations are known. Does there exist a polynomial-time computable posted-price or similarly constructive online policy, using standard value/demand-query access, whose expected welfare is at least $\Omega(1)\cdot\mathrm{OPT}$ for all such instances? More sharply, determine the best possible constant factor and whether static anonymous item prices suffice.
known_results: Feldman, Gravin, and Lucier gave an $O(\log m)$ posted-price prophet inequality for subadditive valuations. Dütting, Kesselheim, and Lucier improved this to a constructive $O(\log\log m)$ guarantee using static anonymous item prices computable with demand-query access, and they prove their equal-marginal approach cannot beat $\Omega(\log\log m)$. They conjecture that unequal-marginal dual prices can yield an $O(1)$ prophet inequality. Saha and Parashar's 2023 survey reports that later work resolves the central open problem of a constant-factor prophet inequality for subadditive valuations, but the known approach is nonconstructive and cannot be implemented using posted prices. Thus the constructive/pricing version and the tight constant remain open.

progress.summary: The constructive posted-price guarantee is $O(\log\log m)$. A constant-factor prophet inequality exists by later nonconstructive work, but this does not give computable posted prices or a simple mechanism.

counterexample_rationale: A lower bound against a class of posted prices may be witnessed by finite valuation profiles. A lower bound against all constructive online policies would require a more structural oracle or communication-complexity argument.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can test candidate price constructions and unequal-marginal distributions on finite subadditive valuation instances. Full progress likely needs LP duality, demand-query algorithms, and mechanism-design proof techniques.

literature.synthesis: The subadditive case exposes a gap between existential prophet inequalities and implementable posted-price mechanisms. Earlier balanced-price approaches give $O(\log m)$ because subadditive valuations are too coarse to support the XOS-style item decomposition used for constants. Dütting-Kesselheim-Lucier's primal-dual approach improves this to $O(\log\log m)$ by considering equal item marginals over a logarithmic ladder of scales; their own lower bound shows that this equal-marginal framework is exhausted. The natural next proof idea is unequal marginals derived from dual solutions of allocation LPs. The later nonconstructive constant-factor existence result shows that the model itself does not require logarithmic loss, but it leaves open the algorithmic and mechanism-design question that matters for posted prices.
