title: High-multiplicity identical-machine scheduling with few processing times
short_statement: A September 2026 preprint claims FPT for fully binary high-multiplicity bin packing, which would settle the corresponding identical-machine makespan target.
full_statement: Consider identical parallel-machine makespan scheduling $P||C_{\max}$ under high-multiplicity input. Instead of listing all jobs individually, the input gives distinct positive integer processing times $a_1,\ldots,a_k$, binary-encoded multiplicities $m_1,\ldots,m_k$, and the number of identical machines $M$. A schedule chooses, for each machine, a vector $c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^k$ of job-type counts, and the total count over all machines must equal $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)$. The load of a machine using configuration $c$ is $\sum_{r=1}^k c_ra_r$, and the objective is to minimize the maximum load. The parameter is $k$, the number of distinct processing times, while multiplicities, machine count, and processing times are part of the compact binary input. The open problem is whether exact makespan minimization is fixed-parameter tractable in $k$, with running time $f(k)\,poly(|I|)$, or whether compact multiplicities make the problem W-hard or otherwise unlikely to be FPT. A September 2026 preprint now claims an FPT decision theorem for the equivalent bin-packing problem. For a candidate makespan $B$, take item sizes $a_r$, multiplicities $m_r$, bin bound $M$, and capacity $B$. Binary search on the integer makespan between zero and total processing load has polynomially many iterations in the binary input length, so the claimed theorem implies FPT computation of the optimum value. This transfer is an inference from the stated decision theorem, not an independent verification of its proof.
background: High-multiplicity encoding is natural in operations settings with many identical jobs of a few types: production lots, cloud tasks, appointment templates, and repeated batch work. It changes the algorithmic question because the explicit number of jobs may be exponentially larger than the input length. For ordinary explicit scheduling, a small number of processing times often enables dynamic programming. Under compact multiplicities, the same intuition can fail because counts are large binary numbers and the algorithm must reason about integer decompositions of machine loads. Mnich and van Bevern include this problem in their parameterized scheduling list as a clean open case at the interface of scheduling, integer programming, and fixed-parameter algorithms. The 2025 high-multiplicity scheduling work sharpens the integer-cone toolkit but did not settle the fully binary case. The September 2026 preprint now claims to do so.
open_problem: Verify the September 2026 FPT claim and its consequence for exact high-multiplicity makespan minimization. The original parameter-$k$ question is no longer listed as an unaddressed target.
known_results:
Koana and Kumabe, 'High-Multiplicity Bin Packing is FPT' (arXiv:2609.16923v1, September 2026), Theorem 1, claim a deterministic $O^*(2^{k^{O(k)}})$ decision algorithm with all sizes, multiplicities, capacity, and bin bound encoded in binary. The suppressed factor is polynomial in binary input length with exponent independent of $k$. Setting bin capacity equal to a candidate makespan and the bin bound equal to the number of machines gives the stated scheduling decision problem exactly. Binary search then yields the optimum makespan in FPT time, assuming the theorem. The preprint's proof has not been independently certified here.

Historical context: Koutecky and Zink (2020) distinguish the ordinary explicit-job problem, which is FPT in the number of processing times, from the high-multiplicity version. Their positive result must not be applied by expanding binary multiplicities. Jansen, Kahler, and Zwanger (CIAC 2025; arXiv v2), Theorem 1.1 and Section 6, give a running time of the form $(\log p_{\max})^{2^{O(k)}}|I|^{O(1)}$. This does not establish $f(k)|I|^{O(1)}$ for binary processing times, because the exponent on their bit length depends on $k$. Their Theorem 0.D.1 relates the target to uniformly related machines parameterized by job and machine types, both with compact multiplicities.

Rohwedder (ICALP 2025), Section 5, obtains $p_{\max}^{O(k)}\langle\mathrm{enc}\rangle^{O(1)}$ for a related uniform-machine formulation with high job multiplicities. This retains numerical dependence on $p_{\max}$ and explicitly lists machine speeds, so it does not resolve the fully compact, parameter-$k$ target here.

A hardness result should keep $k$ as the parameter being lower-bounded. The polynomial exponent must also be independent of k. A runtime with a k-dependent power of the binary input length is XP, not the requested FPT bound.

title: Optimal response-time tail scheduling in the M/G/1 queue
short_statement: Strong asymptotic tail optimality is solved for known-size class-I M/G/1 queues; finite-threshold and full-distribution optimization are different remaining targets.
full_statement: Consider an $M/G/1$ queue with Poisson arrivals of rate $\lambda$, i.i.d. service requirements from a known light-tailed distribution $G$, and load $\rho<1$. A scheduling discipline may be nonanticipative and may use each job's size or class information, depending on the model variant, but it must be work-conserving and stable. For a policy $\pi$, let $T^{\pi}$ be steady-state response time. Classical objectives such as mean response time are solved by policies such as SRPT when sizes are known, while FCFS has attractive asymptotic-tail properties in light-tailed settings. For class-I service distributions with known exact sizes, Yu and Scully (2024) solve strong asymptotic tail optimality using $\gamma$-Boost. Class I means that the moment generating function has a positive convergence endpoint (possibly infinite) and diverges there. This is not stochastic dominance at every finite threshold. The remaining target here is fixed-threshold or finite-percentile optimization, or a rigorously defined attainable-distribution frontier, with size information and preemption permissions fixed in advance.
background: Queueing textbooks give clean optimality theorems for a few objectives: SRPT minimizes mean response time with known sizes, and FCFS has classical asymptotic-tail guarantees for light-tailed service distributions. Modern systems care much more about the entire tail curve, such as the 95th or 99th percentile response time. That objective is still mathematically sharp but much less understood. Grosof, Yang, Scully, and Harchol-Balter showed that a policy called Nudge can stochastically improve upon FCFS, refuting a long-standing belief that FCFS might be strongly tail optimal. Subsequent work identifies asymptotically optimal disciplines, while the finite-threshold objective remains distinct. The model is clean and classical, and the unresolved part is a real theorem about stochastic ordering and stationary queue distributions.
open_problem: Characterize fixed-threshold/finite-percentile performance or the attainable response-time-distribution frontier; do not re-pose solved class-I asymptotic tail-constant optimality.
known_results: SRPT is classically optimal for mean response time in an M/G/1 queue when exact sizes are known, but mean optimality does not imply tail optimality. FCFS is weakly optimal for the asymptotic response-time tail under light-tailed service distributions, meaning that its logarithmic tail decay can be best possible in a limiting sense, but this does not imply optimality at finite quantiles or stochastic dominance. Grosof, Yang, Scully, and Harchol-Balter introduce Nudge and prove that it stochastically improves upon FCFS for relevant light-tailed settings, improving every point of the tail and all moments. Yu and Scully (POMACS 2024) prove strong asymptotic tail optimality of $\gamma$-Boost for known sizes and class-I service distributions. Its boost is $b_\gamma(s)=\gamma^{-1}\log(1/(1-e^{-\gamma s}))$, with $\gamma=\lambda(\mathbb E e^{\gamma S}-1)$. Harlev, Yu, and Scully (POMACS 2025) extend strong tail optimality to unknown/partial-size information using $\gamma$-Gittins in their discrete-step Markov job model. Arrivals are still continuous-time Poisson; service steps are discrete and preemption occurs only at step boundaries. Neither theorem asserts optimality at every finite threshold.

alphaevolve_rationale: Search can discover scheduling rules that improve tail curves for phase-type examples and suggest structural conjectures, but proofs require queueing transforms, coupling, or stochastic-order arguments.

literature.synthesis: Nudge established that FCFS could be improved. Later Boost and Gittins results optimize asymptotic tails under explicit information models. They must not be confused with stochastic ordering of the entire stationary response-time distribution. The unknown-size theorem's service-step restriction also matters; its continuous-service extension is not proved merely by suggesting finer discretization.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Start with two-point or phase-type service distributions and formulate Markov chains for finite policy classes. Compare policies under stochastic orders and search for threshold interchange arguments. Coupling and sample-path exchange arguments are more likely to certify dominance than transform calculations alone.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A solution must specify the admissible information model: exact sizes known on arrival, only size classes known, preemption allowed or forbidden, and whether policies must be work-conserving. A stochastic-dominance claim must compare steady-state response-time distributions for all thresholds $t$, not just a finite set of percentiles. A high-quantile optimality claim must state whether the objective is fixed-$t$, asymptotic $t\to\infty$, or a percentile under the stationary distribution. Numerical tail curves are not enough unless the claim is only to refute a proposed dominance relation; proofs should use coupling, transforms, Markov-chain ordering, or certified finite-state approximations with truncation error. Account for the now-solved asymptotic cases and the discrete-step restriction in the unknown-size theorem.

title: Open-shop unit-time throughput scheduling parameterized by machines
short_statement: Is unit-processing-time open-shop throughput with release dates and weights fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized only by the number of machines?
full_statement: In the problem $O|p_{ij}=1,r_j|\sum_j w_j U_j$, each job $j$ has one unit-time operation on each of $m$ machines. The operations of a job may be processed in any order, but a job cannot be processed on two machines simultaneously and each machine can process at most one job at a time. Job $j$ is released at time $r_j$, has due date $d_j$, and has weight $w_j$. A schedule chooses start times for all operations and a job is counted on time only if all of its operations finish by $d_j$. The objective is to minimize the total weight of tardy jobs, equivalently to maximize the weighted throughput of jobs completed by their due dates. The open problem is whether the exact optimization problem admits an algorithm running in $f(m)\mathrm{poly}(n,\log P)$ time, where $m$ is the number of machines and $P$ denotes the numerical input size, with no additional parameter such as the number of due dates, release dates, weights, or the maximum time horizon.
background: Throughput scheduling asks which jobs should be accepted when not every deadline can be met. In open shop, this acceptance decision is coupled to a flexible routing problem: every accepted job must visit every machine, but the visit order is not fixed. Unit processing times remove one major source of numerical difficulty, so the remaining hardness is structural rather than a modeling artifact. Mnich and van Bevern isolate this as Open Problem 15 in their parameterized-scheduling list. The model is attractive for this repository because the question is not whether open shop is the right model for a factory; it is a clean complexity boundary for a standard shop-scheduling notation. The number of machines is one of the most natural parameters in applications, but the release dates, due dates, and job weights can still encode difficult subset-selection behavior.
open_problem: Determine whether $O|p_{ij}=1,r_j|\sum_j w_j U_j$ is fixed-parameter tractable parameterized by the number of machines $m$ alone, or prove an appropriate W-hardness/lower-bound barrier for this parameterization.
known_results: The open-shop throughput problem sits between several understood cases. Mnich and van Bevern note that $O|p_{ij}=1|\sum_j w_jU_j$ without release dates is fixed-parameter tractable in the number of machines, while $O|p_{ij}=1,r_j|\sum_j U_j$ is NP-hard when the number of machines is unbounded. Baptiste gave a polynomial-time algorithm for the weighted unit-time open-shop problem when the number of machines is fixed as a constant, which places the problem in XP with respect to $m$ but does not give an $f(m)\mathrm{poly}(n)$ running time. The same survey observes an equivalence with a preemptive identical-parallel-machine throughput problem with equal processing times and integer-time preemption. Thus the open part is exactly the parameterized jump from polynomial time for each fixed $m$ to uniform fixed-parameter tractability in $m$.

where_posed.text: Open Problem 15 in Mnich and van Bevern, 'Parameterized complexity of machine scheduling: 15 open problems'.

progress.summary: The release-date-free weighted unit-time open-shop throughput problem is FPT by the number of machines, and the release-date variant is polynomial for each constant number of machines. No FPT algorithm in $m$ alone, and no matching W-hardness result for that exact open-shop formulation, is currently recorded in the cited sources.

counterexample_rationale: The question asks for a uniform FPT algorithm or a parameterized hardness proof. Individual instances can test proposed dynamic programs, but they cannot by themselves resolve the asymptotic classification.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can help discover compressed state representations for small $m$, or generate hard families that defeat natural dominance rules. A final answer needs a rigorous FPT algorithm, XP lower-bound separation, or W-hardness reduction.

literature.synthesis: This problem is a precise parameterized-complexity gap, not a vague call for better heuristics. The release-date-free weighted unit-time case suggests that the number of machines can be powerful enough to control open-shop throughput. Release dates add a temporal packing layer, and current results only give polynomial algorithms when $m$ is treated as a fixed constant. The open problem is therefore whether the exponent hidden in those constant-machine algorithms can be replaced by a dependence $f(m)$ outside the polynomial factor. A resolution would clarify whether unit-time open-shop throughput belongs with the machine-parameter FPT scheduling problems or with problems where release dates encode W-hardness.

title: Terminal equilibria in two-person positive shortest-path games
short_statement: The pure stationary equilibrium question for two-person positive shortest-path games is solved; the remaining open problem asks when a terminal pure stationary equilibrium must exist.
full_statement: A deterministic two-person shortest-path game is played on a directed graph with an initial state and terminal states. At each nonterminal state, one of the two players chooses the outgoing move. Each move has a positive length for each player, and each player seeks to minimize total accumulated length until a terminal is reached; if play cycles forever, the positive-length convention gives infinite cost. A pure stationary strategy profile chooses one outgoing move at every state controlled by each player. The old open question of whether every finite two-person positive shortest-path game has a Nash equilibrium in pure stationary strategies is now solved affirmatively. The remaining open problem is sharper: if there exists at least one directed path from the initial state to a terminal, must there be a pure stationary Nash equilibrium whose induced play reaches a terminal, rather than a cyclic equilibrium with infinite cost?
background: Shortest-path games are a clean deterministic model of strategic routing and dynamic decision-making. They sit at the boundary of combinatorial optimization and game theory: if one decision maker controls all vertices the problem is ordinary shortest path, while multiple controllers create equilibrium questions. Pure stationary equilibria are especially important because they are simple, memoryless, and algorithmically checkable. Boros, Franciosa, Gurvich, and Vyalyi prove a positive theorem for edge-symmetric games with positive lengths and show that related assumptions are essential in other directions. The remaining two-person non-edge-symmetric positive-length case is a crisp existence question: either construct a small counterexample or prove that positivity alone forces equilibrium.
open_problem: In a finite two-person positive shortest-path game with a directed path from the initial state to a terminal, must there exist a terminal Nash equilibrium in pure stationary strategies?
known_results: Boros, Franciosa, Gurvich, and Vyalyi prove that deterministic $n$-person shortest-path games on edge-symmetric digraphs with positive move lengths always have Nash equilibria in pure stationary strategies, and they show that positivity and symmetry are meaningful hypotheses. A later paper by Boros, Elbassioni, Gurvich, and Vyalyi resolves the previously open two-person non-edge-symmetric positive case: every finite two-person positive shortest-path game has a Nash equilibrium in pure stationary strategies, computable in polynomial time. Their proof also covers graphs with finite out-degrees. However, the equilibrium produced may be cyclic, yielding infinite cost for both players. They prove a terminal Nash equilibrium exists if at least one player can force reaching a terminal, and they conjecture that a terminal equilibrium exists whenever there is some directed path from the initial state to a terminal. That terminal-equilibrium conjecture is the remaining open problem.

where_posed.text: Stated in Boros, Franciosa, Gurvich, and Vyalyi, 'Deterministic n-person shortest path and terminal games on symmetric digraphs have Nash equilibria in pure stationary strategies', 2022.

progress.summary: The old pure-stationary existence problem is solved for two-person positive shortest-path games. The residual open question is whether a terminal pure stationary equilibrium exists under the weaker assumption that a terminal is reachable.

links.title: Two-person positive shortest path games have Nash equilibria in pure stationary strategies

counterexample_rationale: A negative answer would be a finite directed game graph with positive edge costs and a verifiable absence of pure stationary Nash equilibria.
alphaevolve_rationale: Finite-game search can enumerate small graphs, cost vectors, and stationary strategy profiles to look for counterexamples or identify structural reasons none exist.

literature.synthesis: The 2024 result changes the status of this record. Positivity alone is now enough for existence of some pure stationary Nash equilibrium in the two-player case, so the original open problem should not be presented as unresolved. The remaining distinction is between cyclic equilibria, where both players incur infinite cost because play never reaches a terminal, and terminal equilibria, where the game reaches an absorbing terminal under equilibrium play. If at least one player can force termination, a terminal equilibrium exists. The conjectured boundary is weaker: mere reachability of a terminal from the initial state may already suffice. A proof would need convert a possibly cyclic equilibrium into a terminal one or construct a new equilibrium using reachability structure; a counterexample would need show that all pure stationary equilibria are necessarily cyclic despite terminal reachability.

title: Optimal length-route tradeoff for spatial networks on random points
short_statement: For networks connecting random points in the plane, determine the optimal tradeoff between total normalized network length and average route excess.
full_statement: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be random points in a planar region, for example iid uniform points in a square of area $n$ so the point density is order one. A connected geometric network $G_n$ consists of straight or rectifiable edges joining the points, possibly with additional Steiner points. Let $L(G_n)$ be its total Euclidean length, normalized by the natural area scale as in Aldous-Shun, and let $d_{G_n}(i,j)$ be shortest-path distance in the network between $X_i$ and $X_j$. Aldous and Shun define a route-length statistic $R$ measuring the average excess of $d_{G_n}(i,j)$ over the Euclidean distance $|X_i-X_j|$ for random pairs of points, with the precise normalization chosen so that proximity-graph families have nontrivial limits. The open problem is to determine the optimal asymptotic tradeoff curve: among all connected spatial networks with limiting normalized length at most $\ell$, what is the infimum possible limiting route-excess statistic $R$, and which network constructions attain or approximate this frontier?
background: This is a clean applied-probability version of a practical network-design question: how much extra infrastructure is needed to make routes nearly Euclidean? Classical objects such as the minimum spanning tree, Delaunay triangulation, relative neighborhood graph, and other proximity graphs give canonical points on the length-versus-route-quality curve. Aldous and Shun proposed a route-length statistic $R$ and studied a one-parameter family of proximity graphs by simulation and theory. The unresolved issue is global optimality. Do proximity graphs, or simple augmentations of them, come close to the best possible tradeoff among all connected spatial networks, or is there a fundamentally different construction? The problem is mathematically precise and does not require inventing a model; the model is random points in the plane, total network length, and shortest-path route excess.
open_problem: Determine the asymptotically optimal tradeoff between total length and route-length statistic $R$ for connected networks over random planar points.
known_results: Aldous and Shun analyze classical proximity-graph families and use Monte Carlo evidence to illustrate a tradeoff between normalized network length and their statistic $R$. Minimum spanning trees, Delaunay triangulations, relative neighborhood graphs, and related proximity graphs provide explicit feasible networks with different points on the length-versus-route curve. They explicitly leave open how close this one-parameter family is to the optimum over all possible connected networks. Related Euclidean optimization theory gives laws of large numbers for structures such as MST and TSP, and geometric spanner theory supplies worst-case stretch constructions, but neither line identifies the average-case optimal length-route tradeoff frontier for random point sets.

where_posed.text: Posed in Aldous and Shun, 'Connected Spatial Networks over Random Points and a Route-Length Statistic', 2010.
where_posed.quote: How close this family comes to the optimal trade-off over all possible networks remains an intriguing open question.

progress.summary: The site has not recorded a later resolution of the full optimal tradeoff question. Known work provides candidate constructions and simulations rather than an optimal frontier.

links.title: Aldous and Shun, 2010

counterexample_rationale: Finite point sets can falsify proposed universal optimality of a construction, but the main question is asymptotic and probabilistic.
alphaevolve_rationale: Construction search can produce new spatial-network families with better empirical length-route tradeoffs, which may then suggest analyzable patterns.

literature.synthesis: Aldous and Shun's paper sits between stochastic geometry and network design. Proximity graphs offer tractable candidates with known or estimable length properties, but the global optimization problem is over all connected geometric networks, possibly including Steiner-like features and hierarchical road-like structures. The main gap is a lower-bound theory strong enough to certify a tradeoff curve, matched by explicit constructions. Existing Euclidean functionals such as MST and TSP constants control extreme points, and geometric spanner theory controls worst-case stretch, but neither directly answers the average-pair route-excess objective. A solution likely needs multiscale continuum lower bounds relating edge-length density to detour, together with constructions that balance local connectivity and long-range shortcuts.

reviewed.result: Introduces statistic $R$ and poses the optimal tradeoff question for spatial networks over random points.

reviewed.result: Background on Euclidean optimization constants and subadditive methods relevant to MST/TSP-like spatial functionals.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Search computationally over geometric spanner constructions, augmented MSTs, and hierarchical road-network designs. For lower bounds, look for continuum relaxations that relate route excess to edge-length density across scales.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A proposed construction should specify the point process, boundary convention, allowed Steiner points, and exact normalization for length and $R$. It should prove convergence or tight bounds for both quantities as $n\to\infty$, not only report Monte Carlo estimates. A proof of optimality must include a lower bound applying to arbitrary connected geometric networks with the same length budget, not only to proximity graphs or planar graphs with bounded degree. If the result uses spanner theory, verify that worst-case stretch translates to the Aldous-Shun average excess statistic under random points.

title: The 5/6 density threshold for pinwheel scheduling with real periods
short_statement: The classical integer-period 5/6 density conjecture for pinwheel scheduling has been settled, but the real-period extension remains conjectural.
full_statement: In classical pinwheel scheduling, each task $i$ has an integer period $a_i$ and a feasible infinite schedule executes one task per day so that task $i$ appears at least once in every block of $a_i$ consecutive days. The density is $\sum_i 1/a_i$. The integer-period $5/6$ conjecture says that density at most $5/6$ guarantees schedulability, and Kawamura has recently proved this integer version. Kawamura's real-period extension assigns each task a positive real period $a_i$ and requires that for every positive integer $\ell$, task $i$ is executed at least $\ell$ times in every block of $\lceil \ell a_i\rceil$ consecutive days. The open problem is whether every finite real-period instance with density $\sum_i 1/a_i\le5/6$ is schedulable under this stronger all-$\ell$ condition.
background: Pinwheel scheduling is a compact model for recurring real-time tasks, maintenance, media streams, and communication requirements. The classical Chan-Chin conjecture asserted that density at most $5/6$ suffices for schedulability in the integer-period model. That conjecture was recently settled, so it should not be listed as open. The remaining real-period version is a sharper modern continuation: it asks whether the same threshold survives after periods are allowed to be nonintegral and feasibility is strengthened through the $\ell$-visit condition. Fujiwara, Miyagi, and Ouchi prove the conjecture when the periods take three distinct real values and explicitly conjecture the full real-period statement. This is a clean scheduling problem: the model is exact, the threshold is explicit, and small instances can be searched for obstructions.
open_problem: Prove or refute the $5/6$ density conjecture for pinwheel scheduling with real periods.
known_results: The classical Chan-Chin $5/6$ density conjecture for integer-period pinwheel scheduling is reported as settled affirmatively by Kawamura, using a reduction to finite cases and computer-assisted ingredients. Before that resolution, Gasieniec, Smith, and Wild verified the integer-period conjecture for all instances with at most 12 tasks and developed Pareto-surface methods. Fujiwara, Miyagi, and Ouchi study Kawamura's real-period extension, where each task with real period $a_i$ must be executed at least $\ell$ times in every block of $\lceil \ell a_i\rceil$ days for every positive integer $\ell$. They prove the real-period conjecture when the periods take three distinct real values and explicitly conjecture the full $5/6$ threshold for arbitrary real periods. Thus the integer-period problem should no longer be listed as open here; the remaining target is the real-period extension.

where_posed.text: Conjectured in Fujiwara, Miyagi, and Ouchi, 'Pinwheel Scheduling with Real Periods', 2025.
where_posed.quote: We hereby conjecture that the conjecture of Chan and Chin is true also for real periods.

progress.summary: The integer-period conjecture is reported as settled, and the real-period version is proved for three distinct period values. The general real-period conjecture remains open.

links.title: Fujiwara, Miyagi, Ouchi, real periods
Kawamura, proof of the integer-period density threshold

counterexample_rationale: A refutation would be an explicit finite set of real periods with density at most $5/6$ and a certificate of unschedulability, though certifying unschedulability can be hard.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can explore real-period instances near density $5/6$, finite-window relaxations, and schedule templates, making this well suited to computational conjecture testing.

literature.synthesis: Kawamura's integer-period proof changes the status of the classical Chan-Chin conjecture: the clean remaining problem is the real-period extension. The all-$\ell$ condition is stronger than simply rounding each real period once, because it controls execution frequencies in every long window. Fujiwara, Miyagi, and Ouchi's three-distinct-period theorem suggests that the integer proof's finite-reduction ideas may extend, but arbitrary real period spectra introduce approximation and limiting issues that are absent in the integer problem. A solution must explain whether real periods can be discretized without increasing density beyond the $5/6$ threshold or whether genuinely irrational period ratios create new obstructions.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Study whether Kawamura's finite reduction for integer periods can be made robust under real-period perturbations. Search for discretization lemmas preserving the all-$\ell$ window constraints, and test irrational period ratios where naive rounding changes density or feasibility.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed solution must address arbitrary finite sets of real periods and the all-$\ell$ window condition, not just integer periods, rational periods with bounded denominators, or a single rounded deadline. A reduction from real to integer periods must control density and all window constraints uniformly. A counterexample must exhibit real periods with total density at most $5/6$ and prove that no infinite schedule satisfies the all-$\ell$ requirements. Computer-assisted finite reductions should include enough certificates to verify both the reduction and the finite schedule enumeration.

title: Optimal policy structure for capacitated stochastic inventory with fixed ordering costs
short_statement: In a single-item periodic-review inventory system with fixed ordering costs and an order-capacity constraint, the natural continuous-order-property conjecture is false. What is the correct exact structural description of the optimal policy?
full_statement: Consider a periodic-review, single-item, single-location stochastic inventory system. At the beginning of period $t$, the state is inventory position $x_t$. The controller may order $q_t \in [0,Q]$, where $Q$ is a fixed order-capacity bound. If $q_t>0$ a fixed ordering cost $K$ is incurred, in addition to any proportional ordering cost. Random demand $D_t$ is then realized, and the system incurs holding and backorder or lost-sales costs according to a specified standard convex one-period cost function. The objective is to minimize expected discounted cost or long-run average cost over an infinite horizon. Classical uncapacitated fixed-cost inventory models have $(s,S)$-type structure, while capacitated models may require multiple reorder regions. The open problem is to characterize the exact structure of an optimal stationary policy under the order-capacity constraint: after the continuous order property and modified multi-$(s,S)$ conjecture fail in general, is there a finite, checkable structural class that is always optimal, or can one prove that no comparably simple threshold description exists?
background: Fixed ordering costs and order-capacity constraints are both standard ingredients in inventory theory. Separately, they lead to fairly interpretable policies: fixed costs suggest $(s,S)$ rules, while capacity constraints create gradual replenishment behavior. Together they produce a surprisingly delicate dynamic program. The state is only one-dimensional, so this is not a vague modelling problem or a curse-of-dimensionality artifact. The hard part is structural: the Bellman operator can create disconnected ordering regions and invalidate the most natural conjectures about when an order should be placed. This makes the problem a useful benchmark for operations-management theory, because a complete answer would say whether the classical threshold-policy paradigm survives once capacity and fixed charges are both present. Rossi, Chen, and Tarim give a numerical counterexample to the continuous order property, showing that the most obvious clean structure is false. The remaining question is not whether practitioners can compute good heuristics; it is whether the exact optimal policy has any parsimonious theorem-level description.
open_problem: Give an exact structural characterization of optimal policies for capacitated stochastic inventory with fixed ordering costs, or prove that no finite threshold-like policy class can represent all optimal policies.
known_results: Classical uncapacitated fixed-cost inventory models admit $(s,S)$-type optimal policies under standard assumptions. Capacitated variants have only partial structural characterizations. Rossi, Chen, and Tarim (2023) show that if the continuous order property held, the optimal policy would have a modified multi-$(s,S)$ form, but they also provide a numerical counterexample in which the continuous order property is violated. Their computations indicate that violations may be rare, and modified multi-$(s,S)$ policies perform extremely well in tested instances. The exact general optimal-policy structure remains open.

where_posed.text: Posed in Rossi, Chen, and Tarim, 'On the stochastic inventory problem under order capacity constraints', 2023.
where_posed.quote: A long-standing problem is that of determining the structure of the optimal control policy when this system is subject to order quantity capacity constraints.

progress.summary: The continuous order property and the resulting modified multi-$(s,S)$ conjecture are known to fail in general, but computational evidence suggests that violations are rare and that the heuristic policy class is often nearly optimal.

links.title: Rossi, Chen, Tarim, 2023

counterexample_rationale: Finite-support demand instances and finite inventory truncations can be searched to refute proposed structural conjectures. The 2023 counterexample already shows that computational search is relevant.
alphaevolve_rationale: An evolutionary search loop can generate small dynamic-programming instances with unusual optimal action regions, helping identify the right structural invariants or further counterexamples.

literature.synthesis: The literature around this model is a good example of a mature operations-management problem where the modelling is settled but the structural theorem is missing. Classical fixed-cost inventory control suggests reorder intervals and order-up-to levels. Capacity constraints complicate this by preventing large corrective orders, so the Bellman recursion may favor ordering over multiple separated state regions. Rossi, Chen, and Tarim isolate the continuous order property as the condition under which a modified multi-$(s,S)$ policy follows, then disprove that property by explicit numerical example. This leaves two possible directions: find a richer exact class that contains all optimal policies, or prove a negative result showing that no simple interval/threshold representation is possible without extra assumptions.

title: FPT algorithms for single-machine total weighted tardiness parameterized by maximum processing time
short_statement: Is single-machine total weighted tardiness fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the maximum processing time?
full_statement: In the single-machine scheduling problem $1||\sum_j w_jT_j$, each job $j$ has integer processing time $p_j$, due date $d_j$, and nonnegative weight $w_j$. A feasible schedule is a permutation of all jobs on one machine. If $C_j$ is the completion time of job $j$, its tardiness is $T_j=\max\{0,C_j-d_j\}$ and the objective is to minimize $\sum_j w_jT_j$. Let $p_{\max}=\max_j p_j$. The open problem asks whether the exact optimization problem is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to $p_{\max}$: does there exist an algorithm with running time $f(p_{\max})\operatorname{poly}(n,L)$, where $L$ is the bit length of the due dates and weights, for arbitrary weights and due dates? The question is not about pseudo-polynomial algorithms in the total processing time or largest due date; those dependencies are too large to establish FPT in $p_{\max}$ alone.
background: Total weighted tardiness is a core single-machine objective in deterministic scheduling. It measures how badly due dates are missed, with job-specific weights representing priority or penalty rates. The model is deliberately parsimonious: one machine, no release dates, no precedence constraints, and a linear tardiness penalty. Despite this simplicity, the weighted problem is strongly NP-hard, while several nearby special cases have dynamic programs or polynomial algorithms. This makes it a useful stress test for parameterized scheduling. Bounding all processing times by a small number seems powerful because it limits the possible job lengths, but it leaves an unbounded number of jobs, due-date positions, and weight tradeoffs. Mnich and van Bevern pose exactly this boundary as Open Problem 1 in their Computers & Operations Research list.
open_problem: Classify $1||\sum_j w_jT_j$ parameterized by $p_{\max}$: either give an FPT algorithm in $p_{\max}$ alone or prove a W-hardness/ETH-type lower bound under the standard parameterized-complexity assumptions.
known_results: The single-machine total weighted tardiness problem $1||\sum w_jT_j$ is strongly NP-hard. When all processing times are equal, $1|p_j=p|\sum w_jT_j$ is polynomial-time solvable by reduction to the classical linear assignment problem. The unweighted total tardiness problem $1||\sum T_j$ is pseudo-polynomial, and Lawler's dynamic program can be interpreted as fixed-parameter tractable in $p_{\max}$ for the unweighted case; it also works for the weighted case under agreeable processing times and weights, where $p_i<p_j$ implies $w_i\ge w_j$. Mnich and van Bevern highlight the remaining gap: the general weighted problem with arbitrary weights and due dates may or may not be FPT in $p_{\max}$. Bounding $p_{\max}$ does not bound the total processing time, the number of distinct due dates, or the range of weights, so existing pseudo-polynomial algorithms do not settle the parameterized question.

where_posed.text: Listed in Mnich and van Bevern, 'Parameterized complexity of machine scheduling: 15 open problems', 2017.

progress.summary: Polynomial/FPT behavior is known for equal processing times, unweighted tardiness, and agreeable weighted instances. The general weighted arbitrary-due-date case remains the cited open boundary.

counterexample_rationale: The question is algorithmic complexity, not a conjecture about a finite object.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search may identify dynamic-programming state compressions for small $p_{\max}$ or reductions suggesting hardness, but a resolution requires a formal FPT algorithm or parameterized lower bound.

literature.synthesis: The known results separate three effects. Equal processing times remove most ordering complexity and lead to an assignment formulation. Dropping weights gives a pseudo-polynomial dynamic program that can exploit bounded processing times. Agreeable weights and processing times impose a monotone structure that also makes Lawler-style dynamic programming effective. The open problem asks whether arbitrary weights reintroduce enough combinatorial freedom to make bounded processing times insufficient. A positive result would likely need a compact representation of partial schedules by counts of each processing time plus a small amount of due-date/weight information. A negative result would need encode a W-hard selection problem while keeping every job length at most $p_{\max}$.

For lower bounds, try reductions from multicolored clique or multidimensional knapsack in which many unit or short jobs encode choices through weights and due dates.

A pseudo-polynomial dynamic program should be checked carefully for hidden dependence on the numerical horizon. A hardness claim should preserve the single-machine, no-release-date, total weighted tardiness model and state whether numbers are binary or unary encoded.

title: Parameterized complexity of unit-time precedence scheduling by poset width
short_statement: Determine whether unit-time precedence-constrained scheduling on identical machines is FPT when parameterized only by the width of the precedence poset.
full_statement: Consider nonpreemptive scheduling on identical parallel machines with precedence constraints. There is a set of unit-processing-time jobs, a partial order $\prec$ on the jobs, and a number of identical machines $m$. A feasible schedule assigns each job to an integer time slot and a machine, processes at most $m$ jobs per slot, and ensures that if $i\prec j$ then $i$ completes before $j$ starts. The width $w$ of the precedence poset is the maximum size of an antichain, equivalently the minimum number of chains in a Dilworth chain decomposition. Given a deadline $T$, decide whether all jobs can be scheduled by time $T$. The open problem is whether this unit-time problem is fixed-parameter tractable in $w$, with running time $f(w)\,poly(n,m,\log T)$, or whether it remains W-hard even when every job has processing time one.
background: Width is one of the most natural structural parameters for precedence-constrained scheduling: a partial order of width $w$ can be decomposed into $w$ chains, suggesting a dynamic program over chain-frontier states. The unit-time parallel-machine case is especially tempting because processing times introduce no numerical variation, leaving only precedence and machine capacity. However, the boundary is delicate. Garey and Johnson's classical OPEN8 asks about the complexity of closely related precedence scheduling for a constant number of machines, and later parameterized work shows that tiny generalizations can already be W-hard. This record isolates the clean unit-time width question as a structural scheduling problem where either an FPT chain-decomposition algorithm or a hardness proof would clarify how much difficulty comes from the partial order alone.
open_problem: Classify the width-parameterized complexity of unit-time precedence-constrained parallel-machine scheduling.
known_results: Van Bevern, Bredereck, Bulteau, Komusiewicz, Talmon, and Woeginger prove W[2]-hardness for $P2|prec,p_j\in\{1,2\}|C_{\max}$ parameterized by partial-order width, and give positive FPT results when width is combined with an additional slack-type parameter measuring the allowed delay beyond earliest starts. Mnich and van Bevern state the unit-time width question as Open Problem 6 and emphasize its connection to the long-standing Garey-Johnson OPEN8 complexity question. The exact unit-time boundary is therefore unresolved: processing times in $\{1,2\}$ are already hard, but this does not settle whether all-unit processing admits an FPT algorithm in the width alone. Simple chain-frontier dynamic programs can have state spaces depending on schedule length or machine capacity, and controlling that dependence is the main algorithmic obstacle.

where_posed.text: Open direction discussed in Mnich and van Bevern, 'Parameterized complexity of machine scheduling: 15 open problems', with partial negative progress by van Bevern et al.

progress.summary: The version with processing times in $\{1,2\}$ is W[2]-hard by van Bevern et al. The all-unit processing-time boundary remains the unresolved case.

counterexample_rationale: Hardness may be witnessed by compact poset gadgets of bounded width, and small examples can test candidate DP state compressions. A final lower bound still needs a parameterized reduction.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can explore chain-decomposition dynamic programs and generate hard bounded-width posets. It may also help discover whether W[2]-hard reductions can be made unit-time.

literature.synthesis: Width is compelling because Dilworth decompositions reduce the precedence structure to a bounded number of chains. Positive algorithms might exploit states describing the frontier along each chain. The challenge is that machine-capacity constraints and makespan feasibility couple the chains globally, so naive frontier dynamic programs can still depend on the horizon. The W[2]-hardness for processing times $1$ and $2$ shows that very small processing-time variation already destroys tractability, but it does not by itself rule out a special unit-time algorithm. Closing this boundary would clarify how much of precedence scheduling hardness comes from order structure alone versus its interaction with processing times.

A positive result should specify how the chain decomposition is obtained or avoided and must be FPT in width alone. A hardness proof should not rely on processing times greater than one.

title: Derandomizing the Exact Matching problem
short_statement: Find a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for Exact Matching, the problem of deciding whether a graph has a perfect matching with exactly $k$ red edges.
full_statement: In the Exact Matching problem, the input is a graph $G=(V,E)$, a color or weight function $c:E\to\{0,1\}$, and an integer $k$. The question is whether $G$ has a perfect matching $M$ satisfying $$\sum_{e\in M} c(e)=k.$$ Equivalently, in a red-blue graph, decide whether there is a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ red edges. The problem is in randomized polynomial time by the Mulmuley-Vazirani-Vazirani algebraic isolation framework. The open problem is to give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary graphs, or to prove a principled barrier showing why such a derandomization would imply a major breakthrough elsewhere. A satisfactory positive solution may derandomize the isolation step, avoid isolation through a different algebraic certificate, or exploit the matching polytope and exact-cardinality constraint in a new way.
background: Exact Matching is a deceptively small extension of ordinary perfect matching. Ordinary matching is one of the central polynomial-time problems in combinatorial optimization, but adding the exact cardinality constraint on one color class moves the known general algorithmic status into randomized polynomial time. The problem also appears as a hardness core inside robust and recoverable assignment models, so it is not just a complexity-theory curiosity. The randomized algorithm of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani is based on algebraic isolation: assign random weights so that a relevant matching is isolated with good probability, then use determinant or Pfaffian computations. Derandomizing this step is a long-standing open problem connected to the broader project of derandomizing isolation lemmas. Recent deterministic fixed-parameter algorithms show that structure helps, but the unrestricted deterministic polynomial-time question remains open.
open_problem: Find a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for Exact Matching, or prove a barrier under a standard derandomization or complexity assumption.
known_results: Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani gave a randomized polynomial-time algorithm via the isolation lemma and algebraic matching computations. The same isolation paradigm underlies many randomized matching algorithms and complexity-theoretic unique-witness reductions. Deterministic algorithms are known for ordinary perfect matching and for several structurally restricted Exact Matching instances. El Maalouly, Steiner, and Wulf gave deterministic FPT algorithms for bipartite graphs parameterized by bipartite independence number. Murakami and Yamaguchi extended deterministic FPT algorithms to more general graphs using odd-cycle-transversal and independence parameters. Fischer, Hartmann, Lendl, and Woeginger show that robust/recoverable assignment variants inherit the unresolved status of Exact Matching. None of these results yields a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for unrestricted Exact Matching.

where_posed.text: The derandomization gap goes back to Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani's randomized algorithm and is stated explicitly in later Exact Matching papers.
where_posed.quote: Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani (1987) proposed a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for this problem, and it is still open whether it can be derandomized.

progress.summary: Randomized polynomial time is known, and deterministic FPT algorithms exist under graph-structure parameters. The unrestricted deterministic polynomial-time problem remains open.

links.title: Murakami and Yamaguchi, FPT algorithms for Exact Matching

counterexample_rationale: The problem asks for an algorithm or derandomization barrier, so a finite counterexample is not the right resolution format. Finite instances can test proposed deterministic algorithms but cannot refute the existence of one.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can look for deterministic isolating weight families, small obstruction patterns for naive derandomizations, or algebraic identities for exact-cardinality matching. A final result needs a proof of polynomial-time correctness or a formal barrier.

literature.synthesis: Exact Matching is close enough to ordinary matching that one expects combinatorial structure, but the exact red-edge constraint blocks direct use of standard augmenting-path algorithms. The randomized MVV approach succeeds by isolating a witness matching and detecting it algebraically; derandomizing this would require deterministic isolation for the relevant family of perfect matchings or a different certificate. Parameterized results show that deterministic algorithms can exploit low independence number or small odd-cycle-transversal structure, while robust assignment reductions show the problem's influence in operations-research models. The unresolved gap is the general graph case with no structural parameter.

title: Heavy-Traffic Queue-Length Distribution for MaxWeight Input-Queued Switches
short_statement: For a general $n\times n$ input-queued switch under MaxWeight, prove the conjectured uniqueness of the transform equation that identifies the steady-state heavy-traffic joint queue-length distribution.
full_statement: Consider an $n\times n$ input-queued switch with queues indexed by input-output pairs $(i,j)$. In each time slot, arrivals $A_{ij}(t)$ join queue $(i,j)$, and the scheduler chooses a matching $M(t)$ between inputs and outputs; queues in the matching receive one unit of service if nonempty. The MaxWeight policy chooses a feasible matching maximizing $\sum_{(i,j)\in M(t)} Q_{ij}(t)$, where $Q_{ij}(t)$ is the queue length. Let the arrival-rate matrix approach the boundary of the switch capacity region in heavy traffic, and consider the steady-state queue-length vector under the usual diffusion/heavy-traffic scaling. For non-complete-resource-pooling regimes, the limiting state-space collapse is multidimensional rather than one-dimensional. Jhunjhunwala and Maguluri derive a candidate Laplace transform for the limiting joint distribution of the collapsed queue-length vector by solving an implicit functional equation, and they obtain a closed-form distribution for special cases. The open problem is to prove, for the general $n\times n$ switch, that the relevant functional equation has a unique admissible solution. Equivalently, prove that the proposed nonlinear function of $2n$ independent exponential random variables is indeed the exact heavy-traffic steady-state joint queue-length distribution for the general MaxWeight input-queued switch, or find a counterexample.
background: Input-queued switches are a canonical stochastic-processing-network model for packet switches, data-center fabrics, and constrained service systems. Each scheduling decision must be a matching, so resource sharing is combinatorial rather than separable across queues. MaxWeight is throughput optimal and has become a central policy in queueing theory, wireless networks, and cloud scheduling. For systems satisfying complete resource pooling, heavy-traffic limits often collapse to one-dimensional reflected Brownian motion, and mean-delay formulas can be comparatively explicit. Input-queued switches under general loads are more subtle: the bottleneck structure can have several active constraints, producing multidimensional state-space collapse and a much harder stationary distribution problem. Mean queue lengths have been characterized in important regimes, but a full joint distribution would be much sharper: it would describe correlations between ports, enable tail approximations, and test whether transform methods can replace more ad hoc interchange-of-limits arguments in non-CRP networks.
known_results: Maguluri and Srikant proved heavy-traffic mean queue-length behavior for MaxWeight input-queued switches when all ports are saturated, settling one version of an earlier conjecture and showing optimal scaling up to a constant factor. Jhunjhunwala and Maguluri introduced a transform method for non-CRP stochastic processing networks. They solved the heavy-traffic joint distribution for the $\mathcal{N}$-system and for a special three-queue input-queued-switch case, and for the general $n\times n$ switch they derived a candidate transform and distribution conditional on a uniqueness conjecture for an implicit functional equation. As of the 2026 literature check, the general uniqueness theorem and hence the full distributional characterization for arbitrary $n$ remain open.

literature.synthesis: The literature has a clear progression from throughput optimality and mean heavy-traffic behavior toward distributional characterization. Maguluri and Srikant gave exact heavy-traffic mean formulas in saturated input-queued switches and established optimal scaling properties of MaxWeight. Jhunjhunwala and Maguluri then developed a transform approach aimed at the full joint distribution in non-CRP systems, where one-dimensional Brownian approximations are insufficient. Their special-case solutions show that explicit distributional answers are possible, but the general switch reduces to uniqueness of an implicit Laplace-transform functional equation. Related BAR methods in multiclass queueing networks suggest that stationary equations can sometimes yield sharp distributional limits, but they also show how delicate truncation, boundary terms, and state-space collapse verification become in multidimensional networks. The remaining gap is a rigorous uniqueness or counterexample theorem for the switch transform.

title: Exact Stability Region for FCFS Multi-Server-Job Queues
short_statement: For FCFS multiserver jobs, saturated-system throughput gives an exact finite-state criterion with Poisson arrivals and phase-type durations. Seek compact or polynomial-complexity criteria and broader input models.
full_statement: Consider a system with $N$ identical servers and $K$ job classes. Class $k$ jobs arrive according to a renewal or Poisson process of rate $\lambda_k$, require $b_k\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ servers simultaneously, and have service-time distribution $S_k$. Jobs wait in a single first-come-first-served queue. When the job at the head of the line requires at most the currently idle servers, it starts service and occupies $b_k$ servers for its service time; otherwise it blocks later jobs even if those later jobs would fit. Let $X(t)$ describe the ordered waiting line, jobs in service, and residual service/interarrival information needed to make the process Markov. For independent Poisson class streams, let $\lambda=\sum_k\lambda_k$ and sample each new job's class with probability $p_k=\lambda_k/\lambda$. With phase-type durations, an exact criterion already exists: $\lambda<\lambda^*(p)$, where $\lambda^*(p)$ is stationary completion throughput of the saturated FCFS system, which replaces each departure immediately and keeps $N$ jobs present. Its finite CTMC can be solved by balance equations. The remaining computational target is a compact closed form or a characterization polynomial in the primitive class/server description, not merely finite-state enumerability. General renewal streams or non-phase-type service require separate assumptions and cannot automatically be replaced by i.i.d. Poisson job marks.
background: Modern cloud, parallel-computing, and machine-learning systems routinely run jobs that need several servers or accelerators at once. This destroys the separability of classical many-server queues: a job may be delayed not because total work is too high, but because the wrong combination of servers is available. Under FCFS, large jobs can block smaller jobs behind them, leaving capacity idle while work waits. The resulting stability problem is a clean stochastic-process question with direct operational meaning: it asks when the queue does not explode. It is not a modeling problem; the FCFS multi-server-job model is fixed and simple to state. The difficulty is that the usual traffic condition $\sum_k\lambda_k b_k\mathbb{E}S_k<N$ is not sufficient in general because fragmentation and head-of-line blocking can waste service capacity.
known_results: Wang, Xie, and Harchol-Balter emphasize that even the exact stability region is very hard, and they derive sufficient conditions for zero queueing in large-system scaling regimes. Grosof, Harchol-Balter, and Scheller-Wolf give a closed-form stability region for the two-class FCFS multiserver-job system with distinct server requirements and exponential service distributions. Grosof, Hong, Harchol-Balter, and Scheller-Wolf (Performance Evaluation 162, 2023, article 102378), Sections 2.2 and 3, describe the saturation-rule criterion for Poisson arrivals with i.i.d. joint server-need/phase-type-duration marks. Appendix C computes the threshold from finite balance equations. Theorem 4.2 further gives mean response time to additive $O(1)$ as arrival rate approaches that threshold. Thus exact finite-state characterization extends beyond two classes. This is not a polynomial-in-input-size complexity theorem.

title: Does BAR Tightness Imply Stability and State-Space Collapse in SBP Queueing Networks?
short_statement: For multiclass queueing networks under static-buffer-priority service, determine whether the BAR tight-matrix condition generally implies the stability and state-space-collapse conditions needed for steady-state heavy-traffic convergence.
full_statement: Consider an open multiclass queueing network operating under a static-buffer-priority (SBP) service discipline. In heavy traffic, the basic adjoint relationship (BAR) method of Braverman, Dai, and Miyazawa establishes steady-state convergence to the associated semimartingale reflected Brownian motion provided three conditions hold: stability of the prelimit networks, state-space collapse (SSC), and tightness of a certain matrix appearing in the BAR/Palm-distribution formulation. In a two-station, five-class reentrant-line example under last-buffer-first-served priority, the tight-matrix condition implies both stability and SSC. The open problem is to decide whether this implication is general. Prove that, for a broad class of SBP multiclass queueing networks in heavy traffic, the tight-matrix condition alone implies the needed stability and SSC conditions; or construct a network and SBP discipline where the tight matrix condition holds but stability or SSC fails.
background: Heavy-traffic theory for multiclass queueing networks is one of the main ways applied probability turns complex service systems into tractable diffusion approximations. The hard part is usually steady state: proving convergence of stationary distributions requires stability, tightness, and interchange of limits, not just process-level weak convergence from a fixed initial condition. The BAR approach attacks the stationary equation directly and has produced sharp results for generalized Jackson networks. Extending it to multiclass networks under static-buffer-priority service is important because priority disciplines are common in manufacturing, healthcare, communication systems, and computing. Braverman, Dai, and Miyazawa isolate three verifiable modules. If one of them, the tight-matrix condition, automatically implied the others, the method would become much more powerful and easier to apply.
known_results: The BAR approach is established for generalized Jackson networks and extended by Braverman, Dai, and Miyazawa to multiclass networks under SBP policies. Their framework shows that steady-state convergence follows from stability, SSC, and tightness of a matrix condition, and they prove all three in reentrant lines under last-buffer-first-served service. In the two-station, five-class reentrant-line case, tightness of the matrix condition implies both stability and SSC. The authors explicitly state that whether this relationship holds generally is open. No general theorem or counterexample was found in the 2026 search.

The BAR method reframes the problem through stationary equations and boundary terms, which can be more modular. Braverman, Dai, and Miyazawa's SBP extension identifies a tight-matrix condition that appears powerful in examples: in a two-station, five-class reentrant line it implies the other two major hypotheses. A positive answer would streamline heavy-traffic stationary analysis; a counterexample would clarify which additional hypotheses are indispensable.

title: Spectral Detection Threshold for Smooth-Kernel Random Geometric Graphs
short_statement: For random geometric graphs generated by a smooth kernel on the sphere, prove or refute the conjecture that the detection threshold against Erdos-Renyi is governed by $n^3\operatorname{tr}^2(\kappa^3)\asymp 1$.
full_statement: Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be independent uniform points on the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Given a symmetric kernel $K:[-1,1]\to[0,1]$, form a graph $G_K(n,d)$ by putting edge $(i,j)$ independently with probability $K(\langle x_i,x_j\rangle)$ conditional on the latent points. Let $p=\mathbb{E}K(\langle x_1,x_2\rangle)$, and compare $G_K(n,d)$ to the Erdos-Renyi graph $G(n,p)$. Let $\kappa$ be the standardized integral operator associated with the centered kernel, normalized so that it captures the signal-to-noise spectrum of the latent geometry. The open problem is to determine the sharp total-variation detection threshold for the hypothesis test $G(n,p)$ versus $G_K(n,d)$ in broad smooth-kernel regimes. Mao, Wu, and Xu conjecture that the critical boundary is $n^3\operatorname{tr}^2(\kappa^3)\asymp 1$: above this scale detection should be possible, and below it the two graph distributions should be contiguous or asymptotically indistinguishable. Prove this conjecture in general, or identify kernels/scalings for which the spectral trace criterion is not sharp.
background: Random geometric graphs are basic models for networks with latent spatial, similarity, or feature geometry. A central inference question is whether an observed graph contains latent geometry at all, or whether it is statistically indistinguishable from an Erdos-Renyi graph with the same edge density. This is a clean testing problem with a long line of work in probability, statistics, information theory, and theoretical computer science. Earlier high-dimensional RGG results focused heavily on hard threshold kernels, where edges are created by spherical caps. Smooth kernels are closer to many statistical network models because edge probabilities vary continuously with latent similarity. Mao, Wu, and Xu showed that smoothness can dramatically change the detection scale: in dense graphs, the critical dimension becomes $d=n^{3/4}$ instead of the much larger hard-threshold scale. Their work suggests that the right general invariant is spectral, not merely dimension or edge density.
known_results: Bubeck, Ding, Eldan, and Racz developed efficient tests and lower bounds for high-dimensional geometric graphs with hard threshold kernels and posed sparse-regime detection conjectures. Liu, Mohanty, Schramm, and Yang nearly resolved the sparse hard-kernel conjecture up to logarithmic factors. Mao, Wu, and Xu proved the sharp $d=n^{3/4}$ detection threshold for dense smooth kernels and extended the analysis to signal-to-noise scalings. They also established an estimation threshold for recovering latent vectors up to rotation. The general spectral trace conjecture $n^3\operatorname{tr}^2(\kappa^3)\asymp 1$ remains open outside the regimes covered by their proof.

literature.synthesis: The hard-kernel RGG testing literature established that latent geometry can remain hidden in very high dimension and that signed subgraph statistics, especially signed triangles, are key in dense regimes. Sparse hard kernels required different techniques, with belief-propagation and posterior conditioning giving near-tight thresholds. Mao, Wu, and Xu move the problem to smooth kernels and show that smoothness changes the dominant statistics and lowers the dense critical dimension to $n^{3/4}$. Their spectral conjecture attempts to unify kernel shape, dimension, and signal-to-noise strength through the standardized operator trace. The gap is to prove both directions of the testing threshold for a broad kernel class, including contiguity below the threshold and an explicit or existential test above it.

title: Optimal Load Balancing for Finite Heterogeneous Parallel-Server Queues
short_statement: For a finite system of parallel queues with heterogeneous service rates, characterize an optimal dispatching policy or prove structural optimality of a simple speed-aware rule.
full_statement: Consider $m$ parallel single-server queues. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process and must be routed immediately and irrevocably to one server. Server $i$ works at exponential rate $\mu_i$, with possibly unequal service rates. A dispatching policy observes the queue-length vector $Q(t)=(Q_1(t),\ldots,Q_m(t))$ and server speeds $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m$, and chooses the destination server for each arrival. For a finite system with fixed $m$ and fixed rates, the objective may be to minimize steady-state mean response time, steady-state expected total queue length, or the discounted/average-cost Markov decision problem with holding cost $\sum_i Q_i(t)$. In the homogeneous case $\mu_i\equiv\mu$, Join-the-Shortest-Queue is optimal for standard objectives. In the heterogeneous case, the open problem is to characterize an optimal finite-system dispatching rule, or to prove/disprove optimality of a natural speed-aware index/JSQ rule. Recent work proves asymptotic optimality of speed-aware JSQ in large-system fluid and Halfin-Whitt regimes, but those limit theorems do not settle exact finite-system optimality.
background: Load balancing is one of the basic controls in service systems, call centers, cloud computing, and data-center scheduling. The homogeneous-server model is classical: routing to the shortest queue has strong optimality properties because servers are exchangeable. Heterogeneous service rates remove that symmetry. A fast server with a longer queue may dominate a slow idle server, but the correct tradeoff depends on the whole queue vector and future arrivals. This makes the finite-system dynamic program natural but hard to understand structurally. The problem is well defined and not primarily about model choice: arrivals, exponential services, observable queues, and a standard holding-cost objective give a concrete continuous-time Markov decision process. The research gap is that the field has increasingly sharp asymptotic policies, while the exact finite-system decision rule remains unknown except in special cases.
known_results: For identical servers, JSQ minimizes standard delay metrics. For heterogeneous systems, Bhambay and Mukhopadhyay prove fluid-limit delay optimality of Speed-Aware JSQ, and Bhambay, Buke, and Mukhopadhyay prove asymptotic optimality in the Halfin-Whitt regime, including steady-state diffusion-scaled optimality among policies using queue lengths and server speeds. Zhou, Shroff, and Wierman resolve a related delayed-information open problem in large heterogeneous systems through an asymptotically optimal local-estimation-driven framework. These results do not identify an exact optimal dispatching policy for a fixed finite heterogeneous system.

literature.synthesis: The finite homogeneous problem has strong monotonicity and exchangeability, making JSQ optimal. Heterogeneity breaks exchangeability and creates a speed-delay tradeoff that is easy to state but hard to solve. Recent papers take an asymptotic route: speed-aware JSQ is delay optimal in fluid limits and remains optimal in Halfin-Whitt heavy traffic, with steady-state interchange justified by Stein and Lyapunov arguments. Related work handles multiple dispatchers and delayed information in large systems. What remains is the finite-system structural problem: identify the exact optimal action regions in queue-length space, or prove that no simple index/threshold characterization can hold generally.

title: Integrality Gap for Min-Sum Single-Machine Scheduling
short_statement: Determine whether the natural knapsack-cover strengthened LP for $1\mid\mid\sum_j f_j(C_j)$ has integrality gap strictly below $4$.
full_statement: In the min-sum single-machine scheduling problem $1\mid\mid\sum_j f_j(C_j)$, there are $n$ jobs. Job $j$ has integral processing time $p_j$, and its cost is a nondecreasing nonnegative function $f_j(C_j)$ of its completion time $C_j$. A feasible schedule is a nonpreemptive ordering of the jobs on one machine, and the objective is to minimize $\sum_{j=1}^n f_j(C_j)$. The known constant-approximation algorithms use time-indexed linear-programming relaxations strengthened by knapsack-cover inequalities. Cheung, Mestre, Shmoys, and Verschae gave a primal-dual analysis whose schedule has cost at most four times the constructed dual bound and asked whether the LP's true integrality gap is less than $4$. The open problem is to prove a bound $4-\delta$ for some universal $\delta>0$, construct instances with gap approaching $4$, or otherwise identify the exact gap/approximability threshold for this LP family.
background: The model $1\mid\mid\sum_j f_j(C_j)$ packages many single-machine sequencing objectives into a single clean abstraction. By choosing the functions $f_j$, one obtains weighted completion-time variants, weighted tardiness-like penalties, deadline penalties, and other nonlinear delay costs. The model is simple enough to state in one line but broad enough that approximation algorithms need ideas beyond Smith's rule or elementary dynamic programming. The key modern approach strengthens a time-indexed LP by knapsack-cover inequalities and rounds it with primal-dual or covering arguments. The open problem is therefore not about finding a model; it is about understanding a very concrete relaxation and whether the factor $4$ is an artifact of analysis or a real barrier.
known_results: Bansal and Pruhs gave the first constant approximation for this general min-sum problem with factor $16$. Cheung, Mestre, Shmoys, and Verschae improved the algorithmic guarantee to $(4+\epsilon)$ and showed that their particular primal-dual analysis is tight at factor $4$, while explicitly leaving open whether the LP integrality gap is actually below $4$. Kurpisz, Leppanen, and Mastrolilli studied Lasserre relaxations for related formulations and showed that some natural hierarchy approaches can still have severe gaps. The lower bound inherited from min-knapsack gives gap at least $2$ for relevant relaxations, but the source-checked gap between $2$ and $4$ remains unresolved.
open_problem: Close the integrality-gap and approximation gap for the knapsack-cover strengthened LP for $1\mid\mid\sum_j f_j(C_j)$, especially whether the gap is strictly less than $4$.

where_posed.text: Explicitly posed in Cheung, Mestre, Shmoys, and Verschae, 'A Primal-Dual Approximation Algorithm for Min-Sum Single-Machine Scheduling Problems'.

literature.synthesis: This problem is a focused LP-gap question inside a broad scheduling model. The 16-approximation of Bansal and Pruhs established that general nondecreasing completion-time costs are approximable by a constant. Cheung-Mestre-Shmoys-Verschae and the related Mestre-Verschae line brought the guarantee to essentially $4$ using knapsack-cover inequalities. The key nuance is that tightness of an analysis is not the same as tightness of the relaxation. Lasserre lower-bound work warns that stronger-looking hierarchies may not automatically solve the problem. The remaining gap is concrete: either find an instance family whose fractional value is nearly one-fourth of the integer optimum, or prove that every fractional solution can be rounded with loss $4-\delta$.

title: Complexity of Unit-Time Precedence Scheduling on Three Machines
short_statement: Determine whether $P3\mid prec, p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$ is polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard.
full_statement: An instance consists of a finite set $J$ of unit-processing-time jobs, three identical parallel machines, and a precedence partial order $\prec$ on $J$. A feasible nonpreemptive schedule assigns each job $j\in J$ to one of the three machines and to an integer time slot, with at most one job processed on each machine in each slot, and with $j$ completed before $k$ starts whenever $j\prec k$. The objective is to minimize the makespan $C_{\max}$, the time at which the last job completes. The open problem is the classical decision complexity of this clean fixed-machine model: given $T$, decide whether there is a feasible schedule of makespan at most $T$ for $P3\mid prec,p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$. Prove that the problem is in P, prove that it is NP-hard, or identify a sharper structural complexity classification that resolves the Garey-Johnson open case.
background: Precedence-constrained scheduling is one of the oldest bridges between operations research and theoretical computer science. Graham's list scheduling gives a simple constant-factor approximation for identical machines, and many variants with arbitrary processing times or many machines are known to be hard. The striking feature of this problem is how little structure remains: all jobs have unit length, the number of machines is fixed at three, and the only combinatorial object is a partial order. For two machines the problem has special structure; for unrestricted machine counts and broader variants there are hardness results. The three-machine case survived the original Garey-Johnson complexity list and remains a benchmark for whether the boundary between polynomial structure and NP-hardness in scheduling can be drawn exactly. Recent approximation work has made the optimization version much better understood for constant $m$, but it has not settled the exact decision complexity of the smallest unresolved fixed-machine case.
known_results: Levey and Rothvoss proved a near-polynomial/quasi-polynomial-time $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation framework for $P\mid prec,p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$ with constant $m$ using LP hierarchies, substantially improving the approximation landscape but not resolving NP-hardness for $m=3$. Garg improved the hierarchy-based running time to quasi-polynomial, Li further improved the dependence, and Das and Wiese gave a simpler QPTAS-style approach. Kulkarni, Li, Tarnawski, and Ye extended hierarchy-based ideas to arbitrary processing lengths in a non-migratory relaxed setting and to communication-delay variants. These results show that constant-machine precedence scheduling is approximable extremely well in quasi-polynomial time, but as of the 2026 literature check they still leave open the exact P-versus-NP status of $P3\mid prec,p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$.
open_problem: Resolve the computational complexity of $P3\mid prec,p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$.

These results are strong evidence that fixed-machine precedence scheduling has substantial hidden structure, but they are not exact algorithms. The 2020 hierarchy-based work also emphasizes that arbitrary processing lengths and communication delays remain harder variants.
