title: Constant-Factor Approximation for Scheduling with Uniform Communication Delays
short_statement: Does $P\mid prec,c\mid C_{\max}$ admit a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation independent of the number of machines and the delay $c$?
full_statement: An instance consists of jobs $J$ with processing times, $m$ identical parallel machines, a precedence DAG on $J$, and a uniform communication delay $c\ge 0$. A nonpreemptive schedule assigns each job to a machine and start time. If $i\prec j$ and $i,j$ are scheduled on the same machine, then $j$ may start after $i$ completes; if they are scheduled on different machines, then $j$ may start only at least $c$ time units after $i$ completes. The objective is to minimize $C_{\max}$. The open problem is whether there is a polynomial-time $O(1)$-approximation for $P\mid prec,c\mid C_{\max}$, where the approximation factor is independent of $m$, $n$, and $c$. A stronger resolution would identify the correct asymptotic approximability, perhaps matching a hardness threshold.
background: Communication-delay scheduling models parallel computation and distributed production systems in which a successor task can start quickly if it stays on the same processor but must wait if intermediate data, materials, or setup information crosses processors. This is a natural extension of precedence-constrained scheduling, but the delay constraint couples assignment and sequencing in a way that breaks many classical list-scheduling arguments. The problem appears in longstanding scheduling open-problem lists, including the Schuurman-Woeginger list and later updates discussed by Bansal and subsequent approximation papers. It is attractive for the ORdos collection because the model is extremely crisp: a precedence DAG, identical machines, and one scalar delay. The difficulty lies not in modeling but in finding an approximation method that avoids paying a factor growing with $c$ or $m$.
known_results: Graham-style list scheduling gives factors that grow with the communication delay. Davies, Kulkarni, Rothvoss, Tarnawski, and Zhang gave a polynomial-time $O(\log c\cdot \log m)$ approximation using Sherali-Adams liftings and randomized clustering, a major improvement over delay-linear bounds but still not constant. For non-uniform communication delays, Davies, Kulkarni, Rothvoss, Sandeep, Tarnawski, and Zhang proved logarithmic hardness under standard quasi-polynomial-time assumptions, showing that the broader delay model cannot have the same constant-factor behavior. Kulkarni, Li, Tarnawski, and Ye developed hierarchy-based algorithms for related precedence and communication-constrained settings. As of the 2026 check, the uniform-delay constant-factor question remains the clean unresolved target.
open_problem: Find a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation for $P\mid prec,c\mid C_{\max}$ with uniform communication delay, or prove that no such approximation exists under a standard complexity assumption.

where_posed.text: Restated as an outstanding Schuurman-Woeginger/Bansal open problem in Davies et al., 'Scheduling with Communication Delays via LP Hierarchies and Clustering'.

title: FPT Status of Single-Machine Scheduling with Forbidden Start and End Times
short_statement: FPT is proved for integer-time forbidden start-and-end instants; the recorded formulation omitted the time-domain restriction.
full_statement: Consider a single machine and a set of nonpreemptive jobs with processing times. There is also a set $F$ of $\tau$ forbidden time points. A feasible schedule processes one job at a time and must avoid starting or completing any job at a forbidden time point; equivalently, every job start time and completion time must lie outside $F$. The objective is to minimize the makespan. The original target is an algorithm with running time $f(\tau)L^{O(1)}$, where $L$ is the encoded input length, or a parameterized hardness classification. The record did not specify the time domain. Gabay, Rapine, and Brauner's Theorem 3 proves FPT for integer data and integer start/completion times, including high-multiplicity encoding. This settles that discrete-time interpretation, not unrestricted real-time schedules without a reduction or discretization argument. The original target is retained with this scope caveat.
background: Forbidden endpoints model auxiliary resources needed to initiate or complete jobs; processing can continue across forbidden instants. Earlier XP bounds motivated parameterized questions. The prior record understated the high-multiplicity Fse result and did not distinguish its integer-time assumptions from unspecified real-time schedules. Forbidden-start-only (Fs) and forbidden-start-and-end (Fse) results also require separate treatment.
known_results: Gabay, Rapine, and Brauner, Journal of Scheduling 19(5), 609-616 (2016), Theorem 3, proves FPT in the number of forbidden start-and-end instants even with high multiplicities. The model requires integer data and integer feasible endpoints. The previous XP-only description is incorrect for that model. Billaut-Sourd concerns forbidden starts; Rapine-Brauner concerns forbidden starts and completions. No conclusion about an unspecified real-time interpretation follows without additional argument.
open_problem: Historical target: classify FPT in the number of forbidden start/end instants. The integer-time interpretation is solved; reconcile any intended nonintegral data or real-time schedules explicitly before extending that conclusion.

title: Total-variation convergence for stationary-ergodic FCFS $G/G/m$ queues
short_statement: For a stable FCFS $G/G/m$ queue driven only by stationary ergodic interarrival and service sequences, does the Kiefer-Wolfowitz workload vector started empty converge in total variation to the minimal stationary distribution?
background: Single-server queues have an unusually clean stability theory. For a stable $G/G/1$ FCFS queue with stationary ergodic input, Loynes' construction gives a unique stationary waiting-time distribution and convergence in total variation from every deterministic initial delay. The natural multi-server analogue is much harder because the state is the ordered vector of residual workloads, not a scalar Lindley recursion. Kiefer and Wolfowitz introduced the workload-vector recursion for the $G/G/m$ queue, and the empty-start recursion is monotone enough to yield weak convergence to the minimal stationary distribution under stability. What is missing is the stronger coupling/total-variation conclusion under only stationary ergodicity. Extra assumptions such as iid, regenerative, or Markovian input allow Harris or renovation arguments, but those assumptions change the theorem. Foss singled this out as a long-standing open problem because it asks whether the classical one-server robustness extends to the most basic many-server FCFS model without any hidden mixing hypothesis.
full_statement: Fix an integer $m\ge 2$. Let $(t_n,\sigma_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ be a stationary ergodic sequence, where $t_n$ is the interarrival time between customers $n$ and $n+1$ and $\sigma_n$ is the service requirement of customer $n$. Consider the FCFS $G/G/m$ queue with $m$ identical servers and ordered workload vector $W_n=(W_{n,1},\ldots,W_{n,m})$, arranged in nondecreasing order immediately before customer $n$ arrives. The Kiefer-Wolfowitz recursion is $$W_{n+1}=R\left((W_{n,1}+\sigma_n-t_{n+1})^+,(W_{n,2}-t_{n+1})^+,\ldots,(W_{n,m}-t_{n+1})^+\right),$$ where $R$ sorts coordinates increasingly. Assume the standard stability condition $\mathbb E[\sigma_1]<m\mathbb E[t_1]$ and start from $W_0=0$. The empty-start Loynes construction gives weak convergence to the minimal stationary distribution $\pi_{\min}$. The open problem is to prove or refute that this convergence is in total variation under no assumptions beyond stationarity, ergodicity, and stability: $$\|\mathcal L(W_n)-\pi_{\min}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\to 0.$$ A stronger resolution would characterize when uniqueness of the stationary workload-vector distribution and convergence from arbitrary deterministic initial workload vectors hold under stationary ergodic input.
open_problem: Prove or refute total-variation convergence to the minimal stationary distribution for the stable FCFS $G/G/m$ queue under stationary ergodic input alone.
known_results: For $m=1$, Loynes' scheme proves existence, uniqueness, and total-variation convergence for the stationary ergodic $G/G/1$ queue under the negative-drift stability condition. For $m\ge2$, the Kiefer-Wolfowitz recursion gives a monotone empty-start construction and weak convergence to the minimal stationary distribution, but not total-variation convergence. Foss notes that multi-server queues can have multiple stationary regimes in general, while iid, regenerative, or Markovian assumptions restore uniqueness and total-variation convergence through Harris recurrence or renovation techniques. The precise stationary-ergodic theorem remains open.

literature.synthesis: The one-server proof works because the workload is the running maximum of a negative-drift stationary ergodic random walk; finite coupling follows from the backward maximum being attained at a finite time. In the multi-server case, the Kiefer-Wolfowitz map preserves enough order to define a minimal stationary workload vector from the empty start, but coordinate sorting and parallel service destroy the scalar random-walk representation. Additional stochastic regularity gives regeneration or small sets, so the issue is not stability itself but whether ergodicity alone forces enough forgetting of initial conditions. The remaining gap is a sharp ergodic theorem for the workload-vector recursion, or an explicit stable stationary ergodic input where weak convergence does not strengthen to total variation.

title: Stability of the nearest-neighbor greedy server on a circle
short_statement: The nearest-neighbor greedy server on a circle is stable at every subcritical arrival rate, for every positive travel speed (Rolla and Sidoravicius, 2017).
background: Spatial queues capture systems in which travel or switching time depends on the geometry of outstanding work. The nearest-neighbor greedy server is perhaps the simplest nontrivial example: requests arrive randomly on a compact space, service consumes fixed time, and the server always moves to the closest waiting request. The policy is locally optimal in travel distance, but local optimality can create global pathologies because new arrivals may repeatedly pull the server around dense regions while remote work accumulates. Foss records that the stability conjecture had already been known for more than twenty years by 2009. The finite-state analogue is much easier, and state-independent routing policies are stable under the natural load condition. Rolla and Sidoravicius subsequently proved the continuous-space conjecture. This entry records that resolution, rather than proposing another search for an instability example.
full_statement: Let the state space be a circle of fixed finite circumference. Particles arrive according to a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$, with iid uniform locations on the circle. A single server moves along the circle at a fixed finite positive speed. Serving a particle takes exactly one unit of time; after service the particle is removed. Whenever a service completion occurs and at least one particle is waiting, the server chooses a waiting particle at minimum circular distance from its current location, moves to that particle, serves it, and repeats. If no particle is waiting, the server idles until the next arrival. Since service itself consumes one unit of time, the obvious necessary condition for stability is $\lambda<1$. This question is resolved: Rolla and Sidoravicius (2017), Theorem 1.1, prove positive recurrence for every $\lambda<1$ and every positive speed. Their convention commits to the chosen customer while traveling, ignoring new arrivals until the next choice. Rescaling space covers each fixed finite circumference; this is not a uniform bound on mean return times over all circumferences and speeds.
open_problem: Resolved for the stated Poisson/uniform-arrival model with deterministic unit service and a target fixed during each journey.
known_results: Rolla and Sidoravicius, Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 70 (2017), 1961-1986, Theorem 1.1, prove stability for Poisson arrivals at uniform circle locations when the arrival rate is below the service rate and travel speed is positive. Deterministic, exponential, and geometric service times are covered. Stability means finite expected time to regeneration at the empty state. Deterministic unit service is exactly the present case. The theorem does not cover a server that changes its destination during travel; the paper explicitly separates that variant. Foss's 2009 open-status statement is historical.

title: Stationary regimes of stationary-ergodic join-the-shortest-queue systems
short_statement: For a stable multi-server join-the-shortest-queue system with stationary ergodic input, characterize stationary regimes, uniqueness, and weak or total-variation convergence.
background: Join-the-shortest-queue is one of the canonical load-balancing policies: arrivals are routed to the currently shorter queue, and the policy is locally sensible in every finite state. Under Markovian assumptions, JSQ systems have a rich and useful stability theory. Foss's open problem asks what survives when the primitive input is only stationary ergodic. This is a natural stress test for queueing stability methods because JSQ lacks the monotonicity that makes FCFS workload recursions tractable. Without monotonicity, Loynes-type constructions do not directly define minimal and maximal stationary versions, and it becomes unclear whether the obvious load condition plus ergodicity determines a unique stationary law. The problem is not about choosing a better model; the routing rule and primitives are fixed. It is a foundational question about whether a simple load-balancing system has robust stability under weak assumptions on the input process.
full_statement: Consider $m\ge2$ single-server queues in parallel. Customers arrive with stationary ergodic interarrival and service primitives satisfying the natural load condition that the long-run offered work per unit time is less than total service capacity. Upon arrival, each customer immediately joins a shortest queue, with ties broken by a fixed deterministic or randomized rule. Services at each queue are FCFS. Let $X_n$ denote the vector of queue lengths and residual workloads seen at arrival epochs, or the corresponding continuous-time Markov/ergodic state descriptor when service times are included. The open problem is to characterize the stationary regimes of this JSQ system under stationary ergodic input alone: how many stationary versions can exist, what additional conditions if any imply uniqueness, and whether $X_n$ started from an empty state converges weakly or in total variation to a stationary law. A particularly sharp target is to prove positive recurrence and uniqueness under the natural load condition, or to construct a stable stationary ergodic input for which multiple stationary regimes or nonconvergence occur.
open_problem: Characterize existence, uniqueness, and convergence of stationary regimes for stable join-the-shortest-queue systems under stationary ergodic input.
known_results: For Markovian and iid models, JSQ stability and stationary behavior can often be handled using Foster-Lyapunov, coupling, fluid-limit, or diffusion techniques. Classical supermarket and JSQ($d$) limits also give detailed behavior in large-server asymptotic regimes, but these rely on independence and Markovian structure that is stronger than stationarity and ergodicity. The stationary-ergodic setting is much less understood because the JSQ routing map is not monotone in the relevant workload state. Foss describes even the two-server stationary-ergodic JSQ problem as open beyond the obvious load condition and asks how many stationary regimes may exist, what assumptions imply uniqueness, and when weak or total-variation convergence holds.

counterexample_rationale: A counterexample could be an explicit stationary ergodic input with stable average load but multiple stationary versions or persistent phase dependence. Constructing and proving such an example would be hard but finite-state or periodic approximations may guide it.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search over deterministic ergodic sequences, Markov-modulated inputs, or adversarial tie-breaking patterns may reveal candidate nonmonotone mechanisms. Verification requires rigorous queueing stability proofs.

literature.synthesis: The contrast with FCFS multi-server queues is instructive. FCFS has an ordered workload-vector recursion with partial monotonicity, which makes Loynes-type stationary constructions possible under weak assumptions. JSQ makes a state-dependent routing decision that can reverse order and amplify small workload differences, so the usual monotone coupling is unavailable. In Markovian settings this is usually handled by Lyapunov drift or regenerative arguments, but stationary ergodic primitives need pathwise constructions rather than transition-kernel recurrence. The known gap is therefore structural: either find a new ergodic stability method for nonmonotone queueing recursions, or exhibit a stationary ergodic input whose long memory defeats uniqueness despite subcritical load.

A uniqueness proof should identify the stationary version and convergence mode. A counterexample must prove stationary ergodicity of the driving process, subcritical load, and the claimed multiplicity or nonconvergence, not merely display a long transient burst pattern.

title: Stable random-access protocols with only success/non-success feedback
short_statement: Can a deterministic update using only current attempt probability and the success bit stabilize a positive rate? Extra-randomization results do not settle this restriction.
background: Random-access channels are among the classical stochastic-network models behind communication protocols. In slotted ALOHA-type systems, many packets contend for a shared channel, and collisions force retransmission. Stability depends strongly on what feedback the protocol receives. If the controller can distinguish empty slots from nonempty slots, or collisions from noncollisions, classical results give the familiar $e^{-1}$ threshold. Foss highlights a feedback restriction: suppose the update can use only the current transmission probability and a single bit saying whether the previous slot had a success. This bit merges empty slots and collisions into the same observation, depriving the protocol of the usual congestion signal. The model is extremely clean, and the question is binary: does any protocol in this information class stabilize the backlog for any positive arrival rate? A later stability theorem uses additional common randomness, so the feedback alphabet alone does not define the admissible protocol class.
full_statement: Time is slotted. In each slot, a Poisson number of new packets with mean $\lambda$ enters a shared single channel. At the beginning of slot $n$, every packet currently in the system attempts transmission independently with probability $p_n$. If exactly one packet transmits, the transmission succeeds and that packet leaves; if zero packets transmit, the slot is idle; if two or more transmit, all attempted transmissions collide and remain in the system. Let $W_n$ be the backlog at the beginning of slot $n$. A protocol is restricted to choose $p_{n+1}$ as a function only of $p_n$ and the binary feedback variable indicating whether slot $n$ had a successful transmission. Thus empty slots and collision slots are observationally identical. The pair $(W_n,p_n)$ is then a time-homogeneous Markov chain. The open problem is whether there exists any such protocol and any $\lambda>0$ for which $(W_n,p_n)$ is positive recurrent. If yes, determine the supremum stabilizable arrival rate under success/non-success feedback; if no, prove impossibility for every positive $\lambda$. Here 'a function only of' means a deterministic update $p_{n+1}=f(p_n,J_n)$, with $J_n$ the success indicator. Independent packet transmission trials are not an extra common random seed for this update. The later doubly randomized theorem belongs to a larger protocol class and is related progress, not a resolution of this target.
open_problem: Original deterministic target: does some update $p_{n+1}=f(p_n,J_n)$ yield positive recurrence at a positive Poisson arrival rate, and what is the supremum stabilizable rate? No answer for this restricted class is certified here.
known_results: Foss-Hajek-Turlikov (2016) constructs stable doubly randomized protocols for iid finite-mean slot arrivals, including Poisson input. For each fixed interval $0<\lambda_0<\lambda_1<e^{-1}$, suitable parameters stabilize all rates in that interval. The feedback merges empty and collision outcomes and no test packets are used. But a shared extra coin randomizes the protocol; the theorem does not establish deterministic f(p,J), nor one parameter choice covering every unknown rate below $e^{-1}$. The original deterministic target is retained without certifying current openness from absence of results.

title: Local-global structure for nonlinear single-machine weighted completion time
short_statement: For $1||\sum_j w_j C_j^\beta$ with fixed $\beta\ne 1$, determine the complexity and resolve the local-global ordering conjecture.
background: The classical single-machine problem $1||\sum_j w_j C_j$ is solved exactly by Smith's rule: order jobs by decreasing $w_j/p_j$. This is one of the cleanest results in deterministic scheduling. Bansal, Duerr, Thang, and Vasquez study the natural nonlinear extension $1||\sum_j w_j C_j^\beta$, where $\beta>0$ is a fixed constant. This objective appears when marginal delay costs are nonlinear, for example through learning effects, convex lateness penalties, or power-like delay disutility. The difficulty is not that the model is vague; the model is completely specified. The difficulty is that for $\beta\ne 1$, a pairwise preference between two jobs can depend on the time at which the pair is scheduled and on other jobs placed before them. Their paper develops dominance relations and a local-global conjecture suggesting that certain local ordering constraints may characterize global optimality. The open problem is to settle this structural conjecture and, more broadly, the computational complexity of the nonlinear problem.
full_statement: Given $n$ jobs on one nonpreemptive single machine, job $j$ has processing time $p_j>0$ and weight $w_j>0$. A schedule is a permutation $\sigma$, completion times are $C_{\sigma(t)}=\sum_{s\le t}p_{\sigma(s)}$, and the objective is $\sum_j w_j C_j^\beta$ for a fixed constant $\beta>0$. For $\beta=1$, Smith's rule gives an optimal ordering by decreasing $w_j/p_j$. For $\beta\ne 1$, determine whether the problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard. More specifically, resolve the local-global conjecture studied by Bansal, Duerr, Thang, and Vasquez: if a schedule satisfies the relevant local dominance/order constraints for all pairs or local moves, must it be globally optimal? A solution should either prove that the local conditions imply global optimality, yielding a structural algorithmic route, or construct an explicit counterexample and then determine the resulting complexity status.
open_problem: Resolve the local-global conjecture for $1||\sum_j w_j C_j^\beta$ and determine the polynomial-time versus NP-hard status of the nonlinear weighted-completion-time problem for fixed $\beta\ne 1$.
known_results: For $\beta=1$, Smith's rule optimally orders jobs by decreasing $w_j/p_j$. Bansal, Duerr, Thang, and Vasquez show that for $\beta\ne 1$ the usual pairwise interchange argument breaks: the preferred order of two jobs may depend on their start time and on intervening jobs. They derive new dominance properties and use them to greatly accelerate exact A* search, but they do not settle the complexity of the problem. Their abstract explicitly states that the complexity status is open for $\beta\ne 1$. The local-global conjecture captures the hope that enough local dominance constraints might still force global optimality, but no proof or counterexample is known from the checked source trail. Thus the remaining gap is very concrete: either turn the local structure into a proof and algorithm, or show by counterexample or reduction that nonlinear power objectives fundamentally break Smith-like orderability.

The linear case has a complete one-line priority rule, while the nonlinear power case is still not classified. The Bansal-Duerr-Thang-Vasquez paper gives enough structure to make computational search meaningful: one can encode local dominance rules, run exact dynamic programming or A* on small instances, and look for either a proof pattern or a smallest obstruction. A full solution would clarify whether the success of Smith's rule is a linear-objective accident or the visible part of a broader nonlinear local-global scheduling principle.

title: Randomized competitive ratio for weighted $k$-server on uniform metrics
short_statement: A 2026 preprint claims an exponential-in-k randomized ratio on uniform metrics; the exact exponential base is not settled.
background: The weighted $k$-server problem is a natural variant of the classical $k$-server problem. There are $k$ servers with different weights, and moving server $i$ through distance $d$ costs $w_i d$. Even on a uniform metric, where every requested point is equally far from every other point, the weighted problem is much less understood than ordinary paging. A request names a point, and the algorithm must ensure that some server is at that point after the request. The unweighted uniform case has logarithmic randomized behavior, while the weighted uniform case has exponential lower bounds and historically only very large upper bounds. Recent work has finally broken the doubly exponential deterministic barrier for randomized algorithms, and an October 2026 preprint claims to close the remaining exponent-order gap. This makes the problem a clean, well-defined constant-in-$n$ but parameterized-in-$k$ competitive-analysis question.
full_statement: Fix $k$ servers with weights $w_1\le\cdots\le w_k$ on a uniform metric space with sufficiently many points. At each online request, a point is revealed; if no server is currently at the point, the algorithm must move one server there and pays that server's weight times the unit distance. The offline optimum knows the full request sequence. Determine the optimal randomized competitive ratio against an oblivious adversary as a function of $k$, or at least close the asymptotic gap between the best lower and upper bounds. In particular, is the true ratio $2^{\Theta(k)}$, $2^{\Theta(k^2)}$, or something else between the known singly exponential lower bound and the previously known $\exp(O(k^2))$ randomized upper bound? Hwang (2026), Theorem 1.3 and Corollary 1.4, claims the $2^{\Theta(k)}$ alternative: ordinary weighted k-server is the diagonal-request special case of its generalized model. This records a preprint claim, not an independently certified proof or the exact optimal exponential base.
open_problem: Historical target: determine the randomized competitive ratio against an oblivious adversary. A preprint claims to close the exponent-order gap to exp(Theta(k)); the exact optimal exponential base is not thereby determined.
known_results: Fiat and Ricklin introduced weighted server variants, and later work showed that the deterministic behavior can be extremely large. Bansal, Elias, Koumoutsos, and Nederlof gave algorithms for generalized $k$-server in uniform metrics and a doubly exponential deterministic guarantee for weighted uniform metrics. Ayyadevara and Chiplunkar proved that the randomized competitive ratio for weighted $k$-server on uniform metrics is at least exponential in $k$, improving the earlier logarithmic-style lower-bound picture. Ayyadevara, Chiplunkar, and Sharma then proposed a decomposition program that reduced part of the randomized upper-bound challenge to relaxed service-pattern problems. Bijoy, Mondal, and Chiplunkar subsequently gave an $\exp(O(k^2))$-competitive randomized algorithm on uniform metrics, the first randomized upper bound beating the doubly exponential deterministic barrier. This left a gap between $\Omega(2^k)$ and $\exp(O(k^2))$. Hwang's arXiv:2610.37192v1, Theorem 1.3, states $\mathbb E[\mathrm{ALG}]\le 20^k\mathrm{OPT}+10^k w_k$ for arbitrary weighted uniform spaces and fixed initial configuration. Corollary 1.4 specializes to ordinary weighted k-server. Combined with the lower bound, this claims exp(Theta(k)) against an oblivious adversary, not a matching exponential base.

title: Stationary short-queue profile in the heavy-traffic supermarket model
short_statement: Prove the Eschenfeldt-Gamarnik conjecture for the stationary short-queue profile of JSQ($d$) in the many-server heavy-traffic supermarket model.
background: The supermarket model is a canonical queueing model for randomized load balancing. There are $n$ parallel single-server queues, arrivals occur at total rate $n\lambda$, each arrival samples $d$ queues uniformly at random, and the job joins a shortest sampled queue. For fixed $\lambda<1$, the power-of-$d$ rule produces a doubly exponential stationary queue-length tail and a maximum queue length of order $\log\log n$. Heavy traffic is subtler: as $\lambda_n\uparrow 1$, the typical queue length grows, and the behavior of queues shorter than the typical scale is not diffusive. Eschenfeldt and Gamarnik identify a deterministic infinite-dimensional dynamical system for the short-queue profile and compute its unique fixed point. They conjecture that this fixed point is the limiting stationary short-queue profile. The open problem is to prove the steady-state version, i.e. an interchange-of-limits theorem and stationary convergence result for this heavy-traffic mean-field system.
full_statement: Consider $n$ queues with exponential service rate $1$ at each server and Poisson arrivals of rate $n\lambda_n$. Each arriving job samples $d\ge2$ queues uniformly and joins a shortest sampled queue, ties arbitrary. Let $Q_i^n(t)$ be the number of queues with length at least $i$ at time $t$. In the heavy-traffic regime $\lambda_n\uparrow1$, with $\lambda_n$ approaching $1$ no faster than the scale specified in Eschenfeldt and Gamarnik, the natural center for queue lengths is approximately $\log_d(1-\lambda_n)^{-1}$. Define a rescaled short-queue profile below this center, for example by tracking the appropriately scaled deficits in $Q_i^n$ for levels $i$ below $\log_d(1-\lambda_n)^{-1}-O(1)$. Eschenfeldt and Gamarnik prove that the transient dynamics of this profile are described by an infinite system of deterministic linear differential equations and that the system has a unique fixed point of the form $\pi_1(d^i-1)/(d-1)$ for $i\ge1$. Prove that, in stationarity, the corresponding rescaled queue-length profile converges to this fixed point. Equivalently, justify the conjectured interchange between the many-server heavy-traffic limit and the stationary distribution for the short-queue process.
open_problem: Prove or refute the conjectured stationary fixed-point limit for the short-queue profile in the heavy-traffic supermarket model.
known_results: Classical supermarket-model work by Vvedenskaya, Dobrushin, and Karpelevich and by Mitzenmacher established the mean-field picture for fixed load $\lambda<1$, including the power-of-two phenomenon and doubly exponential queue tails. Luczak and McDiarmid proved rapid mixing and showed that, in equilibrium for fixed $\lambda<1$, the maximum queue length concentrates on at most two adjacent values around $\log\log n/\log d$. Eschenfeldt and Gamarnik analyze the regime $\lambda_n\uparrow1$. They prove that most queues have length at least $\log_d(1-\lambda_n)^{-1}-O(1)$ with high probability and derive a deterministic infinite-dimensional description for the dynamics of shorter queues after rescaling. They compute the unique fixed point $\pi_1(d^i-1)/(d-1)$ and explicitly conjecture that it describes the steady-state short-queue profile. The remaining difficulty is the steady-state limit: proving tightness, controlling the stationary process, and interchanging the limit in $n$ with the long-time limit.

progress.summary: Transient rescaled dynamics and the candidate fixed point are known. The stationary convergence/interchange-of-limits theorem remains open.

counterexample_rationale: Simulations can test the conjectured stationary profile and may expose missing scaling conditions, but a refutation would still require an asymptotic probabilistic argument or a rigorously analyzed alternative limit.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated experiments can estimate stationary profiles across $n,\lambda_n,d$ and suggest Lyapunov functions or tightness bounds, but the main resolution is analytic.

literature.synthesis: This is a precise open problem about a classical load-balancing queue. The fixed-load supermarket model is well understood, but heavy traffic changes the scale and removes the usual diffusion intuition for short queues. Eschenfeldt and Gamarnik provide the limiting dynamical equations and the unique candidate fixed point, so the remaining task is not to invent a model; it is to prove that the actual stationary distribution follows the candidate limit. A proof would likely require uniform-in-time control of the centered occupancy process, tightness of the short-queue coordinates, and a Lyapunov or generator argument ruling out non-fixed stationary subsequential limits.

title: Constructive description of all gross substitutes valuations
short_statement: Find a constructive grammar or representation theorem for all gross substitutes valuations over indivisible goods.
background: Gross substitutes valuations are one of the central tractable domains in market design with indivisible goods. A valuation $v:2^M\to \mathbb{R}$ has the gross substitutes property if, when some item prices rise and the remaining prices stay fixed, a buyer can choose a new demanded bundle that keeps every previously demanded item whose price did not rise. Kelso and Crawford introduced the condition in matching and salary markets, and Gul and Stacchetti showed its central role in Walrasian equilibrium theory for indivisible goods. Gross substitutes valuations are also equivalent to several discrete-convexity notions and include matroid rank functions and many valuated-matroid-like objects. The class is well characterized by demand behavior and exchange axioms, but these characterizations are not constructive: they do not explain how to build every gross substitutes valuation from simple primitives. Balkanski and Paes Leme frame this construction problem explicitly and show that one natural hope, positive linear combinations of matroid rank functions, is not enough.
full_statement: Let $M$ be a finite set of indivisible goods and let $v:2^M\to\mathbb{R}$ be a normalized valuation. For a price vector $p\in\mathbb{R}^M$, let $D(v,p)$ be the set of bundles maximizing $v(S)-\sum_{j\in S}p_j$. The valuation $v$ is gross substitutes if for any $p\le q$ and any $X\in D(v,p)$, there exists $Y\in D(v,q)$ such that every item in $X$ whose price did not increase remains in $Y$. The open problem is to give a constructive description of exactly this class: identify a set of elementary gross-substitutes primitives and closure operations that generate all and only gross substitutes valuations. A satisfactory answer could be a finite or recursively specified grammar, a decomposition theorem into known discrete-convex objects, or an algorithmic representation that is complete for all finite gross substitutes valuations. It should also explain the role of matroid rank functions, valuated matroids, endowment/merge-type operations, and other known substitute-preserving operations.
open_problem: Give a complete constructive representation of gross substitutes valuations, or prove that no proposed natural family of primitives and substitute-preserving operations is complete.
known_results: Kelso and Crawford introduced gross substitutes in a job-matching model, and Gul and Stacchetti established its connection to Walrasian equilibria and ascending auctions. Discrete convex analysis gives several equivalent ways to recognize the class, including exchange and M-natural-concavity-style conditions; Murota's work clarifies the equivalence between strong no-complementarities and gross substitutes. Shioura showed that a rich subclass of gross substitutes can be represented using sums of matroid rank functions. Balkanski and Paes Leme prove that this particular construction is not complete: some gross substitutes valuations cannot be expressed as positive linear combinations of matroid rank functions. They also give necessary and sufficient conditions for sums to preserve substitutability, identify a new substitute-preserving operation, and completely describe all substitutes on at most four items. Thus the broad construction problem remains open after eliminating one of the most natural candidate representations.

progress.summary: Gross substitutes have many recognition characterizations and several closure operations. Positive combinations of matroid rank functions are not complete, and all four-item substitutes are classified, but no full constructive description is known.

counterexample_rationale: Any proposed constructive grammar can be tested against finite valuation tables. Small counterexamples can refute completeness of a candidate primitive/operation system, as in the matroid-rank-combination obstruction.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search over finite valuation tables can discover gross substitutes valuations outside candidate generated classes, suggest new operations, and test closure conjectures.

literature.synthesis: Gross substitutes sit at the intersection of economics, combinatorial optimization, and discrete convex analysis. Equilibrium existence and ascending-auction algorithms are well understood when valuations are given by demand or value oracles, but the class remains structurally mysterious. The construction problem asks for more than a membership test: it asks for a generative theory comparable to how matroids can be built and recognized through rank, independence, bases, and exchange. Balkanski and Paes Leme's negative result is useful because it shows that the naive matroid-rank-span answer is false while leaving open whether a richer grammar using merge, endowment, valuated matroid operations, or other substitute-preserving transformations is complete.

title: Frontier of combinatorial markets admitting optimal dynamic prices
short_statement: Characterize which valuation domains admit welfare-optimal dynamic posted prices in combinatorial markets.
background: Dynamic posted pricing is a decentralized alternative to direct welfare maximization in markets for indivisible goods. A seller posts prices, buyers arrive sequentially, each buyer chooses a utility-maximizing bundle among remaining items, and prices may be updated after each arrival based on the remaining market. The goal is not revenue learning; it is exact welfare implementation by prices. Unit-demand buyers admit optimal dynamic prices, while coverage valuations can fail to admit them. This creates a clean structural question parallel to the role of gross substitutes in Walrasian equilibrium: which valuation domains are exactly those where dynamic prices can implement an optimal allocation without a central coordinator? Berger, Eden, and Feldman narrow this frontier with positive results for small multi-demand markets and a maximal-domain negative theorem around non-gross-substitutes valuations, but the full characterization remains open.
full_statement: Consider a finite set $M$ of indivisible items and buyers $1,\dots,n$ arriving in a known or adversarially fixed order. Buyer $i$ has valuation $v_i:2^M\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$. A dynamic pricing scheme chooses a price vector $p^t$ over the remaining items before buyer $t$ arrives; the buyer then selects a demanded bundle from the remaining items, and sold items are removed. The scheme is welfare-optimal for a valuation profile if, under an appropriate tie-breaking rule or robust choice condition, the resulting allocation maximizes $\sum_i v_i(S_i)$ over feasible allocations. The open problem is to characterize the valuation domains $\mathcal{V}$ for which every market with buyers from $\mathcal{V}$ admits an efficiently computable welfare-optimal dynamic pricing scheme. In particular, determine whether gross substitutes, multi-demand subclasses, or a different domain form the exact frontier, and settle the status of multi-demand valuations with arbitrary numbers of buyers.
open_problem: Characterize the exact frontier of valuation functions for which optimal dynamic pricing schemes exist in combinatorial markets.
known_results: Cohen-Addad and coauthors showed that unit-demand buyers admit optimal dynamic prices and gave examples, such as coverage valuations, where optimal dynamic prices need not exist. Berger, Eden, and Feldman sharpened the picture. On the positive side, they characterized optimal allocations in multi-demand markets and used this structure to give a polynomial-time optimal dynamic pricing algorithm for up to three multi-demand buyers. On the negative side, they proved a maximal-domain theorem: for every non-gross-substitutes valuation, one can add unit-demand valuations so that the resulting market does not admit optimal dynamic prices. Berczi, Berczi-Kovacs, and Szogi later gave a dual approach, rederived the unit-demand and up-to-three multi-demand results, and proved optimal dynamic prices for bi-demand valuations with an arbitrary number of buyers. These results leave open the full valuation-domain frontier, especially for general multi-demand valuations and for the relationship between gross substitutes and dynamic-price implementability.

progress.summary: Unit-demand markets, up to three multi-demand buyers, and arbitrary many bi-demand buyers are covered. Non-gross-substitutes valuations cannot be included in a maximal universal domain with unit-demand valuations. The exact frontier remains open.

alphaevolve_rationale: Search over small valuation tables, buyer orders, and optimal allocations can find minimal markets that separate candidate valuation domains or suggest new sufficient conditions.

literature.synthesis: The problem is structurally close to Walrasian equilibrium theory but not identical. Gross substitutes are the maximal domain for several equilibrium guarantees, yet dynamic prices are sequential and can condition on previous sales, so the domain could be larger or organized differently. Existing positive results exploit special allocation structure in unit-demand, bi-demand, and small multi-demand markets. Existing negative results show that non-gross-substitutes valuations create obstructions once combined with unit-demand buyers. The unresolved part is to turn these pieces into an exact theorem: either a maximal domain, a complete classification for multi-demand valuations, or a sharp obstruction criterion.

title: Optimal model selection for contextual bandits
short_statement: Can a contextual-bandit learner adapt to the smallest useful class without paying a model-selection penalty? The unrestricted nested-class guarantee has a negative answer; additional structure can permit adaptation.
background:
Model selection tries to avoid paying for an unnecessarily rich hypothesis class. In full-information learning, the same observations can evaluate many alternatives. In a bandit problem, choosing actions also determines which alternatives can be tested. This creates a tension between exploiting a simple model and collecting evidence for a larger one.

The earlier entry mixed policy classes, reward-function classes, and linear dimensions in one claim. These are not interchangeable. It also treated an arbitrary-class costless guarantee as still open without citing the negative answer. A fixed known-class learning theorem is a baseline, not a model-selection result.
full_statement:
Historical target. Let $\Pi_1\subset\cdots\subset\Pi_M$ be finite classes of policies $\mathcal X\to[K]$. At round $t$, the learner observes $x_t$, chooses $a_t$, and observes only the loss $\ell_t(a_t)\in[0,1]$. Define $$R_T(\Pi_m)=\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(a_t)\right]-\min_{\pi\in\Pi_m}\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(\pi(x_t))\right].$$ The COLT 2020 note asks whether, for some fixed $\alpha\in[1/2,1)$, a learner can guarantee simultaneously for all $m$ a bound of order $T^\alpha(\log|\Pi_m|)^{1-\alpha}$, with the stated polynomial dependence on $K,M,\log\log|\Pi_M|$. It also poses a stochastic realizable regression-class version.

The general policy-class question is resolved negatively by Marinov and Zimmert (NeurIPS 2021, Theorem 5). The paper separately states a proper-algorithm stochastic lower bound (Theorem 4) and explains its relation to the realizable variant in footnote 3. Do not infer that every structured realizable or linear subclass is impossible. This record archives the general target, rather than claiming that all questions about adaptive model selection have been settled.
open_problem: Resolved for the unrestricted nested-policy-class target: the requested universal adaptation guarantee is impossible. Structured realizable-class refinements are distinct questions and need their own explicit assumptions.
known_results:
Marinov and Zimmert (NeurIPS 2021) disprove the general COLT policy-class guarantee, even for stochastic data and unrestricted algorithms (Theorem 5). Their matching Pareto-frontier results have a proper-algorithm qualification in the stochastic setting (Theorem 4); this distinction matters when describing what is tight.

Positive results require additional structure. Foster, Krishnamurthy, and Luo's 2019 paper studies nested linear models. Krishnamurthy, Propp, and Athey's revised 2023 manuscript obtains costless adaptation under conditions on class-complexity growth and improvement in policy value. It explicitly treats the unrestricted COLT question as answered negatively. These refinements do not reopen the general conjecture.

title: Tight regret bounds for kernelized bandits with Bernoulli rewards
short_statement: Obtain tight regret bounds for kernelized bandits when observations are Bernoulli samples with mean $f(x)$ rather than sub-Gaussian additive noise.
background: Kernelized bandits are a standard nonparametric model for sequential optimization. A learner chooses points $x_t$ from an action space $\mathcal X$, receives noisy feedback, and wants to compete with the best point in hindsight. In the classical Gaussian-process/RKHS formulation, the unknown reward function $f$ belongs to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space $\mathcal H_k$ with bounded norm, and the feedback is $y_t=f(x_t)+\epsilon_t$ with sub-Gaussian noise. This additive-noise model has a mature theory through GP-UCB, information gain, and self-normalized concentration. Mussi, Drago, and Metelli's COLT open-problem note points out that many applications have binary outcomes instead: a click, conversion, success, or failure, with $y_t\sim \mathrm{Ber}(f(x_t))$. This is not merely a modelling variation. Bernoulli observations are heteroscedastic, bounded, and nonlinear in the likelihood; near $f(x)=0$ or $1$ the variance changes substantially, and standard sub-Gaussian RKHS analyses may lose the sharp dependence that KL-based finite-armed Bernoulli bandits achieve.
full_statement: Let $\mathcal X$ be a compact or finite action set and let $k$ be a positive semidefinite kernel with RKHS $\mathcal H_k$. An unknown function $f:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ satisfies $\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, an adaptive policy chooses $x_t\in\mathcal X$ based on past observations and then observes $Y_t\sim\mathrm{Ber}(f(x_t))$, independently conditional on the past. Regret is $R_T=\sum_{t=1}^T (f(x^*)-f(x_t))$, where $x^*\in\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal X} f(x)$. Determine the minimax and/or instance-dependent order of $R_T$ for this Bernoulli kernelized bandit model. A satisfactory solution should give algorithms and lower bounds with matching dependence on $T$, the RKHS radius $B$, kernel complexity quantities such as maximum information gain or effective dimension, and the Bernoulli geometry. In particular, decide whether the best possible rates coincide with the sub-Gaussian kernelized-bandit rates up to logarithmic factors, improve through Bernoulli-specific KL curvature, or require a different complexity measure.
open_problem: Develop a tight upper-and-lower-bound theory for kernelized bandits with Bernoulli feedback.
known_results: For sub-Gaussian additive noise, Srinivas, Krause, Kakade, and Seeger introduced GP-UCB and obtained regret bounds in terms of information gain; Chowdhury and Gopalan later gave sharper frequentist RKHS confidence bounds and SupKernelUCB-type results. For ordinary finite-armed Bernoulli bandits, KL-UCB and related algorithms exploit Bernoulli likelihoods to obtain sharp logarithmic instance-dependent constants. Logistic and generalized-linear bandits handle binary observations when the mean is linked to a finite-dimensional linear predictor. Mussi, Drago, and Metelli identify the RKHS Bernoulli model $Y_t\sim\mathrm{Ber}(f(x_t))$ as a gap between these lines: it is not finite-dimensional logistic bandits, and the additive-noise kernelized-bandit analysis does not settle tightness for Bernoulli observations. As of the source check, no matching minimax or instance-dependent theorem for this exact model was found.

title: Polynomial kernels above the LP bound for precedence-constrained weighted completion time
short_statement: Decide whether $1|\mathrm{prec}|\sum_j w_j C_j$ has a polynomial kernel when parameterized by the gap between the optimum and the natural LP lower bound.
background: The single-machine precedence-constrained weighted-completion-time problem is a compact classical scheduling model. There is one machine, each job has a processing time and weight, and a precedence partial order restricts the feasible permutations. The objective $\sum_j w_jC_j$ measures total weighted flow through the machine and is central in deterministic scheduling. The problem is NP-hard, but it has strong linear-programming and ordering structure: precedence constraints make it closely related to vertex-cover-like formulations, and several exact and approximation approaches use LP relaxations. Mnich and van Bevern's open-problem list asks for a parameterized-preprocessing result rather than another approximation ratio. If the optimum value is only $k$ above the natural LP lower bound, can the instance be reduced in polynomial time to an equivalent instance whose size is polynomial in $k$? This is a clean question about whether LP structure gives compressible exact instances.
full_statement: An instance consists of jobs $J$, processing times $p_j\in\mathbb N$, weights $w_j\in\mathbb N$, and a precedence partial order $\prec$ on $J$. A feasible schedule is a linear extension $\sigma$ of $\prec$ on a single nonpreemptive machine; completion times are $C_{\sigma(t)}=\sum_{s\le t}p_{\sigma(s)}$, and the objective is $\sum_{j\in J}w_jC_j$. Let $\mathrm{OPT}$ be the minimum objective value and let $\mathrm{LP}$ be the value of the standard natural LP relaxation used for this precedence-constrained weighted-completion-time problem. Parameterize the decision version by $k=\mathrm{OPT}-\mathrm{LP}$, or equivalently by the allowed excess over the LP lower bound. The open problem is whether this parameterized problem admits a polynomial kernel: a polynomial-time preprocessing algorithm that maps every instance with parameter $k$ to an equivalent instance of size $k^{O(1)}$. A positive answer would show that near-LP-tight instances have a finite structural core; a negative answer would likely require cross-composition or related kernel lower-bound machinery.
open_problem: Prove or refute the existence of a polynomial kernel for $1|\mathrm{prec}|\sum_j w_j C_j$ parameterized above the natural LP lower bound.
known_results: The problem $1|\mathrm{prec}|\sum_j w_j C_j$ is NP-hard and has been studied through LP relaxations, ordering polyhedra, and approximation algorithms. Mnich and van Bevern note that it is a special case of weighted vertex cover under a natural formulation, making it tempting to seek kernelization results analogous to above-LP parameterizations in graph problems. Weighted Vertex Cover has polynomial kernels for certain above-guarantee parameterizations, but those results do not directly transfer because scheduling variables encode a linear extension and completion-time costs rather than a plain chosen vertex set. The source list explicitly posed whether the scheduling problem has a polynomial kernel in the excess over the LP bound. A quick status search did not find a later theorem resolving this exact kernelization question.

title: Throughput scheduling with release dates and bounded processing times
short_statement: Resolve the complexity of $1|r_j,p_j\le c|\sum_j U_j$ for constant $c$, and the corresponding weighted/FPT variants.
background: Maximum-throughput scheduling asks which jobs can be completed by their deadlines. It is a clean single-machine model for admission control: each job has a release date, deadline, and processing time; jobs completed late contribute no throughput. The unit-processing-time case is tractable by matching or greedy methods, while arbitrary processing times make the problem NP-hard. The boundary where processing times are bounded by a fixed constant is surprisingly delicate. Sgall's survey and Mnich-van Bevern's parameterized open-problem list highlight the question $1|r_j,p_j\le c|\sum_j U_j$: for each fixed constant $c$, is there a polynomial-time algorithm for maximizing the number of on-time jobs? The weighted version and parameterized versions are also open-looking. This is exactly the kind of problem the repository is meant to include: the model is fixed, small, and classical, but the complexity frontier is not known.
full_statement: An instance consists of jobs $j=1,\ldots,n$ on one nonpreemptive machine. Job $j$ has release date $r_j$, deadline $d_j$, processing time $p_j\in\{1,\ldots,c\}$ for a fixed constant $c$, and optionally weight $w_j$. A schedule chooses a subset of jobs and start times so that each scheduled job starts no earlier than $r_j$, runs for $p_j$ uninterrupted, no two jobs overlap, and job $j$ is counted as on time only if it completes by $d_j$. In Graham notation, the unweighted objective is $1|r_j,p_j\le c|\sum_j U_j$, equivalently maximizing the number of on-time jobs; the weighted objective is $1|r_j,p_j\le c|\sum_j w_jU_j$. Determine whether the unweighted problem is polynomial-time solvable for every fixed constant $c$, whether the weighted version is NP-hard for fixed $c$, and whether the natural parameterized versions are fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by $c$ and/or the number of distinct processing times.
open_problem: Settle the polynomial-time and parameterized complexity of single-machine throughput scheduling with release dates and constant-bounded processing times.
known_results: When all processing times are unit, maximum throughput on one machine with release dates and deadlines has classical polynomial algorithms. With arbitrary processing times, throughput scheduling is NP-hard and heavily studied in approximation and online scheduling. Sgall's survey on maximum throughput scheduling asked whether $1|r_j,p_j\le c|\sum_j U_j$ is polynomial-time solvable for constant $c$; Mnich and van Bevern restate this and add parameterized versions. They also note that the NP-hardness of the weighted case for constant $c$ is open. The issue is that bounded processing times make time-indexed dynamic programs plausible, but release-date/deadline interactions still create global interval-packing structure. A later search did not find a source resolving the exact fixed-$c$ complexity frontier.

title: Polynomial-time constant approximation for Uniform Decision Tree
short_statement: Uniform-prior adaptive identification has strong greedy and subexponential-time guarantees, but the reported 2026 polynomial-time constant approximation was withdrawn.
full_statement:
Let $H$ be a set of $n$ hypotheses, with a uniform prior, and let $T$ be an explicitly given family of tests. Each unit-cost test is a map $\tau:H\to[K]$ specifying the observed outcome for every hypothesis. Assume the tests separate every pair of hypotheses. A decision tree chooses a test at each internal node, branches on its outcome, and identifies the hidden hypothesis at a leaf. Its cost is $C(D)=n^{-1}\sum_{h\in H}\operatorname{depth}_D(h)$, and $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the minimum cost over valid trees.

Does a polynomial-time algorithm always construct a tree with $C(D)\le c\,\mathrm{OPT}$ for a universal constant $c$? State whether the result covers arbitrary outcome arity $K$ or only fixed $K$; even binary tests form a meaningful restricted target. Time must be polynomial in the explicit test table, not subexponential in $n$. Nonuniform hypothesis priors and nonuniform test costs are different models. The constant-factor claim in arXiv:2604.12036v1 was withdrawn in v2; the current v4 paper does not resolve this target.
background: Adaptive identification is useful in diagnosis, active learning, and sequential testing. Uniform priors change the approximation landscape: hardness for an arbitrary prior cannot simply be transferred to equally likely hypotheses. A tree can be optimized by exhaustive recursion on subsets, but this is exponential. The central issue is whether a polynomial-time method can exploit the uniform prior as effectively as the known subexponential algorithms.
open_problem: Find a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation for Uniform Decision Tree, or establish an appropriate stronger hardness result. The withdrawn 2026 constant-factor claim and fixed-order Pandora guarantees do not settle this question.
known_results:
Li, Liang, and Mussmann (arXiv:1906.11385v2), Theorems 3.1-3.2, bound greedy's ratio by $O(\log n/\log C_{\mathrm{OPT}})$ and obtain constant approximations in subexponential time. For fixed outcome arity, this gives a polynomial-time $O(\log n/\log\log n)$ approximation. Their cited hardness threshold is $4-\varepsilon$; their ETH implication limits superconstant NP-hardness results.

Szyfelbein's arXiv:2604.12036v1 claimed a constant ratio, but v2 (April 28, 2026) withdraws it because of a fundamental proof error and a counterexample to the algorithm. Version 4, 'Simpler Logarithmic Approximation Algorithms for the Optimal Decision Tree and Adaptive Set Cover' (October 19, 2026), instead gives logarithmic simultaneous average- and worst-case guarantees. The earlier claim is not current evidence of resolution.

Chawla, Gergatsouli, McMahan, and Tzamos connect UDT to fully adaptive correlated Pandora policies. Bansal, Huang, and Zhu's 2025 ratio-4 result instead benchmarks partially adaptive policies: a fixed box order with adaptive stopping (Section 2.2). It cannot be transferred as a resolution of fully adaptive UDT. The polynomial-time constant-factor question therefore remains open in the reviewed sources.

title: Competitive equilibrium for almost all incomes with additive indivisible goods
short_statement: For additive valuations over indivisible goods, characterize when competitive equilibria exist for almost every income vector.
full_statement: Consider a market with $n$ agents, $m$ indivisible goods, additive nonnegative valuations $v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S} v_{ig}$, and an income vector $b\in\mathbb R_+^n$. A competitive equilibrium consists of prices $p_g\ge 0$ and an allocation of goods to agents such that every allocated bundle is affordable for its owner, every agent receives a utility-maximizing affordable bundle, and all goods with positive price are allocated. Equal incomes can fail to admit a competitive equilibrium even in tiny indivisible markets, so Babaioff, Nisan, and Talgam-Cohen proposed asking whether equilibrium exists for almost every income vector, i.e. outside a measure-zero subset of income space. The open problem is to characterize this almost-everywhere existence question for additive valuations. A central conjectural positive case is two agents with additive valuations and any number of goods. More generally, determine for which pairs $(n,m)$ and valuation classes additive competitive equilibrium exists for almost all incomes, and for which pairs nonexistence persists on a positive-measure set.
background: Competitive equilibrium is one of the cleanest bridges between economics and optimization. With divisible goods and convex preferences, prices decentralize efficient allocations and support fairness properties. Indivisible goods break this theory: exact market-clearing prices may not exist because an agent's demand jumps discontinuously as prices or budgets vary. Generic budgets are a natural repair. Instead of insisting on equal artificial incomes, perturb the income vector and ask whether the nonexistence pathologies are lower-dimensional coincidences. This idea is especially relevant to fair allocation mechanisms such as course allocation, public resource assignment, and allocation with unequal entitlements. The additive-valuation case is the most parsimonious indivisible-goods model: values are fully specified by item-agent weights, with no complementarities. If generic budgets do not restore equilibrium here, the obstruction is fundamental rather than a modeling artifact.
known_results: Babaioff, Nisan, and Talgam-Cohen showed positive results for two agents with equal budgets after generic perturbation, and for several non-equal-budget cases such as identical preferences. Segal-Halevi completed the characterization for monotonically increasing preferences in several small cases left open by the earlier paper: for four goods and three or four agents with general monotone preferences, almost-everywhere equilibrium may fail; for four goods and three additive agents, existence holds. Segal-Halevi also characterized monotone decreasing preferences for chores and proved fairness properties of competitive-equilibrium allocations. The additive-goods frontier remains unresolved. In particular, the broad conjecture that two agents with additive valuations admit competitive equilibrium for almost every income vector and any number of goods is not settled by the known small-$m$ and monotone-preference classifications.

Babaioff, Nisan, and Talgam-Cohen establish the framework and prove important positive cases. title: Tight competitive ratio of greedy online Steiner Forest
short_statement: A 2026 preprint claims the tight greedy online Steiner Forest ratio is $\Theta(\log k\log\log k)$, disproving a logarithmic guarantee.
full_statement: In online Steiner Forest, a weighted undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ is known in advance, but terminal pairs $(s_1,t_1),(s_2,t_2),\ldots,(s_k,t_k)$ arrive one by one. After pair $(s_i,t_i)$ arrives, the algorithm must buy edges so that $s_i$ and $t_i$ are connected in the subgraph bought so far; bought edges cannot be removed. The cost is the total weight of all bought edges, and the benchmark is the offline optimum Steiner forest connecting all $k$ pairs. The greedy algorithm, upon arrival of $(s_i,t_i)$, buys a shortest path between $s_i$ and $t_i$ in the metric obtained after contracting all previously bought edges. Historically, it was known that every online algorithm has competitive ratio $\Omega(\log k)$, while the classical analysis of greedy gives $O(\log^2 k)$. Bamas, Drygala, and Maggiori improved the analysis to $O(\log k\log\log k)$ on a broad class of instances containing all previously known lower-bound examples. The original open problem was to determine whether greedy is $O(\log k)$-competitive on all instances, or whether there is a family forcing a superlogarithmic ratio. An October 29, 2026 preprint by Gholami, Ilya Hajiaghayi, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, and Jabbarzade claims tight $\Theta(\log k\log\log k)$ bounds for this exact greedy algorithm. Its lower bound is independent of tie-breaking; the claimed upper bound covers arbitrary finite positive-cost graphs and feasible demand sequences. Verification is pending.
background: Historical context before October 2026: Online Steiner Forest is a canonical online network-design problem: connectivity demands appear over time, and infrastructure must be built irrevocably. The greedy algorithm is almost unavoidable in this setting: connect the new demand as cheaply as possible using the network already bought. Despite its simplicity, its exact performance has resisted analysis for decades. The problem is attractive because the lower bound for every online algorithm is only logarithmic, so greedy might be optimal up to constants. At the same time, greedy decisions can create subtle long-term effects: a path that is locally shortest may or may not build useful infrastructure for future terminal pairs. The gap between the simple algorithm and the optimal online lower bound is therefore a clean test of whether local metric contraction captures the right online network-design structure. Current status: An October 29, 2026 preprint by Gholami, Ilya Hajiaghayi, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, and Jabbarzade claims tight $\Theta(\log k\log\log k)$ bounds for this exact greedy algorithm.
known_results: Historical context before October 2026: Awerbuch, Azar, and Bartal proved that greedy is $O(\log^2 k)$-competitive, and this remained the main general upper bound for many years. A logarithmic lower bound applies even to randomized algorithms, so no online algorithm can be $o(\log k)$-competitive in general. Bamas, Drygala, and Maggiori improved the analysis of greedy to $O(\log k\log\log k)$ for a wide class of instances, including all lower-bound instances known in the literature. Their result suggests that the extra logarithmic factor in the classical analysis may be an artifact, but it does not settle arbitrary instances. Those earlier papers supplied neither a superlogarithmic greedy lower bound nor a logarithmic general upper bound. Current status: An October 29, 2026 preprint by Gholami, Ilya Hajiaghayi, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, and Jabbarzade claims tight $\Theta(\log k\log\log k)$ bounds for this exact greedy algorithm.

title: Exact random-order ratio of Best-Fit bin packing
short_statement: In online bin packing under uniformly random arrival order, determine the exact asymptotic performance ratio of the classical Best-Fit algorithm.
full_statement: Let $I=\{s_1,\ldots,s_n\}$ be a multiset of item sizes in $(0,1]$. A uniformly random permutation of $I$ is revealed online. The algorithm sees each item size on arrival and must immediately and irrevocably place it into an open unit-capacity bin or open a new bin. The Best-Fit algorithm places an arriving item into a feasible open bin that leaves the smallest remaining capacity after insertion, opening a new bin only when no open bin can fit the item. Let $BF(\pi(I))$ be the number of bins used by Best-Fit on random order $\pi$, and let $OPT(I)$ be the minimum number of bins in an offline packing of $I$. The random-order ratio of Best-Fit is the least $\rho$ such that $\mathbb E_{\pi}[BF(\pi(I))]\le \rho\,OPT(I)+o(OPT(I))$ for all item multisets $I$. Determine this constant $\rho$. Kenyon historically conjectured a value near $1.15$; the published lower bound $1.15582656$ now rules out $1.15$ as an exact upper bound. The open problem is not to design a better algorithm, but to characterize the exact worst-case random-order behavior of one fixed, widely used heuristic. A complete solution would either prove a matching upper and lower bound, or identify the right extremal family showing that the conjectured value is wrong.
known_results: Kenyon's SODA 1996 work established an upper bound of $1.5$ and a lower bound of $1.08$ for the random-order ratio of Best-Fit, and conjectured a value around $1.15$. Albers, Khan, and Ladewig improved the special case in which every item has size larger than $1/3$, giving a $1.25$ upper bound and a $1.1$ lower bound for that restricted regime. Ayyadevara, Dabas, Khan, and Sreenivas settled the iid stochastic model with a $(1+\varepsilon)$-competitive meta-algorithm and made progress on random-order special cases, including items in $(1/4,1/2]$. Hebbar, Khan, and Sreenivas then gave the first general improvement over the $3/2$ barrier, proving an upper bound $1.5-\varepsilon$ for a fixed positive constant $\varepsilon$, and improved the lower bound to $1.144$, close to Kenyon's conjectured value. The exact constant remains open: the best known upper bound is still far from the lower bound, and no known structural theorem identifies the extremal random-order instances. Epstein and Levin (WADS 2025), Theorem 10, improve the asymptotic lower bound to $1.15582656$. Their separate absolute lower bound $1.5$ (Proposition 11) is not an asymptotic bound.

where_posed.text: The conjecture and remaining gap are discussed in Hebbar, Khan, Sreenivas, 'Bin Packing under Random-Order: Breaking the Barrier of 3/2', SODA 2024.

background: Bin packing is one of the canonical models of resource allocation: items of different sizes must be assigned to the minimum number of unit-capacity bins. The online version models packing, memory allocation, scheduling, and admission decisions when future jobs are unknown. Worst-case online bin packing is deliberately pessimistic; adversarial order lets an input designer reveal items in a sequence that is much worse than a typical shuffled instance. Kenyon's random-order model keeps the multiset adversarial but randomizes the arrival order, creating a clean beyond-worst-case benchmark. Best-Fit is especially important because it is simple, deterministic, and used in practice. The random-order analysis asks whether the empirical robustness of Best-Fit has a theorem-level explanation. The problem is also technically attractive: it mixes online irrevocability, random permutations, and packing structure. The main difficulty is that Best-Fit creates state-dependent residual capacities; early random fluctuations determine which gaps remain for later items, and these dependencies are hard to summarize by a small set of statistics.

literature.synthesis: The literature has progressed by separating item-size regimes. Kenyon gave the baseline random-order framework and the original $1.5$ upper bound. Later work improved special intervals such as items larger than $1/3$ or in $(1/4,1/2]$, where the packing structure is much more constrained. Any upper-bound proof must control the distribution of residual bin capacities created by Best-Fit under a random permutation for arbitrary item multisets; any lower-bound proof must turn a finite pattern into an asymptotic family and rigorously compute its expected bin count.

title: Beating the factor-2 barrier for Steiner Forest
short_statement: Resolved: undirected Steiner Forest admits a polynomial-time approximation strictly below $2$; a subsequent algorithm achieves $1.994$.
full_statement: In the undirected Steiner Forest problem, the input is an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with nonnegative edge costs $c_e$ and a collection of terminal pairs $(s_1,t_1),\ldots,(s_k,t_k)$. A feasible solution is a forest $H\subseteq E$ such that, for every $i$, vertices $s_i$ and $t_i$ lie in the same connected component of $(V,H)$. The objective is to minimize $c(H)=\sum_{e\in H} c_e$. The classical primal-dual algorithm gives a factor-$2$ approximation. The historical target was to design a polynomial-time $(2-\varepsilon)$-approximation for some universal constant $\varepsilon>0$, or prove that no such improvement is possible under a standard complexity assumption. This algorithmic target is resolved by Ahmadi et al. (FOCS 2025), followed by Gupta and Traub's $1.994$ algorithm. A separate, still-open LP question asks whether the bidirected-cut relaxation, or another natural relaxation for Steiner Forest, has integrality gap strictly below $2$ and can be rounded constructively. The problem should be distinguished from Steiner Tree, where stronger approximation algorithms are known; multiple disconnected demand components make Steiner Forest harder to couple globally.
background: Steiner Forest is a central network-design problem. It models building the cheapest communication, transportation, or infrastructure network that connects specified pairs, while allowing unrelated demand pairs to live in different components. The problem generalizes Steiner Tree and is one of the flagship successes of primal-dual approximation algorithms: the Agrawal-Klein-Ravi and Goemans-Williamson style moat-growing method gives a clean factor $2$. For decades, factor $2$ remained the best general guarantee, despite the fact that many related network-design problems have seen improvements through LP rounding, iterative rounding, or probabilistic embedding techniques. The difficulty is that local connectivity requirements interact through shared edges but do not require one global connected component. The breakthrough algorithms exploit sharing between terminal pairs better than the primal-dual algorithm without paying for unnecessary connections. The below-$2$ target was resolved in 2025.
known_results: The classical Agrawal-Klein-Ravi and Goemans-Williamson primal-dual algorithms achieve factor $2$. Ahmadi, Gholami, Hajiaghayi, Jabbarzade, and Mahdavi (FOCS 2025) break this barrier with a universal improvement of approximately $10^{-11}$. Gupta and Traub subsequently give a $1.994$ algorithm for arbitrary undirected nonnegative-cost instances (Theorem 1.1). Thus the original target is resolved. APX-hardness does not determine the optimal ratio. Byrka, Grandoni, and Traub prove a $16/9$ guarantee for half-integral bidirected-cut solutions; a general LP gap below $2$ remains a distinct open question.

title: Tight adaptivity gap for subadditive stochastic probing
short_statement: Close the gap between known lower and upper bounds for the adaptivity gap of stochastic probing with general subadditive objectives.
full_statement: Let $U=[n]$ be a set of elements. Each element $i$ has an independent random variable $X_i$ with known distribution. A probing policy adaptively chooses elements to probe; probing reveals $X_i$, and the sequence of probed elements must lie in a prefix-closed feasibility family $\mathcal F$. For a set $P$ of probed elements, the reward is $f(X_P)$, where $f$ is a monotone subadditive objective on realized value vectors and unprobed coordinates are treated as zero. The adaptive optimum is the maximum expected reward over policies whose future probes may depend on observed values. The nonadaptive optimum is the maximum expected reward over a distribution over feasible probe sequences fixed before seeing realizations. The adaptivity gap is the worst-case ratio between these two optima. For Bernoulli probing with binary-XOS objectives, the gap is now known to be $\Theta(\log n/\log\log n)$. For Bernoulli probing with general subadditive objectives, the best known upper bound is $O(\log^3 n)$, while the binary-XOS lower bound still applies. Determine the correct asymptotic adaptivity gap for general subadditive stochastic probing.
background: Stochastic probing is a clean abstraction for sequential testing under uncertainty. It models kidney-exchange edge testing, hiring and inspection, sensor activation, product experimentation, and other settings where observations are costly and feasibility constraints limit what can be tested. Adaptivity is valuable because later tests can react to earlier outcomes, but adaptive policies are often computationally and operationally complex. Adaptivity-gap theorems justify replacing adaptive policies by simpler nonadaptive plans. For submodular and related objectives, constant or near-constant gaps are known in many regimes. General subadditive objectives are much harder: they capture broad complement-free valuation classes but lack the marginal structure used by submodular analyses. The open problem is therefore a precise measure of how much adaptivity is worth when the reward function is complement-free but otherwise arbitrary.
known_results: Gupta, Nagarajan, and Singla and subsequent work developed stochastic probing adaptivity-gap frameworks for submodular, XOS, and related objectives. Bradac, Singla, and Zuzic obtained near-optimal gaps for multi-value probing in several structured settings. Li, Liu, and Zhang resolved an open question for general monotone norms, proving an $O(\log^2 n)$ adaptivity gap and an improved $O(\log r\log n/\log\log n)$ bound where $r$ is the maximum probing length. They also proved a tight $\Theta(\log n/\log\log n)$ gap for Bernoulli probing with binary-XOS objectives and an $O(\log^3 n)$ upper bound for Bernoulli probing with general subadditive objectives. This leaves a polynomial-logarithmic gap for the general subadditive case: the right bound could match binary-XOS, be closer to $\log^3 n$, or require a new intermediate rate.

literature.synthesis: The stochastic-probing literature separates two questions: can one approximate the adaptive optimum efficiently, and how much value is lost by committing to a nonadaptive plan? For submodular and structured objectives, adaptivity gaps are often constant or logarithmic. General subadditive objectives are more expressive and resist marginal-contribution arguments. Li, Liu, and Zhang make major progress by proving polylogarithmic bounds for monotone norms and tight bounds for binary-XOS objectives. Closing this gap would clarify the exact price of adaptivity for one of the broadest complement-free stochastic-optimization models.
