title: Constant approximation for submodular facility location
short_statement: For homogeneous submodular facility location, a 2026 preprint claims tight $\Theta(\log\log n)$ value-oracle approximability; arbitrary facility-specific functions are a different, harder model.
full_statement: Let $C$ be clients, $F$ facilities, and $d$ a metric on $C\cup F$. An assignment $\phi:C\to F$ has cost $\sum_c d(c,\phi(c))+\sum_f g_f(S_f)$, where $S_f=\phi^{-1}(f)$ and each $g_f$ is nonnegative, monotone submodular and zero at the empty set. Model correction: the earlier record allowed arbitrary different $g_f$ but attributed homogeneous results to that generalization. The constant-approximation question posed by the cited literature is for a SINGLE common value-oracle function $g_f=g$ at every facility. Arbitrary facility-specific functions already contain Set Cover and have logarithmic hardness. For common $g$, Abbasi et al. give $O(\log\log|C|)$; their extensions allow $p_f+g(S)$ on nonempty sets or $w_f g(S)$, not arbitrary unrelated functions. The historical question asks for a constant-factor polynomial-query approximation in the homogeneous model. Elmachtoub, Natura, and Neuwohner (October 2026), Theorem 2, claim an $\Omega(\log\log|C|)$ query lower bound even for common matroid-rank costs. This would answer that question negatively; it is a preprint claim, not independently proof-verified here.
background: Facility location is a core operations research model for placing warehouses, servers, depots, and service centers. The classical fixed-charge model assumes a facility has one opening cost independent of which clients it serves. Many applications have richer economies of scale or shared-service effects: the marginal cost of serving an additional client may decrease, overlap with existing fixed costs, or depend on the mix of clients. Submodular facility location captures this by replacing a fixed opening charge with a monotone submodular function of the assigned client set. This is still a clean combinatorial optimization problem: the metric assignment term is classical, and submodularity is the standard mathematical abstraction for diminishing returns. The difficulty is that opening a facility and assigning clients are no longer separable. A local reassignment can change the submodular cost at many marginal scales, and the usual primal-dual and LP-rounding tools for fixed-charge facility location do not directly give constant factors. The exact model matters: the cited iterated-logarithmic guarantee assumes a common submodular function, with specified extensions; independent facility functions encode Set Cover. A 2026 preprint claims the homogeneous oracle threshold is also superconstant.
known_results: Svitkina and Tardos developed hierarchical and submodular facility costs, logarithmic approximation, and constant-factor special cases. Abbasi et al. (ICALP 2024; preprint 2022), Theorems 1.1, 1.3 and 1.4, give $O(\log\log n)$ for a common function and its additive/multiplicative facility-weight extensions. They also improve universal stochastic facility location; classical metric facility location remains a related special case of the facility-weight variants. The unrestricted $g_f$ model already inherits Set Cover hardness. Elmachtoub, Natura, and Neuwohner (2026) claim matching oracle hardness for homogeneous SFL: polynomially many value queries cannot achieve $o(\log\log n)$ with constant success probability, even with unlimited computation. Version 2 (November 4, 2026), Appendix A, Corollary A.2, additionally reports computational hardness: unless $\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{RP}$, no randomized polynomial-time algorithm with constant success probability attains $o(\log\log|F|)$ when the common matroid-rank function is supplied by a polynomial-size evaluation circuit. Note the facility-count parameter here, versus client count in Theorem 2. Neither statement automatically covers every specialized explicit representation.

title: Exact integrality gap of the Goemans-Linial SDP for uniform Sparsest Cut
short_statement: Determine the asymptotic integrality gap of the Goemans-Linial semidefinite relaxation for uniform Sparsest Cut.
full_statement: In uniform Sparsest Cut, the input is an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with $|V|=n$, and the objective is to find a nontrivial cut $S\subset V$ minimizing $$\Phi(S)=\frac{|E(S,V\setminus S)|}{|S|\,|V\setminus S|}$$ up to the conventional normalization. The Goemans-Linial semidefinite relaxation assigns vectors to vertices and enforces squared Euclidean distances satisfying triangle inequalities, producing an SDP value that lower-bounds the optimum cut sparsity. Its integrality gap is the worst-case ratio between the true optimum and the SDP optimum over $n$-vertex instances. The open problem is to determine this gap up to constants or sharp asymptotics. Known lower bounds are superpolylogarithmic in $\log\log n$ but far below the known upper bounds from rounding/embedding theory. Equivalently, characterize how well negative-type metrics embed into $L_1$ for the uniform sparsest-cut setting.
background: Sparsest Cut is a central graph-partitioning problem with applications in clustering, VLSI, divide-and-conquer graph algorithms, metric embeddings, and flow-cut gaps. The Goemans-Linial SDP was one of the major semidefinite relaxations in approximation algorithms. Arora, Rao, and Vazirani's rounding breakthrough gave an $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ approximation for Sparsest Cut and Balanced Separator and made the geometry of negative-type metrics a central object. Understanding the exact performance of this SDP would clarify whether the ARV rounding paradigm is close to optimal or whether a better geometric theorem exists. The problem is clean: the relaxation is fixed, the objective is fixed, and both upper and lower bounds are mathematical statements about finite metrics and graph cuts.
known_results: The ARV framework gives an $O(\sqrt{\log n})$-type upper bound for rounding the SDP. Earlier lower bounds showed an $\Omega(\log\log n)$ integrality gap. Kane and Meka used pseudorandom generators for Lipschitz functions of low-degree polynomials to construct uniform Sparsest Cut instances with Goemans-Linial SDP gap $\exp(\Omega((\log\log n)^{1/2}))$, a near-exponential improvement over the previous lower bound in the iterated-log scale. This still leaves a large gap to the $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ upper bound. Related work on metric embeddings and Unique Games explains why some stronger approximation goals are hard, but the precise integrality gap of this particular SDP in the uniform setting remains unresolved.

title: Tight approximation ratio for the Joint Replenishment Problem
short_statement: Determine the best possible approximation ratio for the deterministic Joint Replenishment Problem with arbitrary waiting costs, and close the gap between APX-hardness, LP gaps, and the best known constant algorithms.
full_statement: In the deterministic Joint Replenishment Problem (JRP), a supplier ships goods to a warehouse and then to retailers. There is a fixed warehouse ordering cost $C$ for each order epoch. If retailer $\rho$ is included in that order, an additional retailer-specific ordering cost $c_\rho$ is paid. Customer demands arrive over time at retailers. In the waiting-cost version, demand $j$ for retailer $\rho(j)$ arrives at time $r_j$ and, if served at time $t\ge r_j$, incurs waiting cost $h_j(t-r_j)$, where $h_j$ is a nondecreasing function. A feasible schedule chooses order times and assigns each demand to an order containing its retailer. The objective is to minimize total warehouse ordering cost plus retailer ordering cost plus waiting cost. In the deadline version JRP-D, each demand must be served by a deadline and has no waiting cost before that deadline. The open problem is to determine the optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for offline JRP, and in particular whether the general arbitrary-waiting-cost problem or the JRP-D special case admits ratios substantially below the current $1.791$ and $1.574$-type bounds, or whether stronger hardness or LP-gap constructions rule this out.
background: Joint replenishment is a classical deterministic inventory model. It captures economies of scale in procurement: placing one warehouse order can serve many retailers, but each participating retailer also has its own setup cost. This two-level fixed-charge structure appears in distribution, retail replenishment, spare-parts logistics, and coordinated ordering. The model is simple enough to be a crisp combinatorial optimization problem, yet rich enough that power-of-two policies and natural LP relaxations leave real gaps. For operations management, the approximation ratio matters because it quantifies the worst-case value of coordination beyond simple periodic policies. For approximation algorithms, JRP is a structured network-design and lot-sizing problem with time, deadlines, and nested fixed charges. The remaining gap is not about choosing a model: the model has been standard for decades. The hard part is understanding the exact algorithmic price of two-level aggregation.
known_results: For the discrete-time JRP with arbitrary waiting cost functions, Bienkowski, Byrka, Chrobak, Jez, and Sgall improved the best offline approximation from $1.8$ to $1.791$. For JRP-D, Bienkowski, Byrka, Chrobak, Dobbs, Nowicki, Sviridenko, Swirszcz, and Young gave a $1.574$ approximation and proved LP lower bounds of $1.207$ and a computer-assisted $1.245$ for the standard relaxation; they also showed APX-hardness, including equal-length demand-period cases with a $1.5$ upper bound and $1.2$ lower bound. Online JRP has separate bounds: the best known upper and lower bounds for arbitrary waiting costs are around $3$ and $2.754$ for the linear-waiting-cost lower-bound regime, while online JRP-D has optimal competitive ratio $2$. In continuous time, Segev recently gave the first quantitative improvements over power-of-two-type guarantees for several long-standing variants. None of these results gives the exact offline approximation threshold for general JRP or JRP-D.

title: Polynomial-time algorithm for mean-payoff games
short_statement: Are finite two-player mean-payoff games solvable in polynomial time?
full_statement: A mean-payoff game is played on a finite directed graph $G=(V,E)$ whose vertices are partitioned into $V_{\max}$ and $V_{\min}$. Each edge $e$ has an integer weight $w(e)$. A token starts at a designated vertex. When the token is at a vertex controlled by Max, Max chooses the outgoing edge; when it is at a vertex controlled by Min, Min chooses. This produces an infinite path $e_1,e_2,\ldots$. Max seeks to maximize and Min seeks to minimize the long-run average payoff $\liminf_{T\to\infty} T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T w(e_t)$, or equivalently the game value. Mean-payoff games are positionally determined and lie in $NP\cap coNP$ for the decision version asking whether the value is at least a threshold. The open problem is to give an algorithm running in time polynomial in the number of vertices, edges, and input bit length, or to prove an appropriate lower-bound/completeness result explaining why such an algorithm should not exist. Equivalent or closely related formulations include energy games, tropical linear programming, and certain policy-iteration/simplex questions.
background: Mean-payoff games are a basic model of infinite-horizon adversarial control. They sit between graph algorithms, optimization, formal verification, and dynamic programming. In verification, they model quantitative properties of reactive systems. In optimization, they are tied to tropical linear programming and policy-improvement methods. In game theory, they are a finite deterministic analogue of average-payoff stochastic games, with positional optimal strategies but unresolved computational complexity. The problem has the same flavor as several central operations-research algorithmic questions: the model is finite and clean, dynamic-programming and strategy-improvement algorithms work well in many cases, but no polynomial worst-case bound is known. The fact that the decision problem lies in $NP\cap coNP$ makes it unlikely to be NP-complete under standard assumptions, yet this membership has not yielded a polynomial algorithm.
known_results: Ehrenfeucht and Mycielski proved positional determinacy for mean-payoff games. Zwick and Paterson gave foundational pseudo-polynomial and exponential algorithms and clarified the complexity landscape. The problem is known to be in $NP\cap coNP$ and is interreducible with energy games and closely related to parity games. Strategy-improvement and value-iteration algorithms are effective in practice but have no polynomial worst-case guarantee; subexponential algorithms are known for related parity/mean-payoff settings. Allamigeon, Benchimol, Gaubert, and Joswig showed that combinatorial simplex algorithms over tropical geometry can solve mean-payoff games, and that a strongly polynomial combinatorial simplex algorithm for linear programming would imply a strongly polynomial algorithm for mean-payoff games. Despite decades of progress on special graph classes and algorithmic frameworks, the general polynomial-time question remains open.

Positional determinacy gives a compact certificate of optimal play, and the threshold decision problem has both NP and coNP certificates. Zwick and Paterson established the classical algorithms and complexity framework. Subsequent work has attacked the problem through strategy improvement, energy games, parity-game reductions, and tropical linear programming. The tropical-simplex connection is especially relevant to optimization: progress on strongly polynomial simplex-type algorithms would propagate to mean-payoff games, while hard mean-payoff instances inform the limits of pivoting methods. The remaining gap is conceptual as much as technical: existing algorithms exploit numerical weights or local improvement structure, but no proof shows that the number of improvement steps or the size of a certificate can be bounded polynomially in all instances.

title: Polynomial-time constant approximation for capacitated $k$-median
short_statement: Does hard-capacitated metric $k$-median admit a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation that violates neither capacities nor the number of open facilities?
full_statement: In the hard-capacitated metric $k$-median problem, the input consists of clients $C$, candidate facility locations $F$, a metric distance $d$ on $C\cup F$, an integer $k$, and capacities $u_f$ for facilities. A feasible solution opens at most $k$ facilities, opens each facility location at most once, and assigns every client $c\in C$ to an open facility $f$ so that no facility receives more than $u_f$ clients. The objective is to minimize total assignment cost $\sum_{c\in C} d(c,\phi(c))$. Uniform capacitated $k$-median is the special case $u_f=U$ for all $f$; nonuniform capacities allow arbitrary $u_f$. The open problem is to give a polynomial-time $O(1)$-approximation for general metric hard-capacitated $k$-median without violating either the capacity constraints or the cardinality constraint, or prove that no such approximation exists under a standard complexity assumption. Bicriteria algorithms that open more than $k$ facilities or exceed capacities do not resolve the problem, and fixed-parameter algorithms whose running time is exponential in $k$ do not resolve the polynomial-time question.
background: Facility location and clustering are core operations research models. The uncapacitated $k$-median problem has a well-developed constant-approximation theory, but realistic service systems often impose capacities: a warehouse, clinic, server, or school cannot serve arbitrarily many clients. Hard capacities are the most natural version when a location can be opened only once. They also create the main algorithmic obstacle. In uncapacitated clustering, one can move clients independently once centers are chosen; in hard-capacitated clustering, moving a client into one facility may force a chain of reassignment moves because capacity slots are scarce. Many algorithms obtain constants by slightly violating capacities or opening extra centers, which is often unacceptable in planning applications. The unresolved problem is therefore exactly aligned with OR practice: can one preserve both operational constraints and still obtain a constant worst-case guarantee in polynomial time?
known_results: Uniform hard-capacitated $k$-median has been called a notorious open problem. Shi Li went beyond the natural LP relaxation, whose integrality gap is unbounded even with substantial cardinality or capacity violation, and obtained an algorithm with a $(1+\varepsilon)$ violation of the number of open facilities and an approximation factor exponential in $1/\varepsilon^2$. Adamczyk, Byrka, Marcinkowski, Meesum, and Wlodarczyk gave a fixed-parameter constant approximation running in $2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}$ time and preserving both capacities and cardinality, with ratio $7+\varepsilon$. Cohen-Addad and Li improved the FPT approximation to $3+\varepsilon$ for capacitated $k$-median in general metrics and obtained PTAS-type results for high-dimensional Euclidean inputs in FPT time. These results show that constant approximation is possible when exponential dependence on $k$ is allowed. However, the best polynomial-time approximation for general metrics remains logarithmic in $k$ for the hard-capacitated setting without violations, and no matching hardness result rules out a constant. Dai and Shi Li's October 2026 preprint gives hard-capacity bicriteria algorithms in $\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\epsilon)$ time: factor $O(\epsilon^{-5})$ with at most $(1+\epsilon)k$ distinct facilities and exact capacities, or factor $O(\epsilon^{-6})$ with at most $k$ facilities and capacity ceiling $\lceil(1+\epsilon)u_f\rceil$. Neither satisfies both original constraints.

literature.synthesis: The capacitated $k$-median literature splits into bicriteria polynomial-time algorithms, stronger relaxations, and fixed-parameter algorithms. The natural LP fails badly; Shi Li's work demonstrated that one can move beyond it, but still pays with cardinality violation. FPT algorithms show that the combinatorial difficulty can be controlled when $k$ is treated as a parameter, culminating in constant factors that preserve all constraints. These results leave a sharp algorithmic gap: the known constant factors are not polynomial in $k$, while the known polynomial-time guarantees either violate constraints or are not constant. A breakthrough may require a relaxation whose extreme points have enough transfer structure to rebalance capacities globally, or a new hardness reduction that explains why exact preservation of both constraints is qualitatively harder than uncapacitated $k$-median. Dai and Shi Li's October 2026 preprint gives hard-capacity bicriteria algorithms in $\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\epsilon)$ time: factor $O(\epsilon^{-5})$ with at most $(1+\epsilon)k$ distinct facilities and exact capacities, or factor $O(\epsilon^{-6})$ with at most $k$ facilities and capacity ceiling $\lceil(1+\epsilon)u_f\rceil$. Neither satisfies both original constraints.

title: Approximability of Densest $k$-Subgraph
short_statement: Close the enormous gap between the $O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})$ algorithm and the best hardness evidence for worst-case Densest $k$-Subgraph.
full_statement: In the Densest $k$-Subgraph problem, the input is an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ on $n$ vertices and an integer $k$. The goal is to find a vertex subset $S\subseteq V$ with $|S|=k$ maximizing the number of induced edges $|E(S)|$. The approximation objective is to output a $k$-vertex subgraph whose edge count is within a factor $\alpha(n,k)$ of the optimum. The best known polynomial-time algorithms achieve roughly $O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})$ approximation for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. On the hardness side, unconditional NP-hardness is much weaker than this, while stronger ETH, Gap-ETH, average-case, and Sum-of-Squares lower bounds provide evidence for polynomial or near-polynomial hardness in certain regimes. The open problem is to determine the correct polynomial-time approximation threshold for worst-case DkS: improve the algorithm below $n^{1/4}$ in a meaningful asymptotic regime, or prove matching hardness under a standard and broadly accepted assumption.
background: Densest $k$-Subgraph is a deceptively simple graph optimization problem with applications in community detection, fraud detection, biological network analysis, and data mining. Unlike ordinary densest subgraph, which is solvable in polynomial time by flow or peeling methods, fixing the cardinality makes the problem dramatically harder. The problem is also a central bridge between worst-case approximation and average-case inference: the same log-density heuristics that guide algorithms for DkS are tied to planted dense subgraph detection and statistical-computational gaps. This makes DkS an unusually important open problem. A better algorithm would reshape graph-mining and approximation techniques; a strong hardness theorem would validate a large body of conditional reasoning that currently relies on DkS hardness assumptions.
known_results: Feige, Kortsarz, and Peleg gave early polynomial-factor approximations. Bhaskara, Charikar, Chlamtac, Feige, and Vijayaraghavan achieved the landmark $O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})$ approximation by exploiting log-density structure and tree-counting ideas. This remains the main worst-case algorithmic benchmark. On the hardness side, Khot ruled out a PTAS under stronger assumptions; Manurangsi proved almost-polynomial ratio ETH-hardness and stronger Gap-ETH consequences, but these still do not match the $n^{1/4}$ algorithmic threshold under standard polynomial-time assumptions. SDP and Sum-of-Squares lower bounds, including work by Bhaskara et al. and Jones, Potechin, Rajendran, and Xu, show that powerful hierarchies fail in regimes predicted by the log-density framework. The remaining gap is therefore not a lack of evidence, but a lack of a definitive algorithm or hardness theorem at the right polynomial scale.

title: Subpolynomial versus KPZ-scale variance in lattice first-passage percolation
short_statement: For i.i.d. first-passage percolation on $\mathbb Z^d$, prove a polynomial sublinear variance bound, or determine the true fluctuation exponent.
full_statement: Consider nearest-neighbor first-passage percolation on $\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge 2$. Each edge $e$ receives an independent nonnegative passage time $t_e$ from a common distribution satisfying the standard assumptions that avoid degeneracy and ensure finite moments. For vertices $x,y\in\mathbb Z^d$, define $$T(x,y)=\inf_{\gamma:x\to y}\sum_{e\in\gamma} t_e,$$ where the infimum is over nearest-neighbor paths. Fix a direction, for instance $e_1=(1,0,\ldots,0)$, and study the variance $\operatorname{Var} T(0,ne_1)$ as $n\to\infty$. The shape theorem gives first-order linear growth. The open problem is to determine the correct fluctuation scale. A concrete intermediate target is to prove that for ordinary i.i.d. lattice FPP there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\operatorname{Var} T(0,ne_1)=O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ under natural moment assumptions. In two dimensions, the KPZ prediction is much sharper: fluctuations should be of order $n^{1/3}$ and variance of order $n^{2/3}$ for broad continuous distributions. None of these polynomial improvements is known for the classical lattice model in this generality.
background: First-passage percolation is one of the central random optimization models in probability. It turns a lattice into a random metric space and asks for the fastest route through a random medium. The model has direct OR intuition: it is a stochastic shortest-path problem on a huge random network. The shape theorem describes the deterministic large-scale growth ball, but the second-order behavior is much harder. In exactly solvable directed last-passage models, KPZ theory predicts and often proves $1/3$ passage-time fluctuations and $2/3$ transversal fluctuations. Undirected lattice FPP is not integrable, so even proving any polynomial improvement over linear variance has resisted the standard concentration and martingale methods. This makes the problem a clean test of whether KPZ-type behavior can be proved without exact formulas.
known_results: Kesten proved foundational concentration and linear-variance-type bounds. Benjamini, Kalai, and Schramm used hypercontractivity to improve the variance upper bound to $O(n/\log n)$ for certain two-valued passage-time distributions, and later work extended sublinear variance bounds under broader assumptions. The Auffinger-Damron-Hanson survey records the state of the art and many related open questions on geodesics, Busemann functions, and fluctuations. For exactly solvable directed last-passage percolation models, KPZ exponents are known in many cases, but these techniques do not transfer to undirected i.i.d. FPP. In 2026, Basu, Sidoravicius, and Sly proved a polynomial variance improvement for a rotationally invariant Riemannian FPP model, breaking the $n/\log n$ barrier in a continuous setting. That result is strong evidence for the right phenomenon, but it does not resolve the classical lattice FPP variance problem.

title: Tight asymptotics of the flatness constant in integer programming
area: Integer Programming and Geometry of Numbers
short_statement: Determine the correct asymptotic order of the maximum lattice width of lattice-free convex bodies.
full_statement: For a convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ and a nonzero integer vector $u\in\mathbb Z^d$, define the width of $K$ in direction $u$ by $$w_u(K)=\max_{x\in K}u\cdot x-\min_{x\in K}u\cdot x.$$ The lattice width is $w(K)=\min_{u\in\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}}w_u(K)$. A convex body is lattice-free if its interior contains no point of $\mathbb Z^d$. The flatness constant is $$\operatorname{Flt}(d)=\sup\{w(K):K\subset\mathbb R^d\text{ convex body with }\operatorname{int}(K)\cap\mathbb Z^d=\emptyset\}.$$ The flatness theorem says $\operatorname{Flt}(d)<\infty$ for every fixed $d$, and it is a key geometric ingredient behind Lenstra-type fixed-dimension integer-programming algorithms. The open problem is to determine the asymptotic growth of $\operatorname{Flt}(d)$, ideally proving whether it is $\Theta(d)$ and identifying the right constant, or showing that a superlinear factor is necessary. Current results give explicit linear lower bounds and near-linear upper bounds with polylogarithmic factors, leaving a clean asymptotic gap.
open_problem: Close the gap between the best lower and upper bounds on $\operatorname{Flt}(d)$; in particular, decide whether the flatness constant is linear in $d$.
background: Flatness is a geometric form of a basic integer-programming principle: if a convex relaxation contains no integer point, then it must be thin in some integer direction. Lenstra's algorithm and its descendants exploit this by branching on a bounded number of integer hyperplanes. Better flatness bounds translate into sharper fixed-dimension integer-programming algorithms and into structural information about maximal lattice-free convex sets, which are also central in cutting-plane theory. The model is parsimonious and fully formal: no stochastic assumptions, no application-specific modeling choices, just convex bodies, lattice points, and width. This makes it exactly the kind of hard, clean OR/open mathematics problem the repository is meant to track.
known_results: Classical geometry-of-numbers arguments prove finiteness of $\operatorname{Flt}(d)$ and polynomial bounds in $d$. Kannan's fixed-dimension integer-programming work and the Kannan-Lovasz covering-minima framework connect flatness to algorithmic integer programming. Dadush's subspace flatness conjecture predicted an essentially logarithmic factor in a related covering-radius comparison, which would imply near-optimal flatness and faster integer programming. Reis and Rothvoss proved this conjecture up to a constant in the exponent, obtaining an upper bound that implies $\operatorname{Flt}(d)=O(d\log^3(2d))$. On the lower-bound side, Mayrhofer, Schade, and Weltge constructed lattice-free simplices with lattice width at least $2d-O(\sqrt d)$, substantially improving previous lower bounds. These are historical bounds, not the current upper-bound frontier. Bizeul's 2026 preprint, Section 3.4 equation (54), gives $O(d\log d)$. Letwin, Reis, and Rothvoss's October 2026 preprint, Corollary 1.4, improves this to $O(d\sqrt{\log d})$ for arbitrary convex bodies. These preprint bounds leave the linear-order question open.

where_posed.text: Recent flatness and subspace-flatness papers explicitly frame the remaining task as closing the asymptotic gap in the flatness constant.

title: Exact Shannon capacity of odd cycles and small graphs
short_statement: Determine the Shannon capacity of basic graphs such as odd cycles beyond $C_5$, especially $C_7$, and clarify the computational complexity of the graph capacity invariant.
full_statement: For a finite graph $G$, let $G^{\boxtimes k}$ denote the $k$-fold strong product of $G$ with itself, and let $\alpha(H)$ be the independence number of a graph $H$. The Shannon capacity of $G$ is $$\Theta(G)=\sup_{k\ge 1}\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}=\lim_{k\to\infty}\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}.$$ Equivalently, $G$ is a confusability graph for a zero-error communication channel, and $\Theta(G)$ is the asymptotic number of distinguishable symbols per channel use. The open problem is to compute or tightly characterize $\Theta(G)$ for fundamental graph families and to determine the computational complexity of approximating or deciding bounds on $\Theta(G)$. A concrete benchmark is the odd cycle $C_7$: determine the exact value of $\Theta(C_7)$, or even close the best upper and lower bounds enough to reveal the correct structural mechanism. A broader resolution would explain whether Shannon capacity admits effective approximation algorithms, semidefinite/asymptotic-spectrum certificates, or inherent noncomputability-like finite-prefix barriers.
open_problem: Compute $\Theta(C_7)$ and, more generally, determine the algorithmic complexity and approximability of graph Shannon capacity.
background: Shannon introduced zero-error capacity to capture communication when the receiver must decode with no possibility of confusion. Translating a channel to its confusability graph gives a beautiful combinatorial invariant: independent sets in strong powers of the graph are zero-error codes. The model is exceptionally clean, but the invariant is hard because it is asymptotic over all powers of the graph. Lovasz's solution for the pentagon $C_5$ via the theta function is one of the classic successes of semidefinite optimization in combinatorics; it also highlights the mystery, because the same machinery does not settle even the next odd cycles. The problem belongs on ORdos because it is a crisp optimization limit, tied to SDP bounds, asymptotic spectra, and finite-object certificate search.
known_results: Shannon defined the capacity invariant and solved several elementary cases. Lovasz introduced the theta number and proved $\Theta(C_5)=\sqrt 5$, giving an efficiently computable semidefinite upper bound that is tight for perfect graphs and some special nonperfect graphs. Haemers introduced rank-based upper bounds that can beat Lovasz theta on some graphs, and later work developed Schrijver, fractional, projective-rank, and asymptotic-spectrum tools. For odd cycles beyond $C_5$, exact capacities remain unknown. Computational and constructive work has improved lower bounds for $C_7$, $C_{11}$, $C_{13}$, $C_{15}$ and related graphs by finding large independent sets in graph powers. Alon and Lubetzky showed that the sequence $\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})$ can have complicated behavior, so no fixed finite prefix of powers can generally approximate capacity within subpolynomial factors. Recent asymptotic-spectrum and graph-limit work provides new language and some improved bounds, but the basic small-instance benchmark $\Theta(C_7)$ remains unresolved. The 2026 construction sequence includes Buys-Polak-Zuiddam's July preprint bound $\Theta(C_7)\ge3.258805369885\ldots$, a later repository update to $3.258827985920\ldots$, and Tandon's August preprint Theorem 2 giving $\Theta(C_7)\ge3.258832620353\ldots$ from an explicit independent set in $C_7^{\boxtimes500}$. The Lovasz upper bound is $7\cos(\pi/7)/(1+\cos(\pi/7))\approx3.317667$. These are lower-bound improvements, not exact capacity.

title: Dimension-free KLS isoperimetry for log-concave measures
short_statement: October 2026 preprints claim a dimension-free KLS bound for all isotropic log-concave measures; the full conjecture is no longer accurately described as having only Chen's near-constant bound.
full_statement: Let $\mu$ be an isotropic log-concave probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$: its barycenter is $0$, its covariance matrix is the identity, and its density has the form $e^{-V(x)}$ for a convex function $V$. Define its Cheeger isoperimetric constant by $$h(\mu)=\inf_{A:0<\mu(A)<1}\frac{\mu^+(A)}{\min\{\mu(A),1-\mu(A)\}},$$ where $\mu^+(A)$ is the usual boundary measure. Let $$\psi_n=\inf\{h(\mu):\mu\text{ is isotropic and log-concave on }\mathbb R^n\}.$$ The Kannan-Lovasz-Simonovits conjecture asks whether there is a universal constant $c>0$, independent of $n$, such that $\psi_n\ge c$ for every dimension. Equivalently, in the reciprocal convention often called the KLS constant, the conjecture asks for a universal upper bound. October 2026 preprints claim this dimension-free bound: Bizeul, Klartag, and Lehec, Theorem 1.1, and Song and Zhang, version 2, Theorem 1.1. Both state a universal Poincare bound for arbitrary isotropic log-concave measures, equivalent here to the requested isoperimetry. This entry records a solution claim, not an independent certification of the proofs. A solution should be stated for arbitrary log-concave measures, not only for uniform measures on centrally symmetric convex bodies or for special product/rotation-invariant classes.
open_problem: Solution claimed for the full dimension-free conjecture; assess the October 2026 proofs before treating it as an unsolved research target.
background: KLS has been one of the central problems at the interface of probability, convex geometry, and algorithms. The model is clean: isotropic log-concave distributions are the canonical high-dimensional convex distributions, and the question asks for a uniform bottleneck/isoperimetric lower bound. The conjecture matters to operations research and theoretical computer science because isoperimetry controls Markov-chain mixing for sampling from convex bodies and log-concave densities, which in turn underlies randomized algorithms for volume computation, integration, and convex optimization. It also sits in a tight web of asymptotic convex-geometry conjectures, including slicing, thin-shell, concentration for Lipschitz functions, and central limit behavior of random projections. The point of the problem is not to choose a better model of demand, service, or uncertainty; the model is already fixed and canonical. The October 2026 proof claims address precisely the dimension dependence.
known_results: Earlier bounds progressed from polynomial losses (Lee and Vempala) to Chen's almost-constant bound, followed by logarithmic improvements. On 4 October 2026 Bizeul, Klartag, and Lehec posted 'Presenting a proof of the Kannan-Lovasz-Simonovits conjecture': Theorem 1.1 states $C_P(\mu)\le C$ for every isotropic log-concave measure in every dimension. Song and Zhang's 'An O(1) Bound for the KLS Constant', arXiv:2610.01447v2, also states the same general conclusion. Its version 1 only claimed $O(4^{\log^* n})$ in reciprocal notation; version 2 is the relevant update. Bizeul, Klartag, and Lehec explicitly build on Song and Zhang's recent criterion involving high-order derivatives of tilt averages; these are not being represented as independent proofs. These are full-conjecture proof claims, not only slicing or thin-shell results. Refereed publication and complete proof verification were not established by this audit.

title: Approximate planning over memoryless stochastic POMDP policies
short_statement: Find an exact or provably approximate algorithm for optimizing stochastic memoryless policies in finite POMDPs.
full_statement: Consider a finite discounted partially observable Markov decision process with state space $S$, action space $A$, observation space $O$, transition kernel $P(s'\mid s,a)$, observation kernel $Z(o\mid s',a)$, reward function $r(s,a)$, initial distribution $\rho$, and discount factor $\gamma\in(0,1)$. A stochastic memoryless policy is a matrix $\pi(a\mid o)$ that maps only the current observation to an action distribution; it does not keep a belief state or history. Its value is $$V(\pi)=\mathbb E_\pi\left[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t r(s_t,a_t)\right].$$ The policy class is finite-dimensional but nonconvex: the stationary occupancy measures and value are rational functions of the policy variables because the hidden state evolves under an observation-action feedback loop. The open problem, as posed in the COLT open-problem paper of Azizzadenesheli, Lazaric, and Anandkumar, is to design a method that finds an exact optimal stochastic memoryless policy or an approximate policy with a provable global guarantee for general finite POMDPs in this class. The problem is not to solve the full belief-state POMDP with arbitrary history-dependent policies; the benchmark is the best policy within the memoryless stochastic class.
open_problem: Give a globally valid exact or approximation algorithm for finite POMDP planning restricted to stochastic memoryless policies.
background: POMDPs are a standard operations-research and AI model for sequential decision making under incomplete state observation. They model maintenance with hidden machine condition, medical treatment with latent patient state, robot navigation with noisy sensors, and inventory/control systems with partial information. Full POMDP planning is difficult because the belief state is continuous and optimal policies may require memory. Memoryless stochastic policies are a natural restricted class: they are compact, implementable, and often used in policy-gradient methods. The surprising difficulty is that even this restricted class is globally nonconvex. This makes the problem a clean theoretical target: the model is already well defined, the policy class is fixed, and the open question is whether there is a tractable exact or approximate global optimizer.
known_results: Classical POMDP theory gives dynamic-programming structure for finite horizons and belief-state formulations for infinite horizons, but those algorithms optimize over history- or belief-dependent policies and scale poorly. Papadimitriou and Tsitsiklis established fundamental computational hardness for Markov decision processes and imperfect-information control models. For memoryless stochastic POMDP policies specifically, Azizzadenesheli, Lazaric, and Anandkumar stated the COLT open problem: despite the small parametric policy class, finding an exact or approximate optimal stochastic memoryless policy remains open. Montufar, Ghazi-Zahedi, and Ay studied the geometry and determinism of optimal stationary control in POMDPs and showed structural facts such as limited stochasticity of optimal memoryless policies. Muller and Montufar later described the value and occupancy geometry as rational functions and polynomial constraints, giving a precise algebraic picture of the nonconvex feasible set. These results clarify the landscape, but they do not provide a polynomial-time approximation theorem or a global optimization method with worst-case guarantees.

title: Polynomial-time algorithm for simple stochastic games
short_statement: Decide whether simple stochastic games can be solved in polynomial time.
full_statement: A simple stochastic game is a finite directed graph whose vertices are partitioned into max vertices, min vertices, random vertices, and terminal vertices. A token starts at a specified vertex. At a max vertex, player Max chooses the outgoing edge; at a min vertex, player Min chooses; at a random vertex, the next edge is chosen according to a specified probability distribution, usually uniform over two outgoing edges in the canonical model. Terminal vertices have fixed payoffs, for example $1$ if Max wins and $0$ otherwise. The value of a vertex is the supremum, over Max strategies, of the infimum, over Min strategies, of the probability of reaching the winning terminal. Positional optimal strategies exist. The computational problem is: given the game and a rational threshold $q$, decide whether the value of the start vertex is at least $q$, or compute all vertex values and optimal strategies. The open problem is to give an algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the number of vertices and input bit length, or prove an appropriate lower bound explaining why such an algorithm is unlikely. The problem is distinct from mean-payoff games, parity games, and discounted MDPs, although it is polynomially related to several of them.
open_problem: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm for solving simple stochastic games?
background: Simple stochastic games are one of the cleanest models of adversarial sequential decision making with randomness. They are turn-based, zero-sum, finite, and have a reachability objective. This puts them close to stochastic dynamic programming and robust control, but the two-player adversarial structure makes the complexity unresolved. Condon introduced the model as a simple form of stochastic game with striking complexity status: it is not known to be polynomial-time solvable, yet it lies in low-looking classes such as NP intersect coNP for the decision version. The problem has become a benchmark for the boundary between dynamic programming, strategy improvement, linear/quadratic programming, and total-search complexity.
known_results: Condon showed that simple stochastic games are in NP intersect coNP and gave foundational reductions and algorithms, but no polynomial-time algorithm. Positional optimal strategies exist, so certificates of value comparisons can be compact in principle. Ludwig gave a subexponential randomized algorithm by adapting strategy-improvement ideas. Gimbert and Horn developed algorithms that are polynomial when the number of random vertices is fixed, using permutation strategies over random vertices. Several strategy-iteration, value-iteration, quadratic-programming, and reduction-based methods perform well in practice, and benchmark work continues to test them. Recent reductions connect simple stochastic games, stochastic mean-payoff games, mean-payoff games, and semidefinite feasibility frameworks, but these do not currently yield a polynomial-time algorithm for the original problem. The exact worst-case complexity remains open.

title: Approximation threshold for complete-graph correlation clustering
short_statement: Close the gap between the best approximation algorithms and hardness/integrality lower bounds for complete-graph correlation clustering.
full_statement: In unweighted complete-graph correlation clustering, the input is a complete graph $K_n$ whose edges are labeled $+$ or $-$. A clustering is a partition $\Pi$ of the vertices. Its disagreement cost is the number of positive edges whose endpoints lie in different parts of $\Pi$ plus the number of negative edges whose endpoints lie in the same part. The objective is to minimize this disagreement cost, with no prescribed number of clusters. The open problem is to determine the polynomial-time approximability threshold of this problem. Published algorithms give constant factors well below the old factor-$2$ barrier, with recent cluster-LP/Sherali-Adams methods reaching about $1.437+\varepsilon$. Known hardness is far weaker, around $24/23$ in the recent cluster-LP work, and the cluster-LP itself has integrality gap at least $4/3$. Close the gap: improve the approximation factor toward the true LP/hardness threshold, strengthen hardness beyond the current small constant, or identify a relaxation whose integrality gap matches the optimal achievable ratio. A July 2026 preprint by Garcia-Soriano and Schohn claims a $(1.3865+\varepsilon)$ algorithm in this same unweighted complete-graph model; the exact threshold remains unresolved.
open_problem: Determine the optimal approximation ratio for complete-graph correlation clustering, or substantially close the current algorithmic/hardness gap.
background: Correlation clustering is a clean model for clustering from inconsistent pairwise similarity data. It does not require choosing the number of clusters in advance, which is why it has become a useful abstraction in data mining, record linkage, entity resolution, computational biology, and consensus clustering. The complete-graph version is the canonical model: every pair of items is labeled similar or dissimilar, and the algorithm chooses the clustering that violates as few labels as possible. The problem is also a crisp combinatorial optimization question about partition metrics, multicut polytopes, and rounding of strong relaxations. Its practical relevance makes fast algorithms important, but the repository-worthy open problem is the theorem gap: the exact approximation threshold is not known.
known_results: Bansal, Blum, and Chawla introduced correlation clustering and gave early approximation results. Ailon, Charikar, and Newman developed the influential randomized Pivot algorithm and a $3$-approximation framework. Chawla, Makarychev, Schramm, and Yaroslavtsev gave a $2.06$-approximation for complete graphs by rounding the standard LP, nearly matching that LP's integrality gap of $2$. Cohen-Addad, Lee, and Newman, followed by Cohen-Addad, Lee, Li, and Newman, broke the factor-$2$ barrier using Sherali-Adams and preclustering ideas, reaching about $1.73$. Cao, Cohen-Addad, Lee, Li, Newman, and Vogl introduced the cluster LP, gave rounding analyses with factors $1.49$ and computationally certified $1.437$, proved a $4/3$ integrality-gap lower bound for the cluster LP, and obtained an NP-hardness ratio of $24/23$. Later work made the cluster-LP approach much faster. The central approximation gap remains: $1.437$ is far above the $24/23$ hardness and above the $4/3$ cluster-LP gap. Garcia-Soriano and Schohn (2026), Theorems 1.1-1.2 and Corollary 1.3, claim a $(1.3865+\varepsilon)$ polynomial-time algorithm. This is a preprint improvement, not independently proof-verified here.

title: PTAS for Euclidean capacitated vehicle routing with arbitrary capacity
short_statement: Does Euclidean capacitated vehicle routing admit a polynomial-time approximation scheme for arbitrary vehicle capacity?
full_statement: In Euclidean capacitated vehicle routing, the input consists of a depot $r\in\mathbb R^2$, customer points $p_1,\ldots,p_n\in\mathbb R^2$, and an integer vehicle capacity $Q$. In the unit-demand version, every customer has demand one; a feasible solution is a collection of tours, each starting and ending at $r$, such that every customer is visited by at least one tour and each tour visits at most $Q$ customers. The objective is to minimize total Euclidean tour length. More general splittable or unsplittable demand variants replace the cardinality bound by a capacity bound on total demand per tour, but the central geometric open problem is already present in the unit-demand arbitrary-$Q$ case. For fixed dimension, determine whether there is a PTAS: for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, an algorithm running in $n^{O_{\varepsilon}(1)}$ time that returns a solution of cost at most $(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}$ for every capacity $Q$. Quasi-polynomial approximation schemes are known, and recent work has reduced the exponent substantially, but a true polynomial-time approximation scheme for arbitrary capacity remains open.
open_problem: Give a PTAS for Euclidean CVRP with arbitrary capacity, or prove that no PTAS exists under a standard complexity assumption.
background: Capacitated vehicle routing is one of the signature models of operations research: a depot must serve geographically located customers using finite-capacity routes. In general metrics, CVRP has stubborn constant-factor approximation gaps, already represented elsewhere in the repository. The Euclidean case is different. For Euclidean TSP, Arora and Mitchell gave PTASs using recursive dissection and portal techniques. CVRP looks close to TSP but adds a global capacity constraint that forces many short tours and couples local geometric choices to depot returns. That capacity coupling is exactly what prevents the classical Euclidean TSP PTAS machinery from applying directly. The problem is therefore a clean test of whether geometric dynamic programming can handle vehicle capacity without paying quasi-polynomial state complexity.
known_results: Dantzig and Ramser introduced vehicle routing in the 1950s, and CVRP has since become a central routing and logistics problem. Arora-style and Mitchell-style dissection methods give PTASs for Euclidean TSP and many geometric network-design problems, but CVRP resisted the same framework for arbitrary capacities. Das and Mathieu gave a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme for Euclidean CVRP in the plane, with running time of the form $n^{\log^{O(1/\varepsilon)} n}$. Jayaprakash and Salavatipour later developed QPTASs for bounded-treewidth, bounded-doubling, and highway-dimension graph metrics, implying another Euclidean-plane approximation scheme in quasi-polynomial time. Sitters recently improved the Euclidean-plane running time to $n^{O_\varepsilon(\log\log n)}$ and reduced CVRP to an $m$-paths problem, explicitly framing the result as a major step toward a PTAS. No source-checked polynomial-time approximation scheme for arbitrary capacity is known as of this sweep.

The question is whether the state space can be compressed to polynomial size as in Euclidean TSP. The obstacle is that capacity makes the number and composition of route pieces crossing a dissection boundary matter; a portal state must remember not only geometry but how partial tours aggregate demand and return to the depot. Sitters' $n^{O(\log\log n)}$ scheme shows that this state explosion can be reduced substantially and proposes the $m$-paths view as an intermediate target. A PTAS may come from a sharper structural theorem for route interactions, while a negative result would need to show that arbitrary capacity fundamentally encodes too much global information even in the plane.

title: Tusnady's problem for low-dimensional boxes
short_statement: Close the logarithmic gaps in Tusnady's discrepancy problem for axis-parallel boxes in dimensions 2, 3, and 4.
full_statement: Let $P\subset[0,1]^d$ be an $n$-point set and let $\mathcal R_d$ be the family of all axis-parallel boxes in $[0,1]^d$. The combinatorial discrepancy of $P$ with respect to boxes is $$\operatorname{disc}(P,\mathcal R_d)=\min_{\chi:P\to\{-1,+1\}}\max_{R\in\mathcal R_d}\left|\sum_{p\in P\cap R}\chi(p)\right|.$$ Tusnady's problem asks for the worst-case asymptotic order $$D_d(n)=\sup_{|P|=n}\operatorname{disc}(P,\mathcal R_d)$$ as a function of $n$ and fixed dimension $d$. The conjectural or benchmark lower-bound scale is roughly $(\log n)^{d-1}$ for fixed $d$. The established general bounds reviewed here are $\Omega_d((\log n)^{d-1})$ and $O_d((\log n)^{d-1/2})$ (Nikolov, Theorem 1). Dutta's claimed stronger bounds and resolution for $d\ge5$ were withdrawn and cannot be used. The open problem is to determine the correct order of $D_d(n)$ for $d=2,3,4$, ideally proving $D_d(n)=\Theta_d((\log n)^{d-1})$ or constructing point sets requiring larger discrepancy.
open_problem: Determine the asymptotic discrepancy of axis-parallel boxes for fixed low dimensions $d=2,3,4$.
background: Geometric discrepancy asks how evenly finite point sets can be two-colored against geometric ranges. It is a bridge between combinatorics, approximation algorithms, numerical integration, data structures, and randomized rounding. Axis-parallel boxes are the most basic multidimensional range family beyond intervals, and Tusnady's problem is the flagship open question for this setting. The problem is clean: the input is an arbitrary finite point set, the allowed ranges are fixed, and the goal is a worst-case logarithmic exponent. It complements the repository's existing Spencer/Komlos/Beck-Fiala discrepancy entries by focusing on a geometric set system where the best known bounds are dimension-sensitive and where existential and algorithmic bounds must be distinguished.
known_results: For intervals, alternating sorted points gives discrepancy at most one. Beck initiated the box-discrepancy problem; Matousek developed geometric decompositions. Nikolov's Theorem 1 gives $O_d(\log^{d-1/2}n)$, compared with lower bound $\Omega_d(\log^{d-1}n)$. Thus verified baseline upper exponents for $d=2,3,4$ are $3/2,5/2,7/2$. Bansal and Garg give algorithmic $O_d(\log^d n)$ bounds. Dutta's 2021 manuscript claimed exponents $7/4,5/2,13/4$ and a matching result for $d\ge5$, but arXiv v2 (February 10, 2022) withdraws it because Claim 4.7 has an unfixable flaw. Those claims are not established progress. No resolution of the intended low-dimensional target was verified in this audit.

title: Relaxation-based approximation for capacitated facility location
short_statement: Find a polynomial-size relaxation with constant integrality gap for metric capacitated facility location, or prove that broad classes of relaxations cannot achieve one.
full_statement: In metric capacitated facility location, there is a set $F$ of facilities, a set $C$ of clients, opening costs $f_i\ge0$, capacities $u_i$, client demands (unit demands in the basic version), and a metric connection cost $d(i,j)$ on $F\cup C$. A feasible integral solution opens facilities and assigns each client to an open facility so that the total demand assigned to facility $i$ is at most $u_i$, paying opening plus connection cost. Constant-factor approximation algorithms are known by combinatorial and local-search methods, but the natural LP relaxation and many strengthened variants have unbounded integrality gap. The open problem is to design a computationally useful linear, convex, or extended formulation of polynomial size with constant integrality gap for capacitated facility location, together with a rounding algorithm, or to prove impossibility for a sufficiently broad class of relaxations. The target is not merely another constant approximation algorithm; it is a relaxation-based explanation comparable to the LP theory for uncapacitated facility location.
open_problem: Does metric capacitated facility location admit a polynomial-time relaxation-based constant-factor approximation, via a relaxation with constant integrality gap and an efficient rounding algorithm?
background: Facility location is one of the central models of operations research, and LP relaxations have been extremely successful for its uncapacitated version. Capacities are operationally unavoidable: warehouses, schools, clinics, and servers all have finite service capacity. Yet the introduction of capacities makes the standard LP picture collapse. A fractional solution can open small fractions of many facilities and route clients cheaply in ways that no integral solution can emulate. Local-search algorithms still obtain constant factors, so the problem is not inapproximable at that level; what is missing is a strong relaxation that captures the combinatorial structure of capacities. This makes the problem especially important for OR: relaxations are not just proof devices but also the basis of exact solvers, decomposition, branch-and-cut, and computational practice.
known_results: The natural LP relaxation for capacitated facility location has unbounded integrality gap. Shmoys and Williamson highlighted the existence of a relaxation-based algorithm for capacitated facility location as one of the top open problems in approximation algorithms. Kolliopoulos and Moysoglou showed that several strengthened formulations still have unbounded gaps, including relaxations obtained after many Lovasz-Schrijver rounds and broad classes of proper relaxations. Their later work with Sherali-Adams gaps, flow-cover inequalities, and generalized configurations gave further negative evidence: even substantial lift-and-project and flow-cover strengthening does not automatically yield a constant-gap relaxation. Separate work on exponential lower bounds shows that, in the natural encoding, small approximate formulations cannot achieve constant gaps. These results do not rule out every possible extended formulation, semidefinite relaxation, or nonstandard configuration system, but they show that the obvious LP-strengthening routes are inadequate.

literature.synthesis: The open problem is sharper than simply approximating capacitated facility location. Constant approximations demonstrate that the integral problem has exploitable structure, but the known algorithms do not pass through a clean polynomial-size relaxation with bounded gap. The negative LP results identify recurring fractional pathologies: facilities can be fractionally opened in tiny amounts, clients can spread demand across many partially open facilities, and common valid inequalities fail to encode the global coupling between opening and assignment. Lift-and-project hierarchies and flow-cover inequalities help in many integer programs, but the Kolliopoulos-Moysoglou results show that substantial levels still leave unbounded gaps in CFL. A breakthrough may require a qualitatively different extended formulation, perhaps with configuration variables that encode demand groups and capacity slack, or a proof that any natural relaxation family must be exponentially large.

title: Constant-factor approximation for minimum feedback arc set in directed graphs
short_statement: Determine whether minimum feedback arc set in general directed graphs has a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation under standard assumptions.
full_statement: Given a directed graph $G=(V,A)$ with nonnegative arc weights $w_a$, a feedback arc set is a set $F\subseteq A$ whose removal makes $G$ acyclic. Equivalently, one can seek a linear ordering of the vertices and pay for arcs directed backward in the ordering; the minimum feedback arc set value is the minimum backward-arc weight over all orders. The problem is NP-hard and is one of the classical cycle-breaking and ranking problems, with applications in deadlock resolution, circuit analysis, graph drawing, and rank aggregation. The best general approximation algorithms for directed feedback arc set are polylogarithmic rather than constant, while strong hardness is known only under assumptions such as the Unique Games Conjecture. The open problem is to determine whether a polynomial-time $O(1)$-approximation exists for weighted or unweighted minimum feedback arc set in general directed graphs under ordinary assumptions such as $P\ne NP$, or whether a superconstant lower bound can be proved.
open_problem: Does general directed minimum feedback arc set admit a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation, or is every polynomial-time approximation necessarily superconstant under a standard complexity assumption?
background: Minimum feedback arc set is a clean ordering problem: find the order of vertices that minimizes the total weight of arcs pointing backward. In tournaments this is the Kemeny/rank-aggregation problem and admits much stronger approximation schemes, but general directed graphs are far less understood. The model is not an application-specific modeling question; it is a fixed graph optimization problem with a direct LP/ordering formulation. The contrast with related problems is striking. Undirected feedback vertex set has constant approximations, maximum acyclic subgraph has a simple constant approximation, and tournament feedback arc set has PTAS-type results. But the minimization version for arbitrary directed graphs remains stuck at a polylogarithmic approximation versus only constant-factor hardness under standard assumptions.
known_results: Karp's original NP-completeness framework includes feedback arc/feedback vertex style cycle-breaking problems, and later work established APX-hardness for directed feedback arc set. Even, Naor, Schieber, and Sudan gave influential polylogarithmic approximation algorithms for minimum feedback sets and directed multicuts; these remain part of the standard approximation baseline. For dense or tournament inputs the situation is much better: feedback arc set in tournaments admits polynomial-time approximation schemes, reflecting the additional ordering structure of complete orientations. Hardness is delicate. Under the Unique Games Conjecture, directed feedback arc set and directed feedback vertex set are hard to approximate within any constant factor, but that conditional result does not give an unconditional superconstant lower bound. Under $P\ne NP$, the known inapproximability is only constant. Thus the central gap is qualitative: either find a constant approximation for arbitrary directed graphs, or prove superconstant hardness from more standard assumptions.

where_posed.text: Standard surveys and problem summaries state that the best approximation for directed feedback arc set is polylogarithmic and that the existence of a constant approximation is open absent Unique-Games-type assumptions.

literature.synthesis: The approximation landscape is asymmetric. Maximizing the number of forward arcs is easy to approximate by taking the better of an order and its reverse, but minimizing the backward arcs is sensitive to the optimum being small. Tournament structure removes sparse pathologies and leads to PTAS results, which is why rank aggregation is algorithmically different from general directed cycle breaking. The Even-Naor-Schieber-Sudan framework connects feedback sets with directed multicut and gives polylogarithmic guarantees, but it does not compress to a constant. Unique-Games hardness suggests a constant approximation may be impossible, yet the repository standard distinguishes UGC evidence from standard-assumption resolution. A breakthrough would either find a new decomposition of directed cycles into orderable pieces or convert conditional hardness intuition into an unconditional superconstant lower bound.

title: Polynomial-time solvability of parity games
short_statement: Determine whether finite parity games can be solved in polynomial time.
full_statement: A parity game is played on a finite directed graph $G=(V,E)$ whose vertices are partitioned into $V_0$ and $V_1$, controlled by players Even and Odd, and equipped with a priority function $p:V\to\{0,1,\ldots,d\}$. A token starts at a vertex. If the token is at a vertex in $V_i$, player $i$ chooses an outgoing edge and the token moves along it. The resulting infinite path is won by Even if the largest priority seen infinitely often is even, and by Odd otherwise; equivalent minimum-priority conventions can be translated by changing priorities. Positional determinacy holds, so if a player can win from a vertex, that player has a memoryless winning strategy. The computational problem is to compute the winning regions and memoryless winning strategies, or decide for a start vertex which player wins. The open problem is to give an algorithm with running time polynomial in $|V|$, $|E|$, and $d$, or to prove a lower-bound result explaining why such an algorithm is unlikely.
open_problem: Are parity games solvable in polynomial time?
background: Parity games sit at the intersection of graph algorithms, automata theory, logic, and verification. They arise in model checking and synthesis for the modal $\mu$-calculus and omega-automata, and they are one of the cleanest finite two-player infinite-duration games with positional strategies. The model is fixed and elementary: a colored directed graph, alternating choices by two players, and a parity acceptance condition. Yet its exact worst-case complexity has resisted classification for decades. The problem resembles mean-payoff and simple stochastic games in that it lies in low nondeterministic complexity classes and has compact certificates, but no polynomial-time algorithm is known. Because practical solvers often perform well, the unresolved question is a sharp theoretical one: is there hidden polynomial structure in strategy improvement, progress measures, or attractor decompositions, or is the quasi-polynomial breakthrough close to the true boundary?
known_results: Emerson and Jutla, Mostowski, and Zielonka established the game-theoretic foundations of parity games, including determinacy and memoryless winning strategies. Jurdzinski proved that deciding the winner lies in $UP\cap coUP$, strengthening the older $NP\cap coNP$ membership and explaining why standard NP-hardness is unlikely. For many years the best general algorithms were exponential or subexponential. In 2017, Calude, Jain, Khoussainov, Li, and Stephan gave a quasi-polynomial-time algorithm, a major breakthrough. Fearnley, Jain, Schewe, Stephan, and Wojtczak showed how to implement the Calude et al. approach in quasi-polynomial time and quasi-linear space, while later work by Parys, Lehtinen, and others produced alternative quasi-polynomial algorithms and progress-measure formulations. Many restricted classes are polynomial-time solvable, and practical strategy-improvement and Zielonka-style algorithms are effective on benchmarks. None of these results gives a polynomial worst-case algorithm for all finite parity games.

where_posed.text: The complexity of parity games is repeatedly identified in the literature as a long-standing open problem; the 2017 quasi-polynomial algorithms were major progress but did not settle polynomial-time solvability.
where_posed.quote: Parity games play an important role in model checking and synthesis.

alphaevolve_rationale: Search can generate hard benchmark games for specific algorithms and discover invariants of progress measures, but proving a polynomial-time algorithm or lower bound requires structural complexity arguments.

literature.synthesis: Parity-game algorithms have repeatedly rediscovered the same tension: memoryless determinacy gives simple certificates, but naive search over strategies can cycle or take exponential time. Progress-measure algorithms encode enough ordinal information to certify wins, Zielonka-style recursive attractor decompositions are fast in practice, and strategy-improvement methods are conceptually simple but hard to analyze. The quasi-polynomial algorithms introduced succinct universal trees, register games, and ordered progress measures that compress the search space much more effectively than earlier exponential techniques. This suggests the right invariant may be near-polynomial, but the remaining logarithmic exponent has not been eliminated. A polynomial-time solution would likely identify a stronger compression of progress certificates or a new monotone potential for strategy improvement; a negative result would require a complexity-theoretic breakthrough because the problem lies in classes where ordinary NP-hardness is implausible.

title: Constant-factor truthful mechanisms for submodular combinatorial auctions
short_statement: Design a polynomial-time truthful mechanism with a constant approximation to welfare for combinatorial auctions with submodular bidders, or prove that no such mechanism exists under a standard model of access to valuations.
full_statement: There are $m$ heterogeneous indivisible items and $n$ bidders. Bidder $i$ has a private normalized monotone submodular valuation $v_i:2^{[m]}\to\mathbb R_+$, accessed through value or demand queries as specified by the mechanism model. An allocation is a tuple of disjoint bundles $(S_1,\ldots,S_n)$, and its welfare is $\sum_i v_i(S_i)$. Without incentive constraints, the submodular welfare maximization problem admits constant-factor approximation algorithms under standard oracle models. The open problem is to obtain a computationally efficient truthful mechanism, preferably universally truthful randomized and using polynomially many demand/value queries, whose expected welfare is within a constant factor of the optimal welfare for every profile of monotone submodular valuations. A solution must include payments and a proof that truthful reporting is a dominant strategy, not merely an allocation algorithm with good welfare. Conversely, a lower bound must specify the mechanism class, oracle model, and truthfulness notion, and must rule out constant approximation for all mechanisms in that class.
open_problem: Is there a polynomial-time truthful constant-approximation mechanism for welfare maximization in combinatorial auctions with monotone submodular bidders?
background: Combinatorial auctions are the canonical algorithmic mechanism-design model for allocating heterogeneous resources when bidders have complementarities or substitutes across bundles. For submodular bidders, valuations have diminishing returns and are expressive enough to model substitutes, budgeted preferences, and many allocation environments in platforms and markets. The algorithmic problem without strategic behavior is well understood at the constant-factor level, but truthfulness changes the problem qualitatively: the allocation rule must be implementable with payments so that bidders prefer to report their valuations honestly. This creates a tension between optimization and incentive compatibility. VCG would be truthful but computationally intractable for exact welfare maximization, while approximate allocation rules are usually not monotone or maximal-in-range in the way needed for truthfulness. The remaining problem is clean because the valuation class and objective are fixed; the missing piece is a theorem-level mechanism or impossibility result.
known_results: Dobzinski, Nisan, and Schapira gave the first computationally efficient truthful mechanism for submodular bidders with an $O(\log^2 m)$ approximation. Dobzinski later broke the logarithmic barrier to obtain an $O(\sqrt{\log m})$ approximation for submodular and XOS valuations. Assadi and Singla then gave a major improvement to an $O((\log\log m)^3)$ approximation in expectation, using only $O(n)$ demand queries and providing a universal truthfulness guarantee. This refuted the possibility that the earlier $\Theta(\sqrt{\log m})$ barrier was inherent. Assadi, Kesselheim, and Singla (SODA 2021), Theorem 2, improve the submodular/XOS guarantee to $O((\log\log m)^2)$ with universal truthfulness and polynomial time; their cubic guarantee is for the broader subadditive class. On the negative side, Dobzinski proved strong value-query lower bounds for universally truthful randomized mechanisms: with only value queries, very good approximations require exponentially many queries. Those lower bounds do not rule out constant-factor mechanisms with demand queries or stronger communication. Thus the main gap remains between the current polyloglog approximation and a constant, with the oracle model and truthfulness notion central to the interpretation. Rubinstein and Singla's October 2026 preprint, Theorem 1.2, claims $O(\log\log m)$ for every fixed XOS profile in uniformly random arrival order, hence also offline after randomizing bidder order. Its constant-factor theorem instead assumes independent distributions and samples, and does not resolve the prior-free target.

where_posed.text: Assadi and Singla describe the problem as a longstanding open problem in algorithmic mechanism design and improve the state of the art to $O((\log\log m)^3)$, leaving the constant-factor frontier open.

literature.synthesis: The literature shows a persistent separation between optimization and truthful optimization. Nontruthful submodular welfare algorithms can use continuous greedy, local search, and rounding to obtain constant factors. Truthful mechanisms are constrained to allocation rules that can be paired with payments, and most approximation algorithms fail monotonicity or maximal-in-range requirements. The Dobzinski line made progress by designing carefully restricted allocation ranges and lottery/partition structures that remain implementable. Assadi-Singla's exponential improvement over the $\sqrt{\log m}$ barrier suggests that the known polylogarithmic losses are not simply information-theoretic, but the value-query impossibility results also warn that the oracle model matters. A convincing resolution must either build a new truthful range/rounding architecture with constant loss, or prove that any such architecture would need communication or queries beyond polynomial size. The 2021 squared-log-log theorem supersedes the older cubic submodular bound. The 2026 random-order/offline claim is another partial improvement, not a prior-free constant approximation.

title: Exact approximation threshold for weighted tree augmentation
short_statement: Determine the true approximability and relaxation gap of weighted tree augmentation after the recent break below the factor-2 barrier.
full_statement: In the weighted tree augmentation problem, the input is an undirected tree $T=(V,E_T)$ and a set $L$ of candidate links, where each link $\ell\in L$ joins two vertices of $T$ and has cost $c_\ell\ge0$. A feasible solution selects links $S\subseteq L$ such that $T\cup S$ is $2$-edge-connected, equivalently every tree edge $e\in E_T$ lies on the unique tree path between the endpoints of at least one selected link. The objective is to minimize $\sum_{\ell\in S}c_\ell$. The unweighted version has approximation ratios below $1.5$, and the weighted version has recently moved from a long-standing factor-$2$ barrier to ratios near and below $1.5$. The open problem is to determine the exact approximation threshold for weighted tree augmentation, or at least close the current gap between lower-bound evidence such as the $1.5$ cut-LP gap and the best approximation algorithms below $1.5$. A parallel LP question asks for the right relaxation and integrality-gap constant.
open_problem: What is the optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio, and the right LP/extended-relaxation gap, for weighted tree augmentation?
background: Tree augmentation is one of the most elementary survivable-network-design problems. Starting from a tree, the goal is to buy extra links so that no single tree edge failure disconnects the network. This is a stylized but precise model for adding redundancy to communication, transportation, and infrastructure backbones. Its appeal is that the base graph is only a tree, so the connectivity requirement reduces to covering a laminar family of cuts. Despite this simplicity, weighted tree augmentation has driven a long line of approximation and LP-rounding work. The old open problem was to beat factor $2$ in the weighted case; that has now been solved. The current repository-worthy question is the next, sharper one: after local search and strong LP relaxations pushed the ratio to around $1.5$ and below, what is the actual barrier?
known_results: The standard cut LP and several classical primal-dual or relative-greedy techniques give factor-$2$ guarantees, and for a long time no better approximation was known for weighted tree augmentation. Kortsarz and Nutov emphasized that weighted TAP was the simplest connectivity network-design problem for which a ratio better than $2$ was unknown, while the unweighted case had better guarantees. Traub and Zenklusen broke the weighted factor-$2$ barrier, first obtaining a $1+\ln2+\varepsilon$ approximation and then a $(1.5+\varepsilon)$ local-search guarantee. Their work also connected weighted tree augmentation to broader weighted connectivity augmentation. In 2026, Cohen-Addad, Drygala, Klein, and Svensson proposed a strong LP relaxation with subset variables and a randomized rounding algorithm below $1.49$. The classical cut LP has gap at least $1.5$, so new relaxations are necessary for LP-based progress below that value. The exact approximation threshold, best possible relaxation gap, and matching hardness remain unknown.
