title: Polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree
short_statement: Determine whether Directed Steiner Tree admits a polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation, or prove a separation between polynomial and quasi-polynomial time.
full_statement: In Directed Steiner Tree, the input is a directed graph $G=(V,E)$ with nonnegative edge costs $c_e$, a root vertex $r\in V$, and a set $K\subseteq V$ of $k$ terminals. A feasible solution is a subgraph, equivalently an $r$-rooted arborescence after pruning, that contains a directed path from $r$ to every terminal $t\in K$. The objective is to minimize the total cost of selected edges. The problem is a central directed network-design model and generalizes Set Cover. The best reliable general results give $O(\log^2 k/\log\log k)$ approximations in quasi-polynomial time and $O(k^\varepsilon)$ approximations in polynomial time for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. The open problem is whether there is a polynomial-time $(\log k)^{O(1)}$-approximation for arbitrary directed graphs, or whether one can prove that quasi-polynomial time is inherently stronger for achieving polylogarithmic ratios. A solution must be for the standard single-root directed Steiner tree problem, not only planar digraphs, bounded-depth graphs, bounded-treewidth graphs, or bicriteria variants.
open_problem: Give a polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree in general directed graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists under a standard complexity assumption.
background: Directed Steiner Tree is one of the basic survivable/network-design problems where directionality changes the approximation landscape completely. Undirected Steiner Tree has constant-factor approximations, while the directed version must choose a rooted arborescence through an asymmetric graph and can encode Set Cover-like structure. The model is clean and operationally meaningful: build the cheapest directed distribution, communication, or dependency network from a source to required sinks. For decades the field has had a striking time-approximation tradeoff. Quasi-polynomial algorithms can achieve polylogarithmic ratios essentially matching known quasi-polynomial hardness, but polynomial-time algorithms are stuck at $k^\varepsilon$. This makes the problem a benchmark for whether lift-and-round, height-reduction, or recursive-density methods can be made efficient without losing the polylogarithmic guarantee.
known_results: Charikar, Chekuri, Cheung, Dai, Goel, Guha, and Li gave the classical quasi-polynomial framework for Directed Steiner Tree. Later work clarified and improved the ratio: Grandoni, Laekhanukit, and Li obtained an $O(\log^2 k/\log\log k)$ approximation in quasi-polynomial time and showed tightness for quasi-polynomial algorithms by tuning Halperin-Krauthgamer-type hardness. Independently, Ghuge and Nagarajan obtained matching quasi-polynomial guarantees through a broader submodular tree-orienteering framework. In polynomial time, the best general guarantee remains $O(k^\varepsilon)$ for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. Planar digraphs are a major positive special case: Friggstad and Mousavi obtained a polynomial-time $O(\log k)$ approximation, and Chekuri, Jain, Kulkarni, Zheng, and Zhu extended tree-embedding and LP ideas to planar directed polymatroid variants. These special cases do not resolve the arbitrary directed-graph problem. A 2024 arXiv attempt claiming a polynomial-time polylogarithmic result for general DST was later marked on arXiv as withdrawn/proof-collapsed, so it should not be treated as a resolution.

literature.synthesis: Directed Steiner Tree has a clean divide between what is possible with quasi-polynomial recursion and what is known in polynomial time. Height-reduction and recursive greedy ideas can reduce the instance to bounded-depth structures, but preserving enough terminal coverage information creates quasi-polynomial state spaces. Sherali-Adams and label-consistent subtree formulations sharpen this into the current $O(\log^2 k/\log\log k)$ quasi-polynomial guarantee. Polynomial time loses this structure and falls back to $k^\varepsilon$ ratios. Planar directed graphs show that graph structure can collapse the difficulty through separators and embeddings, suggesting that the general obstacle is not merely directedness but the absence of compressible decomposition. A resolution likely needs either a new polynomial-size relaxation/rounding framework or a complexity result separating polynomial from quasi-polynomial approximation power for this rooted network-design problem.

title: Exact approximation threshold for Multiway Cut
short_statement: Multiway Cut has a $1.2787$ algorithm; a November 2026 preprint improves the UGC-based lower bound to $1.22232$. The exact threshold remains open.
full_statement: In the undirected Multiway Cut problem, the input is an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with nonnegative edge weights and a set of terminals $T=\{t_1,\ldots,t_k\}$. A feasible solution deletes a set of edges whose removal separates every pair of terminals; equivalently, it partitions $V$ into $k$ parts, each containing exactly one terminal, and pays the total weight of edges crossing between parts. The goal is to minimize this cut cost. The problem is APX-hard for $k\ge3$ and has a canonical geometric LP relaxation due to Calinescu, Karloff, and Rabani, in which vertices are embedded into the $k$-simplex with terminals at simplex corners. The open problem is to determine the exact polynomial-time approximation threshold, or at least close the gap between the best algorithms and the best hardness/integrality-gap constructions for arbitrary $k$.
open_problem: Determine the exact approximation threshold between the $1.2787$ upper bound and lower bounds, including the new preprint $1.22232$ UGC-hardness claim.
background: Graph cut problems are foundational in combinatorial optimization, operations research, image segmentation, clustering, and network interdiction. Multiway Cut is the natural generalization of $s$-$t$ cut from two terminals to many terminals. The two-terminal problem is exactly solvable by max-flow/min-cut, while three or more terminals create an approximation problem with rich geometric structure. The CKR relaxation converts cuts into simplex geometry, and much of the modern theory studies how to randomly round points in that simplex while controlling boundary-crossing probabilities. The model is parsimonious and fully specified, but the constants remain unresolved. This makes it a good repository entry: a clean graph optimization problem with a precise numerical approximation gap and machine-checkable finite gap instances.
known_results: Dahlhaus et al. established early approximation and hardness results; Calinescu, Karloff, and Rabani introduced the simplex LP. Sharma-Vondrak's $1.2965$ algorithm was superseded by Brakensiek, Huang, Potechin, and Zwick (STOC 2026), whose Theorem 1.1 gives $1.2787$ for arbitrary terminal count. Angelidakis-Makarychev-Manurangsi's $1.2$ hardness and the Berczi-Chandrasekaran-Kiraly-Madan $1.20016$ improvement are conditional on UGC when interpreted as approximation hardness, not consequences of $P\ne NP$ alone. The latter is also an unconditional CKR gap lower bound. A November 3, 2026 preprint by Brakensiek et al. claims analytic lower bound $1.22232$, yielding hardness under UGC. Its $1.23003$ figure is numerical evidence, not the proved theorem.

where_posed.text: Historical gap summarized in Berczi et al.; the quoted 1.2965 benchmark has since been improved.

literature.synthesis: The central technical object is the simplex relaxation. Algorithms design randomized partitions of the simplex and bound the probability that an edge segment is separated. Lower bounds construct finite simplex subdivisions and admissible labelings whose boundary behavior forces high cut cost. Sharma and Vondrak's descending-threshold framework gave the historical $1.2965$ constant, while Angelidakis-Makarychev-Manurangsi and Berczi-Chandrasekaran-Kiraly-Madan push the lower-bound side just above $1.2$. The gap is not merely numerical: upper bounds rely on rounding distributions with global simplex symmetries, while lower bounds require understanding higher-dimensional combinatorial topology. A full solution likely needs either a substantially sharper rounding family or a new integrality/hardness construction approaching the algorithmic constant. Large mixtures of rounding schemes improve the upper bound to $1.2787$; a separate new analytic preprint strengthens the lower side. Numerical evidence and conditional hardness must be labeled separately.

title: Tight approximation and LP gap for 0-Extension
short_statement: Close the gap between the $O(\log k/\log\log k)$ upper bound and the $\Omega((\log k)^{2/3})$ lower bound for the 0-Extension metric relaxation.
full_statement: In the $0$-Extension problem, the input is an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with nonnegative edge weights $w_e$, a terminal set $T=\{t_1,\ldots,t_k\}\subseteq V$, and a semimetric $D$ on $T$. A feasible solution maps every vertex $v\in V$ to a terminal $f(v)\in T$ while fixing terminals, $f(t)=t$ for all $t\in T$. The objective is $$\sum_{uv\in E} w_{uv} D(f(u),f(v)).$$ The standard metric or semimetric relaxation extends $D$ from $T$ to all of $V$ and then rounds the extended metric back to a terminal assignment. The best known approximation and relaxation upper bound is $O(\log k/\log\log k)$, while the best lower bound for the relaxation is $\Omega((\log k)^{2/3})$. The open problem is to determine the correct asymptotic integrality gap and approximability of $0$-Extension, and to clarify the corresponding limits of cut/flow vertex sparsifiers.
open_problem: Determine the tight asymptotic approximation ratio and semimetric-LP integrality gap for $0$-Extension.
background: $0$-Extension is a central metric labeling and graph compression problem. It asks how to collapse a graph onto a terminal metric while preserving pairwise terminal distances and minimizing the induced edge cost. This formulation captures clustering with prescribed labels, metric labeling relaxations, and terminal sparsification. Its importance is amplified by its equivalence and close relationship to cut and flow vertex sparsifiers: understanding how well nonterminals can be contracted to terminals tells us how well a large graph can be compressed while preserving terminal cut/flow information. The model is fully specified and finite; the hard question is a theorem-level gap in metric rounding and graph compression, not a modeling choice.
known_results: Calinescu, Karloff, and Rabani developed the metric-relaxation framework and gave an $O(\log k)$-approximation. Fakcharoenphol, Harrelson, Rao, and Talwar improved the rounding guarantee to $O(\log k/\log\log k)$ using metric-decomposition ideas. The lower-bound side moved more slowly. Earlier constructions gave polynomial-in-log lower bounds, and Schwartz and Tur improved the metric-relaxation integrality gap to $\Omega((\log k)^{2/3})$ using randomized graph extensions and a topological obstruction. Chen and Tan studied a version allowing Steiner nodes and proved that related gaps remain superconstant even with many extra Steiner vertices, reinforcing the connection to the major open problem of cut/flow sparsifiers with Steiner nodes. The upper and lower bounds still do not match, and no alternative relaxation or algorithm is known to settle the correct asymptotic behavior.

literature.synthesis: The known algorithms round an extended semimetric by probabilistic terminal decompositions. The $O(\log k/\log\log k)$ bound reflects the best available decomposition quality for arbitrary terminal metrics. Lower bounds have become increasingly geometric: Schwartz and Tur's construction uses randomized graph extensions and a topological no-section argument to beat the earlier square-root-log barrier. Chen and Tan show that even adding many Steiner nodes does not make the corresponding compression problem constant-quality, suggesting the obstruction is not merely the lack of intermediate representatives. The gap remains wide enough that either side could move: a sharper decomposition might close toward $\log^{2/3}k$, or a more powerful topological/metric construction might push the lower bound toward $\log k/\log\log k$.

title: Approximation threshold for the Forest Augmentation Problem
short_statement: Forest Augmentation now has a better-than-2 approximation, but the correct approximation threshold for this basic survivable-network-design problem is still unknown.
full_statement: In the unweighted Forest Augmentation Problem, the input is an undirected forest $F=(V,E_F)$ and a set $L$ of additional candidate links on the same vertex set. The goal is to choose a minimum-cardinality subset $S\subseteq L$ such that the graph $(V,E_F\cup S)$ is 2-edge-connected. This is one of the cleanest survivable-network-design augmentation models beyond Tree Augmentation. Jain's iterative-rounding framework gives a factor-2 approximation for broad survivable network design problems, and for years this was the benchmark for Forest Augmentation. Grandoni, Jabal Ameli, and Traub breached the factor-2 barrier for FAP by reducing to and solving a path-augmentation core. The open problem is to determine the true polynomial-time approximation threshold for Forest Augmentation, and more broadly to understand how far below the Jain factor $2$ one can go for basic augmentation problems whose starting graph is disconnected.
open_problem: Determine the best possible polynomial-time approximation ratio for unweighted Forest Augmentation, or prove a strong hardness/integrality-gap barrier matching the best algorithms.
background: Survivable network design asks for cheap networks that remain connected after failures. The general framework is broad, but augmentation problems isolate the essential combinatorics: start with a graph that is almost connected enough and add links to reach the desired connectivity. Tree Augmentation, where the initial graph is connected, has seen increasingly refined algorithms, including improvements for weighted variants. Forest Augmentation is only a small step away syntactically, but disconnected components remove structural tools that rely on a single tree. The 2021 breakthrough showed that factor 2 is not intrinsic even here, using a reduction to path augmentation and a credit argument. That leaves a clean OR-style approximation problem: identify the actual constant and the right relaxation or hard family.
known_results: Jain's iterative rounding gives a 2-approximation for broad survivable network design settings, and this bound applied to Forest Augmentation. Better-than-2 algorithms were known for Tree Augmentation and related connected-start cases, but those methods did not transfer directly to forests. Grandoni, Jabal Ameli, and Traub give the first better-than-2 approximation for Forest Augmentation and also solve a better-than-2 Path Augmentation subproblem that had been open. The exact achieved constant is not presented as a tight threshold, and known hardness for the clean unweighted FAP model is far from a matching barrier. Thus the remaining open part is to pin down the approximability constant or identify a relaxation whose gap explains the limit. The earlier FAP ratio is $1.9973$. Hommelsheim's 2025 preprint improves it to $1.9955$ (Theorem 2), using a $1.9412$ Path Augmentation guarantee (Theorem 1). The exact unweighted FAP threshold remains open.

title: The true approximation threshold for metric TSP
short_statement: Christofides' $3/2$ barrier for metric TSP was finally beaten, but only by a tiny constant; the true polynomial-time approximation threshold is still unknown.
full_statement: In the symmetric metric Traveling Salesman Problem, the input is a complete graph on vertex set $V$ with nonnegative distances $c_{uv}$ satisfying symmetry and the triangle inequality. A feasible solution is a Hamiltonian cycle, and the goal is to minimize its total length. Christofides' algorithm, independently found by Serdyukov, gives a $3/2$-approximation by combining a minimum spanning tree with a minimum perfect matching on odd-degree vertices. For more than forty years this was the best general polynomial-time guarantee. Karlin, Klein, and Oveis Gharan recently gave a randomized $(3/2-\epsilon)$-approximation for some explicit but extremely small $\epsilon>10^{-36}$, and subsequent work derandomized the guarantee. The open problem is to determine the true polynomial-time approximation threshold for metric TSP: is there a substantially better constant than $3/2$, perhaps approaching the conjectural $4/3$ behavior suggested by the subtour LP, or is there a hardness barrier far above the current $123/122$ inapproximability bound? A solution should apply to arbitrary finite metrics, not only Euclidean, graphic, bounded-genus, or other structured metrics.
open_problem: Close the metric TSP approximability gap: prove a meaningfully better constant-factor approximation than $3/2-10^{-36}$, or prove a substantially stronger hardness threshold for arbitrary symmetric metrics.
background: Metric TSP is one of the canonical routing models in operations research and one of the first problems that made worst-case approximation guarantees central to combinatorial optimization. The model is clean: the metric closure abstracts away road-network details and keeps only pairwise shortest-path distances. Christofides' analysis is also clean, which partly explains why it became a benchmark. The algorithm's two ingredients, a spanning tree and a parity-correction matching, can be interpreted through the subtour-elimination relaxation and $T$-join structure. The long-standing difficulty is that the obvious proof has tight examples, but those examples need not be tight for every algorithm. Modern progress uses maximum-entropy distributions over spanning trees and delicate negative-dependence properties, showing that the old $3/2$ wall was not a theorem-level barrier. The remaining question is whether that breakthrough is the start of a path toward constants such as $4/3$, or whether metric TSP has hard instances requiring ratios much closer to $3/2$.
known_results: Christofides' algorithm gives a $3/2$ approximation for every metric instance, and examples show that this analysis is tight for that algorithm. The strongest general hardness results are much weaker: Karpinski, Lampis, and Schmied prove APX-hardness and an explicit inapproximability threshold of $123/122$ for symmetric metric TSP. Karlin, Klein, and Oveis Gharan break the $3/2$ barrier with a randomized $3/2-\epsilon$ algorithm for an explicit tiny $\epsilon>10^{-36}$; a later paper derandomizes the relevant max-entropy approach. Related work gives slightly improved upper bounds on the subtour-LP integrality gap, and the famous $4/3$ conjecture for the subtour LP remains unresolved. Thus the open part is enormous: the best algorithmic constant is essentially $1.5$, while the best hardness is barely above $1$.

counterexample_rationale: Finite metric instances can refute proposed LP gaps, rounding analyses, or conjectured stronger guarantees for specific algorithm families. Hardness and positive approximation results still require proof, but computational search can produce useful extremal instances.

literature.synthesis: The literature has three distinct layers. The classical algorithmic layer is Christofides' tree-plus-matching method, which gives $3/2$ and remains practically and conceptually central. The LP layer studies the subtour-elimination relaxation and its integrality gap; the conjectured $4/3$ value would imply a much more structured view of metric TSP, but current general upper bounds are still close to $3/2$. The recent max-entropy layer proves that carefully sampled spanning trees have enough structure to beat the old barrier, but the improvement is minuscule. On the hardness side, reductions show APX-hardness but leave a vast gap between $123/122$ and $3/2$. The open problem is therefore not a matter of polishing constants. It asks for either a new global decomposition of metric tours, a much sharper use of the subtour LP, or a reduction that finally explains why routing in arbitrary metrics is hard beyond tiny constant factors.

title: Undecidability of stability for clean multiclass queueing networks
short_statement: Gamarnik and Katz proved queueing-network stability is undecidable for priority networks allowing finite buffers or zero service times; they conjecture the undecidability persists for the cleaner infinite-buffer, positive-service model.
full_statement: Consider a multiclass queueing network with finitely many stations and job classes. External arrivals and service times are deterministic or otherwise specified by rational data; each class has a deterministic route through stations; each station serves jobs according to a fixed nonpreemptive static buffer-priority rule. The stability question asks whether the total queue length remains bounded in the usual stochastic/traffic-intensity sense, or equivalently whether the Markov or deterministic network dynamics are positive recurrent or nondivergent under the specified primitive assumptions. Gamarnik and Katz prove that deciding stability is algorithmically undecidable for a broad class of such networks with deterministic interarrival and service times, allowing finite and infinite buffers and possibly zero service times. They explicitly conjecture that the negative result should remain true for the cleaner model with only infinite buffers and strictly positive service times. The open problem is to prove or refute this conjecture: is there no algorithm that, given the finite rational description of an infinite-buffer multiclass queueing network with positive service times and static priority disciplines, decides stability?
open_problem: Prove or refute undecidability of the stability problem for multiclass static-priority queueing networks when all buffers are infinite and all service times are strictly positive.
background: Queueing-network stability is one of the basic structural questions in applied probability and operations research. If a proposed service discipline is stabilizing, steady-state performance analysis is meaningful; if not, average delay and inventory of unfinished work can explode. For product-form networks stability is transparent, but multiclass networks with priority disciplines can emulate complicated computations. Earlier fluid-model theory showed that traffic intensity conditions alone are not enough and that stable-looking local behavior can produce global instability. Gamarnik and Katz pushed this to a computability boundary by reducing from counter machines. Their theorem is deliberately unsettling: for a natural class of queueing models, a complete constructive characterization of stability cannot exist. The remaining conjecture removes two technical conveniences in the reduction, finite buffers and zero service times, and asks whether the impossibility is intrinsic to ordinary positive-service, infinite-buffer networks.
known_results: Gamarnik and Katz prove undecidability for nonpreemptive static buffer-priority networks with deterministic interarrival and service times, in a formulation that permits finite buffers and possibly zero service times. Their construction extends earlier undecidability ideas for queueing-network stability and uses counter-machine simulation. Classical stability theory gives sufficient and necessary conditions for special classes, and fluid-model methods provide powerful stability certificates or instability witnesses, but they do not yield a general decision procedure. The clean infinite-buffer, positive-service-time case remains open according to the conjecture in the Gamarnik-Katz abstract. Proving undecidability there would show that the obstacle is not a modeling artifact; refuting it would identify a sharp boundary where queueing stability becomes decidable again.

counterexample_rationale: A counterexample to a proposed decidability criterion can be a finite network description. Proving undecidability, however, requires a reduction rather than a finite witness.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search might help transform zero-service or finite-buffer gadgets into positive-service infinite-buffer gadgets, but the main task is a rigorous simulation or decidability proof.

literature.synthesis: Queueing stability sits between stochastic-process analysis and formal computation. Fluid limits often reduce stability questions to deterministic dynamical systems, but multiclass priority networks can encode behavior rich enough to defeat simple load criteria. Gamarnik and Katz show that this richness is not merely analytical inconvenience: in their model, stability is undecidable. The open conjecture is about robustness of the reduction. Zero service times and finite buffers are useful for simulating counters and control logic, but they may be removable by time-scaling, buffer-protection, or gadget amplification. A positive decidability result would be equally interesting because it would isolate a precise modeling feature responsible for undecidability.

title: The true approximation threshold for Sparsest Cut
short_statement: For nonuniform Sparsest Cut, the $O(\sqrt{\log n}\log\log n)$ algorithm and $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ SDP gap do not establish the computational threshold.
full_statement: In the nonuniform Sparsest Cut problem, the input consists of an undirected graph or complete demand network on vertex set $V$, nonnegative capacities $c_{uv}$, and nonnegative demands $d_{uv}$. For a nontrivial cut $S\subset V$, define its sparsity by $$\Phi(S)=\frac{\sum_{u\in S,v\notin S} c_{uv}}{\sum_{u\in S,v\notin S} d_{uv}}.$$ The goal is to find a cut minimizing $\Phi(S)$. The uniform case has demands $d_{uv}=1$ for all pairs. Sparsest Cut is central to graph partitioning, multicommodity flow-cut gaps, and metric embeddings. The Arora-Rao-Vazirani framework gives an $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ approximation for uniform sparsest cut and balanced separator, and later work simplified and accelerated this guarantee. Naor and Young proved an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ integrality gap for the Goemans-Linial SDP relaxation, for nonuniform demands, so that relaxation cannot have smaller gap in that model. The general-demand upper bound is $O(\sqrt{\log n}\log\log n)$; the uniform-demand ARV bound must not be paired with the nonuniform lower bound as an exact match. The open problem is to determine whether polynomial-time algorithms can beat $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ by using stronger relaxations or non-SDP ideas, or whether a comparable hardness result holds under a standard assumption.
open_problem: Determine the nonuniform Sparsest Cut approximation threshold, improving the general-demand upper bound or proving matching computational hardness; distinguish the separate uniform-demand question.
background: Sparsest Cut is a clean mathematical abstraction of partitioning a network while preserving demand pairs. It is also the algorithmic face of a deep metric-embedding question: the flow-cut gap for a demand graph corresponds to how well certain metrics embed into $\ell_1$. Leighton-Rao type methods gave logarithmic approximations through multicommodity flow. The ARV theorem improved this to $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ for uniform demands using a geometric structure theorem for negative-type metrics from semidefinite programming. This was a conceptual breakthrough because it linked graph partitioning to high-dimensional geometry. The $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ lower bound is for nonuniform demands, not a matching uniform ARV gap. A better algorithm would need stronger convex relaxations, hierarchy rounds with new rounding, or a combinatorial method that avoids the known embedding obstruction.
known_results: ARV gives $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ approximation for uniform Sparsest Cut and Balanced Separator. Arora, Lee, and Naor obtained related $O(\sqrt{\log k}\log\log k)$ guarantees for general-demand instances supported on $k$ demand vertices through embeddings of negative-type metrics. Sherman and Kolmogorov give faster and more parallelizable ways to realize essentially the same $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ approximation tradeoff. On the lower-bound side, Khot and Vishnoi refuted the constant-distortion Goemans-Linial conjecture and gave superconstant SDP gaps; Naor and Young later proved an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ gap for the Goemans-Linial SDP. For general demands these upper and lower bounds leave a $\log\log n$ factor, and an SDP gap is not hardness against all algorithms. The nonuniform Naor-Young construction does not give the same uniform-demand gap.

title: Polynomial-time approximation threshold for bimatrix Nash equilibria
short_statement: A 2026 preprint claims additive Nash error $0.30954+\delta$ for general bimatrix games, improving the published $1/3+\delta$ benchmark; the exact threshold remains open.
full_statement: In a two-player normal-form game, the row player has payoff matrix $A\in[0,1]^{m\times n}$ and the column player has payoff matrix $B\in[0,1]^{m\times n}$. A mixed strategy profile $(x,y)$ is an $\varepsilon$-approximate Nash equilibrium if no player can improve expected payoff by more than $\varepsilon$ through a unilateral deviation: $$\max_i e_i^T A y - x^T A y \le \varepsilon,\qquad \max_j x^T B e_j - x^T B y \le \varepsilon.$$ Exact equilibrium exists by Nash's theorem but is PPAD-complete to compute. The open problem is to determine the best additive approximation guarantee achievable in polynomial time for arbitrary bimatrix games. Deligkas, Fasoulakis, and Markakis give a polynomial-time algorithm for $(1/3+\delta)$-approximate Nash equilibria for every constant $\delta>0$. Rubinstein proves quasi-polynomial lower bounds for some positive constant $\varepsilon$ under a PPAD-ETH assumption, but the constant is far below $1/3$ and does not identify the algorithmic threshold. The historical below-$1/3$ target was either to compute $(1/3-\eta)$-approximate equilibria in polynomial time for some universal $\eta>0$, or to prove hardness for approximation at or near the $1/3$ frontier. Dongchen Li and Hanyu Li's October 2026 preprint, Theorem 1, claims an $(r_*+\delta)$-approximate Nash equilibrium for arbitrary bimatrix payoffs in $[0,1]$, where $r_*\approx0.30954$, in time polynomial in input length and $1/\delta$. This claims to cross $1/3$, but does not settle the exact threshold.
open_problem: Determine the exact polynomial-time additive-Nash threshold; verify or improve the new $0.30954+\delta$ preprint guarantee.
background: Bimatrix games are one of the cleanest mathematical models of strategic interaction in economics. They are also a central source problem for PPAD, the complexity class that captures total search problems proved total by parity or fixed-point arguments. Exact Nash equilibrium computation is hard, so approximation became the practical and theoretical fallback. The approximation question is subtle because coarse constant approximations are easy, quasi-polynomial algorithms can achieve arbitrarily small constant error, and PPAD lower bounds become much stronger when the allowed running time is quasi-polynomial rather than polynomial. The historical $1/3$ barrier is important because it is a concrete, model-independent number in the simplest two-player setting. Moving it in either direction would sharpen the computational meaning of Nash equilibrium: either general games admit better polynomial-time strategic predictions than currently known, or the hardness of equilibrium appears already at a visible constant. A new preprint claims to cross it; the overall quantitative threshold is still unresolved.
known_results: Daskalakis, Goldberg, and Papadimitriou and independently Chen, Deng, and Teng established PPAD-completeness for exact Nash equilibrium computation, including the two-player case. Lipton, Markakis, and Mehta showed that $\varepsilon$-approximate equilibria can be found in quasi-polynomial time by enumerating small supports. Tsaknakis and Spirakis gave a long-standing polynomial-time algorithm with guarantee about $0.3393+\delta$. Deligkas, Fasoulakis, and Markakis improved this to $1/3+\delta$ in polynomial time by refining the descent framework and using a richer set of candidate strategies. On the hardness side, Rubinstein proves that, assuming PPAD-ETH, there is a constant $\varepsilon>0$ for which computing an $\varepsilon$-approximate equilibrium requires quasi-polynomial time. This matches the qualitative quasi-polynomial upper bound, but the hard constant is not known to approach $1/3$. Thus the open part remains the quantitative polynomial-time threshold. Dongchen Li and Hanyu Li's October 2026 preprint, Theorem 1, claims an $(r_*+\delta)$-approximate Nash equilibrium for arbitrary bimatrix payoffs in $[0,1]$, where $r_*\approx0.30954$, in time polynomial in input length and $1/\delta$. This audit has not independently verified the proof.

counterexample_rationale: Finite bimatrix games can refute proposed algorithms, descent lemmas, support-size claims, or factor-revealing inequalities. Hardness proofs require reductions, but small games are useful for discovering barriers.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can optimize payoff matrices against candidate algorithms and identify bottleneck games near the $1/3$ boundary.

literature.synthesis: Approximate Nash computation has two different frontiers. The quasi-polynomial frontier is nearly understood: small-support enumeration gives an $n^{O(\log n)}$ algorithm for any fixed error, and Rubinstein gives matching quasi-polynomial lower bounds for some constant error under PPAD-ETH. The polynomial-time frontier is much sharper numerically and much less understood. The Tsaknakis-Spirakis descent framework dominated for years at $0.3393+\delta$, and Deligkas-Fasoulakis-Markakis pushed it to $1/3+\delta$. A further improvement likely needs either a new structural theorem about approximate best responses in arbitrary bimatrix games or a stronger bottleneck analysis of descent-style methods. A hardness result near $1/3$ would require reductions that preserve a much larger approximation constant than current PPAD-hardness technology provides. The new preprint claims a further descent-framework improvement. Do not confuse this general-game result with stronger guarantees restricted to symmetric games.

title: Nonexistence of bigeodesics in two-dimensional first-passage percolation
short_statement: For i.i.d. continuous first-passage percolation on $\mathbb Z^2$, it is famously conjectured that there are almost surely no doubly infinite geodesics.
full_statement: In nearest-neighbor first-passage percolation on $\mathbb Z^2$, assign i.i.d. nonnegative continuous passage times $(t_e)$ to edges, with standard assumptions ensuring finite geodesics and a nondegenerate limit shape. For vertices $x,y$, let $$T(x,y)=\inf_{\gamma:x\to y}\sum_{e\in\gamma} t_e,$$ where the infimum is over nearest-neighbor paths. A finite or infinite path is a geodesic if every finite subpath realizes the passage time between its endpoints. A bigeodesic is a doubly infinite path $(v_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ such that every segment $(v_i,\ldots,v_j)$ is a geodesic between $v_i$ and $v_j$. The open problem is to prove that, under natural continuous i.i.d. edge-weight distributions in two dimensions, almost surely there are no bigeodesics. Equivalently, every infinite geodesic should have only one infinite end, and two-sided globally minimizing paths should not exist in the random metric. A solution should avoid assuming unproved curvature or differentiability properties of the limit shape unless those properties are also proved under the same distributional hypotheses.
open_problem: Prove or refute the no-bigeodesics conjecture for two-dimensional i.i.d. continuous first-passage percolation under standard moment and nondegeneracy assumptions.
background: First-passage percolation turns the lattice into a random metric and asks what large-scale geometry this metric has. The shape theorem gives first-order deterministic growth, but the structure of geodesics remains much less understood. Bigeodesics are especially important because they would be global two-sided minimizers, analogous to geodesic lines in deterministic geometry. In random media they are expected not to exist in two dimensions: geodesics from different points should coalesce, and random fluctuations should prevent a path from being globally optimal in both time directions. The conjecture is tied to Busemann functions, competition interfaces, spin-glass ground states, and the midpoint problem of Benjamini, Kalai, and Schramm. It is a clean fixed-model problem rather than a modeling question: the lattice, randomness, and object of study are all specified.
known_results: Licea and Newman proved strong directional results under assumptions on curvature of the asymptotic shape, including absence of bigeodesics with prescribed directional behavior for a full-measure set of directions. Damron and Hanson proved that, if the boundary of the limit shape is differentiable, there are no bigeodesics with one end directed in any deterministic direction; their work also connects the question to the BKS midpoint problem. Ahlberg and Hoffman developed random coalescing geodesics and solved the midpoint problem, while Brito, Damron, and Hanson proved absence of backward infinite paths in geodesic graphs built from point-to-hyperplane limits in arbitrary dimension. These are substantial advances, but none proves the unconditional two-dimensional no-bigeodesics conjecture for general continuous i.i.d. passage-time distributions.

progress.summary: Directional and conditional nonexistence results are known, but the unconditional two-dimensional no-bigeodesics conjecture remains open.

counterexample_rationale: The conjecture is an almost-sure asymptotic statement about an infinite random metric; finite simulations can illustrate behavior but cannot provide a rigorous counterexample.
alphaevolve_rationale: Computation may help explore geodesic coalescence, midpoint behavior, and candidate finite obstructions, but a proof is likely analytic and probabilistic.

literature.synthesis: The no-bigeodesics problem is part of the broader project of understanding geodesic geometry in FPP beyond the shape theorem. Busemann functions provide one route: if directional Busemann limits exist and geodesics coalesce, one can rule out many two-sided minimizers. Conditional results show that differentiability or curvature of the limit shape would be enough to exclude important classes of bigeodesics, but those shape regularity properties are themselves open for ordinary lattice FPP. Recent random-coalescing-geodesic methods avoid some deterministic shape assumptions and solve related midpoint questions, yet still do not eliminate all possible bigeodesics. A complete solution would likely need a robust coalescence theorem, a new way to control exceptional directions, or a proof that any bigeodesic would force a translation-invariant structure now known to be impossible.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Study Busemann-function constructions, geodesic coalescence, exceptional-direction arguments, and implications of limit-shape differentiability. agent_guidance.verification_notes: A proof must specify distributional assumptions on edge weights and show almost-sure absence of every doubly infinite path whose finite subpaths are geodesics. A conditional result should state exactly which assumptions on the limit shape, curvature, differentiability, or Busemann limits are used, since many known results are conditional in precisely this way. A counterexample would require a passage-time distribution satisfying the standard hypotheses and a rigorous positive-probability construction of a bigeodesic, not only simulations or finite-box geodesic pictures.

title: The GNRS conjecture for minor-free flow-cut gaps
short_statement: The Gupta-Newman-Rabinovich-Sinclair conjecture asks whether every fixed-minor-free graph family has constant multicommodity flow-cut gap.
full_statement: Let $G=(V,E)$ be an undirected supply graph with edge capacities $u_e\ge0$, and let $H$ be a demand graph on the same vertex set with demands $d_{st}\ge0$. The cut condition says that for every cut $S\subset V$, the total capacity crossing $S$ in $G$ is at least the total demand crossing $S$ in $H$. The fractional multicommodity flow-cut gap of a graph family is the smallest constant $C$ such that, whenever the cut condition holds for an instance on a supply graph $G$ in the family, scaling all capacities by $C$ suffices to route all demands fractionally. Equivalently, through the Linial-London-Rabinovich duality, it asks for bounded $\ell_1$ distortion of shortest-path metrics supported by the graph family. The Gupta-Newman-Rabinovich-Sinclair conjecture asserts that for every fixed excluded minor $F$, the class of $F$-minor-free supply graphs has flow-cut gap bounded by a constant depending only on $F$, not on $|V|$ or the demand pattern. The open problem is to prove this constant bound or construct a fixed-minor-free family with unbounded flow-cut gap.
open_problem: Prove or refute the GNRS conjecture: fixed-minor-free undirected graph families should have $O_F(1)$ multicommodity flow-cut gap, equivalently bounded $\ell_1$ distortion for their graph metrics.
background: Multicommodity flow is a central relaxation in network design, routing, graph partitioning, and approximation algorithms. The cut condition is the most basic necessary condition for routing demands, but it is not sufficient in general graphs without capacity augmentation. The worst-case gap between cuts and flows is $\Theta(\log n)$ in general graphs and underlies the logarithmic approximability of Sparsest Cut. Minor-free graph families are much more structured and include planar graphs, bounded-genus graphs, and many networks that arise in geometric or infrastructure settings. The GNRS conjecture says that this structure should collapse the logarithmic gap to a constant. A proof would have algorithmic consequences for routing and cut problems on minor-free networks; a counterexample would show that even topologically simple networks can hide arbitrarily bad multicommodity obstructions.
known_results: General graphs have logarithmic flow-cut gaps, characterized through metric embeddings. The GNRS conjecture predicts constant gaps for every fixed-minor-free family. Several special cases and related bounds are known. Chekuri, Shepherd, and Weibel prove constant integer or fractional flow-cut gap results for important subclasses such as series-parallel and $k$-outerplanar graphs, and they formulate a stronger integer-flow conjecture related to the fractional one. Salmasi, Sidiropoulos, and Sridhar describe the undirected GNRS conjecture as the standard benchmark and obtain first constant directed flow-cut gap results for directed series-parallel graphs, directed bounded-pathwidth graphs, directed trees, and directed cycles. However, the core undirected conjecture remains open even at the level of proving a constant bound for broad fixed-minor-free classes beyond the known special cases.

progress.summary: Constant bounds are known for special graph classes, but the fixed-minor-free conjecture remains open.

counterexample_rationale: Finite supply-demand instances can witness large flow-cut gaps for a graph family and can be checked by linear programming. A refutation would require an infinite family, but computational search can discover candidate gadgets.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search over planar or minor-free supply graphs with demand graphs can produce large finite gaps, suggest recursive constructions, or stress-test embedding conjectures.

literature.synthesis: The GNRS conjecture connects three languages: routing, cuts, and metric embeddings. The routing language asks how much one must scale capacities after all cut inequalities hold. The cut language views this as the integrality/duality gap behind sparsest-cut relaxations. The metric language asks whether shortest-path metrics of minor-free graphs embed into $\ell_1$ with distortion depending only on the excluded minor. General graphs need logarithmic distortion, so the conjecture is a strong structural claim about topology. Known positive results for trees, cycles, series-parallel graphs, and bounded outerplanarity support the conjecture, but the techniques do not yet handle arbitrary planar or fixed-minor-free interactions. A proof may require a new decomposition of minor-free metrics; a counterexample would likely expose a multiscale demand pattern not captured by existing separator or embedding methods.

title: The Gilbert-Pollak Steiner Ratio Conjecture
short_statement: The equilateral triangle gives the apparent worst-case gap between the Euclidean minimum spanning tree and the Euclidean Steiner minimum tree, but no complete proof of this sharp constant is known.
full_statement: Let $P\subset \mathbb R^2$ be a finite set of terminal points. Let $\operatorname{MST}(P)$ be the length of a Euclidean minimum spanning tree on $P$, where edges must join terminals directly. Let $\operatorname{SMT}(P)$ be the length of a Euclidean Steiner minimum tree connecting all terminals in $P$, where the network may use additional Steiner points in the plane. Define the Euclidean Steiner ratio in the $\operatorname{SMT}/\operatorname{MST}$ convention by $\rho = \inf_P \operatorname{SMT}(P)/\operatorname{MST}(P)$. For three terminals forming an equilateral triangle, $\operatorname{SMT}/\operatorname{MST}=\sqrt{3}/2$. The Gilbert-Pollak conjecture asserts that this is the worst case: for every finite $P\subset \mathbb R^2$, $\operatorname{SMT}(P)\ge (\sqrt{3}/2)\operatorname{MST}(P)$. Equivalently, in the reciprocal ratio convention $\Gamma=\sup_P \operatorname{MST}(P)/\operatorname{SMT}(P)$, the conjecture says $\Gamma=2/\sqrt{3}$. The open problem is to prove this inequality for all finite planar point sets or produce a rigorously certified counterexample with ratio below $\sqrt{3}/2$ in the $\operatorname{SMT}/\operatorname{MST}$ convention.
background: The Euclidean Steiner tree problem is one of the classical network-design problems in geometric optimization. The input is already completely specified by finitely many points; the extra modeling choice is not the issue. What is hard is understanding the sharp loss incurred by the minimum spanning tree heuristic when the true optimum is allowed to introduce Steiner points. This sharp constant matters because MST-based networks are simple, canonical, and easy to compute, while Euclidean Steiner trees expose the geometric value of adding junctions. Gilbert and Pollak formulated the conjecture in 1968. A proof announced by Du and Hwang around 1990 was widely cited for years, but later clarification work identified a serious gap, so the conjecture remains open. The problem has recently become relevant to AI-agent mathematics because Ke, Huang, Shu, He, Gai, and Wang use LLM-generated geometric lemmas plus executable verification functions to improve certified lower bounds toward the conjectured constant.
known_results: The equilateral triangle shows that no bound larger than $\sqrt{3}/2$ is possible for $\operatorname{SMT}(P)/\operatorname{MST}(P)$. Classical lower-bound work before the 1990s reached a certified lower bound around $0.824$ in this convention. Du and Hwang published a claimed proof of the exact $\sqrt{3}/2$ bound, but later papers by Innami, Kim, Mashiko, Shiohama and by Ivanov and Tuzhilin explained that the proof has an unresolved gap, so it cannot be used as a resolution. The best widely cited older upper bound on the reciprocal ratio is about $1.2134$, while the conjectured reciprocal value is $2/\sqrt{3}\approx 1.1547$. In 2026, Ke and coauthors reported an AI-assisted certified lower bound of $0.8559$ for $\operatorname{SMT}/\operatorname{MST}$, substantially closer to $\sqrt{3}/2\approx0.8660$ but still short of the conjecture. Thus the open part is not to formulate a new geometric network model; it is to close the remaining constant gap or disprove the sharp equilateral-triangle conjecture.
open_problem: Prove or disprove that every finite planar point set satisfies $\operatorname{SMT}(P)\ge (\sqrt{3}/2)\operatorname{MST}(P)$.

title: Polynomial-Time Complexity of the Square-Root-Sum Problem
short_statement: Many Euclidean optimization algorithms need to compare sums of distances exactly; the basic Turing-model complexity of comparing integer square-root sums is still unresolved.
full_statement: The square-root-sum problem asks, given integers $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb Z$ and positive integers $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb N$, to decide the sign of $E=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\sqrt{a_i}$, for example whether $E\ge 0$. A common equivalent form asks whether $\sum_i \sqrt{a_i}\le t$ for a given integer threshold $t$, or whether one sum of square roots is at most another. The open problem is to determine whether this decision problem is solvable in time polynomial in the bit length of the integer input on an ordinary Turing machine. A sufficiently strong polynomially bounded separation theorem for nonzero values of $E$ would imply such an algorithm, because one could compute the square roots to enough precision and compare safely. Conversely, proving that no such algorithm exists under standard complexity assumptions would separate this exact numerical-comparison problem from the real-RAM intuition that square roots can be manipulated at unit cost.
background: This is a small-looking numerical problem with outsized consequences for computational geometry and geometric optimization. Lengths of Euclidean paths, tours, triangulations, matchings, and Steiner or network-design objects are often sums of square roots of integers. Approximation algorithms can usually avoid exact comparison, but exact decision problems and membership in classes such as NP can depend on whether one can compare such sums within polynomially many bits. For example, the exact complexity of minimum-weight triangulation is entangled with this issue: NP-hardness is known, but NP membership for the Euclidean-length decision version is delicate because a certificate may require comparing sums of radicals. The problem is therefore not about choosing a model of a real-world system; the model is a finite integer expression, and the hard part is the bit-complexity of exact sign determination.
known_results: The problem is easy in a unit-cost real-RAM model but its bit-complexity on Turing machines is open. Allender, Burgisser, Kjeldgaard-Pedersen, and Miltersen placed square-root-sum inside the counting hierarchy, giving a strong upper bound well below arbitrary PSPACE reasoning but not a polynomial-time algorithm. Separation-bound approaches give algorithms whose running time depends on lower bounds for the smallest nonzero value of a square-root sum. Burnikel, Fleischer, Mehlhorn, and Schirra proved a strong computable separation bound for radical expressions, but the dependence remains exponential in the number of terms. Cheng, Meng, Sun, and Chen related the relevant separation quantity to lattice reduction and gave conditional and experimental evidence for sharper behavior. Eisenbrand, Haeberle, and Singer used the subspace theorem to improve the bound to a singly exponential form for fixed radicands, but their constant is ineffective and the result still does not yield a general polynomial-time algorithm. Thus the open part is still the same sharp question: can signs of arbitrary integer square-root sums be decided in polynomial time?
open_problem: Decide whether the square-root-sum problem is solvable in polynomial time on a Turing machine.

counterexample_rationale: There is no finite counterexample to polynomial-time solvability in the usual sense, but explicit near-collisions between square-root sums are valuable because they test proposed separation bounds and precision claims.

literature.synthesis: The square-root-sum problem is a bridge between exact numerical computation and discrete optimization. Its input is completely finite and integer-valued, yet deciding the sign may require ruling out extremely small nonzero gaps between algebraic sums. Allender and coauthors gave a structural upper bound through the counting hierarchy, showing that the problem is not arbitrary real computation. Separation-bound work supplies algorithms by proving that nonzero sums cannot be too close to zero, but known bounds still lead to superpolynomial precision in the number of terms. The Eisenbrand-Haeberle-Singer bound is a real advance for fixed radicands, but because its constant is ineffective and radicands vary with the input, it does not settle the original polynomial-time question. The remaining gap is therefore exact and clean: either prove a polynomial bit-complexity comparison algorithm, likely via stronger effective separation, or show that such a comparison would imply an unexpected complexity collapse.
